abstract: A short account is given of various investigations of neural network properties, beginning with the classic work of McCulloch & Pitts. Early work on neurodynamics and statistical mechanics, analogies with magnetic materials, fault tolerance via parallel distributed processing, memory, learning, and pattern recognition, is described.
originalAbstract: A short account is given of various investigations of neural network properties, beginning with the classic work of McCulloch & Pitts. paragraphs: This paper provides a short historical account of early investigations into neural network properties, beginning with the work of McCulloch and Pitts. Its purpose is to bring several lines of inquiry into one narrative. The topics span how networks behave, what they can store, and how collections of processing elements can support useful computation.

One group of topics concerns neurodynamics, statistical mechanics, and comparisons with magnetic materials. These place network behavior alongside approaches concerned with interacting systems and their collective properties. Another topic is fault tolerance through parallel distributed processing, connecting the organization of computation across many elements with the ability to tolerate faults.

The account also covers memory, learning, and pattern recognition. Taken together, these subjects show the breadth of the early questions examined in neural network research. The paper's contribution is a historical synthesis of those investigations, helping readers relate studies of network dynamics and organization to studies of computational capability. It provides context for understanding these concerns as parts of a shared research history.
summary.tldr: This historical overview connects early neural network studies of dynamics, distributed processing, memory, learning, and pattern recognition.

title: Neural Networks: The Early Days

abstract: Training classifiers on large databases is computationally demand(cid:173) ing. It is desirable to develop efficient procedures for a reliable prediction of a classifier's suitability for implementing a given task, so that resources can be assigned to the most promising candidates or freed for exploring new classifier candidates. We propose such a practical and principled predictive method. Practical because it avoids the costly procedure of training poor classifiers on the whole training set, and principled because of its theoretical foundation. The effectiveness of the proposed procedure is demonstrated for both single- and multi-layer networks. 1

paragraphs: This paper addresses the cost of deciding which classifiers deserve training on a large database. Fully training every candidate can consume resources on models that are poorly suited to the task. The authors propose a predictive procedure intended to assess suitability efficiently, allowing effort to be directed toward more promising candidates.

The title frames the problem through learning curves, their eventual values, and how quickly they approach those values. The practical objective is to predict a classifier's prospects without paying the cost of training an unsuitable candidate on the entire dataset. The authors describe the procedure as principled because it has a theoretical foundation, linking resource allocation to a reasoned prediction of learning behavior.

The method's effectiveness is demonstrated for both single-layer and multilayer networks. Its stated value is in screening candidates before committing the full training budget. Resources saved on poor candidates can support stronger ones or permit exploration of additional classifiers. Thus, the contribution concerns making the model-evaluation process more efficient while retaining a basis for reliable selection.
summary.tldr: A theoretically grounded prediction method screens classifier suitability before expensive training on an entire dataset.

title: Learning Curves: Asymptotic Values and Rate of Convergence

abstract: We present a new algorithm for finding low complexity networks with high generalization capability. The algorithm searches for large connected regions of so-called ''fiat'' minima of the error func(cid:173) tion. In the weight-space environment of a "flat" minimum, the error remains approximately constant. Using an MDL-based ar(cid:173) gument, flat minima can be shown to correspond to low expected overfitting. Although our algorithm requires the computation of second order derivatives, it has backprop's order of complexity. Experiments with feedforward and recurrent nets are described. In an application to stock market prediction, the method outperforms conventional backprop, weight decay, and "optimal brain surgeon" .

paragraphs: This paper proposes a training algorithm that searches for broad, connected regions of low error in a neural network's weight space. Within these flat minima, changing the weights leaves the error approximately unchanged. The objective is to find networks with low complexity and strong generalization by favoring this kind of solution geometry.

The authors use an argument based on minimum description length to connect flat minima with low expected overfitting. This gives the preference for broad low-error regions a model-complexity rationale. The algorithm requires second-order derivatives, but the authors state that its computational complexity has the same order as backpropagation.

Experiments include both feed-forward and recurrent networks. In a stock-market prediction application, the method outperforms conventional backpropagation, weight decay, and optimal brain surgeon. The reported findings connect the theoretical preference for flat solutions with an observed predictive benefit in that application. More broadly, the paper presents the shape of a low-error region as a criterion for selecting among network solutions, alongside the error value itself.
summary.tldr: A training algorithm seeks broad flat minima, linking their geometry to low expected overfitting and improved prediction.

title: SIMPLIFYING NEURAL NETS BY DISCOVERING FLAT MINIMA

abstract: Although TD-Gammon is one of the major successes in machine learn(cid:173) ing, it has not led to similar impressive breakthroughs in temporal dif(cid:173) ference learning for other applications or even other games. We were able to replicate some of the success of TD-Gammon, developing a competitive evaluation function on a 4000 parameter feed-forward neu(cid:173) ral network, without using back-propagation, reinforcement or temporal difference learning methods. Instead we apply simple hill-climbing in a relative fitness environment. These results and further analysis suggest that the surprising success of Tesauro's program had more to do with the co-evolutionary structure of the learning task and the dynamics of the backgammon game itself.

paragraphs: The paper asks which aspects of TD-Gammon explain its success, given that similarly striking results had not followed in other applications or games. The authors investigate this by developing a competitive backgammon evaluation function through a different learning procedure. Their evaluator is a feedforward neural network with 4,000 parameters.

Training uses simple hill climbing in an environment where fitness is relative. It does not use backpropagation, reinforcement learning, or temporal-difference learning. By recovering some of TD-Gammon's success through this alternative procedure, the study examines whether the learning task itself makes successful adaptation possible through more than one algorithm.

The results and further analysis suggest that the co-evolutionary structure of training and the dynamics of backgammon contributed substantially to the original success. This is an interpretation supported by partial replication, rather than a claim that all learning methods behave identically. The broader lesson is to examine the relationship between a training environment, a game's structure, and an algorithm when explaining an impressive result.
summary.tldr: A competitive evaluator trained by hill climbing suggests that backgammon and its co-evolutionary training structure helped explain TD-Gammon's success.

title: Why did TD-Gammon Work?

abstract: The paper is developed in two parts where we discuss a new approach to self-organization in a single-layer linear feed-forward network. First, two novel algorithms for self-organization are derived from a two-layer linear hetero-associative network performing a one-of-m classification, and trained with the constrained least-mean-squared classification error criterion. Second, two adaptive algorithms are derived from these self(cid:173) organizing procedures the principal generalized eigenvectors of two correlation matrices from two sequences of random vectors. These novel adaptive algorithms can be implemented in a single-layer linear feed-forward network. We give a rigorous convergence analysis of the adaptive algorithms by using stochastic approximation theory. As an example, we consider a problem of online signal detection in digital mobile communications.

paragraphs: This paper develops learning algorithms that connect linear neural networks with generalized eigen-decomposition. The construction begins with a two-layer hetero-associative network trained to choose one of several classes. Using a constrained least-mean-squared classification criterion, the authors derive two procedures for self-organization in a single-layer linear feed-forward network.

They then turn those procedures into two adaptive algorithms for finding principal generalized eigenvectors of two correlation matrices. The matrices arise from two sequences of random vectors, so the objective is tied to statistical relationships in incoming data. Both adaptive methods can be implemented in the simpler, single-layer linear architecture.

The paper supplies a rigorous convergence analysis using stochastic approximation theory and considers online signal detection in digital mobile communications as an example. This combination matters because the proposed network updates come with a mathematical account of their convergence. The contribution links a classification-based derivation, an adaptive matrix-computation task, and an implementation that processes data through a linear network.
summary.tldr: Two adaptive linear-network algorithms estimate principal generalized eigenvectors, with convergence established through stochastic approximation theory.

title: Self-Organizing and Adaptive Algorithms for Generalized Eigen-Decomposition

However, cells outside of primary sensory cortex are either gain modulated by postural input or partially shifting. We show that solving classical spatial tasks, like sen(cid:173) sory prediction, multi-sensory integration, sensory-motor transfor(cid:173) mation and motor control requires more complicated intermediate representations that are not invariant in one frame of reference. The brain must be able to use spatial cues coming from different modalities (e.g. vision, audition, touch, proprioception), combine them to infer the position of the object, and compute the appropriate movement. paragraphs: The paper asks how the brain represents locations when information comes from several senses and must guide movement. Vision, hearing, and touch encode position relative to different reference points. Combining these signals therefore requires transformations between representations, and the abstract emphasizes that these transformations become complicated when locations are encoded across populations of neurons.

The authors argue that the spatial tasks they study require intermediate representations that do not stay invariant within one reference frame. They introduce an iterative basis function map using units whose responses are modulated by posture or whose spatial sensitivity shifts partially. These properties connect the proposed computation to the kinds of responses observed outside primary sensory cortex.

The map is presented as performing sensory prediction, multisensory integration, sensory-to-movement transformations, and motor control optimally within the proposed formulation. The authors also test it against neurophysiological and neuropsychological data. Its central contribution is a computational account of why mixed spatial representations can support coordinated spatial behavior.
summary.tldr: An iterative neural map uses mixed spatial representations to combine sensory information and guide movement.

title: A New Model of Spatial Representation in Multimodal Brain Areas

abstract: Estimating the parameters of sparse multinomial distributions is an important component of many statistical learning tasks. Recent approaches have used uncertainty over the vocabulary of symbols in a multinomial distribution as a means of accounting for sparsity. We present a Bayesian approach that allows weak prior knowledge, in the form of a small set of approximate candidate vocabularies, to be used to dramatically improve the resulting estimates. We demonstrate these improvements in applications to text compres(cid:173) sion and estimating distributions over words in newsgroup data.

Recent approaches have used uncertainty over the vocabulary of symbols in a multinomial distribution as a means of accounting for sparsity. We present a Bayesian approach that allows weak prior knowledge, in the form of a small set of approximate candidate vocabularies, to be used to dramatically improve the resulting estimates. We demonstrate these improvements in applications to text compres(cid:173) sion and estimating distributions over words in newsgroup data.

paragraphs: The paper addresses estimation of sparse multinomial distributions, which assign probabilities to discrete symbols. In text applications, those symbols can be words. Sparsity makes estimating their probabilities difficult, and the authors focus on uncertainty about the vocabulary: the set of symbols that belongs in the distribution.

Their Bayesian approach incorporates weak prior knowledge expressed as a small collection of approximate candidate vocabularies. This gives the estimator information about plausible symbol sets without requiring an exact vocabulary in advance. The contribution is to make that limited vocabulary knowledge useful within the probabilistic estimation process, building on approaches that already account for uncertainty about which symbols are possible.

The authors demonstrate dramatic improvements in the resulting estimates through applications to text compression and word distributions in newsgroup data. These findings show that even approximate knowledge of candidate vocabularies can be valuable in the tested sparse-data settings. The methodological point is that prior information about the symbol set itself can improve estimation, in addition to the information supplied by observed symbol occurrences.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian estimator uses a few approximate candidate vocabularies to substantially improve sparse symbol-probability estimates in text applications.

title: Using Vocabulary Knowledge in Bayesian Multinomial Estimation

abstract: The question of whether the nervous system produces movement through the combination of a few discrete elements has long been central to the study of motor control. Muscle synergies, i.e. coordinated patterns of muscle activity, have been proposed as possible building blocks. Here we propose a model based on combinations of muscle synergies with a spe- ciﬁc amplitude and temporal structure. Time-varying synergies provide a realistic basis for the decomposition of the complex patterns observed in natural behaviors. To extract time-varying synergies from simultane- ous recording of EMG activity we developed an algorithm which extends existing non-negative matrix factorization techniques.

paragraphs: The paper addresses whether complex movement can be described through combinations of a few reusable elements. It focuses on muscle synergies: coordinated activity patterns across muscles that have been proposed as building blocks of motor control. The authors develop a model in which those patterns have both an amplitude structure and a structure over time.

Making a synergy time-varying allows the building block itself to describe an unfolding pattern of muscle activity. Combining such elements provides a proposed basis for decomposing the complex muscle patterns seen in natural behavior. The model therefore treats temporal organization as part of each component rather than describing coordination only through muscle activation levels.

To extract these components from simultaneous electromyographic recordings, the authors develop an extension of non-negative matrix factorization. This supplies a computational method for finding the proposed time-varying synergies in recorded muscle activity. The contribution is a model and extraction algorithm for examining modular organization; the abstract presents synergies as possible biological building blocks.
summary.tldr: The paper models muscle activity as combinations of time-varying synergies and extends non-negative matrix factorization to extract them from EMG.

title: Modularity in the motor system: decomposition of muscle patterns as combinations of time-varying synergies

Here, we investigate the properties of this model for a multi-synapse neuron that receives inputs with di(cid:11)erent spike-train statistics. paragraphs: The paper examines a calcium-dependent model of synaptic learning that had already accounted for several rate-based and spike-timing-based plasticity paradigms. It extends the investigation to a neuron with multiple synapses receiving inputs with different spike-train statistics. The question is how the learning model behaves when many inputs act together.

The authors introduce a physiologically motivated form of metaplasticity: regulation of the learning process driven by activity. This mechanism is essential for robustness in the model. It adds a way for activity to influence the conditions under which synaptic changes occur, alongside the calcium-dependent changes themselves.

With this regulation, the modeled neuron develops receptive fields that are both stable and selective under various input statistics. Stability and selectivity are therefore studied within the same learning framework rather than as separate outcomes. The contribution connects a model of synaptic plasticity with organized responses at the level of a neuron, while identifying activity-driven regulation as an essential component of the reported robustness.
summary.tldr: Activity-driven metaplasticity enables robust, stable, selective receptive fields in a multi-synapse calcium-dependent learning model.

title: Selectivity and Metaplasticity in a Unified Calcium-Dependent Model

abstract: This paper extends our earlier analysis on approximate linear program- ming as an approach to approximating the cost-to-go function in a discounted-cost dynamic program [6]. In this paper, we consider the average-cost criterion and a version of approximate linear programming that generates approximations to the optimal average cost and differential cost function. We demonstrate that a naive version of approximate linear programming prioritizes approximation of the optimal average cost and that this may not be well-aligned with the objective of deriving a policy with low average cost. For that, the algorithm should aim at producing a good approximation of the differential cost function. We propose a two- phase variant of approximate linear programming that allows for external control of the relative accuracy of the approximation of the differential cost function over different portions of the state space via state-relevance weights. Performance bounds suggest that the new algorithm is compat- ible with the objective of optimizing performance and provide guidance on appropriate choices for state-relevance weights.

paragraphs: The paper examines approximate linear programming for decision problems evaluated by their long-run average cost. It considers approximations to both the best achievable average cost and the differential cost function, which distinguishes the relative consequences of different states. These quantities have different roles when constructing a decision policy.

The authors show that a naive formulation prioritizes estimating the optimal average cost. That priority may not align with producing a policy that actually incurs low average cost. For policy construction, the approximation should instead give appropriate attention to the differential cost function. Accurately estimating an overall performance level does not necessarily provide the state-specific information needed for good decisions.

A proposed two-phase method introduces state-relevance weights to control relative approximation accuracy across portions of the state space. This lets the formulation direct attention toward selected states. Performance bounds suggest that the revised method aligns with the objective of improving policy performance and help guide weight selection. The contribution connects the approximation objective more closely to the decisions it is meant to support.
summary.tldr: A two-phase approximation method emphasizes state-dependent cost information to better align average-cost dynamic programming with policy performance.

title: Approximate Linear Programming for Average-Cost Dynamic Programming

abstract: Loopy belief propagation (BP) has been successfully used in a num- ber of di–cult graphical models to ﬂnd the most probable conﬂgu- ration of the hidden variables. In applications ranging from protein folding to image analysis one would like to ﬂnd not just the best conﬂguration but rather the top M . While this problem has been solved using the junction tree formalism, in many real world prob- lems the clique size in the junction tree is prohibitively large. In this work we address the problem of ﬂnding the M best conﬂgura- tions when exact inference is impossible. We start by developing a new exact inference algorithm for calculat- ing the best conﬂgurations that uses only max-marginals. For ap- proximate inference, we replace the max-marginals with the beliefs calculated using max-product BP and generalized BP. We show em- pirically that the algorithm can accurately and rapidly approximate the M best conﬂgurations in graphs with hundreds of variables.

paragraphs: Many graphical-model applications need several likely assignments of hidden variables, rather than just the single most probable assignment. The paper addresses finding the top M configurations when exact inference is impractical. Although junction-tree methods can solve this task exactly, the groups of variables they must process together can become prohibitively large.

The authors first develop an exact algorithm that needs only max-marginals, summaries of the best achievable probabilities under specified variable assignments. They then construct an approximate version by substituting beliefs computed with max-product belief propagation or generalized belief propagation. This separates the procedure for finding multiple configurations from the machinery used to obtain its probability summaries.

Experiments show that the approximate algorithm can recover the M best configurations accurately and quickly in graphs containing hundreds of variables. The exactness belongs to the version using the required exact summaries; the belief-propagation version has empirical support as an approximation. The approach makes multiple candidate configurations accessible in settings where exact junction-tree computation is too costly.
summary.tldr: An exact top-M inference procedure becomes a practical approximation when supplied with beliefs from loopy or generalized belief propagation.

title: Finding the M Most Probable Configurations using Loopy Belief Propagation

abstract: Many works have shown that strong connections relate learning from examples to regularization techniques for ill-posed inverse problems. Nevertheless by now there was no formal evidence neither that learning from examples could be seen as an inverse problem nor that theoretical results in learning theory could be independently derived using tools from regularization theory. In this paper we provide a positive answer to both questions. Indeed, considering the square loss, we translate the learning problem in the language of regularization theory and show that consistency results and optimal regularization parameter choice can be derived by the discretization of the corresponding inverse problem.

Indeed, considering the square loss, we translate the learning problem in the language of regularization theory and show that consistency results and optimal regularization parameter choice can be derived by the discretization of the corresponding inverse problem.

paragraphs: Learning from examples and regularizing ill-posed inverse problems have long been recognized as closely related. This paper addresses a stronger question: whether learning can formally be expressed as an inverse problem, and whether regularization theory can independently produce results normally associated with learning theory.

The authors establish this connection for learning with square loss. They translate the learning task into the language of regularization theory and study a discretization of the corresponding inverse problem. Discretization supplies the mathematical route by which the inverse-problem formulation yields conclusions about learning from examples.

Through this formulation, the paper derives consistency results and an optimal choice of regularization parameter. Consistency concerns the behavior of learning as the available evidence grows, while parameter choice determines how regularization enters the procedure. The significance is a formal bridge that makes tools from one theory productive in the other. The square-loss setting is part of the stated result, so the abstract's conclusion should be read within that scope.
summary.tldr: For square loss, the paper formally casts learning as an inverse problem and derives consistency and optimal regularization choices through regularization theory.

title: Learning, Regularization and Ill-Posed Inverse Problems

abstract: We introduce a novel active-learning scenario in which a user wants to work with a learning algorithm to identify useful anomalies. These are distinguished from the traditional statistical definition of anomalies as outliers or merely ill-modeled points. Our distinction is that the useful- ness of anomalies is categorized subjectively by the user. We make two additional assumptions. First, there exist extremely few useful anoma- lies to be hunted down within a massive dataset. Second, both useful and useless anomalies may sometimes exist within tiny classes of similar anomalies. The challenge is thus to identify "rare category" records in an unlabeled noisy set with help (in the form of class labels) from a human expert who has a small budget of datapoints that they are prepared to cat- egorize. We propose a technique to meet this challenge, which assumes a mixture model fit to the data, but otherwise makes no assumptions on the particular form of the mixture components. This property promises wide applicability in real-life scenarios and for various statistical mod- els. We give an overview of several alternative methods, highlighting their strengths and weaknesses, and conclude with a detailed empirical analysis. We show that our method can quickly zoom in on an anomaly set containing a few tens of points in a dataset of hundreds of thousands.

paragraphs: The paper treats anomaly discovery as a collaboration between a learning algorithm and a human expert. An unusual record is useful only if the user considers it useful; statistical unusualness alone does not settle the question. The goal is therefore to find rare categories that matter to the user within a large, noisy, unlabeled dataset.

The setting assumes that useful anomalies are extremely scarce and that both useful and useless anomalies may occur in small groups of similar records. The expert can label only a limited number of examples. The proposed method uses a mixture model fitted to the data but does not require a particular form for its components, allowing flexibility in the statistical model.

The authors discuss alternative methods and evaluate their approach empirically. They show that it can quickly focus on an anomaly group containing only a few dozen records within hundreds of thousands. This supports its usefulness for directing scarce expert attention toward tiny categories, while leaving the user's judgments central to deciding which discoveries actually matter.
summary.tldr: An active learning method uses limited expert labels and a fitted mixture model to locate extremely rare, user-relevant anomaly categories.

title: Active Learning for Anomaly and Rare-Category Detection

abstract: Point process encoding models provide powerful statistical methods for under- standing the responses of neurons to sensory stimuli. Although these models have been successfully applied to neurons in the early sensory pathway, they have fared less well capturing the response properties of neurons in deeper brain areas, ow- ing in part to the fact that they do not take into account multiple stages of pro- cessing. Here we introduce a new twist on the point-process modeling approach: we include unobserved as well as observed spiking neurons in a joint encoding model. The resulting model exhibits richer dynamics and more highly nonlinear response properties, making it more powerful and more ﬂexible for ﬁtting neural data. More importantly, it allows us to estimate connectivity patterns among neu- rons (both observed and unobserved), and may provide insight into how networks process sensory input. We formulate the estimation procedure using variational EM and the wake-sleep algorithm, and illustrate the model’s performance using a simulated example network consisting of two coupled neurons.

paragraphs: Point-process models describe how sensory stimuli relate to the timing of neural spikes. Their success in early sensory pathways has been harder to reproduce in deeper brain regions, partly because standard models omit multiple processing stages. This paper addresses that issue by modeling recorded and unrecorded spiking neurons together.

Including unobserved neurons gives the joint encoding model richer dynamics and more nonlinear stimulus-response behavior. It also allows estimation of connectivity patterns involving both observed and hidden neurons. This makes the model more flexible for fitting neural data and creates a possible route to understanding how networks transform sensory input through interconnected processing.

The authors formulate estimation using variational expectation-maximization and the wake-sleep algorithm. They illustrate performance with a simulated network of two coupled neurons. That demonstration provides a concrete example of the proposed modeling and estimation approach. The broader prospect of gaining insight into sensory computation remains a possibility enabled by the framework, rather than a claim of established biological connectivity recovery.
summary.tldr: Jointly modeling observed and hidden spiking neurons adds nonlinear dynamics and enables connectivity estimation in partially recorded populations.

title: Neural characterization in partially observed populations of spiking neurons

abstract: We propose to use Rademacher complexity, originally developed in computational learning theory, as a measure of human learning capacity. Rademacher complexity measures a learners ability to fit random data, and can be used to bound the learners true error based on the observed training sample error. We first review the definition of Rademacher complexity and its generalization bound. We then describe a learning the noise" procedure to experimentally measure human Rademacher complexities. The results from empirical studies showed that: (i) human Rademacher complexity can be successfully measured, (ii) the complexity depends on the domain and training sample size in intuitive ways, (iii) human learning respects the generalization bounds, (iv) the bounds can be useful in predicting the danger of overfitting in human learning. Finally, we discuss the potential applications of human Rademacher complexity in cognitive science."

paragraphs: The paper proposes measuring human learning capacity with Rademacher complexity, a concept from computational learning theory. It measures how well a learner can fit random data. That ability matters because fitting a training sample can reflect both learning useful structure and accommodating noise, with different implications for performance beyond that sample.

The authors review how Rademacher complexity connects observed training error to a bound on true error. They then introduce an experimental procedure that asks people to learn noise, making the complexity measurable for human learners. This brings a theoretical measure of flexibility into an experimental setting where its dependence on the task and sample size can be examined.

The studies find that human Rademacher complexity can be measured and varies with domain and training-set size in intuitive ways. Human learning in these studies respects the generalization bounds, which can help predict overfitting risk. The paper also discusses potential cognitive-science applications, suggesting a quantitative connection between learning capacity and generalization.
summary.tldr: Experiments measuring how people learn random data connect human learning capacity to theoretical bounds on generalization and overfitting.

title: Human Rademacher Complexity

abstract: This paper discusses the topic of dimensionality reduction for $k$-means clustering. We prove that any set of $n$ points in $d$ dimensions (rows in a matrix $A \in \RR^{n \times d}$) can be projected into $t = \Omega(k / \eps^2)$ dimensions, for any $\eps \in (0,1/3)$, in $O(n d \lceil \eps^{-2} k/ \log(d) \rceil )$ time, such that with constant probability the optimal $k$-partition of the point set is preserved within a factor of $2+\eps$. The projection is done by post-multiplying $A$ with a $d \times t$ random matrix $R$ having entries $+1/\sqrt{t}$ or $-1/\sqrt{t}$ with equal probability. A numerical implementation of our technique and experiments on a large face images dataset verify the speed and the accuracy of our theoretical results.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to reduce the number of coordinates in a dataset while retaining an approximate guarantee for k-means clustering. Its result applies to any collection of n points in d dimensions. The reduced dimension is tied to the number of clusters and the desired approximation parameter.

The projection multiplies the data matrix by a random matrix whose entries are equally likely to be positive or negative 1/sqrt(t). For an approximation parameter epsilon between zero and one third, the stated target dimension is t = Omega(k/epsilon²). With constant probability, the projection preserves the optimal k-partition within a factor of 2 + epsilon.

This is an approximate, probabilistic preservation guarantee. The paper also provides an explicit computation-time bound for constructing the projected data, linking the theoretical guarantee to efficiency. A numerical implementation and experiments on a large face-image dataset support the reported speed and accuracy. The contribution shows how a simple random transformation can reduce dimensionality while retaining a quantified relationship to the original clustering problem.
summary.tldr: A random sign projection reduces dimensions while preserving the optimal k-means partition within a 2 + epsilon factor with constant probability.

title: Random Projections for $k$-means Clustering

abstract: This paper presents an approach that predicts the effectiveness of HIV combination therapies by simultaneously addressing several problems affecting the available HIV clinical data sets: the different treatment backgrounds of the samples, the uneven representation of the levels of therapy experience, the missing treatment history information, the uneven therapy representation and the unbalanced therapy outcome representation. The computational validation on clinical data shows that, compared to the most commonly used approach that does not account for the issues mentioned above, our model has significantly higher predictive power. This is especially true for samples stemming from patients with longer treatment history and samples associated with rare therapies. Furthermore, our approach is at least as powerful for the remaining samples.

paragraphs: Predicting the effectiveness of HIV combination therapies is complicated by how clinical datasets represent patients and treatments. Patients have different treatment backgrounds, levels of therapy experience are unevenly represented, and some treatment-history information is missing. Therapies and their outcomes are also represented unevenly. The proposed approach addresses these issues together.

This joint treatment matters because the prediction problem includes variation in both patient history and the available evidence about therapies. The paper’s history distribution matching approach is designed around that data situation. Its stated comparison is with a commonly used approach that does not account for these issues, making the handling of clinical-data differences central to the evaluation.

Computational validation on clinical data shows significantly higher predictive power for the proposed model. The advantage is especially pronounced for patients with longer treatment histories and for samples involving rare therapies. For the remaining samples, the model is at least as powerful in the reported evaluation. These are findings about predicting therapy effectiveness from the evaluated clinical data.
summary.tldr: Accounting jointly for treatment-history differences, missing information, and data imbalance improves reported predictions of HIV combination-therapy effectiveness.

title: History distribution matching method for predicting effectiveness of HIV combination therapies

abstract: The F-measure, originally introduced in information retrieval, is nowadays routinely used as a performance metric for problems such as binary classification, multi-label classification, and structured output prediction. Optimizing this measure remains a statistically and computationally challenging problem, since no closed-form maximizer exists. Current algorithms are approximate and typically rely on additional assumptions regarding the statistical distribution of the binary response variables. In this paper, we present an algorithm which is not only computationally efficient but also exact, regardless of the underlying distribution. The algorithm requires only a quadratic number of parameters of the joint distribution (with respect to the number of binary responses). We illustrate its practical performance by means of experimental results for multi-label classification.

paragraphs: The F-measure is used to evaluate predictions in tasks including binary classification, multi-label classification, and structured prediction. Directly maximizing it is difficult both statistically and computationally. The paper addresses this optimization problem, where the abstract describes existing algorithms as approximate and typically dependent on extra assumptions about the distribution of binary responses.

The central contribution is an efficient algorithm that finds an exact maximizer regardless of the underlying response distribution. This distributional generality matters because the optimization does not require the additional assumptions used by the approaches discussed in the abstract. Exactness describes the optimization performed using the required distributional information.

The algorithm needs only a number of joint-distribution parameters that grows quadratically with the number of binary responses. This identifies a manageable representation of the information needed for the optimization, rather than requiring every detail of the joint distribution. Experiments in multi-label classification illustrate practical performance, connecting the exact optimization result to a setting where several binary labels must be predicted together.
summary.tldr: An efficient algorithm exactly maximizes F-measure using quadratically many joint-distribution parameters without additional distributional assumptions.

title: An Exact Algorithm for F-Measure Maximization

abstract: We present a novel method for learning densities with bounded support which enables us to incorporate `hard' topological constraints. In particular, we show how emerging techniques from computational algebraic topology and the notion of Persistent Homology can be combined with kernel based methods from Machine Learning for the purpose of density estimation. The proposed formalism facilitates learning of models with bounded support in a principled way, and -- by incorporating Persistent Homology techniques in our approach -- we are able to encode algebraic-topological constraints which are not addressed in current state-of the art probabilistic models. We study the behaviour of our method on two synthetic examples for various sample sizes and exemplify the benefits of the proposed approach on a real-world data-set by learning a motion model for a racecar. We show how to learn a model which respects the underlying topological structure of the racetrack, constraining the trajectories of the car.

paragraphs: The paper develops density estimation for distributions whose possible values lie within a bounded region. It also allows hard constraints on that region’s topology. The aim is to learn a probability model that respects structural restrictions on where data can occur, making those restrictions part of the model itself.

The approach combines kernel-based learning with persistent homology and other tools from computational algebraic topology. These tools allow algebraic-topological information to be encoded as constraints during density estimation. The authors emphasize that this addresses structural requirements not handled by the probabilistic models they compare with conceptually.

They examine the method on two synthetic examples at several sample sizes and apply it to learning a racecar motion model from real data. In that application, the learned model respects the racetrack’s underlying topology and consequently constrains the car’s trajectories. This example explains the practical role of the constraints: a density model can incorporate the structure that governs which movements are possible.
summary.tldr: Combining persistent homology with kernel methods enables bounded-support density models that obey hard topological constraints.

title: Persistent Homology for Learning Densities with Bounded Support

abstract: Statistical learning and sequential prediction are two different but related formalisms to study the quality of predictions. Mapping out their relations and transferring ideas is an active area of investigation. We provide another piece of the puzzle by showing that an important concept in sequential prediction, the mixability of a loss, has a natural counterpart in the statistical setting, which we call stochastic mixability. Just as ordinary mixability characterizes fast rates for the worst-case regret in sequential prediction, stochastic mixability characterizes fast rates in statistical learning. We show that, in the special case of log-loss, stochastic mixability reduces to a well-known (but usually unnamed) martingale condition, which is used in existing convergence theorems for minimum description length and Bayesian inference. In the case of 0/1-loss, it reduces to the margin condition of Mammen and Tsybakov, and in the case that the model under consideration contains all possible predictors, it is equivalent to ordinary mixability.

paragraphs: Statistical learning and sequential prediction study prediction quality through different frameworks. This paper connects them using mixability, a property of losses that characterizes fast worst-case regret rates in sequential prediction. The authors introduce a statistical counterpart, called stochastic mixability, and show that it characterizes fast rates in statistical learning.

The concept also brings together conditions already used in more specialized settings. For log loss, stochastic mixability reduces to a martingale condition appearing in convergence results for minimum description length and Bayesian inference. For zero-one loss, it reduces to the Mammen–Tsybakov margin condition. These connections give the new definition concrete links to established learning theory.

When the model contains every possible predictor, stochastic mixability is equivalent to ordinary mixability. This identifies a setting in which the distinction between the two concepts disappears. The contribution is a common theoretical language for understanding fast prediction rates, showing how apparently separate conditions fit into a relationship between statistical learning and sequential prediction.
summary.tldr: Stochastic mixability characterizes fast statistical-learning rates and connects them to mixability in sequential prediction.

title: Mixability in Statistical Learning

abstract: Inference on high-order graphical models has become increasingly important in recent years. We consider energies with simple 'sparse' high-order potentials. Previous work in this area uses either specialized message-passing or transforms each high-order potential to the pairwise case. We take a fundamentally different approach, transforming the entire original problem into a comparatively small instance of a submodular vertex-cover problem. These vertex-cover instances can then be attacked by standard pairwise methods, where they run much faster (4--15 times) and are often more effective than on the original problem. We evaluate our approach on synthetic data, and we show that our algorithm can be useful in a fast hierarchical clustering and model estimation framework.

paragraphs: High-order graphical models contain interactions involving groups of variables, which can make inference difficult. This paper focuses on energies with simple sparse high-order potentials. Earlier approaches used specialized message passing or converted each high-order potential separately into a pairwise representation that existing methods could process.

The authors instead transform the entire original optimization problem into a comparatively small submodular vertex-cover instance. Standard pairwise methods can then operate on this transformed problem. The important design choice is the scope of the transformation: considering the whole problem produces a different computational representation from reducing each interaction independently.

On the resulting instances, the pairwise methods run four to fifteen times faster and are often more effective than when applied to the original problem. The authors evaluate the approach on synthetic data and show its potential use in fast hierarchical clustering and model estimation. The results concern the sparse high-order setting studied here and demonstrate how a suitable global reformulation can improve the usefulness of existing inference machinery.
summary.tldr: Transforming sparse high-order energy problems into small submodular vertex-cover instances makes standard pairwise methods faster and often more effective.

title: Minimizing Sparse High-Order Energies by Submodular Vertex-Cover

abstract: An increasing number of applications require processing of signals defined on weighted graphs. While wavelets provide a flexible tool for signal processing in the classical setting of regular domains, the existing graph wavelet constructions are less flexible -- they are guided solely by the structure of the underlying graph and do not take directly into consideration the particular class of signals to be processed. This paper introduces a machine learning framework for constructing graph wavelets that can sparsely represent a given class of signals. Our construction uses the lifting scheme, and is based on the observation that the recurrent nature of the lifting scheme gives rise to a structure resembling a deep auto-encoder network. Particular properties that the resulting wavelets must satisfy determine the training objective and the structure of the involved neural networks. The training is unsupervised, and is conducted similarly to the greedy pre-training of a stack of auto-encoders. After training is completed, we obtain a linear wavelet transform that can be applied to any graph signal in time and memory linear in the size of the graph. Improved sparsity of our wavelet transform for the test signals is confirmed via experiments both on synthetic and real data.

paragraphs: Signals defined on weighted graphs need representations that reflect their irregular domain. Existing graph wavelets are guided by graph structure alone, which may miss patterns characteristic of the signals being processed. This paper learns graph wavelets for a given signal class, aiming to represent those signals with fewer significant coefficients.

The construction uses the lifting scheme and observes that its repeated structure resembles a deep autoencoder. Desired wavelet properties shape both the neural network architecture and the training objective. Training is unsupervised and proceeds similarly to greedy training of stacked autoencoders, adapting the transform to signal examples without requiring labels.

After training, the result is a linear wavelet transform that can be applied to any signal on the graph using time and memory proportional to graph size. Experiments on synthetic and real data confirm improved sparsity for the test signals. The contribution combines learning during transform construction with an efficient linear representation afterward, while the reported sparsity benefit concerns the evaluated signals.
summary.tldr: Unsupervised learning adapts graph wavelets to signal classes, producing an efficient linear transform with improved sparsity on tested synthetic and real signals.

title: Wavelets on Graphs via Deep Learning

abstract: This paper considers the sample complexity of the multi-armed bandit with dependencies among the arms. Some of the most successful algorithms for this problem use the principle of optimism in the face of uncertainty to guide exploration. The clearest example of this is the class of upper confidence bound (UCB) algorithms, but recent work has shown that a simple posterior sampling algorithm, sometimes called Thompson sampling, also shares a close theoretical connection with optimistic approaches. In this paper, we develop a regret bound that holds for both classes of algorithms. This bound applies broadly and can be specialized to many model classes. It depends on a new notion we refer to as the eluder dimension, which measures the degree of dependence among action rewards. Compared to UCB algorithm regret bounds for specific model classes, our general bound matches the best available for linear models and is stronger than the best available for generalized linear models.

paragraphs: In a multi-armed bandit with dependent arms, learning about one action can also inform the values of others. This paper studies how that structure affects exploration. It considers optimistic algorithms, including upper confidence bound methods, alongside posterior sampling, which has a close theoretical connection to optimism.

The authors introduce eluder dimension as a measure of the dependence among action rewards. They use it to develop a regret bound that applies to both algorithm classes and can be specialized to many different model families. The contribution is therefore a common analytical framework for relating reward structure to the difficulty of learning which actions to choose.

For linear models, the general bound matches the best available model-specific UCB bounds described in the abstract. For generalized linear models, it improves on the best available bounds in that comparison. These findings show that a broadly applicable complexity measure can retain sharp guarantees in particular settings, while bringing optimistic exploration and posterior sampling under a shared analysis.
summary.tldr: Eluder dimension yields a shared regret analysis for optimistic and posterior-sampling bandit algorithms, with strong guarantees for linear and generalized linear models.

title: Eluder Dimension and the Sample Complexity of Optimistic Exploration

abstract: In principle, zero-shot learning makes it possible to train an object recognition model simply by specifying the category's attributes. For example, with classifiers for generic attributes like striped and four-legged, one can construct a classifier for the zebra category by enumerating which properties it possesses --- even without providing zebra training images. In practice, however, the standard zero-shot paradigm suffers because attribute predictions in novel images are hard to get right. We propose a novel random forest approach to train zero-shot models that explicitly accounts for the unreliability of attribute predictions. By leveraging statistics about each attribute’s error tendencies, our method obtains more robust discriminative models for the unseen classes. We further devise extensions to handle the few-shot scenario and unreliable attribute descriptions. On three datasets, we demonstrate the benefit for visual category learning with zero or few training examples, a critical domain for rare categories or categories defined on the fly.

paragraphs: Zero-shot recognition builds a category classifier from an attribute description without requiring training images of that category. Its practical difficulty is that attributes predicted from new images can be wrong. A description may correctly specify the category’s properties while the visual detectors provide unreliable evidence about whether those properties are present.

This paper proposes a random-forest approach that explicitly incorporates statistics about each attribute’s error tendencies. Those statistics inform the construction of more robust discriminative models for unseen categories. The central idea is to account for the reliability of the evidence when turning an attribute description into a recognition model.

The authors also extend the approach to few-shot learning, where a small number of category examples are available, and to unreliable attribute descriptions themselves. Experiments on three datasets demonstrate benefits for visual category learning with zero or few examples. The work is particularly motivated by rare categories and categories introduced on the fly, where collecting substantial training data may not fit the intended recognition setting.
summary.tldr: A random-forest approach improves zero- and few-shot recognition by accounting for unreliable attribute predictions and descriptions.

title: Zero-shot recognition with unreliable attributes

abstract: Calculation of the log-normalizer is a major computational obstacle in applications of log-linear models with large output spaces. The problem of fast normalizer computation has therefore attracted significant attention in the theoretical and applied machine learning literature. In this paper, we analyze a recently proposed technique known as ``self-normalization'', which introduces a regularization term in training to penalize log normalizers for deviating from zero. This makes it possible to use unnormalized model scores as approximate probabilities. Empirical evidence suggests that self-normalization is extremely effective, but a theoretical understanding of why it should work, and how generally it can be applied, is largely lacking.We prove upper bounds on the loss in accuracy due to self-normalization, describe classes of input distributionsthat self-normalize easily, and construct explicit examples of high-variance input distributions. Our theoretical results make predictions about the difficulty of fitting self-normalized models to several classes of distributions, and we conclude with empirical validation of these predictions on both real and synthetic datasets.

paragraphs: Log-linear models need a normalizing calculation to turn their scores into probabilities, and this can be expensive when there are many possible outputs. Self-normalization addresses that cost by penalizing deviations of the log-normalizer from zero during training. This allows unnormalized scores to serve as approximate probabilities.

The paper analyzes the accuracy consequences of this technique, whose practical effectiveness had outpaced its theoretical explanation. The authors prove upper bounds on the accuracy loss caused by self-normalization. They also identify input-distribution classes that are easy to self-normalize and construct explicit examples of high-variance input distributions.

These results yield predictions about how difficult it will be to fit self-normalized models to different distribution classes. The authors validate those predictions with real and synthetic datasets. The contribution gives theoretical structure to the computational tradeoff: simplifying probability calculation has an accuracy cost that can be bounded, and the suitability of the approach depends on properties of the input distribution.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds accuracy losses from self-normalization and explains how input distributions affect its suitability.

title: On the Accuracy of Self-Normalized Log-Linear Models

abstract: We present the Mind the Gap Model (MGM), an approach for interpretable feature extraction and selection. By placing interpretability criteria directly into the model, we allow for the model to both optimize parameters related to interpretability and to directly report a global set of distinguishable dimensions to assist with further data exploration and hypothesis generation. MGM extracts distinguishing features on real-world datasets of animal features, recipes ingredients, and disease co-occurrence. It also maintains or improves performance when compared to related approaches. We perform a user study with domain experts to show the MGM's ability to help with dataset exploration.

MGM extracts distinguishing features on real-world datasets of animal features, recipes ingredients, and disease co-occurrence. It also maintains or improves performance when compared to related approaches. We perform a user study with domain experts to show the MGM's ability to help with dataset exploration.

paragraphs: The Mind the Gap Model addresses feature selection and extraction with interpretability built into the model itself. The aim is to identify dimensions that people can distinguish and use when exploring data. Its output is a global set of such dimensions, providing a view of the dataset that can support further investigation and hypothesis generation.

The central design choice is to include interpretability criteria directly in modeling. This allows parameters related to interpretability to be optimized during learning and lets the model report the resulting dimensions directly. Interpretability therefore shapes the representation being learned, making the selected or extracted features part of the model’s intended explanatory output.

The authors demonstrate distinguishing features in datasets covering animals, recipe ingredients, and disease co-occurrence. They report maintained or improved performance relative to related approaches and conduct a study with domain experts showing usefulness for dataset exploration. These findings connect the model’s design to both computational performance and human use, supporting its role as an exploratory tool.
summary.tldr: Mind the Gap builds interpretability into feature learning and reports useful distinguishing dimensions for expert-guided data exploration.

title: Mind the Gap: A Generative Approach to Interpretable Feature Selection and Extraction

abstract: We provide a theoretical framework for analyzing basis function construction for linear value function approximation in Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). We show that important existing methods, such as Krylov bases and Bellman-error-based methods are a special case of the general framework we develop. We provide a general algorithmic framework for computing basis function refinements which “respect” the dynamics of the environment, and we derive approximation error bounds that apply for any algorithm respecting this general framework. We also show how, using ideas related to bisimulation metrics, one can translate basis refinement into a process of finding “prototypes” that are diverse enough to represent the given MDP.

paragraphs: Linear value-function approximation represents the value of states through a weighted combination of basis functions. The choice of these functions determines what the approximation can express. This paper studies how to construct and refine them in Markov decision processes, placing several existing approaches within a common theoretical framework.

The framework includes Krylov bases and methods driven by Bellman error as special cases. It also provides a general procedure for refinements that account for the environment's dynamics. The authors derive approximation-error bounds for any algorithm that follows this framework, so the analysis applies to a family of construction methods rather than only one particular refinement rule.

A further connection uses ideas related to bisimulation metrics to interpret refinement as selecting representative prototypes. These prototypes must be sufficiently diverse to represent the given decision process. This perspective connects the algebraic task of expanding a basis with the more concrete task of choosing useful representatives, while keeping the dynamics central to how representation quality is assessed.
summary.tldr: A unified framework explains how to refine value-function bases around an environment's dynamics and bounds the resulting approximation error.

title: Basis refinement strategies for linear value function approximation in MDPs

abstract: Low rank matrix completion plays a fundamental role in collaborative filtering applications, the key idea being that the variables lie in a smaller subspace than the ambient space. Often, additional information about the variables is known, and it is reasonable to assume that incorporating this information will lead to better predictions. We tackle the problem of matrix completion when pairwise relationships among variables are known, via a graph. We formulate and derive a highly efficient, conjugate gradient based alternating minimization scheme that solves optimizations with over 55 million observations up to 2 orders of magnitude faster than state-of-the-art (stochastic) gradient-descent based methods. On the theoretical front, we show that such methods generalize weighted nuclear norm formulations, and derive statistical consistency guarantees. We validate our results on both real and synthetic datasets.

paragraphs: Collaborative filtering often predicts missing entries in a matrix by assuming that the observed variables share a lower-dimensional structure. This paper asks how to use additional information about relationships between those variables. It represents known pairwise relationships as a graph and incorporates that graph into the matrix completion problem.

The computational contribution is an alternating minimization scheme built around conjugate gradients. Alternating minimization divides the optimization into successive subproblems, while the conjugate gradient component supports efficient solution. The authors report handling more than 55 million observations and running up to two orders of magnitude faster than the state-of-the-art gradient-based methods used in their comparisons.

The paper also connects these methods to a broader mathematical formulation, showing that they generalize weighted nuclear norm approaches and deriving statistical consistency guarantees. Validation uses both real and synthetic data. These results make the contribution more than a speed improvement: the framework brings graph information, scalable optimization, and statistical justification into the same approach to recovering missing entries.
summary.tldr: Graph-informed matrix completion combines statistical consistency guarantees with an alternating solver reported to be up to two orders of magnitude faster.

title: Collaborative Filtering with Graph Information: Consistency and Scalable Methods

abstract: We consider tractable representations of probability distributions and the polytime operations they support. In particular, we consider a recently proposed arithmetic circuit representation, the Probabilistic Sentential Decision Diagram (PSDD). We show that PSDD supports a polytime multiplication operator, while they do not support a polytime operator for summing-out variables. A polytime multiplication operator make PSDDs suitable for a broader class of applications compared to arithmetic circuits, which do not in general support multiplication. As one example, we show that PSDD multiplication leads to a very simple but effective compilation algorithm for probabilistic graphical models: represent each model factor as a PSDD, and then multiply them.

This paper studies that question for Probabilistic Sentential Decision Diagrams, or PSDDs, a type of arithmetic circuit representation. Its focus is on combining distributions by multiplication and eliminating variables by summing them out.

The authors show that PSDDs support polynomial-time multiplication but do not support a polynomial-time operator for summing out variables. This establishes a specific combination of capabilities and limits. General arithmetic circuits do not support multiplication efficiently in all cases, so the PSDD result enables a broader class of applications involving that operation.

As a concrete use, the paper gives a compilation algorithm for probabilistic graphical models. Each factor of the model is first represented as a PSDD, and the factors are then multiplied together. The authors describe this procedure as simple and effective. The broader lesson is that efficient multiplication can make a representation useful for constructing probabilistic models even when other transformations remain intractable.
summary.tldr: PSDDs support efficient multiplication, enabling straightforward graphical-model compilation, but do not support a general polynomial-time summing-out operator.

title: Tractable Operations for Arithmetic Circuits of Probabilistic Models

abstract: Deep metric learning has gained much popularity in recent years, following the success of deep learning. However, existing frameworks of deep metric learning based on contrastive loss and triplet loss often suffer from slow convergence, partially because they employ only one negative example while not interacting with the other negative classes in each update. In this paper, we propose to address this problem with a new metric learning objective called multi-class N-pair loss. The proposed objective function firstly generalizes triplet loss by allowing joint comparison among more than one negative examples – more specifically, N-1 negative examples – and secondly reduces the computational burden of evaluating deep embedding vectors via an efficient batch construction strategy using only N pairs of examples, instead of (N+1)×N. We demonstrate the superiority of our proposed loss to the triplet loss as well as other competing loss functions for a variety of tasks on several visual recognition benchmark, including fine-grained object recognition and verification, image clustering and retrieval, and face verification and identification.

paragraphs: Deep metric learning trains representations for comparing examples. The paper identifies a weakness in common contrastive and triplet-loss approaches: an update often uses only one negative example, leaving other negative classes out of that comparison. The authors describe this limited interaction as one contributor to slow convergence.

Their multi-class N-pair loss generalizes triplet loss by comparing against N−1 negative examples jointly. This gives each update information about several competing classes. The paper also introduces a batch-construction strategy that uses only N pairs of examples instead of (N+1)×N examples, reducing the work required to compute deep embeddings for these comparisons.

The authors report better results than triplet loss and other competing objectives across several visual-recognition benchmarks. The tasks include fine-grained recognition and verification, image clustering and retrieval, and face verification and identification. These findings support the usefulness of considering multiple negative classes together, while the batch strategy addresses the computational burden that would otherwise accompany richer comparisons.
summary.tldr: Multi-class N-pair loss compares several negative classes per update and uses efficient batches to improve deep metric learning.

title: Improved Deep Metric Learning with Multi-class N-pair Loss Objective

abstract: Deep convolutional neural networks (CNN) have achieved great success. On the other hand, modeling structural information has been proved critical in many vision problems. It is of great interest to integrate them effectively. In a classical neural network, there is no message passing between neurons in the same layer. In this paper, we propose a CRF-CNN framework which can simultaneously model structural information in both output and hidden feature layers in a probabilistic way, and it is applied to human pose estimation. A message passing scheme is proposed, so that in various layers each body joint receives messages from all the others in an efficient way. Such message passing can be implemented with convolution between features maps in the same layer, and it is also integrated with feedforward propagation in neural networks. Finally, a neural network implementation of end-to-end learning CRF-CNN is provided. Its effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments on two benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Human pose estimation involves predicting related body joints, so the structure connecting those predictions matters. This paper combines convolutional neural networks with a probabilistic framework for representing that structure. Its motivation is that a classical neural network does not pass messages between neurons within the same layer, limiting that particular route for exchanging information among joint representations.

The proposed CRF-CNN models structural relationships in both hidden feature layers and the output layer. Its message-passing scheme allows each body joint to receive information from all the others at multiple layers. Thus, relationships among joints can influence the internal features used for prediction as well as the final joint estimates.

The authors implement message passing through convolutions between feature maps in the same layer and integrate it with ordinary forward propagation. This yields a neural-network implementation that can be trained end to end. Experiments on two benchmark datasets demonstrate the framework’s effectiveness, supporting the value of incorporating structured interactions throughout the pose-estimation network.
summary.tldr: CRF-CNN improves structured human pose modeling by passing messages among body-joint representations in hidden layers and outputs.

title: CRF-CNN: Modeling Structured Information in Human Pose Estimation

abstract: We study the problem of maximizing a function that is approximately submodular under a cardinality constraint. Approximate submodularity implicitly appears in a wide range of applications as in many cases errors in evaluation of a submodular function break submodularity. Say that $F$ is $\eps$-approximately submodular if there exists a submodular function $f$ such that $(1-\eps)f(S) \leq F(S)\leq (1+\eps)f(S)$ for all subsets $S$. We are interested in characterizing the query-complexity of maximizing $F$ subject to a cardinality constraint $k$ as a function of the error level $\eps > 0$. We provide both lower and upper bounds: for $\eps > n^{-1/2}$ we show an exponential query-complexity lower bound. In contrast, when $\eps < {1}/{k}$ or under a stronger bounded curvature assumption, we give constant approximation algorithms.

paragraphs: Submodular optimization relies on diminishing returns, but errors in evaluating an objective can destroy that property. This paper studies maximizing a function that remains multiplicatively close to some submodular function. For every subset, its value must lie between one minus epsilon and one plus epsilon times the corresponding submodular value.

The selection is limited to at most k items, and the central question is how many function queries are needed as the error level changes. The authors establish an exponential query-complexity lower bound when epsilon exceeds n to the power of negative one-half, where n is the number of available items. Thus, closeness to a submodular function alone can still leave a difficult optimization problem.

They also identify favorable regimes. When epsilon is smaller than one divided by k, or when a stronger bounded-curvature assumption holds, they provide constant-factor approximation algorithms. These results show why the size of evaluation errors and additional structural assumptions matter: approximate submodularity can support efficient guarantees, but does not automatically inherit the benefits of exact submodularity.
summary.tldr: Approximately submodular maximization has sharply different query guarantees depending on evaluation error, selection size, and additional structural assumptions.

title: Maximization of Approximately Submodular Functions

abstract: Semi-supervised clustering algorithms have been proposed to identify data clusters that align with user perceived ones via the aid of side information such as seeds or pairwise constrains. However, traditional side information is mostly at the instance level and subject to the sampling bias, where non-randomly sampled instances in the supervision can mislead the algorithms to wrong clusters. In this paper, we propose learning from the feature-level supervision. We show that this kind of supervision can be easily obtained in the form of perception vectors in many applications. Then we present novel algorithms, called Perception Embedded (PE) clustering, that exploit the perception vectors as well as traditional side information to find clusters perceived by the user. Extensive experiments are conducted on real datasets and the results demonstrate the effectiveness of PE empirically.

In this paper, we propose learning from the feature-level supervision. We show that this kind of supervision can be easily obtained in the form of perception vectors in many applications. Then we present novel algorithms, called Perception Embedded (PE) clustering, that exploit the perception vectors as well as traditional side information to find clusters perceived by the user. Extensive experiments are conducted on real datasets and the results demonstrate the effectiveness of PE empirically.

paragraphs: Clustering guided by a user aims to recover groups that match the user's perception. Traditional guidance often concerns particular examples, such as seed assignments or constraints on pairs. If those examples are selected nonrandomly, their sampling bias can steer the algorithm toward groups that fail to reflect the intended organization.

This paper proposes adding supervision at the feature level. It represents such guidance through perception vectors, which the authors say can be obtained easily in many applications. Their Perception Embedded clustering algorithms use these vectors together with traditional side information to find groups aligned with the user's view.

The approach changes how the user's intended grouping is communicated: guidance can describe relevant features as well as relationships among selected instances. This directly addresses the concern that instance-level supervision may offer a biased picture of the desired clusters. Extensive experiments on real datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of Perception Embedded clustering empirically. Those results support feature-level supervision as a useful source of guidance, without establishing that sampling bias is eliminated in every application.
summary.tldr: Perception Embedded clustering combines feature-level perception vectors with traditional supervision to better recover user-perceived groups.

title: Learning User Perceived Clusters with Feature-Level Supervision

abstract: This work is motivated by the engineering task of achieving a near state-of-the-art face recognition on a minimal computing budget running on an embedded system. Our main technical contribution centers around a novel training method, called Multibatch, for similarity learning, i.e., for the task of generating an invariant ``face signature'' through training pairs of ``same'' and ``not-same'' face images. The Multibatch method first generates signatures for a mini-batch of $k$ face images and then constructs an unbiased estimate of the full gradient by relying on all $k^2-k$ pairs from the mini-batch. We prove that the variance of the Multibatch estimator is bounded by $O(1/k^2)$, under some mild conditions. In contrast, the standard gradient estimator that relies on random $k/2$ pairs has a variance of order $1/k$. The smaller variance of the Multibatch estimator significantly speeds up the convergence rate of stochastic gradient descent. Using the Multibatch method we train a deep convolutional neural network that achieves an accuracy of $98.2\%$ on the LFW benchmark, while its prediction runtime takes only $30$msec on a single ARM Cortex A9 core. Furthermore, the entire training process took only 12 hours on a single Titan X GPU.

It learns a face signature from pairs labeled as showing the same or different people. Its main contribution, Multibatch, changes how training pairs are used so that a batch of computed signatures supplies a more informative gradient estimate.
