summary.tldr: Multibatch reuses all image pairs within a batch to reduce gradient variance and train an efficient face-recognition network.

title: Learning a Metric Embedding for Face Recognition using the Multibatch Method

abstract: Functional brain networks are well described and estimated from data with Gaussian Graphical Models (GGMs), e.g.\ using sparse inverse covariance estimators. Comparing functional connectivity of subjects in two populations calls for comparing these estimated GGMs. Our goal is to identify differences in GGMs known to have similar structure. We characterize the uncertainty of differences with confidence intervals obtained using a parametric distribution on parameters of a sparse estimator. Sparse penalties enable statistical guarantees and interpretable models even in high-dimensional and low-sample settings. Characterizing the distributions of sparse models is inherently challenging as the penalties produce a biased estimator. Recent work invokes the sparsity assumptions to effectively remove the bias from a sparse estimator such as the lasso. These distributions can be used to give confidence intervals on edges in GGMs, and by extension their differences. However, in the case of comparing GGMs, these estimators do not make use of any assumed joint structure among the GGMs. Inspired by priors from brain functional connectivity we derive the distribution of parameter differences under a joint penalty when parameters are known to be sparse in the difference. This leads us to introduce the debiased multi-task fused lasso, whose distribution can be characterized in an efficient manner. We then show how the debiased lasso and multi-task fused lasso can be used to obtain confidence intervals on edge differences in GGMs. We validate the techniques proposed on a set of synthetic examples as well as neuro-imaging dataset created for the study of autism.

paragraphs: Comparing functional brain connectivity across populations requires deciding which network differences are supported by data. This paper studies Gaussian graphical models known to have similar structure and seeks confidence intervals for differences between their edges. The focus is uncertainty about changes, beyond simply producing two estimated networks.

Sparse estimation helps produce interpretable models when variables are numerous and samples are limited, but its penalties introduce bias. Existing debiasing approaches can support edge confidence intervals without using the assumed relationship between the networks. The authors instead derive the distribution of parameter differences under a joint penalty, using the assumption that only a sparse set of parameters differs.

This leads to the debiased multi-task fused lasso, whose distribution can be characterized efficiently. The paper shows how both this method and the debiased lasso yield confidence intervals for edge differences. Synthetic examples and a neuroimaging dataset assembled for autism research validate the proposed techniques. The contribution is a way to incorporate shared network structure into uncertainty estimates when comparing closely related graphical models.
summary.tldr: A debiased joint estimator provides confidence intervals for differences between Gaussian graphical models when their parameter differences are sparse.

title: Testing for Differences in Gaussian Graphical Models: Applications to Brain Connectivity

abstract: Compressing neural networks by pruning weights with small magnitudes can significantly reduce the computation and storage cost. Although pruning makes the model smaller, it is difficult to get practical speedup in modern computing platforms such as CPU and GPU due to the irregularity. Structural pruning has attract a lot of research interest to make sparsity hardware-friendly. Increasing the sparsity granularity can lead to better hardware utilization, but it will compromise the sparsity for maintaining accuracy. In this work, we propose a novel method, TETRIS, to achieve both better hardware utilization and higher sparsity. Just like a tile-matching game, we cluster the irregularly distributed weights with small value into structured groups by reordering the input/output dimension and structurally prune them. Results show that it can achieve comparable sparsity with the irregular element-wise pruning and demonstrate negligible accuracy loss. The experiments also shows ideal speedup, which is proportional to the sparsity, on GPU platforms. Our proposed method provides a new solution toward algorithm and architecture co-optimization for accuracy-efficiency trade-off.

paragraphs: Removing small neural-network weights can reduce storage and arithmetic, but irregularly scattered removals are difficult for CPUs and GPUs to exploit efficiently. Pruning larger structured groups improves hardware utilization, yet can require retaining more weights to preserve accuracy. TETRIS aims to combine the sparsity of individual-weight pruning with the practicality of structured pruning.

The method reorders input and output dimensions so that small weights, initially scattered through the network, become concentrated in structured groups. Those groups can then be pruned. The tile-matching analogy describes this rearrangement: changing how weights are organized creates groups that are better suited to removal and hardware execution.

The reported results achieve sparsity comparable to irregular element-wise pruning with negligible accuracy loss. GPU experiments also show speedup proportional to sparsity. These are empirical findings from the evaluated settings, connecting the organization of removed weights with actual execution gains. The contribution is an approach to the accuracy-efficiency tradeoff that coordinates the pruning algorithm with the structured work that computing hardware can use effectively.
summary.tldr: TETRIS rearranges small weights into structured groups, achieving high sparsity and proportional GPU speedups in the reported experiments.

title: TETRIS: TilE-matching the TRemendous Irregular Sparsity

abstract: Knowledge distillation is effective to train the small and generalisable network models for meeting the low-memory and fast running requirements. Existing offline distillation methods rely on a strong pre-trained teacher, which enables favourable knowledge discovery and transfer but requires a complex two-phase training procedure. Online counterparts address this limitation at the price of lacking a high-capacity teacher. In this work, we present an On-the-fly Native Ensemble (ONE) learning strategy for one-stage online distillation. Specifically, ONE only trains a single multi-branch network while simultaneously establishing a strong teacher on-the-fly to enhance the learning of target network. Extensive evaluations show that ONE improves the generalisation performance of a variety of deep neural networks more significantly than alternative methods on four image classification dataset: CIFAR10, CIFAR100, SVHN, and ImageNet, whilst having the computational efficiency advantages.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation uses a teacher model to help train a smaller model with good generalization. A strong pretrained teacher can provide useful guidance, but preparing it creates a separate training phase. Existing online approaches avoid that two-stage procedure, while the paper identifies their lack of a high-capacity teacher as a drawback.

On-the-fly Native Ensemble, or ONE, builds a strong teacher during the same training process as the target network. It trains a single network with multiple branches and establishes the teacher on the fly. This provides a one-stage online distillation strategy in which teacher construction and target-model learning happen together.

Evaluations cover a variety of deep networks on CIFAR10, CIFAR100, SVHN, and ImageNet. The authors report larger generalization improvements than alternative methods, together with computational-efficiency advantages. The contribution is a way to combine the guidance of a strong teacher with a unified training procedure. Its reported benefits concern both the quality of the learned models and the efficiency of obtaining them.
summary.tldr: ONE creates a strong teacher inside a single multi-branch training process, improving online knowledge distillation and reported generalization.

title: Knowledge Distillation by On-the-Fly Native Ensemble

abstract: We present Memory Augmented Policy Optimization (MAPO), a simple and novel way to leverage a memory buffer of promising trajectories to reduce the variance of policy gradient estimate. MAPO is applicable to deterministic environments with discrete actions, such as structured prediction and combinatorial optimization tasks. We express the expected return objective as a weighted sum of two terms: an expectation over the high-reward trajectories inside the memory buffer, and a separate expectation over trajectories outside the buffer. To make an efficient algorithm of MAPO, we propose: (1) memory weight clipping to accelerate and stabilize training; (2) systematic exploration to discover high-reward trajectories; (3) distributed sampling from inside and outside of the memory buffer to scale up training. MAPO improves the sample efficiency and robustness of policy gradient, especially on tasks with sparse rewards. We evaluate MAPO on weakly supervised program synthesis from natural language (semantic parsing). On the WikiTableQuestions benchmark, we improve the state-of-the-art by 2.6%, achieving an accuracy of 46.3%. On the WikiSQL benchmark, MAPO achieves an accuracy of 74.9% with only weak supervision, outperforming several strong baselines with full supervision. Our source code is available at https://goo.gl/TXBp4e

MAPO is applicable to deterministic environments with discrete actions, such as structured prediction and combinatorial optimization tasks. We express the expected return objective as a weighted sum of two terms: an expectation over the high-reward trajectories inside the memory buffer, and a separate expectation over trajectories outside the buffer. To make an efficient algorithm of MAPO, we propose: (1) memory weight clipping to accelerate and stabilize training; (2) systematic exploration to discover high-reward trajectories; (3) distributed sampling from inside and outside of the memory buffer to scale up training. MAPO improves the sample efficiency and robustness of policy gradient, especially on tasks with sparse rewards. We evaluate MAPO on weakly supervised program synthesis from natural language (semantic parsing). On the WikiTableQuestions benchmark, we improve the state-of-the-art by 2.6%, achieving an accuracy of 46.3%. On the WikiSQL benchmark, MAPO achieves an accuracy of 74.9% with only weak supervision, outperforming several strong baselines with full supervision. Our source code is available at https://goo.gl/TXBp4e

paragraphs: MAPO uses a memory of promising action sequences to reduce variance in policy-gradient estimates. It applies to deterministic environments with discrete actions, including structured prediction and combinatorial optimization. The motivation is particularly relevant when rewards are sparse: useful trajectories can be difficult to discover, making effective reuse of them valuable.

The method expresses expected return as a weighted combination of two expectations, one over high-reward trajectories in memory and another over trajectories outside it. Memory weight clipping helps accelerate and stabilize training, systematic exploration seeks additional high-reward trajectories, and distributed sampling from both groups supports larger-scale training.

The authors report improved sample efficiency and robustness, evaluating MAPO on weakly supervised program synthesis from natural language. It reaches 46.3% accuracy on WikiTableQuestions, with a reported 2.6% improvement over the state of the art. On WikiSQL it reaches 74.9% accuracy with weak supervision, exceeding several strong fully supervised baselines. These results demonstrate the memory-based approach in semantic parsing under the stated environment setting.
summary.tldr: MAPO reuses high-reward trajectories through a memory buffer to improve policy-gradient learning, especially when rewards are sparse.

title: Memory Augmented Policy Optimization for Program Synthesis and Semantic Parsing

abstract: Flow-based generative models, conceptually attractive due to tractability of both the exact log-likelihood computation and latent-variable inference, and efficiency of both training and sampling, has led to a number of impressive empirical successes and spawned many advanced variants and theoretical investigations. Despite their computational efficiency, the density estimation performance of flow-based generative models significantly falls behind those of state-of-the-art autoregressive models. In this work, we introduce masked convolutional generative flow (MaCow), a simple yet effective architecture of generative flow using masked convolution. By restricting the local connectivity in a small kernel, MaCow enjoys the properties of fast and stable training, and efficient sampling, while achieving significant improvements over Glow for density estimation on standard image benchmarks, considerably narrowing the gap to autoregressive models.

However, the paper identifies a substantial density-estimation gap between these models and leading autoregressive approaches. MaCow is designed to improve that aspect of flow modeling while retaining useful computational properties.

The proposed architecture uses masked convolutions with local connectivity restricted to a small kernel. This makes the pattern of connections a central architectural choice. The authors report that the resulting generative flow supports fast, stable training and efficient sampling, connecting its constrained local structure with practical computation.

On standard image benchmarks, MaCow significantly improves density estimation over Glow and substantially narrows the gap to autoregressive models. The claim is an improvement and a narrowing of that gap, rather than elimination of it. The paper’s contribution is a simple flow architecture that brings better density modeling together with the training and sampling advantages that motivate this model family.
summary.tldr: MaCow uses locally masked convolutions to improve flow-based image density estimation while retaining fast training and efficient sampling.

title: MaCow: Masked Convolutional Generative Flow

abstract: Algorithm configuration methods optimize the performance of a parameterized heuristic algorithm on a given distribution of problem instances. Recent work introduced an algorithm configuration procedure ( Structured Procrastination'') that provably achieves near optimal performance with high probability and with nearly minimal runtime in the worst case. It also offers an anytime property: it keeps tightening its optimality guarantees the longer it is run. Unfortunately, Structured Procrastination is not adaptive to characteristics of the parameterized algorithm: it treats every input like the worst case. Follow-up work ( LeapsAndBounds'') achieves adaptivity but trades away the anytime property. This paper introduces a new algorithm, ``Structured Procrastination with Confidence'', that preserves the near-optimality and anytime properties of Structured Procrastination while adding adaptivity. In particular, the new algorithm will perform dramatically faster in settings where many algorithm configurations perform poorly. We show empirically both that such settings arise frequently in practice and that the anytime property is useful for finding good configurations quickly.

However, it treated inputs according to the worst case. Another method gained adaptivity but gave up that anytime behavior.

Structured Procrastination with Confidence combines those properties. It preserves near-optimality and progressively improving guarantees while adapting to characteristics of the algorithm being configured. In particular, the authors show that it can run dramatically faster when many candidate configurations perform poorly, a condition that makes treating all candidates as worst cases unnecessarily costly.

Empirical results show that these favorable conditions occur frequently in practice. They also demonstrate the usefulness of the anytime property for finding good configurations quickly. The contribution therefore concerns both how efficiently the search responds to its candidates and how the quality assurances improve as more computation becomes available, without requiring a fixed stopping point to obtain useful results.
summary.tldr: Structured Procrastination with Confidence combines adaptive configuration search with near-optimality guarantees that tighten as it runs.

title: Procrastinating with Confidence: Near-Optimal, Anytime, Adaptive Algorithm Configuration

abstract: We introduce a variant of the $k$-nearest neighbor classifier in which $k$ is chosen adaptively for each query, rather than supplied as a parameter. The choice of $k$ depends on properties of each neighborhood, and therefore may significantly vary between different points. (For example, the algorithm will use larger $k$ for predicting the labels of points in noisy regions.) We provide theory and experiments that demonstrate that the algorithm performs comparably to, and sometimes better than, $k$-NN with an optimal choice of $k$. In particular, we derive bounds on the convergence rates of our classifier that depend on a local quantity we call the ``advantage'' which is significantly weaker than the Lipschitz conditions used in previous convergence rate proofs. These generalization bounds hinge on a variant of the seminal Uniform Convergence Theorem due to Vapnik and Chervonenkis; this variant concerns conditional probabilities and may be of independent interest.

paragraphs: Nearest-neighbor classification predicts a label from nearby examples, but choosing how many neighbors to consult is consequential. This paper replaces a single supplied value of k with a choice made separately for each query. The neighborhood itself determines how much evidence the classifier uses, allowing different parts of the data to receive different treatment.

For example, the method uses more neighbors when predicting labels in noisy regions. Theory and experiments indicate that this adaptive rule performs comparably to, and sometimes better than, nearest-neighbor classification with an optimal choice of k. The stated benefit is therefore the ability to adjust locally while remaining competitive with a well-chosen fixed setting.

The analysis also changes how convergence is characterized. Its bounds depend on a local quantity called advantage, using a substantially weaker condition than the Lipschitz conditions in earlier convergence proofs. Supporting these bounds is a version of the Vapnik–Chervonenkis uniform convergence theorem for conditional probabilities. That result supplies the theoretical foundation for the classifier and may also be useful independently.
summary.tldr: An adaptive nearest-neighbor classifier chooses its neighborhood size per query and competes with optimally tuned fixed-k classification under weaker convergence conditions.

title: An adaptive nearest neighbor rule for classification

abstract: Detecting 3D objects from a single RGB image is intrinsically ambiguous, thus requiring appropriate prior knowledge and intermediate representations as constraints to reduce the uncertainties and improve the consistencies between the 2D image plane and the 3D world coordinate. To address this challenge, we propose to adopt perspective points as a new intermediate representation for 3D object detection, defined as the 2D projections of local Manhattan 3D keypoints to locate an object; these perspective points satisfy geometric constraints imposed by the perspective projection. We further devise PerspectiveNet, an end-to-end trainable model that simultaneously detects the 2D bounding box, 2D perspective points, and 3D object bounding box for each object from a single RGB image. PerspectiveNet yields three unique advantages: (i) 3D object bounding boxes are estimated based on perspective points, bridging the gap between 2D and 3D bounding boxes without the need of category-specific 3D shape priors. (ii) It predicts the perspective points by a template-based method, and a perspective loss is formulated to maintain the perspective constraints. (iii) It maintains the consistency between the 2D perspective points and 3D bounding boxes via a differentiable projective function. Experiments on SUN RGB-D dataset show that the proposed method significantly outperforms existing RGB-based approaches for 3D object detection.

paragraphs: A single RGB image leaves ambiguity about an object's three-dimensional location and extent. PerspectiveNet addresses this by introducing an intermediate representation that connects image coordinates to 3D geometry. Its perspective points are the 2D projections of local Manhattan 3D keypoints, and their arrangement must satisfy constraints imposed by perspective projection.

The end-to-end model jointly predicts each object's 2D bounding box, perspective points, and 3D bounding box. It predicts the points through a template-based method and uses a perspective loss to enforce their geometric constraints. A differentiable projective function also maintains consistency between the predicted 2D points and 3D boxes, tying the outputs together during learning.

Estimating 3D boxes through these points avoids the need for category-specific 3D shape priors in the proposed approach. Experiments on SUN RGB-D show significant improvements over existing RGB-based 3D detection methods. The findings support using a geometrically constrained intermediate representation to reduce ambiguity and improve agreement between image-space predictions and three-dimensional object estimates.
summary.tldr: PerspectiveNet connects 2D and 3D object detection through geometrically constrained perspective points, improving single-image detection on SUN RGB-D.

title: PerspectiveNet: 3D Object Detection from a Single RGB Image via Perspective Points

abstract: In this work we propose a differential geometric motivation for Nesterov's accelerated gradient method (AGM) for strongly-convex problems. By considering the optimization procedure as occurring on a Riemannian manifold with a natural structure, The AGM method can be seen as the proximal point method applied in this curved space. This viewpoint can also be extended to the continuous time case, where the accelerated gradient method arises from the natural block-implicit Euler discretization of an ODE on the manifold. We provide an analysis of the convergence rate of this ODE for quadratic objectives.
originalAbstract: In this work we propose a differential geometric motivation for Nesterov's accelerated gradient method (AGM) for strongly-convex problems. By considering the optimization procedure as occurring on a Riemannian manifold with a natural structure, The AGM method can be seen as the proximal point method applied in this curved space. This viewpoint can also be extended to the continuous time case, where the accelerated gradient method arises from the natural block-implicit Euler discretization of an ODE on the manifold. We provide an analysis of the convergence rate of this ODE for quadratic objectives.

paragraphs: Nesterov's accelerated gradient method is the subject of this paper's geometric interpretation. For strongly convex problems, the authors view optimization as taking place on a Riemannian manifold, a space equipped with a geometry that can be curved. The aim is to explain the accelerated update through that geometry.

In this formulation, the accelerated method can be understood as a proximal point method applied in the curved space. This connects two optimization procedures by changing the geometric setting in which the updates are interpreted. The contribution is therefore a mathematical explanation of acceleration, with the manifold's natural structure playing a central role in the correspondence.

The perspective also extends to continuous time through an ordinary differential equation on the manifold. A natural block-implicit Euler discretization of that equation gives rise to the accelerated gradient method. The authors analyze the equation's convergence rate for quadratic objectives. This scope distinguishes the broader strongly convex motivation from the particular class of objectives covered by the stated continuous-time convergence analysis.
summary.tldr: The paper interprets Nesterov acceleration as a proximal point method on a curved manifold and analyzes related continuous-time dynamics for quadratic objectives.

title: On the Curved Geometry of Accelerated Optimization

abstract: Semi-implicit graph variational auto-encoder (SIG-VAE) is proposed to expand the flexibility of variational graph auto-encoders (VGAE) to model graph data. SIG-VAE employs a hierarchical variational framework to enable neighboring node sharing for better generative modeling of graph dependency structure, together with a Bernoulli-Poisson link decoder. Not only does this hierarchical construction provide a more flexible generative graph model to better capture real-world graph properties, but also does SIG-VAE naturally lead to semi-implicit hierarchical variational inference that allows faithful modeling of implicit posteriors of given graph data, which may exhibit heavy tails, multiple modes, skewness, and rich dependency structures. SIG-VAE integrates a carefully designed generative model, well suited to model real-world sparse graphs, and a sophisticated variational inference network, which propagates the graph structural information and distribution uncertainty to capture complex posteriors. SIG-VAE clearly outperforms a simple combination of VGAE with variational inference, including semi-implicit variational inference~(SIVI) or normalizing flow (NF), which does not propagate uncertainty in its inference network, and provides more interpretable latent representations than VGAE does. Extensive experiments with a variety of graph data show that SIG-VAE significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods on several different graph analytic tasks.

paragraphs: Graph generative models must represent relationships among nodes and uncertainty about their hidden representations. The paper introduces SIG-VAE to expand the flexibility of variational graph autoencoders. Its hierarchical framework enables information sharing among neighboring nodes and uses a Bernoulli-Poisson link decoder in a model designed for sparse graphs.

A central feature is an inference network that propagates both graph structure and distributional uncertainty. The resulting semi-implicit hierarchical inference can represent complex posterior shapes, including heavy tails, multiple modes, skewness, and dependencies. This flexibility matters because uncertainty about a graph’s hidden representation need not fit a simple distribution, and neighboring nodes may carry related uncertainty.

The authors report that SIG-VAE outperforms straightforward combinations of a graph variational autoencoder with semi-implicit inference or normalizing flows that do not propagate uncertainty through the inference network. They also report more interpretable latent representations than VGAE and significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods across several graph analysis tasks. The findings emphasize the joint design of graph generation and uncertainty-aware inference.
summary.tldr: SIG-VAE improves graph generative modeling by sharing structural information and uncertainty through a flexible hierarchical inference network.

title: Semi-Implicit Graph Variational Auto-Encoders

abstract: The success of generative modeling in continuous domains has led to a surge of interest in generating discrete data such as molecules, source code, and graphs. However, construction histories for these discrete objects are typically not unique and so generative models must reason about intractably large spaces in order to learn. Additionally, structured discrete domains are often characterized by strict constraints on what constitutes a valid object and generative models must respect these requirements in order to produce useful novel samples. Here, we present a generative model for discrete objects employing a Markov chain where transitions are restricted to a set of local operations that preserve validity. Building off of generative interpretations of denoising autoencoders, the Markov chain alternates between producing 1) a sequence of corrupted objects that are valid but not from the data distribution, and 2) a learned reconstruction distribution that attempts to fix the corruptions while also preserving validity. This approach constrains the generative model to only produce valid objects, requires the learner to only discover local modifications to the objects, and avoids marginalization over an unknown and potentially large space of construction histories. We evaluate the proposed approach on two highly structured discrete domains, molecules and Laman graphs, and find that it compares favorably to alternative methods at capturing distributional statistics for a host of semantically relevant metrics.

paragraphs: Generating structured discrete objects presents two difficulties: an object may have many construction histories, and only some objects satisfy the domain’s validity rules. Learning across all possible histories can become intractable. The paper addresses these issues with a generative process built from local operations that preserve validity.

The model uses a Markov chain that alternates between corruption and learned reconstruction. Corruption produces objects that remain valid but depart from the data distribution. The reconstruction model then learns local changes that attempt to repair those corruptions while continuing to respect validity. This design restricts generated objects to valid ones and avoids summing over an unknown, potentially enormous collection of construction histories.

The authors evaluate the approach on molecules and Laman graphs, two domains with strong structural requirements. They report favorable comparisons with alternative methods in capturing distributional statistics across semantically relevant measures. The results support learning a sequence of valid local modifications as a way to model complex discrete objects while keeping their structural constraints built into generation.
summary.tldr: A generative Markov chain learns validity-preserving local repairs to produce structured discrete objects without enumerating their construction histories.

title: Discrete Object Generation with Reversible Inductive Construction

abstract: Despite the vulnerability of object detectors to adversarial attacks, very few defenses are known to date. While adversarial training can improve the empirical robustness of image classifiers, a direct extension to object detection is very expensive. This work is motivated by recent progress on certified classification by randomized smoothing. We start by presenting a reduction from object detection to a regression problem. Then, to enable certified regression, where standard mean smoothing fails, we propose median smoothing, which is of independent interest. We obtain the first model-agnostic, training-free, and certified defense for object detection against $\ell_2$-bounded attacks.

This work is motivated by recent progress on certified classification by randomized smoothing. We start by presenting a reduction from object detection to a regression problem. Then, to enable certified regression, where standard mean smoothing fails, we propose median smoothing, which is of independent interest. We obtain the first model-agnostic, training-free, and certified defense for object detection against $\ell_2$-bounded attacks.

paragraphs: Object detectors are vulnerable to adversarial changes in their inputs, yet defending them poses different challenges from defending image classifiers. The paper notes that directly extending adversarial training to detection is very expensive. It instead pursues a certified defense: a method that supplies a mathematical robustness guarantee for a specified class of input changes.

The authors first reformulate object detection as a regression problem. This step creates a route for adapting ideas from randomized smoothing, which had supported certified classification. However, standard smoothing based on the mean fails for the certified regression problem considered here. The proposed alternative is median smoothing, which provides the needed regression certification mechanism.

Combining the reduction with median smoothing yields what the authors describe as the first model-agnostic, training-free certified defense for object detection against attacks bounded in l_2 magnitude. These properties matter because the defense does not depend on a particular detector architecture or require defensive retraining. The guarantee is specifically tied to the stated perturbation class. Median smoothing is also presented as a contribution with relevance beyond its use in object detection.
summary.tldr: Reducing detection to regression and using median smoothing yields a training-free certified defense against l_2-bounded attacks.

title: Detection as Regression: Certified Object Detection with Median Smoothing

abstract: The strong lottery ticket hypothesis (LTH) postulates that one can approximate any target neural network by only pruning the weights of a sufficiently over-parameterized random network. A recent work by Malach et al. [MYSS20] establishes the first theoretical analysis for the strong LTH: one can provably approximate a neural network of width $d$ and depth $l$, by pruning a random one that is a factor $O(d^4 l^2)$ wider and twice as deep. This polynomial over-parameterization requirement is at odds with recent experimental research that achieves good approximation with networks that are a small factor wider than the target. In this work, we close the gap and offer an exponential improvement to the over-parameterization requirement for the existence of lottery tickets. We show that any target network of width $d$ and depth $l$ can be approximated by pruning a random network that is a factor $O(log(dl))$ wider and twice as deep. Our analysis heavily relies on connecting pruning random ReLU networks to random instances of the Subset Sum problem. We then show that this logarithmic over-parameterization is essentially optimal for constant depth networks. Finally, we verify several of our theoretical insights with experiments.

paragraphs: The strong lottery ticket hypothesis asks whether pruning alone can uncover a network that approximates a chosen target inside a sufficiently large random network. Earlier theory established this possibility but required a polynomial increase in width. That requirement was much larger than the small width increases associated with successful experimental approximations.

This paper proves that a random network only O(log(dl)) times wider than a target of width d and depth l, and twice as deep, is sufficient for approximation through pruning. The result is an exponential improvement over the previous width requirement. It concerns the existence of suitable subnetworks within the random network.

The proof connects pruning random ReLU networks with random instances of the Subset Sum problem. This connection provides the mathematical route to the sharper width bound. The authors further show that logarithmic over-parameterization is essentially optimal for networks of constant depth and experimentally verify several theoretical insights. The results substantially narrow the gap between earlier existence guarantees and the modest over-parameterization seen in experiments.
summary.tldr: A logarithmic increase in width and a doubling of depth suffice for random networks to contain pruned approximations of target networks.

title: Optimal Lottery Tickets via Subset Sum: Logarithmic Over-Parameterization is Sufficient

abstract: We introduce Sparse Symplectically Integrated Neural Networks (SSINNs), a novel model for learning Hamiltonian dynamical systems from data. SSINNs combine fourth-order symplectic integration with a learned parameterization of the Hamiltonian obtained using sparse regression through a mathematically elegant function space. This allows for interpretable models that incorporate symplectic inductive biases and have low memory requirements. We evaluate SSINNs on four classical Hamiltonian dynamical problems: the Hénon-Heiles system, nonlinearly coupled oscillators, a multi-particle mass-spring system, and a pendulum system. Our results demonstrate promise in both system prediction and conservation of energy, often outperforming the current state-of-the-art black-box prediction techniques by an order of magnitude. Further, SSINNs successfully converge to true governing equations from highly limited and noisy data, demonstrating potential applicability in the discovery of new physical governing equations.

paragraphs: This paper learns Hamiltonian dynamical systems from observed data while building physical structure into the model. Sparse Symplectically Integrated Neural Networks combine a learned Hamiltonian with fourth-order symplectic integration. The Hamiltonian is obtained through sparse regression in a chosen function space, producing a compact mathematical representation of the dynamics.

The combination is intended to make the learned system interpretable, incorporate symplectic inductive biases, and keep memory requirements low. The authors evaluate it on four classical problems: the Hénon–Heiles system, nonlinearly coupled oscillators, a multiparticle mass-spring system, and a pendulum. These tests examine prediction of motion alongside conservation of energy.

The reported results show promise on both objectives, often improving on leading black-box prediction techniques by an order of magnitude. The models also recover true governing equations from highly limited and noisy data in the studied problems. That recovery motivates possible use in discovering new physical laws. The demonstrated result is equation recovery on the evaluated systems; discovering previously unknown governing equations remains a potential application supported by those findings.
summary.tldr: SSINNs combine sparse Hamiltonian learning with symplectic integration to produce interpretable dynamics models and recover equations from limited, noisy data.

title: Sparse Symplectically Integrated Neural Networks

abstract: In safety-critical applications, autonomous agents may need to learn in an environment where mistakes can be very costly. In such settings, the agent needs to behave safely not only after but also while learning. To achieve this, existing safe reinforcement learning methods make an agent rely on priors that let it avoid dangerous situations during exploration with high probability, but both the probabilistic guarantees and the smoothness assumptions inherent in the priors are not viable in many scenarios of interest such as autonomous driving. This paper presents an alternative approach inspired by human teaching, where an agent learns under the supervision of an automatic instructor that saves the agent from violating constraints during learning. In this model, we introduce the monitor that neither needs to know how to do well at the task the agent is learning nor needs to know how the environment works. Instead, it has a library of reset controllers that it activates when the agent starts behaving dangerously, preventing it from doing damage. Crucially, the choices of which reset controller to apply in which situation affect the speed of agent learning. Based on observing agents' progress the teacher itself learns a policy for choosing the reset controllers, a curriculum, to optimize the agent's final policy reward. Our experiments use this framework in two environments to induce curricula for safe and efficient learning.

Crucially, the choices of which reset controller to apply in which situation affect the speed of agent learning. Our experiments use this framework in two environments to induce curricula for safe and efficient learning.

paragraphs: An agent in a safety-critical environment must avoid costly mistakes while it is still learning. This paper proposes an instructor-based alternative to exploration methods that depend on particular smoothness assumptions and probabilistic safety priors.

A monitor has a library of reset controllers and activates them when the agent begins behaving dangerously. It need not know how to solve the task or possess a model of the environment. Because different interventions affect learning progress differently, a teacher learns a policy for selecting reset controllers, creating a curriculum aimed at improving final policy reward.

Experiments in two environments demonstrate curricula for safe and efficient learning. The abstract does not give numerical results or describe how reset-controller reliability is established. The safety mechanism depends on that intervention library and monitoring setup; it is not evidence that an arbitrary unmonitored agent can explore real-world environments safely.
summary.tldr: An automatic instructor learns when to activate reset controllers during reinforcement learning.

title: Safe Reinforcement Learning via Curriculum Induction

abstract: Offline Reinforcement Learning (RL) is a promising approach for learning optimal policies in environments where direct exploration is expensive or unfeasible. However, the adoption of such policies in practice is often challenging, as they are hard to interpret within the application context, and lack measures of uncertainty for the learned policy value and its decisions. To overcome these issues, we propose an Expert-Supervised RL (ESRL) framework which uses uncertainty quantification for offline policy learning. In particular, we have three contributions: 1) the method can learn safe and optimal policies through hypothesis testing, 2) ESRL allows for different levels of risk averse implementations tailored to the application context, and finally, 3) we propose a way to interpret ESRL’s policy at every state through posterior distributions, and use this framework to compute off-policy value function posteriors. We provide theoretical guarantees for our estimators and regret bounds consistent with Posterior Sampling for RL (PSRL). Sample efficiency of ESRL is independent of the chosen risk aversion threshold and quality of the behavior policy.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning uses existing experience to learn policies when direct exploration is costly or infeasible. Practical adoption can be difficult when the resulting decisions are hard to interpret and the method does not express uncertainty about their value. Expert-Supervised Reinforcement Learning addresses these issues by making uncertainty quantification part of offline policy learning.

The framework uses hypothesis testing to learn safe and optimal policies and supports different degrees of risk aversion for different applications. It also represents uncertainty through posterior distributions, providing a way to interpret the policy at each state. The same framework computes posterior distributions over off-policy value functions, so evaluation includes uncertainty about the value of a policy.

The paper provides theoretical guarantees for its estimators and regret bounds consistent with Posterior Sampling for Reinforcement Learning. It further states that sample efficiency is independent of the chosen risk aversion threshold and the quality of the behavior policy that generated the data. Together, these contributions connect policy learning, uncertainty-aware evaluation, and adjustable risk preferences within one framework.
summary.tldr: ESRL uses uncertainty estimates and hypothesis testing to support interpretable offline policy learning with adjustable risk aversion and theoretical guarantees.

title: Expert-Supervised Reinforcement Learning for Offline Policy Learning and Evaluation

abstract: The ability to perform effective planning is crucial for building an instruction-following agent. When navigating through a new environment, an agent is challenged with (1) connecting the natural language instructions with its progressively growing knowledge of the world; and (2) performing long-range planning and decision making in the form of effective exploration and error correction. Current methods are still limited on both fronts despite extensive efforts. In this paper, we introduce Evolving Graphical Planner (EGP), a module that allows global planning for navigation based on raw sensory input. The module dynamically constructs a graphical representation, generalizes the local action space to allow for more flexible decision making, and performs efficient planning on a proxy representation. We demonstrate our model on a challenging Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) task with photorealistic images, and achieve superior performance compared to previous navigation architectures. Concretely, we achieve 53% success rate on the test split of Room-to-Room navigation task (Anderson et al.) through pure imitation learning, outperforming previous architectures by up to 5%.

paragraphs: An instruction-following navigation agent must relate language to an environment it is still discovering. It also needs to plan beyond its next move, explore effectively, and recover from mistakes. The paper presents Evolving Graphical Planner, or EGP, as a module for addressing these linked demands using raw sensory input.

EGP dynamically builds a graph representation as the agent acquires knowledge of the environment. It expands the local action space to support more flexible decisions and carries out planning on a proxy representation. Together, these components provide a mechanism for global planning while the agent's available understanding of the world continues to grow.

The authors evaluate the model on vision-and-language navigation with photorealistic images. Using pure imitation learning, it achieves a 53% success rate on the Room-to-Room test split and reports an improvement of up to 5% over previous architectures. The findings support the value of an evolving graph for connecting ongoing perception with longer-range navigation decisions in the evaluated task.
summary.tldr: EGP builds an evolving graph for global navigation planning and achieves 53% success on Room-to-Room using imitation learning.

title: Evolving Graphical Planner: Contextual Global Planning for Vision-and-Language Navigation

abstract: Tensor factorization based models have shown great power in knowledge graph completion (KGC). However, their performance usually suffers from the overfitting problem seriously. This motivates various regularizers---such as the squared Frobenius norm and tensor nuclear norm regulariers---while the limited applicability significantly limits their practical usage. To address this challenge, we propose a novel regularizer---namely, \textbf{DU}ality-induced \textbf{R}egul\textbf{A}rizer (DURA)---which is not only effective in improving the performance of existing models but widely applicable to various methods. The major novelty of DURA is based on the observation that, for an existing tensor factorization based KGC model (\textit{primal}), there is often another distance based KGC model (\textit{dual}) closely associated with it.

paragraphs: Knowledge graph completion uses models to infer missing relationships. Tensor-factorization approaches are powerful for this task, but the paper identifies serious overfitting as a recurring problem. Regularizers can restrain that tendency, yet existing choices such as squared Frobenius and tensor nuclear norm penalties have limited applicability across methods.

The proposed Duality-Induced Regularizer, or DURA, builds on a relationship between two ways of modeling the same completion problem. A tensor-factorization model often has a closely associated model based on distances. The paper calls the factorization model the primal and its distance-based counterpart the dual, and uses this connection as the basis for regularization.

The stated contribution combines improved performance with broad applicability to existing factorization methods. This matters because a useful regularizer must fit the models people actually use, alongside controlling overfitting. The central insight is that an associated distance-based formulation can guide the regularization of a factorization model. The abstract presents this relationship as occurring often, rather than asserting that every possible factorization model has such a counterpart.
summary.tldr: DURA uses connections between tensor-factorization and distance-based models to regularize knowledge graph completion across a broad range of methods.

title: Duality-Induced Regularizer for Tensor Factorization Based Knowledge Graph Completion

abstract: We introduce a conceptually simple yet effective model for self-supervised representation learning with graph data. It follows the previous methods that generate two views of an input graph through data augmentation. However, unlike contrastive methods that focus on instance-level discrimination, we optimize an innovative feature-level objective inspired by classical Canonical Correlation Analysis. Compared with other works, our approach requires none of the parameterized mutual information estimator, additional projector, asymmetric structures, and most importantly, negative samples which can be costly. We show that the new objective essentially 1) aims at discarding augmentation-variant information by learning invariant representations, and 2) can prevent degenerated solutions by decorrelating features in different dimensions. Our theoretical analysis further provides an understanding for the new objective which can be equivalently seen as an instantiation of the Information Bottleneck Principle under the self-supervised setting. Despite its simplicity, our method performs competitively on seven public graph datasets.

paragraphs: This paper learns graph representations without labels by generating two augmented views of the same graph. Its central choice is to compare learned features through an objective inspired by canonical correlation analysis. This shifts the learning emphasis from distinguishing individual instances to organizing the information carried by representation dimensions.

The objective encourages representations to retain information that stays consistent across augmentations while discarding information that changes with them. It also decorrelates different feature dimensions, which can prevent degenerate solutions. The method does not require negative samples, an additional projector, asymmetric structures, or a parameterized mutual-information estimator, simplifying the machinery needed for training.

The theoretical analysis interprets the objective as an instance of the information bottleneck principle in a self-supervised setting. This gives a second account of how the objective controls retained information. Empirically, the approach performs competitively on seven public graph datasets. Together, these results support the usefulness of feature-level invariance and decorrelation as a comparatively simple approach to self-supervised graph learning.
summary.tldr: A correlation-inspired graph-learning objective combines augmentation invariance with feature decorrelation, achieving competitive results without negative samples or several common auxiliary components.

title: From Canonical Correlation Analysis to Self-supervised Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Approximate Bayesian inference for neural networks is considered a robust alternative to standard training, often providing good performance on out-of-distribution data. However, Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) with high-fidelity approximate inference via full-batch Hamiltonian Monte Carlo achieve poor generalization under covariate shift, even underperforming classical estimation. We explain this surprising result, showing how a Bayesian model average can in fact be problematic under covariate shift, particularly in cases where linear dependencies in the input features cause a lack of posterior contraction. We additionally show why the same issue does not affect many approximate inference procedures, or classical maximum a-posteriori (MAP) training. Finally, we propose novel priors that improve the robustness of BNNs to many sources of covariate shift.

We additionally show why the same issue does not affect many approximate inference procedures, or classical maximum a-posteriori (MAP) training. paragraphs: Bayesian neural networks are often viewed as a robust alternative to standard training, including when inputs differ from those seen during training. This paper examines a surprising failure: networks using high-fidelity approximate inference through full-batch Hamiltonian Monte Carlo generalize poorly under covariate shift, even falling behind classical estimation in the reported setting.

The explanation concerns Bayesian model averaging itself. In particular, linear dependencies among input features can prevent the posterior from concentrating. Averaging predictions under that posterior can then become problematic when the input distribution changes. The paper identifies this mechanism as especially relevant to the observed failures, rather than claiming that Bayesian averaging always fails under shift.

The authors also explain why many approximate inference procedures and maximum a-posteriori training avoid the same issue. They propose new priors that improve Bayesian networks' robustness to many sources of covariate shift. The findings show that inference fidelity alone does not ensure robustness: the interaction between input dependencies, posterior behavior, and prior choice can matter substantially.
summary.tldr: Bayesian model averaging can fail under covariate shift when feature dependencies prevent posterior concentration, and alternative priors can improve robustness.

title: Dangers of Bayesian Model Averaging under Covariate Shift

abstract: Increasingly, copious amounts of consumer data are used to learn high-revenue mechanisms via machine learning. Existing research on mechanism design via machine learning assumes that there is a distribution over the buyers' values for the items for sale and that the learning algorithm's input is a training set sampled from this distribution. This setup makes the strong assumption that no noise is introduced during data collection. In order to help place mechanism design via machine learning on firm foundations, we investigate the extent to which this learning process is robust to noise. Optimizing revenue using noisy data is challenging because revenue functions are extremely volatile: an infinitesimal change in the buyers' values can cause a steep drop in revenue. Nonetheless, we provide guarantees when arbitrarily correlated noise is added to the training set; we only require that the noise has bounded magnitude or is sub-Gaussian. We conclude with an application of our guarantees to multi-task mechanism design, where there are multiple distributions over buyers' values and the goal is to learn a high-revenue mechanism per distribution. To our knowledge, we are the first to study mechanism design via machine learning with noisy data as well as multi-task mechanism design.

paragraphs: Learning a revenue-maximizing sales mechanism usually starts with examples of buyers' values. Existing formulations assume those examples are sampled without collection noise. This paper asks how robust the learning process remains when the training values are corrupted, addressing a gap between that clean-data setup and learning from noisy observations.

The challenge is that revenue can change abruptly: even a tiny alteration in buyers' values can cause a large revenue decrease. The authors nevertheless establish guarantees allowing noise to be arbitrarily correlated. The noise must have bounded magnitude or be sub-Gaussian, so the result permits dependence while retaining a restriction on the size or tail behavior of disturbances.

The paper also applies these guarantees to multi-task mechanism design. In that setting, several distributions describe buyers' values, and the objective is to learn a high-revenue mechanism for each distribution. The contribution provides theoretical support for revenue learning with noisy data and extends that support to multiple related learning objectives, despite the underlying sensitivity of revenue functions.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes revenue-learning guarantees under arbitrarily correlated noise with bounded magnitude or sub-Gaussian tails, including a multi-task application.

title: Revenue maximization via machine learning with noisy data

abstract: We give a fast algorithm to compose privacy guarantees of differentially private (DP) algorithms to arbitrary accuracy. Our method is based on the notion of privacy loss random variables to quantify the privacy loss of DP algorithms. The running time and memory needed for our algorithm to approximate the privacy curve of a DP algorithm composed with itself $k$ times is $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{k})$. This improves over the best prior method by Koskela et al. (2020) which requires $\tilde{\Omega}(k^{1.5})$ running time. We demonstrate the utility of our algorithm by accurately computing the privacy loss of DP-SGD algorithm of Abadi et al. (2016) and showing that our algorithm speeds up the privacy computations by a few orders of magnitude compared to prior work, while maintaining similar accuracy.

paragraphs: A privacy guarantee for one algorithmic operation does not by itself describe the privacy cost of repeating that operation many times. This paper develops a fast numerical method for composing differential-privacy guarantees to arbitrary accuracy. The task is to calculate the combined privacy curve efficiently as the number of repetitions grows.

The method represents privacy loss through random variables. For an algorithm composed with itself k times, its running time and memory scale as roughly the square root of k, with logarithmic factors suppressed. The cited prior method requires running time growing at least roughly as k to the three-halves power, again ignoring logarithmic factors.

The authors demonstrate the method by calculating privacy loss for differentially private stochastic gradient descent. In that evaluation, privacy computations become a few orders of magnitude faster while retaining similar accuracy. The contribution concerns the cost of accounting for privacy: more efficient numerical composition makes it less expensive to determine the guarantee associated with repeated private computations.
summary.tldr: A numerical privacy accountant composes repeated differential-privacy guarantees with substantially improved runtime and memory scaling.

title: Numerical Composition of Differential Privacy

abstract: This paper discusses model estimation in offline model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL), which is important for subsequent policy improvement using an estimated model. From the viewpoint of covariate shift, a natural idea is model estimation weighted by the ratio of the state-action distributions of offline data and real future data. However, estimating such a natural weight is one of the main challenges for off-policy evaluation, which is not easy to use. As an artificial alternative, this paper considers weighting with the state-action distribution ratio of offline data and simulated future data, which can be estimated relatively easily by standard density ratio estimation techniques for supervised learning. Based on the artificial weight, this paper defines a loss function for offline MBRL and presents an algorithm to optimize it. Weighting with the artificial weight is justified as evaluating an upper bound of the policy evaluation error. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of weighting with the artificial weight.

paragraphs: Offline model-based reinforcement learning estimates an environment model from existing data, then uses it to improve a policy. A difficulty is that future state-action visits may differ from those represented in the dataset. Weighting model estimation to account for this shift is natural, but weights involving real future visits are hard to estimate.

The paper substitutes a more accessible distribution: future state-action visits simulated using the model. It constructs artificial weights from the ratio involving offline and simulated state-action distributions. Standard density-ratio estimation methods from supervised learning can estimate these weights relatively easily, making the correction more usable.

Using the artificial weights, the authors define a loss for offline model-based reinforcement learning and provide an optimization algorithm. The theoretical justification connects the weighted objective to an upper bound on policy-evaluation error. Numerical experiments support the effectiveness of this weighting approach. The contribution is a tractable surrogate correction with an error-bound rationale for improving model estimation from fixed data.
summary.tldr: Weights based on simulated future state-action distributions provide a tractable, theoretically justified objective for offline model estimation.

title: Weighted model estimation for offline model-based reinforcement learning

abstract: Graph Neural Networks~(GNNs) are a powerful class of architectures for solving learning problems on graphs. While many variants of GNNs have been proposed in the literature and have achieved strong empirical performance, their theoretical properties are less well understood. In this work we study the convergence properties of the gradient descent algorithm when used to train GNNs. In particular, we consider the realizable setting where the data is generated from a network with unknown weights and our goal is to study conditions under which gradient descent on a GNN architecture can recover near optimal solutions. While such analysis has been performed in recent years for other architectures such as fully connected feed-forward networks, the message passing nature of the updates in a GNN poses a new challenge in understanding the nature of the gradient descent updates. We take a step towards overcoming this by proving that for the case of deep linear GNNs gradient descent provably recovers solutions up to error $\epsilon$ in $O(\text{log}(1/\epsilon))$ iterations, under natural assumptions on the data distribution. Furthermore, for the case of one-round GNNs with ReLU activations, we show that gradient descent provably recovers solutions up to error $\epsilon$ in $O(\frac{1}{\epsilon^2} \log(\frac{1}{\epsilon}))$ iterations.

paragraphs: This paper studies when gradient descent can successfully train a graph neural network. Its setting is realizable: the data comes from a network with unknown weights, and training aims to recover a solution with nearly optimal error. The central difficulty is that a graph network passes information between connected nodes, making its training dynamics harder to analyze than those of a standard feed-forward network.

The authors establish convergence results for two architectures. For deep linear graph networks, under assumptions on the data distribution, reaching error ε requires O(log(1/ε)) iterations. For graph networks with one round of message passing and ReLU activations, they prove a bound of O((1/ε²) log(1/ε)) iterations.

These results provide mathematical support for successful optimization in the specific settings analyzed. They also distinguish how the proven iteration requirements depend on the requested accuracy for the two architectures. The contribution is a step toward understanding graph-network training through its message-passing structure, with guarantees tied to the stated model and data conditions.
summary.tldr: The paper proves gradient-descent convergence rates for deep linear and one-round ReLU graph networks in a realizable setting.

title: A Convergence Analysis of Gradient Descent on Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Sortition is an age-old democratic paradigm, widely manifested today through the random selection of citizens' assemblies. Recently-deployed algorithms select assemblies \textit{maximally fairly}, meaning that subject to demographic quotas, they give all potential participants as equal a chance as possible of being chosen. While these fairness gains can bolster the legitimacy of citizens' assemblies and facilitate their uptake, existing algorithms remain limited by their lack of transparency. To overcome this hurdle, in this work we focus on panel selection by uniform lottery, which is easy to realize in an observable way. By this approach, the final assembly is selected by uniformly sampling some pre-selected set of $m$ possible assemblies.We provide theoretical guarantees on the fairness attainable via this type of uniform lottery, as compared to the existing maximally fair but opaque algorithms, for two different fairness objectives. We complement these results with experiments on real-world instances that demonstrate the viability of the uniform lottery approach as a method of selecting assemblies both fairly and transparently.

paragraphs: Citizens’ assemblies often select participants randomly while meeting demographic quotas. Fair selection tries to make each eligible person’s chance of participation as equal as those quotas allow. Existing algorithms can optimize this goal, but their complexity makes the selection process harder for the public to observe and understand.

The paper investigates a more transparent mechanism: first prepare a collection of m possible assemblies, then choose one through a uniform lottery. Each assembly in that collection has the same chance of winning. Individual participation chances depend on how often each person appears across the collection, so choosing the collection is central to achieving fairness.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees comparing the fairness available through this lottery with that of existing maximally fair algorithms. They study two fairness objectives, making the comparison broader than a single definition of fair participation. Experiments on real-world instances demonstrate the approach’s viability. The contribution is a way to connect measurable fairness with a final selection step that can be carried out observably.
summary.tldr: Uniform lotteries over carefully selected possible assemblies offer a transparent selection process with theoretical fairness guarantees and practical support.

title: Fair Sortition Made Transparent

abstract: In this work we seek to bridge the concepts of topographic organization and equivariance in neural networks. To accomplish this, we introduce the Topographic VAE: a novel method for efficiently training deep generative models with topographically organized latent variables. We show that such a model indeed learns to organize its activations according to salient characteristics such as digit class, width, and style on MNIST. Furthermore, through topographic organization over time (i.e. temporal coherence), we demonstrate how predefined latent space transformation operators can be encouraged for observed transformed input sequences -- a primitive form of unsupervised learned equivariance. We demonstrate that this model successfully learns sets of approximately equivariant features (i.e. "capsules") directly from sequences and achieves higher likelihood on correspondingly transforming test sequences. Equivariance is verified quantitatively by measuring the approximate commutativity of the inference network and the sequence transformations. Finally, we demonstrate approximate equivariance to complex transformations, expanding upon the capabilities of existing group equivariant neural networks.

We show that such a model indeed learns to organize its activations according to salient characteristics such as digit class, width, and style on MNIST. Furthermore, through topographic organization over time (i.e. temporal coherence), we demonstrate how predefined latent space transformation operators can be encouraged for observed transformed input sequences -- a primitive form of unsupervised learned equivariance. We demonstrate that this model successfully learns sets of approximately equivariant features (i.e. "capsules") directly from sequences and achieves higher likelihood on correspondingly transforming test sequences. Equivariance is verified quantitatively by measuring the approximate commutativity of the inference network and the sequence transformations. paragraphs: The Topographic VAE connects organized latent representations with equivariance: representations changing predictably when inputs transform. It introduces a way to train deep generative models whose latent variables have a topographic organization. On MNIST, the model organizes activations around salient properties including digit class, width, and style.

The authors extend this organization over time using temporal coherence. For sequences of transformed inputs, this encourages predefined transformation operators in latent space. The resulting feature groups, called capsules, learn approximately equivariant behavior directly from sequences. The claim is about encouraged, approximate correspondence between input and representation transformations.

The model achieves higher likelihood on test sequences undergoing corresponding transformations. The authors also measure equivariance by checking approximate commutativity: whether transforming an input and then encoding it agrees with the corresponding transformation of its encoding. Demonstrations include complex transformations, expanding the capabilities described for existing group-equivariant networks. The findings show how temporal organization can help a generative model learn structured responses to transformations without supervised equivariance targets.
summary.tldr: Topographic VAEs use spatial and temporal latent organization to learn feature groups that transform approximately equivariantly.

title: Topographic VAEs learn Equivariant Capsules

abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms, which learn a dynamics model from logged experience and perform conservative planning under the learned model, have emerged as a promising paradigm for offline reinforcement learning (offline RL). However, practical variants of such model-based algorithms rely on explicit uncertainty quantification for incorporating conservatism. Uncertainty estimation with complex models, such as deep neural networks, can be difficult and unreliable. We empirically find that uncertainty estimation is not accurate and leads to poor performance in certain scenarios in offline model-based RL. We overcome this limitation by developing a new model-based offline RL algorithm, COMBO, that trains a value function using both the offline dataset and data generated using rollouts under the model while also additionally regularizing the value function on out-of-support state-action tuples generated via model rollouts. This results in a conservative estimate of the value function for out-of-support state-action tuples, without requiring explicit uncertainty estimation. Theoretically, we show that COMBO satisfies a policy improvement guarantee in the offline setting. Through extensive experiments, we find that COMBO attains greater performance compared to prior offline RL on problems that demand generalization to related but previously unseen tasks, and also consistently matches or outperforms prior offline RL methods on widely studied offline RL benchmarks, including image-based tasks.
originalAbstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms, which learn a dynamics model from logged experience and perform conservative planning under the learned model, have emerged as a promising paradigm for offline reinforcement learning (offline RL). However, practical variants of such model-based algorithms rely on explicit uncertainty quantification for incorporating conservatism. Uncertainty estimation with complex models, such as deep neural networks, can be difficult and unreliable. We empirically find that uncertainty estimation is not accurate and leads to poor performance in certain scenarios in offline model-based RL. We overcome this limitation by developing a new model-based offline RL algorithm, COMBO, that trains a value function using both the offline dataset and data generated using rollouts under the model while also additionally regularizing the value function on out-of-support state-action tuples generated via model rollouts. This results in a conservative estimate of the value function for out-of-support state-action tuples, without requiring explicit uncertainty estimation. Theoretically, we show that COMBO satisfies a policy improvement guarantee in the offline setting. Through extensive experiments, we find that COMBO attains greater performance compared to prior offline RL on problems that demand generalization to related but previously unseen tasks, and also consistently matches or outperforms prior offline RL methods on widely studied offline RL benchmarks, including image-based tasks.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must learn decisions from logged experience. Model-based approaches build a dynamics model from those records and use it to plan conservatively. Many practical methods rely on estimating the model's uncertainty, but this paper finds empirically that inaccurate uncertainty estimates can cause poor performance in some settings.

COMBO instead learns a value function from both the recorded dataset and trajectories generated by the learned model. It additionally regularizes values for model-generated state-action combinations outside the dataset's support. This produces conservative value estimates for those combinations without requiring an explicit uncertainty estimate. The method therefore places caution directly into value learning while still using model rollouts to expand training experience.

The authors establish a theoretical policy-improvement guarantee in the offline setting. Their experiments find stronger performance than prior offline methods on problems requiring transfer to related, previously unseen tasks. COMBO also matches or exceeds prior methods across the studied offline benchmarks, including image-based tasks. Together, these findings support conservative value regularization as a useful alternative to explicit uncertainty estimation.
summary.tldr: COMBO learns conservative values from logged and model-generated experience, enabling offline policy optimization without explicit uncertainty estimation.

title: COMBO: Conservative Offline Model-Based Policy Optimization

abstract: Existing neural information retrieval (IR) models have often been studied in homogeneous and narrow settings, which has considerably limited insights into their out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization capabilities. To address this, and to facilitate researchers to broadly evaluate the effectiveness of their models, we introduce Benchmarking-IR (BEIR), a robust and heterogeneous evaluation benchmark for information retrieval. We leverage a careful selection of 18 publicly available datasets from diverse text retrieval tasks and domains and evaluate 10 state-of-the-art retrieval systems including lexical, sparse, dense, late-interaction, and re-ranking architectures on the BEIR benchmark. Our results show BM25 is a robust baseline and re-ranking and late-interaction based models on average achieve the best zero-shot performances, however, at high computational costs. In contrast, dense and sparse-retrieval models are computationally more efficient but often underperform other approaches, highlighting the considerable room for improvement in their generalization capabilities. We hope this framework allows us to better evaluate and understand existing retrieval systems and contributes to accelerating progress towards more robust and generalizable systems in the future. BEIR is publicly available at https://github.com/UKPLab/beir.

paragraphs: BEIR evaluates whether text retrieval systems work beyond the narrow settings in which they are commonly studied. It combines 18 public datasets covering different tasks and domains. This diversity makes generalization a central part of evaluation, allowing researchers to examine retrieval effectiveness across a broader range of conditions.

The authors compare 10 systems representing lexical, sparse, dense, late-interaction, and re-ranking approaches. Their results identify BM25 as a robust baseline. Re-ranking and late-interaction methods achieve the strongest zero-shot results on average, but require substantial computation. The average qualification matters: the finding describes performance across the benchmark rather than establishing a winner for every individual task.

Dense and sparse retrieval approaches are more computationally efficient in these comparisons, yet often perform worse than other approaches. This exposes a trade-off between retrieval quality and computational cost, along with room to improve generalization. BEIR supplies a shared framework for examining that trade-off across varied retrieval settings.
summary.tldr: BEIR compares retrieval systems across 18 diverse datasets, revealing generalization gaps and trade-offs between zero-shot quality and computation.

title: BEIR: A Heterogeneous Benchmark for Zero-shot Evaluation of Information Retrieval Models

abstract: Popular object detection models generate bounding boxes in a different way than we humans. As an example, modern detectors yield object box either upon the regression of its center and width/height (center-guided detector), or by grouping paired estimated corners (corner-guided detector). However, that is not the pattern we manually label an object due to high degrees of freedom in searching centers or low efficiency of grouping corners. Empirically, humans run two steps to locate an object bounding box manually: 1) click the mouse at the top-left corner of object, and then drag the mouse to the bottom-right corner; 2) refine the corner positions to make the bounding box more precisely, if necessary. Inspired by this manual labeling process, we propose a novel human-like detector, termed as HumanLiker, which is devised as a two-stage end-to-end detector to simulate the two aforementioned. Like we humans in manual labeling, HumanLiker can effectively avert both the thorny center searching and heuristic corner grouping. Different from the mainstream detector branches, i.e., the center/corner-guided methods, the HumanLiker provides a new paradigm which integrates the advantages of both branches to balance the detection efficiency and bounding box quality. On MS-COCO test-dev set, HumanLiker can achieve 50.2%/51.6% and 53.8%/55.6% in term of AP with ResNeXt-101 and SwinTransformer backbones in single/multi-scale testing, outperforming current popular center/corner-guided baselines (e.g., DETR/CornerNet) by a large margin, with much less training epochs and higher inference FPS. Code will be available soon.
