paragraphs: HumanLiker takes inspiration from how people draw bounding boxes around objects. A person typically starts at the top-left corner, drags to the bottom-right corner, and then adjusts the box if needed. The paper turns this sequence into a two-stage detector trained end to end, using the manual workflow as an organizing principle.

The motivation is that common detector designs approach boxes differently. Some estimate a centre together with width and height, while others predict corners and then group them. HumanLiker aims to avoid the difficult centre search and heuristic corner pairing associated with those approaches. Its two-stage structure instead combines initial localization with refinement, balancing detection efficiency and box quality.

On MS-COCO test-dev, the authors report higher average precision than popular centre- and corner-guided baselines, including DETR and CornerNet, alongside fewer training epochs and faster inference. Results are reported with both ResNeXt-101 and SwinTransformer backbones under single- and multi-scale testing. The findings support the human-inspired localization workflow as an effective detector design in the evaluated configurations.
summary.tldr: HumanLiker models box drawing and refinement as a two-stage detector, reporting stronger accuracy and efficiency than popular comparison methods.

title: HumanLiker: A Human-like Object Detector to Model the Manual Labeling Process

abstract: We formulate the first differentiable analog quantum computing framework with specific parameterization design at the analog signal (pulse) level to better exploit near-term quantum devices via variational methods. We further propose a scalable approach to estimate the gradients of quantum dynamics using a forward pass with Monte Carlo sampling, which leads to a quantum stochastic gradient descent algorithm for scalable gradient-based training in our framework. Applying our framework to quantum optimization and control, we observe a significant advantage of differentiable analog quantum computing against SOTAs based on parameterized digital quantum circuits by {\em orders of magnitude}.

We further propose a scalable approach to estimate the gradients of quantum dynamics using a forward pass with Monte Carlo sampling, which leads to a quantum stochastic gradient descent algorithm for scalable gradient-based training in our framework. Applying our framework to quantum optimization and control, we observe a significant advantage of differentiable analog quantum computing against SOTAs based on parameterized digital quantum circuits by {\em orders of magnitude}.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a differentiable framework for analog quantum computing. The adjustable parameters are defined at the level of analog control signals, or pulses. The aim is to make variational methods better exploit near-term quantum devices by optimizing this signal-level description of the computation.

A central technical contribution concerns obtaining gradients of quantum dynamics. The authors propose a scalable estimator that uses a forward pass together with Monte Carlo sampling. Those estimated gradients lead to a quantum stochastic gradient descent algorithm for training the framework. This connects the choice of pulse parameters with a procedure for updating them, making gradient-based optimization part of the proposed analog computing approach.

The authors apply the framework to quantum optimization and control and report an advantage of orders of magnitude over state-of-the-art approaches based on parameterized digital quantum circuits. This is an observed result for the studied applications. The contribution combines pulse-level parameterization with a scalable gradient estimation method, providing both a way to represent the computation and a way to train it.
summary.tldr: A pulse-level analog quantum computing framework uses sampled gradient estimates and reports orders-of-magnitude advantages in studied optimization and control applications.

title: Differentiable Analog Quantum Computing for Optimization and Control

abstract: Recent advances in contrastive representation learning over paired image-text data have led to models such as CLIP that achieve state-of-the-art performance for zero-shot classification and distributional robustness. Such models typically require joint reasoning in the image and text representation spaces for downstream inference tasks. Contrary to prior beliefs, we demonstrate that the image and text representations learned via a standard contrastive objective are not interchangeable and can lead to inconsistent downstream predictions. To mitigate this issue, we formalize consistency and propose CyCLIP, a framework for contrastive representation learning that explicitly optimizes for the learned representations to be geometrically consistent in the image and text space. In particular, we show that consistent representations can be learned by explicitly symmetrizing (a) the similarity between the two mismatched image-text pairs (cross-modal consistency); and (b) the similarity between the image-image pair and the text-text pair (in-modal consistency). Empirically, we show that the improved consistency in CyCLIP translates to significant gains over CLIP, with gains ranging from 10%-24% for zero-shot classification on standard benchmarks (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet1K) and 10%-27% for robustness to various natural distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Models such as CLIP learn representations from paired images and text so that the two forms of information can support shared predictions. This paper shows that standard contrastive training does not make those representations interchangeable. Reasoning through the image space or the text space can produce inconsistent downstream predictions.

CyCLIP addresses this mismatch by explicitly encouraging geometric consistency. One constraint symmetrizes similarities between mismatched image-text pairs. Another aligns the similarity between two images with the similarity between their corresponding texts. Together, these constraints make the relationships within and across the two representation spaces more consistent, going beyond simply bringing matched image-text examples together.

The experiments report gains over CLIP of 10%–24% for zero-shot classification on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet1K, and 10%–27% for robustness under natural distribution shifts. These empirical improvements connect the proposed consistency objective to downstream performance. The paper's broader point is that the geometry linking modalities deserves explicit attention when predictions depend on reasoning across both image and text representations.
summary.tldr: CyCLIP explicitly aligns image-text representation geometry, improving zero-shot classification and robustness in the reported experiments.

title: CyCLIP: Cyclic Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining

abstract: Neural networks (NNs) struggle to efficiently solve certain problems, such as learning parities, even when there are simple learning algorithms for those problems. Can NNs discover learning algorithms on their own? We exhibit a NN architecture that, in polynomial time, learns as well as any efficient learning algorithm describable by a constant-sized program. For example, on parity problems, the NN learns as well as Gaussian elimination, an efficient algorithm that can be succinctly described. Our architecture combines both recurrent weight sharing between layers and convolutional weight sharing to reduce the number of parameters down to a constant, even though the network itself may have trillions of nodes. While in practice the constants in our analysis are too large to be directly meaningful, our work suggests that the synergy of Recurrent and Convolutional NNs (RCNNs) may be more natural and powerful than either alone, particularly for concisely parameterizing discrete algorithms.

paragraphs: Some problems have simple, efficient learning algorithms but remain difficult for neural networks to learn efficiently. The paper asks whether a network can discover such algorithms itself. It provides a theoretical architecture that learns in polynomial time as well as any efficient learning algorithm expressible by a constant-sized program.

The construction combines recurrent weight sharing across layers with convolutional weight sharing. Together, these mechanisms keep the number of parameters constant even when the network has an enormous number of nodes. Parity learning illustrates the result: the network can learn as well as Gaussian elimination, an efficient algorithm with a concise description.

The distinction between parameter count and overall computational scale is central to interpreting the finding. The architecture can contain trillions of nodes, and the authors explicitly state that the constants in their analysis are too large for direct practical significance. The result instead suggests a theoretical advantage of combining recurrence and convolution when representing discrete learning algorithms concisely; it does not establish a ready-to-use practical learner.
summary.tldr: A theoretical recurrent-convolutional architecture can match succinct efficient learning algorithms, although its constants make the construction impractical.

title: Recurrent Convolutional Neural Networks Learn Succinct Learning Algorithms

abstract: We propose a general purpose Bayesian inference algorithm for expensive likelihoods, replacing the stochastic term in the Langevin equation with a deterministic density gradient term. The particle density is evaluated from the current particle positions using a Normalizing Flow (NF), which is differentiable and has good generalization properties in high dimensions. We take advantage of NF preconditioning and NF based Metropolis-Hastings updates for a faster convergence. We show on various examples that the method is competitive against state of the art sampling methods.

We take advantage of NF preconditioning and NF based Metropolis-Hastings updates for a faster convergence. We show on various examples that the method is competitive against state of the art sampling methods.

paragraphs: This paper develops a general-purpose Bayesian inference algorithm for situations where likelihood evaluations are expensive. Its starting point is Langevin sampling, which includes a stochastic term in its update equation. The proposed method replaces that term with a deterministic term based on a density gradient, changing how the collection of sampling particles moves.

To obtain that gradient, the method estimates the particle density from the particles’ current positions using a normalizing flow. The flow supplies a differentiable density model, allowing density information to guide the updates. The authors emphasize the model’s generalization properties in high dimensions, where representing the evolving particle distribution is an important part of the approach.

The normalizing flow serves additional roles through preconditioning and flow-based Metropolis–Hastings updates, which the authors use to accelerate convergence. Across several examples, the complete method is competitive with state-of-the-art sampling methods. The stated result supports combining learned density information with sampling updates for expensive inference problems; it is an empirical competitiveness claim across those examples.
summary.tldr: A normalizing flow supplies density gradients and sampling updates for a Bayesian inference method competitive on several examples.

title: Deterministic Langevin Monte Carlo with Normalizing Flows for Bayesian Inference

abstract: Most existing 3D point cloud object detection approaches heavily rely on large amounts of labeled training data. However, the labeling process is costly and time-consuming. This paper considers few-shot 3D point cloud object detection, where only a few annotated samples of novel classes are needed with abundant samples of base classes. To this end, we propose Prototypical VoteNet to recognize and localize novel instances, which incorporates two new modules: Prototypical Vote Module (PVM) and Prototypical Head Module (PHM). Specifically, as the 3D basic geometric structures can be shared among categories, PVM is designed to leverage class-agnostic geometric prototypes, which are learned from base classes, to refine local features of novel categories. Then PHM is proposed to utilize class prototypes to enhance the global feature of each object, facilitating subsequent object localization and classification, which is trained by the episodic training strategy. To evaluate the model in this new setting, we contribute two new benchmark datasets, FS-ScanNet and FS-SUNRGBD. We conduct extensive experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of Prototypical VoteNet, and our proposed method shows significant and consistent improvements compared to baselines on two benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Detecting objects in 3D point clouds usually requires extensive annotation. This paper studies a setting with plentiful labeled examples for base classes but only a few for novel classes. The challenge is both to recognize new object categories and to locate their instances using that limited additional supervision.

Prototypical VoteNet addresses the problem with two modules. The Prototypical Vote Module learns class-independent geometric prototypes from base classes and uses them to refine local features of novel objects. Its motivation is that basic 3D structures can be shared across categories. The Prototypical Head Module uses class prototypes to strengthen each object’s overall representation for localization and classification.

The head module is trained through an episodic strategy. To evaluate the few-shot detection setting, the authors introduce FS-ScanNet and FS-SUNRGBD benchmarks. Their experiments show significant, consistent improvements over baselines on both datasets. The results support combining transferable local geometry with class-level object representations, while retaining the important setup assumption that abundant base-class training data is available.
summary.tldr: Prototypical VoteNet transfers geometric and class prototypes to detect novel 3D objects from only a few annotated examples.

title: Prototypical VoteNet for Few-Shot 3D Point Cloud Object Detection

abstract: The Dark Web represents a hotbed for illicit activity, where users communicate on different market forums in order to exchange goods and services. Law enforcement agencies benefit from forensic tools that perform authorship analysis, in order to identify and profile users based on their textual content. However, authorship analysis has been traditionally studied using corpora featuring literary texts such as fragments from novels or fan fiction, which may not be suitable in a cybercrime context. Moreover, the few works that employ authorship analysis tools for cybercrime prevention usually employ ad-hoc experimental setups and datasets. To address these issues, we release VeriDark: a benchmark comprised of three large scale authorship verification datasets and one authorship identification dataset obtained from user activity from either Dark Web related Reddit communities or popular illicit Dark Web market forums. We evaluate competitive NLP baselines on the three datasets and perform an analysis of the predictions to better understand the limitations of such approaches. We make the datasets and baselines publicly available at https://github.com/bit-ml/VeriDark .

paragraphs: Authorship analysis examines who wrote a text and can support forensic investigation of online activity. However, much previous research used literary material such as novels or fan fiction. VeriDark addresses the concern that such data may not represent the writing encountered in cybercrime investigations, where prior studies have also relied on ad hoc datasets and evaluation setups.

The benchmark contains three large-scale authorship-verification datasets and one authorship-identification dataset. Verification concerns whether texts share an author, while identification concerns assigning authorship. The source material comes from user activity in Dark Web-related Reddit communities or popular illicit Dark Web market forums, bringing the benchmark closer to the stated application context.

The authors evaluate competitive natural-language-processing baselines on the three verification datasets and analyze their predictions to better understand the approaches' limitations. Both datasets and baselines are publicly released. The main contribution is a shared evaluation resource for studying authorship analysis on relevant online writing, accompanied by baseline results and analysis that future methods can build upon.
summary.tldr: VeriDark provides public authorship-analysis datasets and baselines drawn from Dark Web forums and related Reddit communities.

title: VeriDark: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Authorship Verification on the Dark Web

abstract: Score-based generative models are shown to achieve remarkable empirical performances in various applications such as image generation and audio synthesis. However, a theoretical understanding of score-based diffusion models is still incomplete. Recently, Song et al. showed that the training objective of score-based generative models is equivalent to minimizing the Kullback-Leibler divergence of the generated distribution from the data distribution. In this work, we show that score-based models also minimize the Wasserstein distance between them. Specifically, we prove that the Wasserstein distance is upper bounded by the square root of the objective function up to multiplicative constants and a fixed constant offset. Our proof is based on a novel application of the theory of optimal transport, which can be of independent interest to the society. Our numerical experiments support our findings. By analyzing our upper bounds, we provide a few techniques to obtain tighter upper bounds.

paragraphs: Score-based generative models perform strongly in applications such as image generation and audio synthesis, but the meaning of their training objective is still being developed theoretically. This paper connects that objective to Wasserstein distance, a measure of discrepancy between the generated distribution and the data distribution.

The precise result is an upper bound: Wasserstein distance is bounded by a constant multiple of the square root of the training objective, plus a fixed offset. Lowering the objective therefore reduces the objective-dependent part of this bound. The fixed offset matters because the theorem does not simply equate the objective with Wasserstein distance or say that zero objective necessarily makes the distance zero.

The proof uses optimal-transport theory, adding another interpretation alongside the previously established connection to Kullback-Leibler divergence. Numerical experiments support the findings. By examining the derived bounds, the authors also propose techniques for tightening them. The contribution gives a mathematical link between score-based training and distributional closeness while retaining the constants and offset that qualify that link.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds Wasserstein distance by a scaled square root of the score-model objective plus a fixed offset.

title: Score-based Generative Modeling Secretly Minimizes the Wasserstein Distance

abstract: Contrastive learning is a highly effective method for learning representations from unlabeled data. Recent works show that contrastive representations can transfer across domains, leading to simple state-of-the-art algorithms for unsupervised domain adaptation. In particular, a linear classifier trained to separate the representations on the source domain can also predict classes on the target domain accurately, even though the representations of the two domains are far from each other. We refer to this phenomenon as linear transferability. This paper analyzes when and why contrastive representations exhibit linear transferability in a general unsupervised domain adaptation setting. We prove that linear transferability can occur when data from the same class in different domains (e.g., photo dogs and cartoon dogs) are more related with each other than data from different classes in different domains (e.g., photo dogs and cartoon cats) are. Our analyses are in a realistic regime where the source and target domains can have unbounded density ratios and be weakly related, and they have distant representations across domains.

In particular, a linear classifier trained to separate the representations on the source domain can also predict classes on the target domain accurately, even though the representations of the two domains are far from each other. We refer to this phenomenon as linear transferability. This paper analyzes when and why contrastive representations exhibit linear transferability in a general unsupervised domain adaptation setting. We prove that linear transferability can occur when data from the same class in different domains (e.g., photo dogs and cartoon dogs) are more related with each other than data from different classes in different domains (e.g., photo dogs and cartoon cats) are. Our analyses are in a realistic regime where the source and target domains can have unbounded density ratios and be weakly related, and they have distant representations across domains.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning can produce representations that support classification across domains. A linear classifier trained on one domain may also classify another accurately, even when the two domains occupy distant regions of the representation space. The paper calls this linear transferability and investigates why it can happen in unsupervised domain adaptation.

The analysis focuses on how examples relate across domains. The authors prove that transferability can occur when examples belonging to the same class across domains are more related than examples belonging to different classes across domains. For instance, the relevant relationship is whether dogs in photographs connect more strongly to cartoon dogs than to cartoon cats.

The result does not require the domains to have nearby representations. The analysis permits weak relationships and unbounded density ratios between source and target data. This matters because successful transfer can depend on the organization of class relationships even when domain differences remain pronounced. The stated condition explains a route to transferability; it is not presented as a guarantee for every contrastively learned representation.
summary.tldr: Contrastive representations can support linear transfer across distant domains when cross-domain relationships favor matching classes.

title: Beyond Separability: Analyzing the Linear Transferability of Contrastive Representations to Related Subpopulations

abstract: AI-empowered drug recommendation has become an important task in healthcare research areas, which offers an additional perspective to assist human doctors with more accurate and more efficient drug prescriptions. Generally, drug recommendation is based on patients' diagnosis results in the electronic health records. We assume that there are three key factors to be addressed in drug recommendation: 1) elimination of recommendation bias due to limitations of observable information, 2) better utilization of historical health condition and 3) coordination of multiple drugs to control safety. To this end, we propose DrugRec, a causal inference based drug recommendation model. The causal graphical model can identify and deconfound the recommendation bias with front-door adjustment. Meanwhile, we model the multi-visit in the causal graph to characterize a patient's historical health conditions. Comprehensive experiment results show that our proposed model achieves state-of-the-art performance on the widely used datasets MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV, demonstrating the effectiveness and safety of our method.

title: Debiased, Longitudinal and Coordinated Drug Recommendation through Multi-Visit Clinic Records

abstract: As in-the-wild data are increasingly involved in the training stage, machine learning applications become more susceptible to data poisoning attacks. Such attacks typically lead to test-time accuracy degradation or controlled misprediction. In this paper, we investigate the third type of exploitation of data poisoning - increasing the risks of privacy leakage of benign training samples. To this end, we demonstrate a set of data poisoning attacks to amplify the membership exposure of the targeted class. We first propose a generic dirty-label attack for supervised classification algorithms. We then propose an optimization-based clean-label attack in the transfer learning scenario, whereby the poisoning samples are correctly labeled and look "natural" to evade human moderation. We extensively evaluate our attacks on computer vision benchmarks. Our results show that the proposed attacks can substantially increase the membership inference precision with minimum overall test-time model performance degradation. To mitigate the potential negative impacts of our attacks, we also investigate feasible countermeasures.

paragraphs: Data poisoning is usually discussed as a way to damage a model's accuracy or induce particular wrong predictions. This paper investigates a different consequence: making it easier to determine whether legitimate examples were part of the training data. The attacks target membership exposure for a chosen class, linking manipulation of training data to privacy risks for otherwise benign samples.

The authors introduce two forms of poisoning. One is a generic dirty-label attack for supervised classification, involving incorrectly labeled poison examples. The other is an optimization-based clean-label attack in a transfer-learning setting. In the latter, the injected examples retain correct labels and appear natural, with the aim of avoiding detection through human moderation.

Evaluations on computer vision benchmarks show substantial increases in membership-inference precision with minimal degradation of overall test performance. This means a model can continue to appear effective on its main prediction task while becoming more revealing about its training data. The paper also investigates feasible countermeasures, treating privacy exposure as a poisoning outcome that merits attention alongside predictive accuracy.
summary.tldr: Data poisoning can substantially increase training-data membership exposure while causing little overall loss of prediction performance.

title: Amplifying Membership Exposure via Data Poisoning

abstract: Humans are remarkably flexible in understanding viewpoint changes due to visual cortex supporting the perception of 3D structure. In contrast, most of the computer vision models that learn visual representation from a pool of 2D images often fail to generalize over novel camera viewpoints. Recently, the vision architectures have shifted towards convolution-free architectures, visual Transformers, which operate on tokens derived from image patches. However, these Transformers do not perform explicit operations to learn viewpoint-agnostic representation for visual understanding. To this end, we propose a 3D Token Representation Layer (3DTRL) that estimates the 3D positional information of the visual tokens and leverages it for learning viewpoint-agnostic representations. The key elements of 3DTRL include a pseudo-depth estimator and a learned camera matrix to impose geometric transformations on the tokens, trained in an unsupervised fashion. These enable 3DTRL to recover the 3D positional information of the tokens from 2D patches. In practice, 3DTRL is easily plugged-in into a Transformer. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of 3DTRL in many vision tasks including image classification, multi-view video alignment, and action recognition. The models with 3DTRL outperform their backbone Transformers in all the tasks with minimal added computation. Our code is available at https://github.com/elicassion/3DTRL.

This paper introduces a layer intended to make viewpoint changes more directly accessible to the representation.

The 3D Token Representation Layer, or 3DTRL, estimates tokens' 3D positions using a pseudo-depth estimator and a learned camera matrix. Trained without supervision for this process, these components impose geometric transformations on tokens recovered from 2D patches. The resulting positional information supports learning representations that are less tied to a particular viewpoint.

The layer can be inserted into a Transformer with minimal additional computation. In experiments on image classification, multi-view video alignment, and action recognition, models containing 3DTRL outperform their corresponding backbone Transformers across the evaluated tasks. These results support adding estimated 3D structure as a useful representation component across several types of visual understanding.
summary.tldr: 3DTRL adds estimated 3D token positions to Transformers, improving the evaluated visual tasks with minimal extra computation.

title: Learning Viewpoint-Agnostic Visual Representations by Recovering Tokens in 3D Space

abstract: We study the question of last-iterate convergence rate of the extragradient algorithm by Korpelevich [1976] and the optimistic gradient algorithm by Popov [1980] in multi-player games. We show that both algorithms with constant step-size have last-iterate convergence rate of $O(\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}})$ to a Nash equilibrium in terms of the gap function in smooth monotone games, where each player's action set is an arbitrary convex set. Previous results only study the unconstrained setting, where each player's action set is the entire Euclidean space. Our results address an open question raised in several recent work by Hsieh et al. [2019], Golowich et al. [2020a,b], who ask for last-iterate convergence rate of either the extragradient or the optimistic gradient algorithm in the constrained setting. Our convergence rates for both algorithms are tight and match the lower bounds by Golowich et al. [2020a,b]. At the core of our results lies a new notion -- the tangent residual, which we use to measure the proximity to equilibrium. We use the tangent residual (or a slight variation of the tangent residual) as the the potential function in our analysis of the extragradient algorithm (or the optimistic gradient algorithm) and prove that it is non-increasing between two consecutive iterates.

paragraphs: When several players learn simultaneously, a central question is whether their current actions approach a Nash equilibrium. This paper studies last-iterate convergence for extragradient and optimistic gradient methods. Last-iterate guarantees concern the actual current output of learning, making them directly relevant to what an algorithm returns after a fixed number of updates.

The authors prove that both methods, with constant step sizes, achieve an equilibrium gap decreasing at order one over the square root of the number of iterations. The result assumes smooth monotone games and allows each player's action set to be an arbitrary convex set. This extends earlier results that treated only unrestricted Euclidean action spaces.

The main analytical tool is a new measure of equilibrium proximity called the tangent residual. The authors use it, or a slight variant, as a potential function and show that it never increases between consecutive iterates. The resulting rates match existing lower bounds, establishing tight convergence guarantees and resolving the stated open question for constrained games.
summary.tldr: Extragradient and optimistic gradient achieve tight last-iterate convergence rates in smooth monotone games with arbitrary convex action sets.

title: Finite-Time Last-Iterate Convergence for Learning in Multi-Player Games

abstract: Large-scale driving datasets such as Waymo Open Dataset and nuScenes substantially accelerate autonomous driving research, especially for perception tasks such as 3D detection and trajectory forecasting. Since the driving logs in these datasets contain HD maps and detailed object annotations which accurately reflect the real-world complexity of traffic behaviors, we can harvest a massive number of complex traffic scenarios and recreate their digital twins in simulation. Compared to the hand-crafted scenarios often used in existing simulators, data-driven scenarios collected from the real world can facilitate many research opportunities in machine learning and autonomous driving. In this work, we present ScenarioNet, an open-source platform for large-scale traffic scenario modeling and simulation. ScenarioNet defines a unified scenario description format and collects a large-scale repository of real-world traffic scenarios from the heterogeneous data in various driving datasets including Waymo, nuScenes, Lyft L5, and nuPlan datasets. These scenarios can be further replayed and interacted with in multiple views from Bird-Eye-View layout to realistic 3D rendering in MetaDrive simulator. This provides a benchmark for evaluating the safety of autonomous driving stacks in simulation before their real-world deployment. We further demonstrate the strengths of ScenarioNet on large-scale scenario generation, imitation learning, and reinforcement learning in both single-agent and multi-agent settings. Code, demo videos, and website are available at https://github.com/metadriverse/scenarionet

Views range from an overhead layout to realistic three-dimensional rendering, allowing the same underlying situation to support different forms of inspection and interaction.

The authors demonstrate uses in large-scale scenario generation, imitation learning, and reinforcement learning, including both single-agent and multi-agent settings. ScenarioNet also provides a simulation benchmark for assessing autonomous-driving safety before deployment. Its contribution is shared infrastructure that connects recorded traffic situations to reproducible simulated environments in which driving systems can be studied.
summary.tldr: ScenarioNet converts diverse driving datasets into a unified repository of interactive traffic simulations for research and evaluation.

title: ScenarioNet: Open-Source Platform for Large-Scale Traffic Scenario Simulation and Modeling

abstract: As an efficient alternative to conventional full fine-tuning, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) is becoming the prevailing method to adapt pretrained language models. In PEFT, a lightweight module is learned on each dataset while the underlying pretrained language model remains unchanged, resulting in multiple compact modules representing diverse skills when applied to various domains and tasks. In this paper, we propose to compose these parameter-efficient modules through linear arithmetic operations in the weight space, thereby integrating different module capabilities. Specifically, we first define an addition and negation operator for the module, and then further compose these two basic operators to perform flexible arithmetic. Our approach requires no additional training and enables highly flexible module composition. We apply different arithmetic operations to compose the parameter-efficient modules for (1) distribution generalization, (2) multi-tasking, (3) detoxifying, and (4) domain transfer. Additionally, we extend our approach to detoxify Alpaca-LoRA, the latest instruction-tuned large language model based on LLaMA. Empirical results demonstrate that our approach produces new and effective parameter-efficient modules that significantly outperform existing ones across all settings.

paragraphs: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning adapts a pretrained language model by learning a small module while keeping the underlying model fixed. Training on different tasks or domains therefore produces a collection of compact modules with different capabilities. This paper investigates whether those learned modules can become reusable ingredients for further adaptations.

The proposed method combines modules through linear arithmetic on their weights. The authors define addition and negation operations, then compose them into more flexible expressions. Once the original modules have been learned, producing a combined module requires no additional training. The approach therefore operates directly on the stored adaptations.

The paper applies this arithmetic to distribution generalization, multitasking, detoxification, and domain transfer, including detoxification of Alpaca-LoRA. Across the evaluated settings, the resulting modules significantly outperform existing ones. These findings support module arithmetic as a practical way to reuse learned adaptations. The evidence concerns the tested compositions and tasks; it does not establish that every combination of module weights will preserve or combine capabilities successfully.
summary.tldr: Linear arithmetic on lightweight adaptation modules produces useful combined language-model capabilities without additional training.

title: Composing Parameter-Efficient Modules with Arithmetic Operation

abstract: Text-attributed graphs (TAGs) are prevalent in various real-world scenarios, where each node is associated with a text description. The cornerstone of representation learning on TAGs lies in the seamless integration of textual semantics within individual nodes and the topological connections across nodes. Recent advancements in pre-trained language models (PLMs) and graph neural networks (GNNs) have facilitated effective learning on TAGs, garnering increased research interest. However, the absence of meaningful benchmark datasets and standardized evaluation procedures for TAGs has impeded progress in this field. In this paper, we propose CS-TAG, a comprehensive and diverse collection of challenging benchmark datasets for TAGs. The CS-TAG datasets are notably large in scale and encompass a wide range of domains, spanning from citation networks to purchase graphs. In addition to building the datasets, we conduct extensive benchmark experiments over CS-TAG with various learning paradigms, including PLMs, GNNs, PLM-GNN co-training methods, and the proposed novel topological pre-training of language models. In a nutshell, we provide an overview of the CS-TAG datasets, standardized evaluation procedures, and present baseline experiments. The entire CS-TAG project is publicly accessible at \url{https://github.com/sktsherlock/TAG-Benchmark}.

paragraphs: Text-attributed graphs combine two sources of information: descriptions attached to individual nodes and connections between those nodes. Learning useful representations requires integrating what the text says with how the graph is organized. The paper addresses a practical obstacle to studying this integration: a shortage of meaningful datasets and standardized evaluation procedures.

The authors introduce CS-TAG, a collection of large, challenging datasets covering multiple domains, including citation networks and purchase graphs. This breadth provides a shared setting for examining approaches across different kinds of textual and structural information. Standardized procedures accompany the datasets, making evaluation a central part of the contribution.

The study benchmarks pretrained language models, graph neural networks, and methods that train the two together. It also proposes topological pretraining of language models, bringing graph structure into language-model pretraining. The contribution is a benchmark collection, evaluation framework, and set of baseline experiments for investigating these learning choices. The abstract establishes this comparative foundation without declaring a single learning paradigm the overall winner.
summary.tldr: CS-TAG provides large, diverse text-attributed graph datasets and standardized experiments for studying how language and graph models interact.

title: A Comprehensive Study on Text-attributed Graphs: Benchmarking and Rethinking

abstract: Robots often rely on a repertoire of previously-learned motion policies for performing tasks of diverse complexities. When facing unseen task conditions or when new task requirements arise, robots must adapt their motion policies accordingly. In this context, policy optimization is the \emph{de facto} paradigm to adapt robot policies as a function of task-specific objectives. Most commonly-used motion policies carry particular structures that are often overlooked in policy optimization algorithms. We instead propose to leverage the structure of probabilistic policies by casting the policy optimization as an optimal transport problem. Specifically, we focus on robot motion policies that build on Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) and formulate the policy optimization as a Wassertein gradient flow over the GMMs space. This naturally allows us to constrain the policy updates via the $L^2$-Wasserstein distance between GMMs to enhance the stability of the policy optimization process. Furthermore, we leverage the geometry of the Bures-Wasserstein manifold to optimize the Gaussian distributions of the GMM policy via Riemannian optimization. We evaluate our approach on common robotic settings: Reaching motions, collision-avoidance behaviors, and multi-goal tasks. Our results show that our method outperforms common policy optimization baselines in terms of task success rate and low-variance solutions.

paragraphs: Robots often adapt previously learned motion policies when tasks or operating conditions change. This paper focuses on policies represented by Gaussian mixture models, which combine several Gaussian distributions. It argues that policy optimization can benefit from explicitly respecting this probabilistic structure when modifying a robot’s behavior.

The authors formulate policy optimization as an optimal transport problem and describe updates through a Wasserstein gradient flow over Gaussian mixtures. The Wasserstein distance constrains how far a policy moves between updates, supporting a more stable optimization process. They also use Bures–Wasserstein geometry to optimize the individual Gaussian components with Riemannian methods.

Evaluations cover reaching, collision avoidance, and tasks with multiple goals. The method outperforms common policy-optimization baselines in task success and in producing low-variance solutions. The contribution is a geometry-aware way to adapt structured motion policies: both the overall mixture update and its Gaussian components are optimized using distances and geometry suited to probability distributions, with the reported benefits demonstrated in the evaluated robotic settings.
summary.tldr: Optimal-transport geometry guides Gaussian-mixture robot policy updates, improving task success and reducing solution variance in the evaluated settings.

title: Wasserstein Gradient Flows for Optimizing Gaussian Mixture Policies

abstract: Token embeddings, a mapping from discrete lexical symbols to continuous vectors, are at the heart of any language model (LM). However, lexical symbol meanings can also be determined and even redefined by their structural role in a long context. In this paper, we ask: is it possible for a language model to be performant without \emph{any} fixed token embeddings? Such a language model would have to rely entirely on the co-occurence and repetition of tokens in the context rather than the \textit{a priori} identity of any token. To answer this, we study \textit{lexinvariant}language models that are invariant to lexical symbols and therefore do not need fixed token embeddings in practice. First, we prove that we can construct a lexinvariant LM to converge to the true language model at a uniform rate that is polynomial in terms of the context length, with a constant factor that is sublinear in the vocabulary size. Second, to build a lexinvariant LM, we simply encode tokens using random Gaussian vectors, such that each token maps to the same representation within each sequence but different representations across sequences. Empirically, we demonstrate that it can indeed attain perplexity comparable to that of a standard language model, given a sufficiently long context. We further explore two properties of the lexinvariant language models: First, given text generated from a substitution cipher of English, it implicitly implements Bayesian in-context deciphering and infers the mapping to the underlying real tokens with high accuracy. Second, it has on average 4X better accuracy over synthetic in-context reasoning tasks. Finally, we discuss regularizing standard language models towards lexinvariance and potential practical applications.

A lexinvariant model does not depend on the identities assigned to lexical symbols, forcing contextual structure to carry the information.

These findings show how much token meaning can be recovered from structure in the tested settings and motivate exploring lexinvariance as a regularizer for standard language models.
summary.tldr: Lexinvariant language models replace fixed token embeddings with sequence-specific random vectors and can achieve comparable perplexity with sufficiently long context.

title: Lexinvariant Language Models

abstract: We study the problem of combining neural networks with symbolic reasoning. Recently introduced frameworks for Probabilistic Neurosymbolic Learning (PNL), such as DeepProbLog, perform exponential-time exact inference, limiting the scalability of PNL solutions. We introduce Approximate Neurosymbolic Inference (A-NeSI): a new framework for PNL that uses neural networks for scalable approximate inference. A-NeSI 1) performs approximate inference in polynomial time without changing the semantics of probabilistic logics; 2) is trained using data generated by the background knowledge; 3) can generate symbolic explanations of predictions; and 4) can guarantee the satisfaction of logical constraints at test time, which is vital in safety-critical applications. Our experiments show that A-NeSI is the first end-to-end method to solve three neurosymbolic tasks with exponential combinatorial scaling. Finally, our experiments show that A-NeSI achieves explainability and safety without a penalty in performance.

paragraphs: Probabilistic neurosymbolic learning combines neural networks with reasoning expressed through logical rules and probabilities. Exact reasoning in existing frameworks can require computation that grows exponentially with the problem, restricting the size of tasks they can handle. A-NeSI addresses this bottleneck by learning neural networks that approximate the inference process.

The framework performs approximate inference in polynomial time while retaining the meaning of the underlying probabilistic logic. It trains on examples generated from background knowledge, connecting the learned inference procedure to the supplied rules. It can also produce symbolic explanations for predictions and can guarantee that logical constraints are satisfied during testing.

The experiments report that A-NeSI is the first end-to-end method to solve three neurosymbolic tasks with exponentially growing combinatorial structure. They also show explainability and constraint-based safety without a performance penalty in those experiments. The contribution is therefore a way to make probabilistic logical reasoning more scalable while preserving useful connections between neural predictions, explicit explanations, and enforceable rules.
summary.tldr: A-NeSI uses neural networks to approximate probabilistic logical inference efficiently while supporting symbolic explanations and guaranteed logical constraints.

title: A-NeSI: A Scalable Approximate Method for Probabilistic Neurosymbolic Inference

abstract: An intelligent conversational agent (a.k.a., chat-bot) could embrace conversational technologies to obtain user preferences online, to overcome inherent limitations of recommender systems trained over the offline historical user behaviors. In this paper, we propose CORE, a new offline-training and online-checking framework to plug a COnversational agent into REcommender systems. Unlike most prior conversational recommendation approaches that systemically combine conversational and recommender parts through a reinforcement learning framework, CORE bridges the conversational agent and recommender system through a unified uncertainty minimization framework, which can be easily applied to any existing recommendation approach. Concretely, CORE treats a recommender system as an offline estimator to produce an estimated relevance score for each item, while CORE regards a conversational agent as an online checker that checks these estimated scores in each online session. We define uncertainty as the sum of unchecked relevance scores. In this regard, the conversational agent acts to minimize uncertainty via querying either attributes or items. Towards uncertainty minimization, we derive the certainty gain of querying each attribute and item, and develop a novel online decision tree algorithm to decide what to query at each turn. Our theoretical analysis reveals the bound of the expected number of turns of CORE in a cold-start setting. Experimental results demonstrate that CORE can be seamlessly employed on a variety of recommendation approaches, and can consistently bring significant improvements in both hot-start and cold-start settings.

Experiments show that CORE works with varied recommendation approaches and consistently improves results in both hot-start and cold-start settings. summary.tldr: CORE improves recommendations by selecting conversational questions that reduce uncertainty in an existing recommender's relevance estimates.

title: Lending Interaction Wings to Recommender Systems with Conversational Agents

abstract: Adversarial Robustness Distillation (ARD) aims to transfer the robustness of large teacher models to small student models, facilitating the attainment of robust performance on resource-limited devices. However, existing research on ARD primarily focuses on the overall robustness of student models, overlooking the crucial aspect of $\textit{robust fairness}$. Specifically, these models may demonstrate strong robustness on some classes of data while exhibiting high vulnerability on other classes. Unfortunately, the "buckets effect" implies that the robustness of the deployed model depends on the classes with the lowest level of robustness. In this paper, we first investigate the inheritance of robust fairness during ARD and reveal that student models only partially inherit robust fairness from teacher models. We further validate this issue through fine-grained experiments with various model capacities and find that it may arise due to the gap in capacity between teacher and student models, as well as the existing methods treating each class equally during distillation. Based on these observations, we propose $\textbf{Fair}$ $\textbf{A}$dversarial $\textbf{R}$obustness $\textbf{D}$istillation (Fair-ARD), a novel framework for enhancing the robust fairness of student models by increasing the weights of difficult classes, and design a geometric perspective-based method to quantify the difficulty of different classes for determining the weights. Extensive experiments show that Fair-ARD surpasses both state-of-the-art ARD methods and existing robust fairness algorithms in terms of robust fairness (e.g., the worst-class robustness under AutoAttack is improved by at most 12.3\% and 5.3\% using ResNet18 on CIFAR10, respectively), while also slightly improving overall robustness. Our code is available at: [https://github.com/NISP-official/Fair-ARD](https://github.com/NISP-official/Fair-ARD).

Overall robustness can conceal uneven protection: some data classes may remain much easier to attack than others. This paper examines that imbalance, using robust fairness to describe how robustness is distributed across classes.

The authors find that students inherit only part of their teachers' robust fairness. Experiments across model capacities suggest that the teacher-student capacity gap and equal treatment of classes during distillation may contribute. Their proposed Fair-ARD framework increases the weights of difficult classes, using a geometrically motivated measure of class difficulty to determine those weights.

summary.tldr: Fair-ARD emphasizes difficult classes during robustness distillation, improving worst-class protection and slightly improving overall robustness in experiments.

title: Revisiting Adversarial Robustness Distillation from the Perspective of Robust Fairness

abstract: Table Representation Learning (TRL) models are commonly pre-trained on large open-domain datasets comprising millions of tables and then used to address downstream tasks. Choosing the right TRL model to use on proprietary data can be challenging, as the best results depend on the content domain, schema, and data quality. Our purpose is to support end-users in testing TRL models on proprietary data in two established SQL-centric tasks, i.e., Question Answering (QA) and Semantic Parsing (SP). We present QATCH (Query-Aided TRL Checklist), a toolbox to highlight TRL models’ strengths and weaknesses on relational tables unseen at training time. For an input table, QATCH automatically generates a testing checklist tailored to QA and SP. Checklist generation is driven by a SQL query engine that crafts tests of different complexity. This design facilitates inherent portability, allowing the checks to be used by alternative models. We also introduce a set of cross-task performance metrics evaluating the TRL model’s performance over its output. Finally, we show how QATCH automatically generates tests for proprietary datasets to evaluate various state-of-the-art models including TAPAS, TAPEX, and CHATGPT.

Given an input table, QATCH automatically creates a testing checklist tailored to those tasks. A SQL query engine constructs tests with different levels of complexity. This portability supports examining different systems on a common set of table-specific challenges.

The authors demonstrate automatic test generation for proprietary datasets and evaluation of models including TAPAS, TAPEX, and ChatGPT. QATCH’s contribution is a practical way to expose strengths and weaknesses on relational tables that were unseen during training.

title: QATCH: Benchmarking SQL-centric tasks with Table Representation Learning Models on Your Data

abstract: We study benign overfitting in two-layer ReLU networks trained using gradient descent and hinge loss on noisy data for binary classification. In particular, we consider linearly separable data for which a relatively small proportion of labels are corrupted or flipped. We identify conditions on the margin of the clean data that give rise to three distinct training outcomes: benign overfitting, in which zero loss is achieved and with high probability test data is classified correctly; overfitting, in which zero loss is achieved but test data is misclassified with probability lower bounded by a constant; and non-overfitting, in which clean points, but not corrupt points, achieve zero loss and again with high probability test data is classified correctly. Our analysis provides a fine-grained description of the dynamics of neurons throughout training and reveals two distinct phases: in the first phase clean points achieve close to zero loss, in the second phase clean points oscillate on the boundary of zero loss while corrupt points either converge towards zero loss or are eventually zeroed by the network. We prove these results using a combinatorial approach that involves bounding the number of clean versus corrupt updates during these phases of training.

paragraphs: Fitting corrupted training labels does not always imply poor predictions on new examples. This paper studies that distinction for two-layer ReLU networks trained with gradient descent and hinge loss. The setting assumes linearly separable clean data with a relatively small proportion of labels flipped or corrupted.

The authors identify clean-data margin conditions producing three outcomes. In benign overfitting, training loss reaches zero while test classification is correct with high probability. In harmful overfitting, training loss also reaches zero, but test error has a constant lower bound. In non-overfitting, clean points reach zero loss while corrupted points do not, and test classification is again correct with high probability.

The proof follows neuron behavior through two training phases. Clean examples first approach zero loss; later, they oscillate near its boundary while corrupted examples either approach zero loss or are eventually zeroed by the network. By counting clean and corrupted updates, the analysis connects data geometry to whether fitting noisy labels helps, harms, or is avoided during training.
summary.tldr: Margin conditions distinguish benign, harmful, and avoided overfitting in shallow ReLU networks trained on lightly corrupted labels.

title: Training shallow ReLU networks on noisy data using hinge loss: when do we overfit and is it benign?

abstract: We study the node classification problem on feature-decorated graphs in the sparse setting, i.e., when the expected degree of a node is $O(1)$ in the number of nodes, in the fixed-dimensional asymptotic regime, i.e., the dimension of the feature data is fixed while the number of nodes is large. Such graphs are typically known to be locally tree-like. We introduce a notion of Bayes optimality for node classification tasks, called asymptotic local Bayes optimality, and compute the optimal classifier according to this criterion for a fairly general statistical data model with arbitrary distributions of the node features and edge connectivity. The optimal classifier is implementable using a message-passing graph neural network architecture. We then compute the generalization error of this classifier and compare its performance against existing learning methods theoretically on a well-studied statistical model with naturally identifiable signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) in the data. We find that the optimal message-passing architecture interpolates between a standard MLP in the regime of low graph signal and a typical convolution in the regime of high graph signal. Furthermore, we prove a corresponding non-asymptotic result.

paragraphs: The paper studies node classification on graphs that have node features and remain sparse as they grow. Specifically, expected node degree stays bounded while feature dimension remains fixed. Such graphs are typically locally tree-like, providing a setting for analyzing what information a local classifier can use.

The authors define asymptotic local Bayes optimality and derive the classifier that satisfies this criterion for a broad statistical model allowing arbitrary feature and edge-connectivity distributions. They show that the resulting classifier can be implemented as a message-passing graph neural network. Its optimality is therefore attached to a specified local criterion and statistical setting.

A corresponding non-asymptotic result is also proved. These findings explain how the useful degree of graph-based processing changes with the strength of structural information.
summary.tldr: Under a local Bayes-optimality criterion for sparse graphs, an optimal message-passing classifier adapts between MLP-like and convolution-like behavior.

title: Optimality of Message-Passing Architectures for Sparse Graphs

abstract: Reductive Lie Groups, such as the orthogonal groups, the Lorentz group, or the unitary groups, play essential roles across scientific fields as diverse as high energy physics, quantum mechanics, quantum chromodynamics, molecular dynamics, computer vision, and imaging. In this paper, we present a general Equivariant Neural Network architecture capable of respecting the symmetries of the finite-dimensional representations of any reductive Lie Group. Our approach generalizes the successful ACE and MACE architectures for atomistic point clouds to any data equivariant to a reductive Lie group action. We also introduce the lie-nn software library, which provides all the necessary tools to develop and implement such general G-equivariant neural networks. It implements routines for the reduction of generic tensor products of representations into irreducible representations, making it easy to apply our architecture to a wide range of problems and groups. The generality and performance of our approach are demonstrated by applying it to the tasks of top quark decay tagging (Lorentz group) and shape recognition (orthogonal group).

paragraphs: Many scientific datasets come with transformations that a predictive model should respect. An equivariant network preserves the relationship between transforming its input and transforming its output. This paper develops a general architecture for symmetries described by finite-dimensional representations of reductive Lie groups, a family that includes orthogonal, Lorentz, and unitary groups.

The approach extends the ACE and MACE architectures beyond their atomistic point-cloud setting. Its scope is data that transforms according to an action of a reductive Lie group. The authors also introduce lie-nn, a software library supporting construction of these networks. A central capability decomposes tensor products of representations into irreducible representations, providing mathematical building blocks for implementing the architecture across different groups.

The authors demonstrate the framework on top quark decay tagging using Lorentz symmetry and shape recognition using orthogonal symmetry. These applications illustrate how one architectural framework can accommodate distinct transformation rules. The contribution combines a broad symmetry-respecting construction with implementation tools and demonstrations in two different problem settings.
summary.tldr: A general architecture and supporting library extend equivariant neural networks to finite-dimensional representations of any reductive Lie group.

title: A General Framework for Equivariant Neural Networks on Reductive Lie Groups

abstract: Humans and animals have a rich and flexible understanding of the physical world, which enables them to infer the underlying dynamical trajectories of objects and events, plausible future states, and use that to plan and anticipate the consequences of actions.However, the neural mechanisms underlying these computations are unclear.We combine a goal-driven modeling approach with dense neurophysiological data and high-throughput human behavioral readouts that contain thousands of comparisons to directly impinge on this question.Specifically, we construct and evaluate several classes of sensory-cognitive networks to predict the future state of rich, ethologically-relevant environments, ranging from self-supervised end-to-end models with pixel-wise or object-slot objectives, to models that future predict in the latent space of purely static image-pretrained or dynamic video-pretrained foundation models.We find that ``scale is \emph{not} all you need'', and that many state-of-the-art machine learning models fail to perform well on our neural and behavioral benchmarks for future prediction.In fact, only one class of models matches these data well overall.We find that neural responses are currently best predicted by models trained to predict the future state of their environment in the \emph{latent} space of pretrained foundation models optimized for \emph{dynamic} scenes in a self-supervised manner.These models also approach the neurons' ability to predict the environmental state variables that are visually hidden from view, despite not being explicitly trained to do so.Finally, we find that not all foundation model latents are equal.Notably, models that future predict in the latent space of video foundation models that are optimized to support a \emph{diverse} range of egocentric sensorimotor tasks, reasonably match \emph{both} human behavioral error patterns and neural dynamics across all environmental scenarios that we were able to test.Overall, these findings suggest that the neural mechanisms and behaviors of primate mental simulation have strong inductive biases associated with them, and are thus far most consistent with being optimized to future predict on \emph{reusable} visual representations that are useful for Embodied AI more generally.

paragraphs: This paper investigates which computational models best resemble how primates anticipate the future of physical scenes. The authors compare several families of prediction networks against dense neural recordings and human behavioral measurements containing thousands of comparisons. Candidate models predict pixels, object-based representations, or internal representations learned by image and video foundation models.

Many advanced models perform poorly on these neural and behavioral tests, suggesting that increasing scale alone is insufficient. Neural responses are best predicted by models trained to forecast future states in the latent space of self-supervised foundation models trained on dynamic scenes. These models also approach neurons' ability to predict visually hidden environmental variables without explicit training for that capability.

The strongest overall agreement comes from prediction in representations learned for diverse first-person sensorimotor tasks. Those models reasonably match both human error patterns and neural dynamics across the tested scenarios. The findings suggest that mental simulation favors reusable visual representations shaped by interaction-relevant tasks, while remaining evidence about model–brain correspondence rather than a definitive identification of the brain's mechanism.
summary.tldr: Predicting future states in representations learned from dynamic sensorimotor scenes best matches the study's neural and behavioral evidence.

title: Neural Foundations of Mental Simulation: Future Prediction of Latent Representations on Dynamic Scenes

abstract: The design and analysis of randomized experiments is fundamental to many areas, from the physical and social sciences to industrial settings. Regression adjustment is a popular technique to reduce the variance of estimates obtained from experiments, by utilizing information contained in auxiliary covariates. While there is a large literature within the statistics community studying various approaches to regression adjustment and their asymptotic properties, little focus has been given to approaches in the finite population setting with non-asymptotic accuracy bounds. Further, prior work typically assumes that an entire population is exposed to an experiment, whereas practitioners often seek to minimize the number of subjects exposed to an experiment, for ethical and pragmatic reasons.In this work, we study the problems of estimating the sample mean, individual treatment effects, and average treatment effect with regression adjustment. We propose approaches that use techniques from randomized numerical linear algebra to sample a subset of the population on which to perform an experiment. We give non-asymptotic accuracy bounds for our methods and demonstrate that they compare favorably with prior approaches.

paragraphs: Regression adjustment uses auxiliary information about experimental subjects to reduce variation in estimated outcomes or treatment effects. This paper examines that idea for a finite population, with particular attention to experiments that expose only a subset of people to treatment. Limiting participation can matter for both practical and ethical reasons.

The authors study estimation of the sample mean, individual treatment effects, and the average treatment effect. Their methods draw on randomized numerical linear algebra to choose a subset of the population on which to run the experiment. This brings the selection of experimental subjects into the same methodological picture as the subsequent regression-adjusted estimation.

The analysis supplies non-asymptotic accuracy bounds, meaning guarantees stated for finite settings rather than only through limiting behavior as sample sizes grow. The authors also demonstrate favorable comparisons with prior approaches. The central contribution is therefore a combination of subset selection, regression adjustment, and finite-data accuracy analysis. It addresses the practical situation where experimenting on an entire population is undesirable while accurate estimation remains important.
summary.tldr: The paper combines population subsampling and regression adjustment with finite-data accuracy guarantees for mean and treatment-effect estimation.

title: Finite Population Regression Adjustment and Non-asymptotic Guarantees for Treatment Effect Estimation

abstract: Recent advances in neural image compression (NIC) have produced models that are starting to outperform classic codecs. While this has led to growing excitement about using NIC in real-world applications, the successful adoption of any machine learning system in the wild requires it to generalize (and be robust) to unseen distribution shifts at deployment. Unfortunately, current research lacks comprehensive datasets and informative tools to evaluate and understand NIC performance in real-world settings. To bridge this crucial gap, first, this paper presents a comprehensive benchmark suite to evaluate the out-of-distribution (OOD) performance of image compression methods. Specifically, we provide CLIC-C and Kodak-C by introducing 15 corruptions to the popular CLIC and Kodak benchmarks. Next, we propose spectrally-inspired inspection tools to gain deeper insight into errors introduced by image compression methods as well as their OOD performance. We then carry out a detailed performance comparison of several classic codecs and NIC variants, revealing intriguing findings that challenge our current understanding of the strengths and limitations of NIC. Finally, we corroborate our empirical findings with theoretical analysis, providing an in-depth view of the OOD performance of NIC and its dependence on the spectral properties of the data. Our benchmarks, spectral inspection tools, and findings provide a crucial bridge to the real-world adoption of NIC. We hope that our work will propel future efforts in designing robust and generalizable NIC methods. Code and data will be made available at https://github.com/klieberman/ood_nic.

summary.tldr: New corruption benchmarks and spectral inspection tools examine how neural image compression behaves under distribution shifts and connect that behavior to data properties.

title: Neural Image Compression: Generalization, Robustness, and Spectral Biases

abstract: Machine learning models are increasingly being scaled in both sequence length and model dimension to reach longer contexts and better performance. However, existing architectures such as Transformers scale quadratically along both these axes. We ask: are there performant architectures that can scale sub-quadratically along sequence length and model dimension? We introduce Monarch Mixer (M2), a new architecture that uses the same sub-quadratic primitive along both sequence length and model dimension: Monarch matrices, a simple class of expressive structured matrices that captures many linear transforms, achieves high hardware efficiency on GPUs, and scales sub-quadratically. As a proof of concept, we explore the performance of M2 in three domains: non-causal BERT-style language modeling, ViT-style image classification, and causal GPT-style language modeling. For non-causal BERT-style modeling, M2 matches BERT-base and BERT-large in downstream GLUE quality with up to 27% fewer parameters, and achieves up to 9.1$\times$ higher throughput at sequence length 4K. On ImageNet, M2 outperforms ViT-b by 1% in accuracy, with only half the parameters. Causal GPT-style models introduce a technical challenge: enforcing causality via masking introduces a quadratic bottleneck. To alleviate this bottleneck, we develop a novel theoretical view of Monarch matrices based on multivariate polynomial evaluation and interpolation, which lets us parameterize M2 to be causal while remaining sub-quadratic. Using this parameterization, M2 matches GPT-style Transformers at 360M parameters in pretraining perplexity on The PILE—showing for the first time that it may be possible to match Transformer quality without attention or MLPs.

Its common building block is the Monarch matrix, a structured matrix class that supports expressive linear transformations and efficient GPU computation. title: Monarch Mixer: A Simple Sub-Quadratic GEMM-Based Architecture

abstract: The extraordinary ability of generative models to generate photographic images has intensified concerns about the spread of disinformation, thereby leading to the demand for detectors capable of distinguishing between AI-generated fake images and real images. However, the lack of large datasets containing images from the most advanced image generators poses an obstacle to the development of such detectors. In this paper, we introduce the GenImage dataset, which has the following advantages: 1) Plenty of Images, including over one million pairs of AI-generated fake images and collected real images. 2) Rich Image Content, encompassing a broad range of image classes. 3) State-of-the-art Generators, synthesizing images with advanced diffusion models and GANs. The aforementioned advantages allow the detectors trained on GenImage to undergo a thorough evaluation and demonstrate strong applicability to diverse images. We conduct a comprehensive analysis of the dataset and propose two tasks for evaluating the detection method in resembling real-world scenarios. The cross-generator image classification task measures the performance of a detector trained on one generator when tested on the others. The degraded image classification task assesses the capability of the detectors in handling degraded images such as low-resolution, blurred, and compressed images. With the GenImage dataset, researchers can effectively expedite the development and evaluation of superior AI-generated image detectors in comparison to prevailing methodologies.

paragraphs: Detecting generated images requires evaluation data that reflect the variety of images and generators a detector may encounter. GenImage addresses a shortage of large datasets containing outputs from advanced image-generation systems. It includes more than one million pairs of generated and collected real images, spanning many image classes.

The generated portion includes outputs from diffusion models and generative adversarial networks. Beyond assembling the data, the authors define two evaluation tasks. Cross-generator classification trains a detector on one generator and tests it on others, examining whether its learned distinctions transfer beyond the source used for training.

The second task evaluates detection after image degradation, including reduced resolution, blur, and compression. Together, these tasks assess two different demands: recognizing outputs from other generators and handling changes to image quality. The paper contributes a large, varied dataset and an evaluation framework for developing and comparing detectors under conditions intended to resemble practical use. Its stated value lies in enabling more thorough assessment across image content, generator families, and degradation conditions.
summary.tldr: GenImage provides a million-scale dataset and tests for evaluating generated-image detectors across generators and degraded image conditions.

title: GenImage: A Million-Scale Benchmark for Detecting AI-Generated Image

abstract: Given the ubiquity of graph data and its applications in diverse domains, building a Graph Foundation Model (GFM) that can work well across different graphs and tasks with a unified backbone has recently garnered significant interests. A major obstacle to achieving this goal stems from the fact that graphs from different domains often exhibit diverse node features. Inspired by multi-modal models that align different modalities with natural language, the text has recently been adopted to provide a unified feature space for diverse graphs. Despite the great potential of these text-space GFMs, current research in this field is hampered by two problems. First, the absence of a comprehensive benchmark with unified problem settings hinders a clear understanding of the comparative effectiveness and practical value of different text-space GFMs. Second, there is a lack of sufficient datasets to thoroughly explore the methods' full potential and verify their effectiveness across diverse settings. To address these issues, we conduct a comprehensive benchmark providing novel text-space datasets and comprehensive evaluation under unified problem settings. Empirical results provide new insights and inspire future research directions. Our code and data are publicly available from https://github.com/CurryTang/TSGFM.
