paragraphs: A graph foundation model aims to use one backbone across different graphs and tasks. A major obstacle is that nodes from different domains can have very different features. Text-space approaches use natural language as a shared feature space, drawing inspiration from multimodal systems that align different kinds of information with language.

This paper focuses on the evidence needed to evaluate that strategy. Existing research lacks both a comprehensive benchmark with consistent problem settings and enough datasets to examine performance across diverse conditions. Without those shared resources, it is difficult to compare methods clearly or assess their practical value.

The authors contribute new text-space graph datasets and a broad evaluation under unified settings. Their empirical study produces insights intended to guide subsequent research. The contribution is primarily an evaluation foundation: a more consistent basis for studying how well text can unify graph features and support transfer across tasks and domains. It expands the resources available for comparison without claiming that one approach is universally best.
summary.tldr: New datasets and unified evaluations provide a more comprehensive benchmark for graph foundation models that use text as a shared feature space.

title: Text-space Graph Foundation Models: Comprehensive Benchmarks and New Insights

abstract: We propose an unsupervised adaptation framework, Self-TAught Recognizer (STAR), which leverages unlabeled data to enhance the robustness of automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems in diverse target domains, such as noise and accents. STAR is developed for prevalent speech foundation models based on Transformer-related architecture with auto-regressive decoding (e.g., Whisper, Canary). Specifically, we propose a novel indicator that empirically integrates step-wise information during decoding to assess the token-level quality of pseudo labels without ground truth, thereby guiding model updates for effective unsupervised adaptation. Experimental results show that STAR achieves an average of 13.5% relative reduction in word error rate across 14 target domains, and it sometimes even approaches the upper-bound performance of supervised adaptation. Surprisingly, we also observe that STAR prevents the adapted model from the common catastrophic forgetting problem without recalling source-domain data. Furthermore, STAR exhibits high data efficiency that only requires less than one-hour unlabeled data, and seamless generality to alternative large speech models and speech translation tasks. Our code aims to open source to the research communities.

paragraphs: Speech recognizers need to adapt to target conditions such as unfamiliar accents and noise, but labeled recordings may be unavailable. Self-TAught Recognizer, or STAR, adapts speech foundation models using unlabeled audio. It targets Transformer-related models with autoregressive decoding, including Whisper and Canary.

The key component is an indicator that assesses the quality of individual tokens in automatically generated transcripts without access to correct transcripts. It combines information produced step by step during decoding and uses that assessment to guide model updates. This gives adaptation a way to distinguish more useful pseudo-label information from less reliable information within the same generated output.

Across 14 target domains, STAR achieves an average 13.5% relative reduction in word error rate and sometimes approaches supervised adaptation performance. The authors also observe avoidance of catastrophic forgetting without revisiting source-domain data. Experiments report effectiveness with less than one hour of unlabeled data and applicability to other large speech models and speech translation. These findings support quality-aware pseudo-labeling as a practical route to efficient unsupervised adaptation.
summary.tldr: STAR uses decoding-based token quality estimates to adapt speech models from unlabeled audio, reducing word error rates across diverse target domains.

title: Self-Taught Recognizer: Toward Unsupervised Adaptation for Speech Foundation Models

abstract: Training and inference with large machine learning models that far exceed the memory capacity of individual devices necessitates the design of distributed architectures, forcing one to contend with communication constraints. We present a framework for distributed computation over a quantum network in which data is encoded into specialized quantum states. We prove that for models within this framework, inference and training using gradient descent can be performed with exponentially less communication compared to their classical analogs, and with relatively modest overhead relative to standard gradient-based methods. We show that certain graph neural networks are particularly amenable to implementation within this framework, and moreover present empirical evidence that they perform well on standard benchmarks.To our knowledge, this is the first example of exponential quantum advantage for a generic class of machine learning problems that hold regardless of the data encoding cost. Moreover, we show that models in this class can encode highly nonlinear features of their inputs, and their expressivity increases exponentially with model depth.We also delineate the space of models for which exponential communication advantages hold by showing that they cannot hold for linear classification. Communication of quantum states that potentially limit the amount of information that can be extracted from them about the data and model parameters may also lead to improved privacy guarantees for distributed computation. Taken as a whole, these findings form a promising foundation for distributed machine learning over quantum networks.

paragraphs: When a machine learning model exceeds the memory of one device, computation must be distributed and information exchanged between devices. This paper develops a quantum-network framework that encodes data in specialized quantum states. Its central objective is to reduce the communication required for inference and gradient-descent training.

For models within this framework, the authors prove an exponential communication advantage over classical counterparts, with relatively modest overhead compared with standard gradient-based methods. The stated advantage holds regardless of data encoding cost. Certain graph neural networks fit the framework particularly well, and experiments provide evidence that these models perform well on standard benchmarks.

The framework can represent highly nonlinear input features, and its expressivity grows exponentially with depth. The paper also establishes a boundary: the exponential communication advantage cannot hold for linear classification. Finally, the authors suggest that limits on information extractable from transmitted quantum states may improve privacy. That privacy benefit is presented as a possibility, while the communication advantage is a theorem for the specified model class.
summary.tldr: A quantum-network framework provably reduces communication exponentially for a specified class of distributed learning and inference models.

title: Exponential Quantum Communication Advantage in Distributed Inference and Learning

abstract: Despite significant advancements in text generation and reasoning, Large Language Models (LLMs) still face challenges in accurately performing complex arithmetic operations. Language model systems often enable LLMs to generate code for arithmetic operations to achieve accurate calculations. However, this approach compromises speed and security, and fine-tuning risks the language model losing prior capabilities. We propose a framework that enables exact arithmetic in *a single autoregressive step*, providing faster, more secure, and more interpretable LLM systems with arithmetic capabilities. We use the hidden states of a LLM to control a symbolic architecture that performs arithmetic. Our implementation using Llama 3 with OccamNet as a symbolic model (OccamLlama) achieves 100\% accuracy on single arithmetic operations ($+,-,\times,\div,\sin{},\cos{},\log{},\exp{},\sqrt{}$), outperforming GPT 4o with and without a code interpreter. Furthermore, OccamLlama outperforms GPT 4o with and without a code interpreter on average across a range of mathematical problem solving benchmarks, demonstrating that OccamLLMs can excel in arithmetic tasks, even surpassing much larger models. Code is available at https://github.com/druidowm/OccamLLM.

paragraphs: Language models can produce fluent explanations while still making arithmetic mistakes. Generating code for calculations can improve accuracy, but the paper identifies speed and security costs in that approach. OccamLLM connects a language model to a symbolic arithmetic architecture, aiming to perform exact calculations within a single autoregressive step.

The language model's hidden states control the symbolic component that carries out arithmetic. The implementation, OccamLlama, combines Llama 3 with OccamNet. This gives the model an arithmetic mechanism whose operations are explicit, supporting the framework's stated goals of faster, more secure, and more interpretable calculation.

OccamLlama achieves one hundred percent accuracy in the reported tests of individual operations, including basic arithmetic, trigonometric functions, logarithms, exponentials, and square roots. It outperforms GPT-4o with and without a code interpreter on those tests and on average across the evaluated mathematical problem-solving benchmarks. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of symbolic integration for the tested arithmetic tasks, including comparisons with a much larger language model.
summary.tldr: OccamLLM uses language-model hidden states to control symbolic arithmetic, enabling exact calculations in a single autoregressive step.

title: OccamLLM: Fast and Exact Language Model Arithmetic in a Single Step

abstract: Pre-trained large language models (LLMs) based on Transformer have demonstrated striking in-context learning (ICL) abilities. With a few demonstration input-label pairs, they can predict the label for an unseen input without any parameter updates. In this paper, we show an exciting phenomenon that SVD-based weight pruning can enhance ICL performance, and more surprising, pruning weights in deep layers often results in more stable performance improvements than in shallow layers. However, the underlying mechanism of those findings still remains an open question. To reveal those findings, we conduct an in-depth theoretical analysis by presenting the implicit gradient descent (GD) trajectories of ICL and giving the mutual information based generalization bounds of ICL via full implicit GD trajectories. This helps us reasonably explain the surprising experimental findings. Besides, based on all our experimental and theoretical insights, we intuitively propose a simple, model-compression and derivative-free algorithm for downstream tasks in enhancing ICL inference. Experiments on benchmark datasets and open source LLMs display the method effectiveness.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a language model use example input-label pairs to predict a new label without updating its parameters. This paper investigates an unexpected observation: pruning model weights using singular value decomposition can improve that ability. Pruning deeper layers also often produces more stable improvements than pruning shallower ones.

To explain these observations, the authors analyze in-context learning through implicit gradient-descent trajectories. They derive generalization bounds based on mutual information using the full trajectories. This provides a theoretical account connecting the internal learning process to the observed effects of pruning, including the differing behavior of deep and shallow layers.

The experimental and theoretical insights motivate a simple derivative-free algorithm that combines model compression with improved in-context inference for downstream tasks. Experiments on benchmark datasets and open-source language models demonstrate its effectiveness. The significance is that removing parts of the weight representation can sometimes improve how a model uses demonstrations, in addition to compressing it. The reported deeper-layer advantage remains an empirical tendency rather than a guarantee for every model.
summary.tldr: SVD-based weight pruning can improve in-context learning, with implicit gradient-descent analysis helping explain the observed gains.

title: Enhancing In-Context Learning Performance with just SVD-Based Weight Pruning: A Theoretical Perspective

abstract: Generative models hold great promise for small molecule discovery, significantly increasing the size of search space compared to traditional in silico screening libraries. However, most existing machine learning methods for small molecule generation suffer from poor synthesizability of candidate compounds, making experimental validation difficult. In this paper we propose Reaction-GFlowNet (RGFN), an extension of the GFlowNet framework that operates directly in the space of chemical reactions, thereby allowing out-of-the-box synthesizability while maintaining comparable quality of generated candidates. We demonstrate that with the proposed set of reactions and building blocks, it is possible to obtain a search space of molecules orders of magnitude larger than existing screening libraries coupled with low cost of synthesis. We also show that the approach scales to very large fragment libraries, further increasing the number of potential molecules. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach across a range of oracle models, including pretrained proxy models and GPU-accelerated docking.

paragraphs: Molecular generators can search beyond the compounds available in fixed screening libraries, but their proposed molecules may be difficult to synthesize. That creates a practical obstacle to experimental validation. Reaction-GFlowNet, or RGFN, addresses this by making chemical reactions the space in which generation operates.

RGFN extends the GFlowNet framework to construct candidates using a proposed collection of reactions and building blocks. The authors report that this provides synthesizability directly within generation while maintaining comparable candidate quality. With their chosen reactions and building blocks, the accessible molecular space is orders of magnitude larger than existing screening libraries and is coupled with low synthesis cost.

The approach also scales to very large fragment libraries, further expanding the possible compounds. Evaluations use several kinds of oracle models, including pretrained proxies and GPU-accelerated docking, to demonstrate effectiveness. The significance is the connection between search breadth and construction feasibility: the model explores a large space through reaction-based choices, so synthesis considerations are built into how candidates are produced.
summary.tldr: RGFN generates molecules through chemical reactions, combining a large search space with synthesis-aware candidate construction.

title: RGFN: Synthesizable Molecular Generation Using GFlowNets

abstract: In today’s era, whatever we can measure at scale, we can optimize. So far, measuring the interpretability of units in deep neural networks (DNNs) for computer vision still requires direct human evaluation and is not scalable. As a result, the inner workings of DNNs remain a mystery despite the remarkable progress we have seen in their applications. In this work, we introduce the first scalable method to measure the per-unit interpretability in vision DNNs. This method does not require any human evaluations, yet its prediction correlates well with existing human interpretability measurements. We validate its predictive power through an interventional human psychophysics study. We demonstrate the usefulness of this measure by performing previously infeasible experiments: (1) A large-scale interpretability analysis across more than 70 million units from 835 computer vision models, and (2) an extensive analysis of how units transform during training. We find an anticorrelation between a model's downstream classification performance and per-unit interpretability, which is also observable during model training. Furthermore, we see that a layer's location and width influence its interpretability.

We validate its predictive power through an interventional human psychophysics study. paragraphs: Understanding individual units inside a vision network usually requires people to judge whether those units have understandable behavior. That makes broad comparisons expensive. This paper introduces an automated measure of per-unit interpretability, allowing researchers to examine far more units than direct human evaluation would make practical.

The measure's predictions correlate well with existing human interpretability measurements. The authors also validate its predictive power through an interventional human psychophysics study. Human evaluation therefore helps establish the measure's usefulness, while applying the measure itself does not require new human judgments for every unit being assessed.

The authors use it to analyze more than 70 million units across 835 vision models and to examine how units change during training. They find a negative relationship between downstream classification performance and per-unit interpretability, including during training. Layer position and width also influence interpretability. These findings describe relationships at the level of individual units; the reported anticorrelation does not by itself establish that lower interpretability causes higher accuracy.
summary.tldr: An automated interpretability measure enables analysis of over 70 million vision-network units and reveals a negative association with classification performance.

title: Measuring Per-Unit Interpretability at Scale Without Humans

abstract: We present *knowledge continuity*, a novel definition inspired by Lipschitz continuity which aims to certify the robustness of neural networks across input domains (such as continuous and discrete domains in vision and language, respectively). Most existing approaches that seek to certify robustness, especially Lipschitz continuity, lie within the continuous domain with norm and distribution-dependent guarantees. In contrast, our proposed definition yields certification guarantees that depend only on the loss function and the intermediate learned metric spaces of the neural network. These bounds are independent of domain modality, norms, and distribution. We further demonstrate that the expressiveness of a model class is not at odds with its knowledge continuity. This implies that achieving robustness by maximizing knowledge continuity should not theoretically hinder inferential performance. Finally, to complement our theoretical results, we present several applications of knowledge continuity such as regularization, a certification algorithm, and show that knowledge continuity can be used to localize vulnerable components of a neural network.

Most existing approaches that seek to certify robustness, especially Lipschitz continuity, lie within the continuous domain with norm and distribution-dependent guarantees. In contrast, our proposed definition yields certification guarantees that depend only on the loss function and the intermediate learned metric spaces of the neural network. These bounds are independent of domain modality, norms, and distribution. We further demonstrate that the expressiveness of a model class is not at odds with its knowledge continuity. This implies that achieving robustness by maximizing knowledge continuity should not theoretically hinder inferential performance. Finally, to complement our theoretical results, we present several applications of knowledge continuity such as regularization, a certification algorithm, and show that knowledge continuity can be used to localize vulnerable components of a neural network.

paragraphs: Robustness certification seeks mathematical guarantees about how a neural network behaves under changes to its input. Many existing approaches express those guarantees through distances in continuous input spaces. This paper introduces knowledge continuity to support certification across different kinds of inputs, including continuous visual data and discrete language data.

The definition draws inspiration from Lipschitz continuity but bases its guarantees on the loss function and metric spaces learned inside the network. The resulting bounds are independent of input modality, norms, and distribution. This shifts the mathematical basis of certification toward the model’s learned representations and the quantity used to assess its errors.

The authors also show that knowledge continuity is compatible with the expressiveness of a model class. Their theoretical result suggests that maximizing it for robustness should not inherently restrict inferential performance. They complement the theory with applications to regularization, a certification algorithm, and locating vulnerable network components. Together, these contributions connect a general robustness definition to ways of training, certifying, and inspecting models.
summary.tldr: Knowledge continuity provides robustness guarantees based on learned representations and loss, independent of input modality, norms, and distribution.

title: Achieving Domain-Independent Certified Robustness via Knowledge Continuity

abstract: Non-monotone constrained submodular maximization plays a crucial role in various machine learning applications. However, existing algorithms often struggle with a trade-off between approximation guarantees and practical efficiency. The current state-of-the-art is a recent $0.401$-approximation algorithm, but its computational complexity makes it highly impractical. The best practical algorithms for the problem only guarantee $1/e$-approximation. In this work, we present a novel algorithm for submodular maximization subject to a cardinality constraint that combines a guarantee of $0.385$-approximation with a low and practical query complexity of $O(n+k^2)$. Furthermore, we evaluate our algorithm's performance through extensive machine learning applications, including Movie Recommendation, Image Summarization, and more. These evaluations demonstrate the efficacy of our approach.

The current state-of-the-art is a recent $0.401$-approximation algorithm, but its computational complexity makes it highly impractical. The best practical algorithms for the problem only guarantee $1/e$-approximation. In this work, we present a novel algorithm for submodular maximization subject to a cardinality constraint that combines a guarantee of $0.385$-approximation with a low and practical query complexity of $O(n+k^2)$. Furthermore, we evaluate our algorithm's performance through extensive machine learning applications, including Movie Recommendation, Image Summarization, and more. These evaluations demonstrate the efficacy of our approach.

paragraphs: Many selection problems ask for a useful subset while restricting how many items may be chosen. Submodular objectives capture diminishing returns: an item's extra contribution can shrink as the selected set grows. In the non-monotone case considered here, adding items does not always improve the objective, making good selection more challenging.

The paper addresses the tradeoff between a provable approximation guarantee and practical computational effort. It presents an algorithm with a 0.385 approximation guarantee under a cardinality constraint and query complexity O(n + k²). The abstract contrasts this with a stronger 0.401 guarantee from an algorithm described as impractical, and the 1/e guarantees of the best practical alternatives.

The new result improves the stated guarantee available with practical query complexity, without claiming the strongest approximation ratio overall. Evaluations on machine-learning applications, including movie recommendation and image summarization, demonstrate the method's effectiveness. Its contribution is a combination of theoretical solution quality and manageable evaluation cost for constrained subset-selection problems.
summary.tldr: A new subset-selection algorithm combines a 0.385 approximation guarantee with practical O(n + k²) query complexity.

title: Practical $0.385$-Approximation for Submodular Maximization Subject to a Cardinality Constraint

abstract: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) methods have shown promise in enabling agents to learn a shared communication protocol from scratch and accomplish challenging team tasks. However, the learned language is usually not interpretable to humans or other agents not co-trained together, limiting its applicability in ad-hoc teamwork scenarios. In this work, we propose a novel computational pipeline that aligns the communication space between MARL agents with an embedding space of human natural language by grounding agent communications on synthetic data generated by embodied Large Language Models (LLMs) in interactive teamwork scenarios. Our results demonstrate that introducing language grounding not only maintains task performance but also accelerates the emergence of communication. Furthermore, the learned communication protocols exhibit zero-shot generalization capabilities in ad-hoc teamwork scenarios with unseen teammates and novel task states. This work presents a significant step toward enabling effective communication and collaboration between artificial agents and humans in real-world teamwork settings.

paragraphs: Agents trained together through multi-agent reinforcement learning can invent communication protocols that help them cooperate. The proposed pipeline aligns the agents' communication space with an embedding space for human natural language. It grounds their messages using synthetic data generated by embodied language models in interactive teamwork scenarios. Human-language representations thereby provide a shared reference for communication that would otherwise emerge solely from joint reinforcement learning.

The learned protocols also generalize without additional training to teamwork with unseen teammates and unfamiliar task states. The work presents this as progress toward collaboration between artificial agents and humans, rather than reporting universal real-world teamwork capability.
summary.tldr: Grounding agent communication in natural-language embeddings preserves performance and enables reported zero-shot teamwork with unfamiliar partners and states.

title: Language Grounded Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning with Human-interpretable Communication

abstract: Causal video question answering (QA) has garnered increasing interest, yet existing datasets often lack depth in causal reasoning. To address this gap, we capitalize on the unique properties of cartoons and construct CausalChaos!, a novel, challenging causal Why-QA dataset built upon the iconic "Tom and Jerry" cartoon series. Cartoons use the principles of animation that allow animators to create expressive, unambiguous causal relationships between events to form a coherent storyline. Utilizing these properties, along with thought-provoking questions and multi-level answers (answer and detailed causal explanation), our questions involve causal chains that interconnect multiple dynamic interactions between characters and visual scenes. These factors demand models to solve more challenging, yet well-defined causal relationships. We also introduce hard incorrect answer mining, including a causally confusing version that is even more challenging. While models perform well, there is much room for improvement, especially, on open-ended answers. We identify more advanced/explicit causal relationship modeling \& joint modeling of vision and language as the immediate areas for future efforts to focus upon. Along with the other complementary datasets, our new challenging dataset will pave the way for these developments in the field. Dataset and Code: https://github.com/LUNAProject22/CausalChaos

paragraphs: Causal video question answering requires understanding why events happen, including how earlier interactions lead to later outcomes. CausalChaos! is a dataset built from Tom and Jerry cartoons to test this ability through longer causal chains. The authors use animation's expressive depiction of events to construct causal questions with clear relationships despite their complexity.

Each question comes with both an answer and a more detailed causal explanation. Answering can require connecting several interactions between characters and their surroundings, rather than recognizing an isolated action. The dataset also includes deliberately difficult incorrect answers, with an additional version designed to create confusion specifically about causal relationships.

The evaluation finds that models perform well in some respects but still have considerable room to improve, particularly when generating open-ended answers. The authors identify explicit causal relationship modeling and joint treatment of vision and language as promising next directions. The dataset's contribution is to make demanding, visually grounded causal reasoning available for evaluation alongside complementary existing datasets.
summary.tldr: CausalChaos! uses cartoon scenes and detailed explanations to test video models on longer causal chains and challenging why questions.

title: CausalChaos! Dataset for Comprehensive Causal Action Question Answering Over Longer Causal Chains Grounded in Dynamic Visual Scenes

abstract: In this work we investigate the generalization performance of random feature ridge regression (RFRR). Our main contribution is a general deterministic equivalent for the test error of RFRR. Specifically, under a certain concentration property, we show that the test error is well approximated by a closed-form expression that only depends on the feature map eigenvalues. Notably, our approximation guarantee is non-asymptotic, multiplicative, and independent of the feature map dimension---allowing for infinite-dimensional features. We expect this deterministic equivalent to hold broadly beyond our theoretical analysis, and we empirically validate its predictions on various real and synthetic datasets. As an application, we derive sharp excess error rates under standard power-law assumptions of the spectrum and target decay. In particular, we provide a tight result for the smallest number of features achieving optimal minimax error rate.

paragraphs: Random feature ridge regression learns a predictor using a randomized collection of features and regularization. This paper studies its test error: how well the resulting predictor performs on new examples. Its main contribution is a deterministic formula that approximates that error using the eigenvalues of the feature map, giving a tractable description of a quantity affected by randomness.

The theoretical guarantee requires a particular concentration property. Under that condition, the approximation is multiplicative, applies at finite sample sizes, and does not depend on the feature map's dimension. This last property allows the analysis to include infinite-dimensional feature maps. Experiments on real and synthetic datasets support the formula's predictions, and the authors expect it to apply beyond the settings covered by their proof.

The paper then assumes standard power-law behavior for the spectrum and target decay to derive sharp excess-error rates. It also identifies a tight feature-count requirement for attaining the optimal minimax rate. These results connect prediction quality with the number of random features needed under the stated assumptions.
summary.tldr: Under a concentration assumption, a dimension-independent formula predicts random feature regression error and yields sharp feature-count scaling results.

title: Dimension-free deterministic equivalents and scaling laws for random feature regression

abstract: Monocular depth estimation (MDE) is fundamental for deriving 3D scene structures from 2D images. While state-of-the-art monocular relative depth estimation (MRDE) excels in estimating relative depths for in-the-wild images, current monocular metric depth estimation (MMDE) approaches still face challenges in handling unseen scenes. Since MMDE can be viewed as the composition of MRDE and metric scale recovery, we attribute this difficulty to scene dependency, where MMDE models rely on scenes observed during supervised training for predicting scene scales during inference. To address this issue, we propose to use humans as landmarks for distilling scene-independent metric scale priors from generative painting models. Our approach, Metric from Human (MfH), bridges from generalizable MRDE to zero-shot MMDE in a generate-and-estimate manner. Specifically, MfH generates humans on the input image with generative painting and estimates human dimensions with an off-the-shelf human mesh recovery (HMR) model. Based on MRDE predictions, it propagates the metric information from painted humans to the contexts, resulting in metric depth estimations for the original input. Through this annotation-free test-time adaptation, MfH achieves superior zero-shot performance in MMDE, demonstrating its strong generalization ability.

paragraphs: A model can estimate which parts of an image are nearer or farther without knowing their distances in real-world units. This paper separates monocular metric depth estimation into relative depth estimation and scale recovery. The authors attribute difficulty on unseen scenes to scale predictions that depend on scene types encountered during supervised training.

Metric from Human uses generated people as landmarks for recovering scale. A generative painting model inserts humans into the input image, and an existing human mesh recovery model estimates their dimensions. The method then combines that metric information with relative depth predictions and propagates it into the surrounding scene, producing metric depth for the original input.

This process adapts at test time without requiring annotations. It aims to draw scene-independent scale information from the generative model through the painted humans, connecting generalizable relative depth with metric measurements. The authors report superior zero-shot metric depth performance, supporting the approach as a way to improve generalization to scenes beyond those used for supervised metric-depth training.
summary.tldr: Metric from Human inserts generated people into images to recover real-world depth scale without test-time annotations.

title: Metric from Human: Zero-shot Monocular Metric Depth Estimation via Test-time Adaptation

abstract: Multi-instance point cloud registration aims to estimate the pose of all instances of a model point cloud in the whole scene. Existing methods all adopt the strategy of first obtaining the global correspondence and then clustering to obtain the pose of each instance. However, due to the cluttered and occluded objects in the scene, it is difficult to obtain an accurate correspondence between the model point cloud and all instances in the scene. To this end, we propose a simple yet powerful 3D focusing-and-matching network for multi-instance point cloud registration by learning the multiple pair-wise point cloud registration. Specifically, we first present a 3D multi-object focusing module to locate the center of each object and generate object proposals. By using self-attention and cross-attention to associate the model point cloud with structurally similar objects, we can locate potential matching instances by regressing object centers. Then, we propose a 3D dual-masking instance matching module to estimate the pose between the model point cloud and each object proposal. It performs instance mask and overlap mask masks to accurately predict the pair-wise correspondence. Extensive experiments on two public benchmarks, Scan2CAD and ROBI, show that our method achieves a new state-of-the-art performance on the multi-instance point cloud registration task.

Then, we propose a 3D dual-masking instance matching module to estimate the pose between the model point cloud and each object proposal. It performs instance mask and overlap mask masks to accurately predict the pair-wise correspondence. paragraphs: Multi-instance point cloud registration means finding the position and orientation of every occurrence of a reference object in a three-dimensional scene. Clutter and occlusion make this difficult: points belonging to different objects can become hard to distinguish. Existing approaches first establish matches across the whole scene and then group those matches into individual instances.

This paper changes the sequence by locating candidate objects before matching their points. A focusing module uses self-attention and cross-attention to relate the reference point cloud to structurally similar objects. It predicts object centers and produces candidate regions. A second module then estimates a separate pose for each candidate, turning the overall problem into multiple pairwise registration problems.

The matching module uses both an instance mask and an overlap mask to improve point correspondences. These address which points belong to the candidate instance and which participate in the shared region. Experiments on Scan2CAD and ROBI report state-of-the-art results, supporting the effectiveness of focusing on individual objects before detailed matching.
summary.tldr: A two-stage network locates candidate objects before matching their points, improving multi-instance 3D pose estimation on two benchmarks.

title: 3D Focusing-and-Matching Network for Multi-Instance Point Cloud Registration

abstract: While following different technical routes, both low-rank and orthogonal adaptation techniques can efficiently adapt large-scale pre-training models in specific tasks or domains based on a small piece of trainable parameters. In this study, we bridge the gap between these two techniques, proposing a simple but effective adaptation method based on Householder reflections. Given a pre-trained model, our method fine-tunes its layers by multiplying each frozen weight matrix with an orthogonal matrix constructed by a chain of learnable Householder reflections (HRs). This HR-based orthogonal fine-tuning is equivalent to an adaptive low-rank adaptation. Moreover, we show that the orthogonality of the reflection planes corresponding to the HRs impacts the model capacity and regularity. The analysis motivates us to regularize the orthogonality of the HRs, leading to different implementations of the proposed Householder reflection adaptation (HRA) method. Compared with state-of-the-art methods, HRA achieves superior performance with fewer learnable parameters when adapting large language models and conditional image generators. The code of the experiments is available at https://github.com/DaShenZi721/HRA, and the method has been merged into the [PEFT](https://github.com/huggingface/peft) package.

paragraphs: Adapting a large pretrained model can involve learning a small set of parameters while keeping its original weights fixed. This paper connects two approaches to that goal: low-rank adaptation and orthogonal adaptation. It introduces Householder reflection adaptation, or HRA, as a construction that links their mathematical descriptions.

HRA multiplies each frozen weight matrix by an orthogonal matrix built from a sequence of learnable Householder reflections. The authors show that this transformation is equivalent to an adaptive low-rank adaptation. They also analyze how the orthogonality of the reflection planes affects model capacity and regularity, motivating versions of HRA that explicitly regularize those relationships.

In experiments adapting large language models and conditional image generators, HRA achieves better performance than the compared state-of-the-art methods while using fewer trainable parameters. The connection matters because it gives a common interpretation to adaptation techniques that initially appear technically different. It also turns the analysis of reflection geometry into a concrete design choice for efficient fine-tuning.
summary.tldr: Householder reflection adaptation links orthogonal and adaptive low-rank fine-tuning, with reported gains using fewer trainable parameters.

title: Bridging The Gap between Low-rank and Orthogonal Adaptation via Householder Reflection Adaptation

abstract: An important line of research in the field of explainability is to extract a small subset of crucial rationales from the full input. The most widely used criterion for rationale extraction is the maximum mutual information (MMI) criterion. However, in certain datasets, there are spurious features non-causally correlated with the label and also get high mutual information, complicating the loss landscape of MMI. Although some penalty-based methods have been developed to penalize the spurious features (e.g., invariance penalty, intervention penalty, etc) to help MMI work better, these are merely remedial measures. In the optimization objectives of these methods, spurious features are still distinguished from plain noise, which hinders the discovery of causal rationales. This paper aims to develop a new criterion that treats spurious features as plain noise, allowing the model to work on datasets rich in spurious features as if it were working on clean datasets, thereby making rationale extraction easier.We theoretically observe that removing either plain noise or spurious features from the input does not alter the conditional distribution of the remaining components relative to the task label. However, significant changes in the conditional distribution occur only when causal features are eliminated.Based on this discovery, the paper proposes a criterion for \textbf{M}aximizing the \textbf{R}emaining \textbf{D}iscrepancy (MRD). Experiments on six widely used datasets show that our MRD criterion improves rationale quality (measured by the overlap with human-annotated rationales) by up to $10.4\%$ as compared to several recent competitive MMI variants. Code: \url{https://github.com/jugechengzi/Rationalization-MRD}.

paragraphs: Rationale extraction seeks a small part of an input that explains a prediction. A common objective maximizes mutual information with the label, rewarding features that are informative about the answer. The difficulty is that spurious features can also be highly informative without being causal, making them attractive to the same objective.

The paper proposes Maximizing the Remaining Discrepancy, or MRD. Its theoretical observation is that removing noise or spurious features leaves the relevant conditional distribution of the remaining components unchanged, whereas removing causal features produces a substantial change. MRD builds on this distinction to treat spurious features like plain noise during rationale extraction, instead of preserving their special status as label-correlated features.

Experiments on six datasets evaluate rationale quality through overlap with human annotations. The authors report improvements of up to 10.4% over several recent competitive variants of mutual-information-based methods. These findings support the proposed criterion for extracting human-aligned rationales in the evaluated settings. The measured result concerns annotation overlap, while the method's motivation and theoretical analysis concern separating causal information from spurious correlations.
summary.tldr: MRD uses changes caused by feature removal to seek causal rationales, improving overlap with human explanations by up to 10.4% in evaluated datasets.

title: Is the MMI Criterion Necessary for Interpretability? Degenerating Non-causal Features to Plain Noise for Self-Rationalization

abstract: Accurately predicting the future fluid is vital to extensive areas such as meteorology, oceanology, and aerodynamics. However, since the fluid is usually observed from the Eulerian perspective, its moving and intricate dynamics are seriously obscured and confounded in static grids, bringing thorny challenges to the prediction. This paper introduces a new Lagrangian-Eulerian combined paradigm to tackle the tanglesome fluid dynamics. Instead of solely predicting the future based on Eulerian observations, we propose DeepLag to discover hidden Lagrangian dynamics within the fluid by tracking the movements of adaptively sampled key particles. Further, DeepLag presents a new paradigm for fluid prediction, where the Lagrangian movement of the tracked particles is inferred from Eulerian observations, and their accumulated Lagrangian dynamics information is incorporated into global Eulerian evolving features to guide future prediction respectively. Tracking key particles not only provides a transparent and interpretable clue for fluid dynamics but also makes our model free from modeling complex correlations among massive grids for better efficiency. Experimentally, DeepLag excels in three challenging fluid prediction tasks covering 2D and 3D, simulated and real-world fluids. Code is available at this repository: https://github.com/thuml/DeepLag.

paragraphs: Fluid observations often describe what happens at fixed grid locations, an Eulerian view. Moving fluid structures can be difficult to follow in that representation because their motion is spread across changing locations. DeepLag combines this fixed-grid perspective with a Lagrangian perspective, which follows particles as they move through the fluid.

The model adaptively selects key particles and infers their movement from grid-based observations. It then feeds accumulated information about these particle trajectories back into the evolving global grid features used for prediction. The two views therefore play complementary roles: particle tracking captures motion, while grid features retain the broader description of the fluid.

Tracking selected particles gives an interpretable indication of fluid dynamics and reduces the need to model complex relationships among large numbers of grid cells. The authors report strong performance on three challenging prediction tasks spanning two- and three-dimensional fluids and simulated and real-world data. These findings support combining representations of where fluid is observed and how it moves to improve prediction and efficiency.
summary.tldr: DeepLag improves fluid prediction by combining fixed-grid observations with learned trajectories of selected moving particles.

title: DeepLag: Discovering Deep Lagrangian Dynamics for Intuitive Fluid Prediction

abstract: We propose RABBit, a Branch-and-Bound-based verifier for verifying relational properties defined over Deep Neural Networks, such as robustness against universal adversarial perturbations (UAP). Existing SOTA complete $L_{\infty}$-robustness verifiers can not reason about dependencies between multiple executions and, as a result, are imprecise for relational verification. In contrast, existing SOTA relational verifiers only apply a single bounding step and do not utilize any branching strategies to refine the obtained bounds, thus producing imprecise results. We develop the first scalable Branch-and-Bound-based relational verifier, RABBit, which efficiently combines branching over multiple executions with cross-executional bound refinement to utilize relational constraints, gaining substantial precision over SOTA baselines on a wide range of datasets and networks. Our code is at https://github.com/uiuc-focal-lab/RABBit.

Existing SOTA complete $L_{\infty}$-robustness verifiers can not reason about dependencies between multiple executions and, as a result, are imprecise for relational verification. In contrast, existing SOTA relational verifiers only apply a single bounding step and do not utilize any branching strategies to refine the obtained bounds, thus producing imprecise results. paragraphs: Some neural-network properties concern relationships between multiple executions. Robustness against a universal adversarial perturbation is one example, because the same perturbation connects the executions being analyzed. RABBit targets these relational properties, where treating executions independently can discard useful constraints and produce imprecise verification results.

The paper identifies two gaps in existing tools. Complete infinity-norm robustness verifiers do not reason about dependencies across executions, while existing relational verifiers use only one bounding step without branching to refine it. RABBit combines branch-and-bound across multiple executions with bound refinement that uses cross-execution relationships. This gives the verifier a way to progressively sharpen its analysis while retaining relational constraints.

Experiments across a broad range of datasets and networks report substantially greater precision than state-of-the-art baselines. The contribution is a scalable relational verification procedure that brings branching and relational reasoning together. The findings show the value of considering dependencies during refinement when the property being checked spans several executions of a network.
summary.tldr: RABBit improves relational neural-network verification by combining branching across executions with bounds that preserve their dependencies.

title: Relational Verification Leaps Forward with RABBit

abstract: In this paper, we derive *entrywise* error bounds for low-rank approximations of kernel matrices obtained using the truncated eigen-decomposition (or singular value decomposition). While this approximation is well-known to be optimal with respect to the spectral and Frobenius norm error, little is known about the statistical behaviour of individual entries. Our error bounds fill this gap. A key technical innovation is a delocalisation result for the eigenvectors of the kernel matrix corresponding to small eigenvalues, which takes inspiration from the field of Random Matrix Theory. Finally, we validate our theory with an empirical study of a collection of synthetic and real-world datasets.

While this approximation is well-known to be optimal with respect to the spectral and Frobenius norm error, little is known about the statistical behaviour of individual entries. Our error bounds fill this gap. A key technical innovation is a delocalisation result for the eigenvectors of the kernel matrix corresponding to small eigenvalues, which takes inspiration from the field of Random Matrix Theory. Finally, we validate our theory with an empirical study of a collection of synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: A low-rank approximation compresses a kernel matrix by retaining only part of its eigen-decomposition or singular value decomposition. This familiar construction is optimal under spectral and Frobenius error measures. Those whole-matrix criteria, however, leave a separate statistical question: how accurately does the approximation preserve each individual entry of the original matrix?

The paper derives error bounds that address entries directly. Its main technical ingredient is a delocalization result for eigenvectors associated with small eigenvalues. Delocalization describes how these vectors spread their weight across coordinates. Understanding that spread helps the analysis connect the components omitted by truncation with the errors appearing at individual matrix locations.

The authors draw inspiration from random matrix theory and evaluate their theoretical findings using synthetic and real-world datasets. The contribution is a finer view of an established approximation method, extending analysis beyond aggregate error criteria. It gives a way to study local approximation accuracy even when the method's optimality at the level of the entire matrix is already understood.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds individual-entry errors in truncated kernel-matrix approximations using a new eigenvector delocalization result.

title: Entrywise error bounds for low-rank approximations of kernel matrices

abstract: When reading long-form text, human cognition is complex and structurized. While large language models (LLMs) process input contexts through a causal and sequential perspective, this approach can potentially limit their ability to handle intricate and complex inputs effectively. To enhance LLM’s cognition capability, this paper presents a novel concept of context structurization. Specifically, we transform the plain, unordered contextual sentences into well-ordered and hierarchically structurized elements. By doing so, LLMs can better grasp intricate and extended contexts through precise attention and information-seeking along the organized structures. Extensive evaluations are conducted across various model architectures and sizes (including a series of auto-regressive LLMs as well as BERT-like masking models) on a diverse set of NLP tasks (e.g., context-based question-answering, exhaustive hallucination evaluation, and passage-level dense retrieval). Empirical results show consistent and significant performance gains afforded by a single-round structurization. In particular, we boost the open-sourced LLaMA2-70B model to achieve comparable performance against GPT-3.5-Turbo as the halluci- nation evaluator. Besides, we show the feasibility of distilling advanced LLMs’ language processing abilities to a smaller yet effective StruXGPT-7B to execute structurization, addressing the practicality of our approach. Code is available at https://github.com/alibaba/struxgpt.

title: Enhancing LLM’s Cognition via Structurization

abstract: Multimodal representation learning techniques typically require paired samples to learn shared representations, but collecting paired samples can be challenging in fields like biology, where measurement devices often destroy the samples. This paper presents an approach to address the challenge of aligning unpaired samples across disparate modalities in multimodal representation learning. We draw an analogy between potential outcomes in causal inference and potential views in multimodal observations, allowing us to leverage Rubin's framework to estimate a common space for matching samples. Our approach assumes experimentally perturbed samples by treatments, and uses this to estimate a propensity score from each modality. We show that the propensity score encapsulates all shared information between a latent state and treatment, and can be used to define a distance between samples. We experiment with two alignment techniques that leverage this distance---shared nearest neighbours (SNN) and optimal transport (OT) matching---and find that OT matching results in significant improvements over state-of-the-art alignment approaches in on synthetic multi-modal tasks, in real-world data from NeurIPS Multimodal Single-Cell Integration Challenge, and on a single cell microscopy to expression prediction task.

paragraphs: Learning across measurement types often relies on paired observations of the same sample. In biology, some measurements destroy the sample, making such pairing difficult. This paper proposes aligning unpaired observations by using information about experimental treatments, drawing a connection between missing views in multimodal data and potential outcomes in causal inference.

The approach assumes that samples have been experimentally perturbed by treatments. It estimates a propensity score separately from each modality and uses these scores to define distances between samples. The authors show that the score captures all information shared between the latent state and treatment. This supplies a common matching basis tied to treatment-related information across otherwise different measurement spaces.

The paper evaluates shared-nearest-neighbor and optimal-transport matching using that distance. Optimal transport produces significant improvements over leading alignment approaches on synthetic tasks, data from the NeurIPS Multimodal Single-Cell Integration Challenge, and a microscopy-to-expression prediction task. These results support treatment-derived propensity scores as useful alignment signals in the experimentally perturbed settings studied.
summary.tldr: Treatment-derived propensity scores provide a shared distance for aligning unpaired modalities, with strong results using optimal-transport matching.

title: Propensity Score Alignment of Unpaired Multimodal Data

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved unprecedented performance by leveraging vast pretraining corpora, yet their performance remains suboptimal in knowledge-intensive domains such as medicine and scientific research, where high factual precision is required. While synthetic data provides a promising avenue for augmenting domain knowledge, existing methods frequently generate redundant samples that do not align with the model’s true knowledge gaps. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel Structural Entropy-guided Knowledge Navigator (SENATOR) framework that addresses the intrinsic knowledge deficiencies of LLMs. Our approach employs the Structure Entropy (SE) metric to quantify uncertainty along knowledge graph paths and leverages Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to selectively explore regions where the model lacks domain-specific knowledge. Guided by these insights, the framework generates targeted synthetic data for supervised fine-tuning, enabling continuous self-improvement. Experimental results on LLaMA-3 and Qwen2 across multiple domain-specific benchmarks show that SENATOR effectively detects and repairs knowledge deficiencies, achieving notable performance improvements.

paragraphs: Synthetic data can strengthen domain knowledge, but generating many redundant examples may miss a model’s actual weaknesses. SENATOR, the Structural Entropy-guided Knowledge Navigator, aims to direct data generation toward those deficiencies.

The framework quantifies uncertainty along knowledge-graph paths using structural entropy and explores them with Monte Carlo tree search. The selected regions guide targeted synthetic examples for supervised fine-tuning, creating a cycle of identifying gaps and updating the model.

Experiments with LLaMA-3 and Qwen2 on domain-specific benchmarks show improved performance and effective identification of knowledge weaknesses. The contribution is a selection mechanism for synthetic supervision rather than simply increasing its volume. Its application to knowledge-intensive fields is motivated by factual precision, while benchmark gains alone do not establish clinical reliability or eliminate the need to check generated training facts.
summary.tldr: SENATOR targets synthetic training data at knowledge-graph regions where a model appears uncertain.

title: Structural Entropy Guided Agent for Detecting and Repairing Knowledge Deficiencies in LLMs

abstract: We study online learning in finite-horizon episodic Markov decision processes (MDPs) under the challenging \textit{aggregate bandit feedback} model, where the learner observes only the cumulative loss incurred in each episode, rather than individual losses at each state-action pair. While prior work in this setting has focused exclusively on worst-case analysis, we initiate the study of \textit{best-of-both-worlds} (BOBW) algorithms that achieve low regret in both stochastic and adversarial environments. We propose the first BOBW algorithms for episodic tabular MDPs with aggregate bandit feedback. In the case of known transitions, our algorithms achieve $O(\log T)$ regret in stochastic settings and ${O}(\sqrt{T})$ regret in adversarial ones. Importantly, we also establish matching lower bounds, showing the optimality of our algorithms in this setting. We further extend our approach to unknown-transition settings by incorporating confidence-based techniques. Our results rely on a combination of FTRL over occupancy measures, self-bounding techniques, and new loss estimators inspired by recent advances in online shortest path problems. Along the way, we also provide the first individual-gap-dependent lower bounds and demonstrate near-optimal BOBW algorithms for shortest path problems with bandit feedback.

paragraphs: Learning which decisions work is difficult when feedback arrives only as a total loss after an entire episode. The learner cannot directly see which individual actions caused that loss. This paper studies that setting in finite-horizon, tabular Markov decision processes, aiming for algorithms that perform well both when losses follow a stochastic pattern and when they are adversarial.

The proposed algorithms combine a decision-making framework based on occupancy measures with new estimators that extract useful learning signals from episode totals. Occupancy measures describe how frequently a policy visits different state-action combinations. Additional self-bounding arguments support sharper guarantees in stochastic environments, while confidence-based techniques extend the approach to unknown transitions.

With known transitions, the algorithms achieve regret growing as O(log T) in stochastic settings and O(√T) in adversarial settings. Matching lower bounds establish optimality in that setting. The unknown-transition extension is a separate contribution; the abstract does not assign it these same rates. Related results also provide individual-gap-dependent lower bounds and near-optimal algorithms for shortest-path learning with bandit feedback.
summary.tldr: New algorithms learn from episode-total losses while achieving optimal stochastic and adversarial regret rates when transitions are known.

title: Adapting to Stochastic and Adversarial Losses in Episodic MDPs with Aggregate Bandit Feedback

abstract: Curriculum learning has emerged as an effective strategy to enhance the training efficiency and generalization of machine learning models. However, its theoretical underpinnings remain relatively underexplored. In this work, we develop a theoretical framework for curriculum learning based on biased regularized empirical risk minimization (RERM), identifying conditions under which curriculum learning provably improves generalization. We introduce a sufficient condition that characterizes a "good" curriculum and analyze a multi-task curriculum framework, where solving a sequence of convex tasks can facilitate better generalization. We also demonstrate how these theoretical insights translate to practical benefits when using stochastic gradient descent (SGD) as an optimization method. Beyond convex settings, we explore the utility of curriculum learning for non-convex tasks. Empirical evaluations on synthetic datasets and MNIST validate our theoretical findings and highlight the practical efficacy of curriculum-based training.

paragraphs: Curriculum learning organizes training into a sequence intended to make later learning more effective. This paper asks when that organization can improve generalization, moving beyond the observation that curricula sometimes help. It develops a theoretical framework based on biased regularized empirical risk minimization.

The authors identify a sufficient condition for a good curriculum and analyze a multi-task setting in which solving a sequence of convex tasks can improve generalization. A sufficient condition establishes circumstances where an improvement is provable; it does not establish that every beneficial curriculum must satisfy that condition. The analysis also connects these insights to practical training with stochastic gradient descent.

The paper further explores curriculum learning for non-convex tasks and evaluates the approach on synthetic datasets and MNIST. Those experiments support the theoretical findings and demonstrate practical benefits in the tested settings. The contribution is an account of conditions under which task sequencing helps, paired with evidence that the theoretical perspective can inform actual optimization. Its claims remain tied to the analyzed conditions and evaluated training problems.
summary.tldr: A theoretical framework identifies sufficient conditions for curricula to improve generalization and connects them with practical training results.

title: When Does Curriculum Learning Help? A Theoretical Perspective

abstract: Worldwide image geolocalization—the task of predicting GPS coordinates from images taken anywhere on Earth—poses a fundamental challenge due to the vast diversity in visual content across regions. While recent approaches adopt a two-stage pipeline of retrieving candidates and selecting the best match, they typically rely on simplistic similarity heuristics and point-wise supervision, failing to model spatial relationships among candidates. In this paper, we propose **GeoRanker**, a distance-aware ranking framework that leverages large vision-language models to jointly encode query–candidate interactions and predict geographic proximity. In addition, we introduce a *multi-order distance loss* that ranks both absolute and relative distances, enabling the model to reason over structured spatial relationships. To support this, we curate GeoRanking, the first dataset explicitly designed for geographic ranking tasks with multimodal candidate information. GeoRanker achieves state-of-the-art results on two well-established benchmarks (IM2GPS3K and YFCC4K), significantly outperforming current best methods. We also release our code, checkpoint, and dataset online for ease of reproduction.

paragraphs: Predicting where an image was taken requires distinguishing visually plausible places across the world. Many approaches first retrieve candidate locations and then select a match. GeoRanker focuses on this selection stage, where simple similarity scores and separate judgments of individual candidates can miss geographic relationships between the options.

The framework uses a large vision-language model to jointly represent interactions between the query image and its candidates and predict geographic proximity. Its multi-order distance loss trains the model to rank both absolute and relative distances. This makes structured spatial relationships part of the learning objective, rather than relying only on whether a candidate looks similar.

The authors also introduce GeoRanking, a dataset designed specifically for geographic ranking with multimodal candidate information. GeoRanker achieves state-of-the-art results on IM2GPS3K and YFCC4K, significantly outperforming the strongest existing methods in those evaluations. The results support treating candidate selection as a geographic ranking problem, with supervision that captures how the possible locations relate spatially to the query and to one another.
summary.tldr: GeoRanker improves image geolocation by learning to rank candidate locations using absolute and relative geographic distances.

title: GeoRanker: Distance-Aware Ranking for Worldwide Image Geolocalization

abstract: Online structured prediction is a task of sequentially predicting outputs with complex structures based on inputs and past observations, encompassing online classification. Recent studies showed that in the full-information setting, we can achieve finite bounds on the *surrogate regret*, *i.e.,* the extra target loss relative to the best possible surrogate loss. In practice, however, full-information feedback is often unrealistic as it requires immediate access to the whole structure of complex outputs. Motivated by this, we propose algorithms that work with less demanding feedback, *bandit* and *delayed* feedback. For bandit feedback, by using a standard inverse-weighted gradient estimator, we achieve a surrogate regret bound of $O(\sqrt{KT})$ for the time horizon $T$ and the size of the output set $K$. However, $K$ can be extremely large when outputs are highly complex, resulting in an undesirable bound. To address this issue, we propose another algorithm that achieves a surrogate regret bound of $O(T^{2/3})$, which is independent of $K$. This is achieved with a carefully designed pseudo-inverse matrix estimator. Furthermore, we numerically compare the performance of these algorithms, as well as existing ones. Regarding delayed feedback, we provide algorithms and regret analyses that cover various scenarios, including full-information and bandit feedback, as well as fixed and variable delays.

paragraphs: Online structured prediction involves repeatedly predicting complex outputs and learning from feedback. Existing theory can assume immediate access to complete feedback, an expensive requirement when outputs have substantial structure. This paper develops algorithms for settings where feedback is partial, delayed, or both, and studies surrogate regret: extra target loss relative to the best achievable surrogate loss.

For bandit feedback, an inverse-weighted gradient estimator yields a regret bound of O(sqrt(KT)), where K is the number of possible outputs and T is the number of rounds. That dependence becomes troublesome when structured outputs create a huge output space. A second algorithm uses a carefully constructed pseudoinverse matrix estimator to obtain an O(T^(2/3)) bound independent of K.

These bounds expose a tradeoff between dependence on output-space size and dependence on the time horizon. The paper also compares algorithms numerically and analyzes delayed feedback across full-information and bandit settings, including fixed and varying delays. Its contribution is to extend performance guarantees to feedback conditions that demand less immediate information from the learning environment.
summary.tldr: The paper gives structured-prediction algorithms and regret guarantees for partial or delayed feedback, including a bandit bound independent of output-space size.

title: Bandit and Delayed Feedback in Online Structured Prediction

abstract: Continual learning is often motivated by the idea, known as the big world hypothesis, that the "world is bigger" than the agent. Recent problem formulations capture this idea by explicitly constraining an agent relative to the environment. These constraints lead to solutions in which the agent continually adapts to best use its limited capacity, rather than converging to a fixed solution. However, explicit constraints can be ad hoc, difficult to incorporate, and limiting to the effectiveness of scaling up the agent's capacity. In this paper, we characterize a problem setting in which an agent, regardless of its capacity, is implicitly constrained by being embedded in the environment. In particular, we introduce a computationally-embedded perspective that represents an embedded agent as an automaton simulated within a universal (formal) computer. We prove that such an automaton is implicitly constrained and that it is equivalent to an agent that interacts with a partially observable Markov decision process over a countably infinite state-space. We then propose an objective for this setting, which we call interactivity, that measures an agent's ability to continually adapt its behaviour and to continually learn new predictions. We develop a reinforcement learning algorithm for maximizing interactivity and a synthetic benchmark to experimentation on continual learning. Our results indicate that deep nonlinear networks struggle to sustain interactivity whereas deep linear networks can achieve higher interactivity as capacity increases.

Formalizing this idea through explicit resource limits can require arbitrary choices and complicate scaling. This paper instead studies an agent whose limitations follow from being computationally embedded inside its environment, regardless of how much capacity the agent has.

The authors represent the agent as an automaton simulated within a universal formal computer. They prove that this embedding implicitly constrains the agent and is equivalent to interaction with a partially observable Markov decision process over countably infinitely many states. They then define interactivity, an objective measuring the ability to keep adapting behavior and learning new predictions.

These findings concern the proposed setting and benchmark, offering a formal way to study sustained adaptation and an empirical distinction between the tested network types.
summary.tldr: A computationally embedded agent model formalizes inherent limits and introduces interactivity as an objective for sustained adaptation and prediction learning.

title: The World Is Bigger! A Computationally-Embedded Perspective on the Big World Hypothesis

abstract: Efficiently solving constrained optimization problems is crucial for numerous real-world applications, yet traditional solvers are often computationally prohibitive for real-time use. Machine learning-based approaches have emerged as a promising alternative to provide approximate solutions at faster speeds, but they struggle to strictly enforce constraints, leading to infeasible solutions in practice. To address this, we propose the Feasibility-Seeking Neural Network (FSNet), which integrates a feasibility-seeking step directly into its solution procedure to ensure constraint satisfaction. This feasibility-seeking step solves an unconstrained optimization problem that minimizes constraint violations in a differentiable manner, enabling end-to-end training and providing guarantees on feasibility and convergence. Our experiments across a range of different optimization problems, including both smooth/nonsmooth and convex/nonconvex problems, demonstrate that FSNet can provide feasible solutions with solution quality comparable to (or in some cases better than) traditional solvers, at significantly faster speeds.

paragraphs: A constrained optimization solution must satisfy its rules as well as achieve a good objective value. Traditional solvers can be too expensive for real-time use, while faster learned approximations may violate constraints. FSNet tackles this tension by making a feasibility-seeking operation part of the neural network’s solution procedure.

That operation solves an unconstrained optimization problem whose objective measures constraint violations. In effect, the procedure explicitly seeks to remove violations while remaining differentiable, allowing it to participate in end-to-end training. The authors provide feasibility and convergence guarantees for the approach. This connects the speed-oriented learned solution process with an explicit mechanism for enforcing the original problem’s constraints.

Experiments cover smooth and nonsmooth problems as well as convex and nonconvex ones. FSNet produces feasible solutions with quality comparable to traditional solvers, and sometimes better quality, at substantially faster speeds. These results suggest that embedding feasibility into the solution process can make learned optimization more practically useful when a fast answer must also obey the problem’s requirements.
summary.tldr: FSNet embeds a differentiable feasibility-seeking step into learned optimization to produce fast solutions with constraint-satisfaction guarantees.

title: FSNet: Feasibility-Seeking Neural Network for Constrained Optimization with Guarantees

abstract: Sparse and low-rank matrix composite approximation has emerged as a promising paradigm for compressing large language models (LLMs), offering a more flexible pruning structure than conventional methods based solely on sparse matrices. The significant variation in weight redundancy across layers, along with the differing rank and sparsity structures of weight matrices, makes identifying the globally optimal pruning structure extremely challenging. Existing methods often depend on uniform or manually designed heuristic rules to allocate weight sparsity across layers, subsequently compressing each matrix using matrix approximation techniques. Given the above theoretical difficulty in global compression of LLMs and the limited computational and data resources available compared to the training phase, we argue that a collaboration between learning and matrix approximation is essential for effective compression. In this paper, we propose a novel LLM compression framework based on generalized bilevel optimization that naturally formulates an effective collaborative mechanism. Specifically, the outer loop frames the weight allocation task as a probabilistic optimization problem, enabling the automatic learning of both layer-wise sparsities and matrix-wise retained ranks, while the inner loop solves the corresponding sparsity and rank-constrained model compression problem via matrix approximation. Our main technical contributions include two key innovations for efficiently solving this bilevel optimization problem. First, we introduce a truncated Gaussian prior-based probabilistic parameterization integrated with a policy gradient estimator, which avoids expensive backpropagation and stabilizes the optimization process. Second, we design an adapted QR-based matrix approximation algorithm that significantly accelerates inner loop computations. Extensive experiments on Phi-3 and the LLama-2/3 family demonstrate the effectiveness of our method. Notably, it maintains over 95\% zero-shot accuracy under 50\% sparsity and achieves up to 2× inference speedup.

summary.tldr: A two-loop compression framework learns sparsity and rank allocations while efficiently constructing the corresponding compressed language-model weights.

title: Compress Large Language Models via Collaboration Between Learning and Matrix Approximation

abstract: Earth observation foundation models have shown strong generalization across multiple Earth observation tasks, but their robustness under real-world perturbations remains underexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce REOBench, the first comprehensive benchmark for evaluating the robustness of Earth observation foundation models across six tasks and twelve types of image corruptions, including both appearance-based and geometric perturbations. To ensure realistic and fine-grained evaluation, our benchmark focuses on high-resolution optical remote sensing images, which are widely used in critical applications such as urban planning and disaster response. We conduct a systematic evaluation of a broad range of models trained using masked image modeling, contrastive learning, and vision-language pre-training paradigms. Our results reveal that (1) existing Earth observation foundation models experience significant performance degradation when exposed to input corruptions. (2) The severity of degradation varies across tasks, model architectures, backbone sizes, and types of corruption, with performance drop varying from less than 1% to over 25%. (3) Vision-language models show enhanced robustness, particularly in multimodal tasks. REOBench underscores the vulnerability of current Earth observation foundation models to real-world corruptions and provides actionable insights for developing more robust and reliable models.
