paragraphs: Earth observation foundation models can generalize across tasks, but that does not establish how well they handle corrupted inputs. REOBench evaluates this question using high-resolution optical remote sensing imagery. It covers six tasks and twelve corruption types, including changes to image appearance and geometry.

The benchmark compares models pretrained through masked image modeling, contrastive learning, and vision-language objectives. This design supports analysis across training approaches as well as architectures and backbone sizes. Its focus on high-resolution optical imagery connects the evaluation to applications such as urban planning and disaster response, where robustness is relevant to model reliability.

The size of the decline depends on the task, architecture, backbone size, and corruption type. Vision-language models show stronger robustness, particularly on multimodal tasks. These findings provide a more differentiated view of reliability than clean-input performance alone and identify factors associated with stronger or weaker resistance to input corruption.
summary.tldr: REOBench finds substantial, task-dependent robustness gaps in Earth observation foundation models across twelve image corruption types.

title: REOBench: Benchmarking Robustness of Earth Observation Foundation Models

abstract: Algorithmic fairness has become a central topic in machine learning, and mitigating disparities across different subpopulations has emerged as a rapidly growing research area. In this paper, we systematically study the classification of functional data under fairness constraints, ensuring the disparity level of the classifier is controlled below a pre-specified threshold. We propose a unified framework for fairness-aware functional classification, tackling an infinite-dimensional functional space, addressing key challenges from the absence of density ratios and intractability of posterior probabilities, and discussing unique phenomena in functional classification. We further design a post-processing algorithm Fair Functional Linear Discriminant Analysis classifier (Fair-FLDA), which targets at homoscedastic Gaussian processes and achieves fairness via group-wise thresholding. Under weak structural assumptions on eigenspace, theoretical guarantees on fairness and excess risk controls are established. As a byproduct, our results cover the excess risk control of the standard FLDA as a special case, which, to the best of our knowledge, is first time seen. Our theoretical findings are complemented by extensive numerical experiments on synthetic and real datasets, highlighting the practicality of our designed algorithm.

paragraphs: Functional classification works with inputs that are entire functions, creating an infinite-dimensional learning problem. This paper asks how to classify such inputs while keeping disparity across subpopulations below a chosen threshold. Standard tools become difficult to use because density ratios may be unavailable and posterior probabilities can be intractable.

The authors develop a unified framework for this setting and introduce Fair Functional Linear Discriminant Analysis, or Fair-FLDA. The algorithm targets homoscedastic Gaussian processes, which share a covariance structure, and applies group-specific decision thresholds as a post-processing step. Those thresholds provide a way to adjust fairness in the classifier's decisions.

Under weak structural assumptions on the eigenspace, the paper establishes guarantees controlling both fairness and excess classification risk. Its risk analysis also includes standard FLDA as a special case. Numerical experiments on synthetic and real datasets complement the theory, supporting the practicality of the algorithm within the functional-data setting and assumptions studied.
summary.tldr: Fair-FLDA uses group-specific thresholds to control disparity in functional classification, with fairness and risk guarantees under stated structural assumptions.

title: Fairness-aware Bayes Optimal Functional Classification

abstract: Initialization plays a critical role in Deep Neural Network training, directly influencing convergence, stability, and generalization. Common approaches such as Glorot and He initializations rely on randomness, which can produce uneven weight distributions across layer connections. In this paper, we introduce the Sinusoidal initialization, a novel deterministic method that employs sinusoidal functions to construct structured weight matrices expressly to improve the spread and balance of weights throughout the network while simultaneously fostering a more uniform, well‑conditioned distribution of neuron activation states from the very first forward pass. Because Sinusoidal initialization begins with weights and activations that are already evenly and efficiently utilized, it delivers consistently faster convergence, greater training stability, and higher final accuracy across a wide range of models, including convolutional neural networks, vision transformers, and large language models. On average, our experiments show an increase of 4.8 % in final validation accuracy and 20.9 % in convergence speed. By replacing randomness with structure, this initialization provides a stronger and more reliable foundation for Deep Learning systems.

paragraphs: A neural network's starting weights influence how reliably and quickly it learns. This paper introduces a deterministic alternative that constructs initial weight matrices using sinusoidal functions.

The method is designed to distribute weights more evenly while producing balanced, well-conditioned neuron activations from the first forward pass. Its rationale is that both connections and activations should be usefully engaged at the start of training. Structured initialization therefore changes the network's initial state before any learning updates take place.

Experiments across convolutional networks, vision transformers, and large language models report consistently faster convergence, improved training stability, and higher final accuracy. The authors report average increases of 4.8% in final validation accuracy and 20.9% in convergence speed. These are empirical findings across the evaluated models. They support the paper's argument that deliberately structured initial weights can provide a stronger starting point for training across several model families.
summary.tldr: Sinusoidal initialization uses deterministic structured weights and reports improved accuracy, convergence speed, and stability across several neural network families.

title: Sinusoidal Initialization, Time for a New Start

abstract: Counterfactual explanations play a pivotal role in explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) by offering intuitive, human-understandable alternatives that elucidate machine learning model decisions. Despite their significance, existing methods for generating counterfactuals often require constant access to the predictive model, involve computationally intensive optimization for each instance, and lack the flexibility to adapt to new user-defined constraints without retraining. In this paper, we propose DiCoFlex, a novel model-agnostic, conditional generative framework that produces multiple diverse counterfactuals in a single forward pass. Leveraging conditional normalizing flows trained solely on labeled data, DiCoFlex addresses key limitations by enabling real-time, user-driven customization of constraints such as sparsity and actionability at inference time. Extensive experiments on standard benchmark datasets show that DiCoFlex outperforms existing methods in terms of validity, diversity, proximity, and constraint adherence, making it a practical and scalable solution for counterfactual generation in sensitive decision-making domains.

paragraphs: Counterfactual explanations describe alternative inputs that would lead to a different model decision. Their usefulness depends on offering changes a person can understand and potentially act on. Many existing generators repeatedly query the predictive model, solve a costly optimization problem for each case, or require retraining when users introduce new constraints.

DiCoFlex uses a conditional generative model to produce several diverse alternatives in one forward pass. Its conditional normalizing flows are trained solely on labeled data, supporting a model-agnostic approach. Users can adjust constraints during inference, including sparsity, which concerns how many features change, and actionability, which concerns whether the proposed changes are usable.

On standard benchmark datasets, the method outperforms existing approaches in validity, diversity, proximity, and adherence to constraints. Together, these criteria assess whether alternatives achieve the desired decision, differ from one another, stay close to the original case, and respect user requirements. The contribution combines efficient generation with flexible control, making counterfactual explanations more adaptable to individual decision-making needs.
summary.tldr: DiCoFlex generates diverse counterfactual explanations in one pass while letting users change constraints at inference time without retraining.

title: DiCoFlex: Model-Agnostic Diverse Counterfactuals with Flexible Control

abstract: We propose Equivariance by Contrast (EbC) to learn equivariant embeddings from observation pairs $(\mathbf{y}, g \cdot \mathbf{y})$, where $g$ is drawn from a finite group acting on the data. Our method jointly learns a latent space and a group representation in which group actions correspond to invertible linear maps—without relying on group-specific inductive biases. We validate our approach on the infinite dSprites dataset with structured transformations defined by the finite group $G:= (R_m \times \mathbb{Z}_n \times \mathbb{Z}_n)$, combining discrete rotations and periodic translations. The resulting embeddings exhibit high-fidelity equivariance, with group operations faithfully reproduced in latent space. On synthetic data, we further validate the approach on the non-abelian orthogonal group $O(n)$ and the general linear group $GL(n)$. We also provide a theoretical proof for identifiability. While broad evaluation across diverse group types on real-world data remains future work, our results constitute the first successful demonstration of general-purpose encoder-only equivariant learning from group action observations alone, including non-trivial non-abelian groups and a product group motivated by modeling affine equivariances in computer vision.

paragraphs: An equivariant representation changes predictably when its input undergoes a transformation. Equivariance by Contrast learns such representations from pairs containing an observation and a transformed version. The proposed setup uses actions from a finite group and avoids building group-specific structural assumptions into the encoder.

The method jointly learns an embedding space and a representation of transformations as invertible linear maps. This means transformations of the data can be reproduced through corresponding operations on embeddings. The authors also provide an identifiability proof, giving theoretical support for recovering the intended structure from observations.

Experiments on infinite dSprites combine discrete rotations with periodic translations and produce embeddings that reproduce group operations with high fidelity. Synthetic experiments additionally examine the orthogonal and general linear groups, including non-commuting transformations. The authors present these results as a first demonstration of general-purpose, encoder-only equivariant learning from group-action observations alone. They explicitly leave broad evaluation across diverse groups on real-world data for future work, so the empirical evidence is centered on the reported structured and synthetic settings.
summary.tldr: Equivariance by Contrast jointly learns embeddings and linear transformation rules from observation pairs, with identifiability theory and structured-data validation.

title: Equivariance by Contrast: Identifiable Equivariant Embeddings from Unlabeled Finite Group Actions

abstract: Survey papers are foundational to the scholarly progress of research communities, offering structured overviews that guide both novices and experts across disciplines. However, the recent surge of AI-generated surveys, especially enabled by large language models (LLMs), has transformed this traditionally labor-intensive genre into a low-effort, high-volume output. While such automation lowers entry barriers, it also introduces a critical threat: the phenomenon we term the "survey paper DDoS attack" to the research community. This refers to the unchecked proliferation of superficially comprehensive but often redundant, low-quality, or even hallucinated survey manuscripts, which floods preprint platforms, overwhelms researchers, and erodes trust in the scientific record. In this position paper, we argue that we must stop uploading massive amounts of AI-generated survey papers (i.e., survey paper DDoS attack) to the research community, by instituting strong norms for AI-assisted review writing. We call for restoring expert oversight and transparency in AI usage and, moreover, developing new infrastructures such as Dynamic Live Surveys, community-maintained, version-controlled repositories that blend automated updates with human curation. Through quantitative trend analysis, quality audits, and cultural impact discussion, we show that safeguarding the integrity of surveys is no longer optional but imperative to the research community.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that high-volume AI-generated survey papers can overwhelm the research community's ability to assess and use scholarly summaries. The concern is the combined burden on researchers and trust in the scientific record.

The authors support their argument through quantitative trend analysis, quality audits, and discussion of cultural effects. They call for stronger norms around AI-assisted review writing, including expert oversight and transparency about AI use. These proposals address the tension between lowering the effort needed to produce a survey and maintaining the judgment that makes surveys valuable.

The paper also proposes Dynamic Live Surveys: community-maintained repositories with version control that combine automated updates with human curation. This would make survey knowledge an ongoing collaborative resource. The contribution is a diagnosis and a set of community proposals, emphasizing that useful automation needs processes for expert review, maintenance, and accountability.
summary.tldr: This position paper calls for expert oversight, transparent AI use, and community-maintained live surveys to address low-quality survey proliferation.

title: Stop DDoS Attacking the Research Community with AI-Generated Survey Papers

abstract: Spatial location and molecular interactions have long been linked to the connectivity patterns of neural circuits. Yet, at the macroscale of human brain networks, the interplay between spatial position, gene expression, and connectivity remains incompletely understood. Recent efforts to map the human transcriptome and connectome have yielded spatially resolved brain atlases, however modeling the relationship between high-dimensional transcriptomic data and connectivity while accounting for inherent spatial confounds presents a significant challenge. In this paper, we present the first deep learning approaches for predicting whole-brain functional connectivity from gene expression and regional spatial coordinates, including our proposed Spatiomolecular Transformer (SMT). SMT explicitly models biological context by tokenizing genes based on their transcription start site (TSS) order to capture multi-scale genomic organization, and incorporating regional 3D spatial location via a dedicated context [CLS] token within its multi-head self-attention mechanism. We rigorously benchmark context-aware neural networks, including SMT and a single-gene resolution Multilayer-Perceptron (MLP), to established rules-based and bilinear methods. Crucially, to ensure that learned relationships in any model are not mere artifacts of spatial proximity, we introduce novel spatiomolecular null maps, preserving both spatial and transcriptomic autocorrelation. Context-aware neural networks outperform linear methods, significantly exceed our stringent null shuffle models, and generalize across diverse connectomic datasets and parcellation resolutions. Together, these findings demonstrate a strong, predictable link between the spatial distributions of gene expression and functional brain network architecture, and establish a rigorously validated deep learning framework for decoding this relationship. Code to reproduce our results is available at: github.com/neuroinfolab/GeneEx2Conn.

paragraphs: This paper predicts functional connections across the brain from regional gene expression and spatial coordinates. A central challenge is that nearby brain regions can share both expression patterns and connectivity characteristics. A model might therefore appear to discover a meaningful molecular relationship while mostly exploiting spatial proximity.

The proposed Spatiomolecular Transformer organizes gene tokens by transcription-start-site order, allowing attention to reflect genomic organization at multiple scales. A dedicated context token introduces each region's three-dimensional position. The authors benchmark this model and other context-aware networks, including a single-gene-resolution multilayer perceptron, against established rules-based and bilinear approaches.

To test whether predictions go beyond spatial artifacts, the study introduces null maps that preserve both spatial and transcriptomic autocorrelation. Context-aware networks outperform linear methods, significantly exceed these stringent shuffled controls, and generalize across connectomic datasets and region-partitioning resolutions. The findings support a strong predictive relationship between the spatial distribution of gene expression and functional connectivity. The structured controls are crucial because they make that relationship harder to explain through proximity alone.
summary.tldr: Context-aware networks predict brain connectivity from gene expression and location, outperforming controls that preserve spatial and transcriptomic structure.

title: Predicting Functional Brain Connectivity with Context-Aware Deep Neural Networks

abstract: We introduce a framework for Thompson sampling (TS) contextual bandit algorithms, in which the algorithm's ability to quantify uncertainty and make decisions depends on the quality of a generative model that is learned offline. Instead of viewing uncertainty in the environment as arising from unobservable latent parameters, our algorithm treats uncertainty as stemming from missing, but potentially observable outcomes (including both future and counterfactual outcomes). If these outcomes were all observed, one could simply make decisions using an "oracle" policy fit on the complete dataset. Inspired by this conceptualization, at each decision-time, our algorithm uses a generative model to probabilistically impute missing outcomes, fits a policy using the imputed complete dataset, and uses that policy to select the next action. We formally show that this algorithm is a generative formulation of TS and establish a state-of-the-art regret bound. Notably, our regret bound depends on the generative model only through the quality of its offline prediction loss, and applies to any method of fitting the "oracle" policy.

paragraphs: This paper reframes uncertainty in contextual bandit decisions around missing outcomes. These include results that have not happened yet and counterfactual results from actions that were not chosen. If every such outcome were available, a decision-maker could fit an oracle policy to the complete dataset and use it to choose actions.

The proposed algorithm approximates this situation with a generative model trained offline. At each decision, it samples plausible values for missing outcomes, fits a policy to the resulting completed dataset, and follows that policy for the next action. Different sampled completions represent different possibilities about the environment, allowing uncertainty to influence action selection through the generated data.

The authors formally establish this procedure as a generative version of Thompson sampling and derive a state-of-the-art regret bound. The bound depends on the generative model through its offline prediction loss and accommodates any method for fitting the oracle policy. This connects decision quality to a measurable prediction objective while allowing flexibility in the policy-fitting procedure.
summary.tldr: The paper formulates Thompson sampling by generating missing outcomes and links its regret guarantee to offline predictive quality.

title: Contextual Thompson Sampling via Generation of Missing Data

abstract: Multimodal dataset distillation aims to synthesize a small set of image-text pairs that enables efficient training of large-scale vision-language models. While dataset distillation has shown promise in unimodal tasks, extending it to multimodal contrastive learning presents key challenges: learning cross-modal alignment and managing the high computational cost of large encoders. Prior approaches address scalability by freezing the text encoder and update only the image encoder and text projection layer. However, we find this severely limits semantic alignment and becomes a bottleneck for performance scaling. We propose CovMatch, a scalable dataset distillation framework that aligns the cross-covariance of real and synthetic features while regularizing feature distributions within each modality. Unlike prior approaches, CovMatch enables joint optimization of both encoders, leading to stronger cross-modal alignment and improved performance. Evaluated on Flickr30K and COCO, CovMatch outperforms state-of-the-art multimodal distillation methods and achieves up to 6.8\% absolute gains in retrieval accuracy using only 500 synthetic pairs.

paragraphs: Multimodal dataset distillation creates a small synthetic collection of image-text pairs intended to support efficient training of vision-language models. A central challenge is preserving the relationship between images and language while keeping large encoders computationally manageable. Earlier approaches freeze the text encoder, but the authors find that this restricts semantic alignment and limits improvements as performance scales.

CovMatch matches the cross-covariance of real and synthetic features, targeting how image and text representations vary together. It also regularizes feature distributions separately within each modality. This framework allows both the image encoder and text encoder to be optimized jointly, giving the language side room to adapt as cross-modal alignment is learned.

On Flickr30K and COCO, CovMatch outperforms state-of-the-art multimodal distillation methods. The reported gains reach 6.8 percentage points in retrieval accuracy with only 500 synthetic pairs. The findings indicate that preserving relationships between modalities and allowing both encoders to learn can improve how much useful training information a compact synthetic dataset carries.
summary.tldr: CovMatch distills image-text data by matching cross-modal feature relationships while allowing both encoders to train.

title: CovMatch: Cross-Covariance Guided Multimodal Dataset Distillation with Trainable Text Encoder

abstract: Dark matter makes up approximately 85\% of total matter in our universe, yet it has never been directly observed in any laboratory on Earth. The origin of dark matter is one of the most important questions in contemporary physics, and a convincing detection of dark matter would be a Nobel-Prize-level breakthrough in fundamental science. The ABRACADABRA experiment was specifically designed to search for dark matter. Although it has not yet made a discovery, ABRACADABRA has produced several dark matter search results widely endorsed by the physics community. The experiment generates ultra-long time-series data at a rate of 10 million samples per second, where the dark matter signal would manifest itself as a sinusoidal oscillation mode within the ultra-long time series. In this paper, we present the TIDMAD --- a comprehensive data release from the ABRACADABRA experiment including three key components: an ultra-long time series dataset divided into training, validation, and science subsets; a carefully-designed denoising score for direct model benchmarking; and a complete analysis framework which produces a physics community-standard dark matter search result suitable for publication as a physics paper. This data release enables core AI algorithms to extract the dark matter signal and produce real physics results thereby advancing fundamental science.

paragraphs: TIDMAD makes data from the ABRACADABRA dark-matter experiment available for developing and evaluating AI denoising methods. The experiment records ten million samples per second, producing extremely long time series. A dark-matter signal, if present in this search, would appear as a sinusoidal oscillation within those measurements, making signal extraction the central computational task.

It provides training, validation, and science subsets of the time-series data; a denoising score for comparing models directly; and a complete analysis framework that turns processed measurements into a dark-matter search result meeting physics-community standards. This connects algorithm development with the downstream scientific analysis.

The abstract explicitly states that ABRACADABRA has not made a discovery, although it has produced established search results. TIDMAD enables AI researchers to test whether their denoising methods can extract relevant signals and contribute to publishable physics results using data from an actual experiment.
summary.tldr: TIDMAD provides experimental time series, denoising benchmarks, and a physics analysis pipeline for applying AI to dark-matter searches.

title: TIDMAD: Time Series Dataset for Discovering Dark Matter with AI Denoising

abstract: In this work, we consider the problem of Bayesian Optimization (BO) under reward model uncertainty—that is, when the underlying distribution type of the reward is unknown and potentially intractable to specify. This challenge is particularly evident in many modern applications, where the reward distribution is highly ill-behaved, often non-stationary, multi-modal, or heavy-tailed. In such settings, classical Gaussian Process (GP)-based BO methods often fail due to their strong modeling assumptions. To address this challenge, we propose a novel surrogate model, the infinity-Gaussian Process ($\infty$-GP), which represents a sequential spatial Dirichlet Process mixture with a GP baseline. The $\infty$-GP quantifies both value uncertainty and model uncertainty, enabling more flexible modeling of complex reward structures. Combined with Thompson Sampling, the $\infty$-GP facilitates principled exploration and exploitation in the distributional space of reward models. Theoretically, we prove that the $\infty$-GP surrogate model can approximate a broad class of reward distributions by effectively exploring the distribution space, achieving near-minimax-optimal posterior contraction rates. Empirically, our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in various challenging scenarios, including highly non-stationary and heavy-tailed reward settings where classical GP-based BO often fails.

title: Exploring and Exploiting Model Uncertainty in Bayesian Optimization

abstract: We examine hypothesis testing within a principal-agent framework, where a strategic agent, holding private beliefs about the effectiveness of a product, submits data to a principal who decides on approval. The principal employs a hypothesis testing rule, aiming to pick a p-value threshold that balances false positives and false negatives while anticipating the agent’s incentive to maximize expected profitability. Building on prior work, we develop a game-theoretic model that captures how the agent’s participation and reporting behavior respond to the principal’s statistical decision rule. Despite the complexity of the interaction, we show that the principal's errors exhibit clear monotonic behavior when segmented by an efficiently computable critical p-value threshold, leading to an interpretable characterization of their optimal p-value threshold. We empirically validate our model and these insights using publicly available data on drug approvals. Overall, our work offers a comprehensive perspective on strategic interactions within the hypothesis testing framework, providing technical and regulatory insights.

paragraphs: An approval rule can affect which evidence is submitted for approval. This paper studies that feedback through a principal-agent model: an agent privately assesses a product’s effectiveness and submits data, while a principal chooses a p-value threshold for approval. The agent seeks expected profit, and the principal balances false positives against false negatives.

The game-theoretic model captures how the agent’s participation and reporting respond to the statistical rule. This makes threshold selection a strategic problem because changing the rule can change the evidence-generating interaction. The authors show that the principal’s errors follow clear monotonic patterns when divided into regions by an efficiently computable critical p-value threshold.

That structure yields an interpretable characterization of the principal’s optimal threshold despite the complexity of the interaction. The authors empirically validate the model and its insights using public drug-approval data. The contribution connects statistical testing with the incentives of those supplying evidence, offering a way to analyze approval standards while accounting for how interested parties respond to them.
summary.tldr: A game-theoretic model characterizes optimal testing thresholds when approval rules influence strategic participation and evidence reporting.

title: Strategic Hypothesis Testing

abstract: According to Algorithmic Information Theory (AIT), intelligent representations compress data into the shortest possible program while remaining predictive of its content—exhibiting low Kolmogorov Complexity (KC). In contrast, most visual representation learning systems assign fixed-length representations to all inputs, ignoring variations in complexity or familiarity. Recent adaptive tokenization methods address this by allocating variable-length representations but typically require test-time search over multiple hypotheses to identify the most predictive one. Inspired by KC principles, we propose a one-shot adaptive tokenizer, KARL, that predicts the appropriate number of tokens for an image in a single forward pass, halting once its approximate KC is reached. The token count serves as a proxy for the minimum description length. KARL performs comparably to recent adaptive tokenizers while operating in a one-pass manner. Additionally, we present a conceptual study showing a correlation between adaptive tokenization and core ideas from AIT. We demonstrate that adaptive tokenization not only aligns with KC but also reveals empirical signals approximating AIT concepts such as sophistication and logical depth. Finally, we analyze predicted image complexity and interestingness across axes such as structure vs. noise and in-distribution vs. out-of-distribution familiarity, highlighting alignment with human annotations.

This paper instead draws on algorithmic information theory: an informative representation should compress an input while retaining what is needed to predict its content. Images that differ in complexity or familiarity may therefore call for different numbers of tokens.

KARL predicts that token allocation in a single forward pass. It stops when it reaches an approximate measure of Kolmogorov complexity, with token count serving as a proxy for minimum description length. summary.tldr: KARL allocates image tokens in one pass, matching recent adaptive tokenizers while using token count as an approximate description-length measure.

title: Single-pass Adaptive Image Tokenization for Minimum Program Search

abstract: We propose LiteReality, a novel pipeline that converts RGB-D scans of indoor environments into compact, realistic, and interactive 3D virtual replicas. LiteReality not only reconstructs scenes that visually resemble reality but also supports key features essential for graphics pipelines—such as object individuality, articulation, high-quality physically based rendering materials. At its core, LiteReality first performs scene understanding and parses the results into a coherent 3D layout and objects, with the help of a structured scene graph. It then reconstructs the scene by retrieving the most visually similar 3D artist-crafted models from a curated asset database. Later, the Material Painting module enhances the realism of retrieved objects by recovering high-quality, spatially varying materials. Finally, the reconstructed scene is integrated into a simulation engine with basic physical properties applied to enable interactive behavior. The resulting scenes are compact, editable, and fully compatible with standard graphics pipelines, making them suitable for applications in AR/VR, gaming, robotics, and digital twins. In addition, LiteReality introduces a training-free object retrieval module that achieves state-of-the-art similarity performance, as benchmarked on the Scan2CAD dataset, along with a robust Material Painting module capable of transferring appearances from images of any style to 3D assets—even in the presence of severe misalignment, occlusion, and poor lighting. We demonstrate the effectiveness of LiteReality on both real-life scans and public datasets.

The approach matters because its outputs already have the object structure, materials, and compatibility needed for graphics pipelines, supporting applications such as virtual environments, robotics, and digital twins.
summary.tldr: LiteReality turns indoor color-and-depth scans into editable, interactive 3D scenes using retrieved assets and recovered materials.

title: LiteReality: Graphics-Ready 3D Scene Reconstruction from RGB-D Scans

abstract: Medical Visual Question Answering (Med-VQA) holds significant potential for clinical decision support, yet existing efforts primarily focus on 2D imaging with limited task diversity. This paper presents 3D-RAD, a large-scale dataset designed to advance 3D Med-VQA using radiology CT scans. The 3D-RAD dataset encompasses six diverse VQA tasks: anomaly detection, image observation, medical computation, existence detection, static temporal diagnosis, and longitudinal temporal diagnosis. It supports both open- and closed-ended questions while introducing complex reasoning challenges, including computational tasks and multi-stage temporal analysis, to enable comprehensive benchmarking. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that existing vision-language models (VLMs), especially medical VLMs exhibit limited generalization, particularly in multi-temporal tasks, underscoring the challenges of real-world 3D diagnostic reasoning. To drive future advancements, we release a high-quality training set 3D-RAD-T of 136,195 expert-aligned samples, showing that fine-tuning on this dataset could significantly enhance model performance. Our dataset and code, aiming to catalyze multimodal medical AI research and establish a robust foundation for 3D medical visual understanding, are publicly available.

paragraphs: 3D-RAD expands medical visual question answering from predominantly two-dimensional images to three-dimensional CT scans. Its purpose is to test a wider range of diagnostic reasoning abilities than existing datasets typically cover. The questions include both open responses and answers drawn from a restricted set, allowing different forms of model behavior to be assessed.

The dataset covers six tasks: anomaly detection, image observation, medical computation, existence detection, static temporal diagnosis, and longitudinal temporal diagnosis. This variety makes the benchmark about more than recognizing visible findings. Computational questions and multiple stages of temporal analysis also test whether a model can reason about information within and across examinations.

The evaluations find limited generalization among existing vision-language models, particularly medical models and particularly on tasks involving multiple times. The authors also provide 3D-RAD-T, a training collection containing 136,195 expert-aligned examples, and report that fine-tuning on it could substantially improve performance. Together, the benchmark and training set identify difficult capabilities while providing data intended to help develop them.
summary.tldr: 3D-RAD benchmarks diverse question-answering tasks on CT scans and exposes weaknesses in models’ reasoning across time.

title: 3D-RAD: A Comprehensive 3D Radiology Med-VQA Dataset with Multi-Temporal Analysis and Diverse Diagnostic Tasks

abstract: A new model is developed for joint analysis of ordered, categorical, real and count data. The ordered and categorical data are answers to questionnaires, the (word) count data correspond to the text questions from the questionnaires, and the real data correspond to fMRI responses for each subject. The Bayesian model employs the von Mises distribution in a novel manner to infer sparse graphical models jointly across people, questions, fMRI stimuli and brain region, with this integrated within a new matrix factorization based on latent binary features. The model is compared with simpler alternatives on two real datasets. We also demonstrate the ability to predict the response of the brain to visual stimuli (as measured by fMRI), based on knowledge of how the associated person answered classical questionnaires.

paragraphs: This paper brings questionnaire responses, questionnaire text, and brain-imaging measurements into a single statistical model. These sources have different forms: answers can be ordered or categorical, question text is represented through word counts, and fMRI responses are real-valued measurements. Joint analysis needs to accommodate those differences while learning connections across the sources.

The proposed Bayesian model combines a matrix factorization based on latent binary features with sparse graphical models. It uses the von Mises distribution in a new way to infer relationships jointly across people, questions, imaging stimuli, and brain regions. The latent representation provides a shared modeling structure for these otherwise heterogeneous observations.

The authors compare the model with simpler alternatives on two real datasets. They also demonstrate prediction of a person’s brain response to visual stimuli, as measured by fMRI, from that person’s answers to classical questionnaires. This finding illustrates the practical purpose of integration: information from questionnaire responses can support predictions about a different type of measurement within the studied setting.
summary.tldr: A joint Bayesian model integrates questionnaire data and fMRI, demonstrating prediction of visual-stimulus brain responses from questionnaire answers.

title: Exploring the Mind: Integrating Questionnaires and fMRI

abstract: High-level skills relieve planning algorithms from low-level details. But when the skills are poorly designed for the domain, the resulting plan may be severely suboptimal. Sutton et al. 1999 made an important step towards resolving this problem by introducing a rule that automatically improves a set of skills called options. This rule terminates an option early whenever switching to another option gives a higher value than continuing with the current option. However, they only analyzed the case where the improvement rule is applied once. We show conditions where this rule converges to the optimal set of options. A new Bellman-like operator that simultaneously improves the set of options is at the core of our analysis. One problem with the update rule is that it tends to favor lower-level skills. Therefore we introduce a regularization term that favors longer duration skills. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach can derive a good set of high-level skills even when the original set of skills cannot solve the problem.

paragraphs: High-level skills simplify planning by hiding low-level decisions, but poorly chosen skills can lead to severely suboptimal plans. This paper studies an interruption rule for skills called options: stop the current option whenever switching to another has higher value. Earlier analysis considered applying that rule once; this work examines its repeated application.

The authors identify conditions under which the rule converges to an optimal set of options. A new Bellman-like operator, which improves the options together, forms the core of the analysis. The convergence statement is conditional, so the result establishes when repeated interruption-based improvement works rather than claiming that it succeeds for every possible starting situation.

The update rule also tends to favor lower-level skills, which can undermine the purpose of planning with high-level actions. The authors add a regularization term favoring longer-duration skills to address that tendency. Experiments show that the resulting approach can derive useful high-level skills even when the original set cannot solve the problem, combining skill improvement with a preference for temporal abstraction.
summary.tldr: TRIO combines interruption-based option improvement with a preference for longer skills, supported by conditional convergence analysis and experiments.

title: Time-Regularized Interrupting Options (TRIO)

abstract: In this paper, we present results on ordered representations of data in which different dimensions have different degrees of importance. To learn these representations we introduce nested dropout, a procedure for stochastically removing coherent nested sets of hidden units in a neural network. We first present a sequence of theoretical results in the simple case of a semi-linear autoencoder. We rigorously show that the application of nested dropout enforces identifiability of the units, which leads to an exact equivalence with PCA. We then extend the algorithm to deep models and demonstrate the relevance of ordered representations to a number of applications. Specifically, we use the ordered property of the learned codes to construct hash-based data structures that permit very fast retrieval, achieving retrieval in time logarithmic in the database size and independent of the dimensionality of the representation. This allows the use of codes that are hundreds of times longer than currently feasible for retrieval. We therefore avoid the diminished quality associated with short codes, while still performing retrieval that is competitive in speed with existing methods. We also show that ordered representations are a promising way to learn adaptive compression for efficient online data reconstruction.

paragraphs: This paper learns representations whose dimensions have an order of importance. Its training procedure, nested dropout, randomly removes coherent nested sets of hidden units. The objective is to make the arrangement of information within a learned code useful, rather than treating all representation dimensions as interchangeable.

For a semi-linear autoencoder, the authors prove that nested dropout makes the units identifiable and leads to an exact equivalence with principal component analysis. They then extend the procedure to deep models. The exact PCA connection belongs to the analyzed semi-linear setting, while the deep-model extension supports a broader set of applications.

The ordered codes enable hash-based retrieval structures with lookup time logarithmic in database size and independent of representation dimensionality. The authors report using codes hundreds of times longer than previously feasible for retrieval, avoiding the quality loss associated with short codes while retaining competitive retrieval speed. They also show that ordered representations are promising for adaptive compression and efficient online reconstruction. Across these applications, ordering makes representation length a more usable computational choice.
summary.tldr: Nested dropout orders representation dimensions by importance, enabling long-code retrieval and promising adaptive compression.

title: Learning Ordered Representations with Nested Dropout

abstract: The Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) has been studied for years. Traditional ADMM algorithms need to compute, at each iteration, an (empirical) expected loss function on all training examples, resulting in a computational complexity proportional to the number of training examples. To reduce the complexity, stochastic ADMM algorithms were proposed to replace the expected loss function with a random loss function associated with one uniformly drawn example plus a Bregman divergence term. The Bregman divergence, however, is derived from a simple 2nd-order proximal function, i.e., the half squared norm, which could be a suboptimal choice. In this paper, we present a new family of stochastic ADMM algorithms with optimal 2nd-order proximal functions, which produce a new family of adaptive stochastic ADMM methods. We theoretically prove that the regret bounds are as good as the bounds which could be achieved by the best proximal function that can be chosen in hindsight. Encouraging empirical results on a variety of real-world datasets confirm the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper improves stochastic versions of the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers, or ADMM. Traditional ADMM evaluates an empirical expected loss over all training examples at each iteration, making that part of the computation grow with dataset size. Stochastic variants reduce this cost by using the loss from a single uniformly sampled example.

Those stochastic variants also use a Bregman divergence term derived from a proximal function, which influences the geometry of the update. The authors argue that the customary choice based on half the squared norm can be suboptimal. They introduce a family of adaptive methods using optimized second-order proximal functions instead of committing to that simple choice.

Their theoretical result concerns regret: the adaptive methods achieve bounds as good as those available from the best proximal function chosen in hindsight. This gives a precise comparison for the adaptation, rather than merely asserting that a more flexible update should help. Experiments on several real-world datasets provide encouraging evidence of effectiveness and efficiency for the proposed algorithm family.
summary.tldr: Adaptive stochastic ADMM chooses better proximal geometry and achieves regret bounds matching the best proximal choice available in hindsight.

title: Adaptive Stochastic Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers

abstract: We consider the problem of designing locality sensitive hashes (LSH) for inner product similarity, and of the power of asymmetric hashes in this context. Shrivastava and Li (2014a) argue that there is no symmetric LSH for the problem and propose an asymmetric LSH based on different mappings for query and database points. However, we show there does exist a simple symmetric LSH that enjoys stronger guarantees and better empirical performance than the asymmetric LSH they suggest. We also show a variant of the settings where asymmetry is in-fact needed, but there a different asymmetric LSH is required.

Shrivastava and Li (2014a) argue that there is no symmetric LSH for the problem and propose an asymmetric LSH based on different mappings for query and database points. However, we show there does exist a simple symmetric LSH that enjoys stronger guarantees and better empirical performance than the asymmetric LSH they suggest. paragraphs: Inner-product search looks for database points that score highly against a query using their inner product. Locality-sensitive hashing aims to support similarity search through hash mappings. This paper examines whether query points and database points need different mappings, called asymmetry, or whether the same mapping can work for both.

The authors challenge an earlier claim that symmetric hashing is unavailable for the problem. They construct a simple symmetric locality-sensitive hash and show that it has stronger guarantees and better empirical performance than the proposed asymmetric alternative they study. This establishes that asymmetry is not required in the setting addressed by that construction.

The paper also identifies a variant of the setting where asymmetry really is necessary. In that variant, however, a different asymmetric hash is needed. The two findings together clarify that the usefulness and necessity of separate mappings depend on the precise search setting. They support neither a blanket rejection of asymmetry nor a universal claim that symmetric hashing suffices.
summary.tldr: Symmetric hashing works well for one inner-product search setting, while a related variant genuinely requires a different asymmetric construction.

title: On Symmetric and Asymmetric LSHs for Inner Product Search

abstract: We propose an extension to Hawkes processes by treating the levels of self-excitation as a stochastic differential equation. Our new point process allows better approximation in application domains where events and intensities accelerate each other with correlated levels of contagion. We generalize a recent algorithm for simulating draws from Hawkes processes whose levels of excitation are stochastic processes, and propose a hybrid Markov chain Monte Carlo approach for model fitting. Our sampling procedure scales linearly with the number of required events and does not require stationarity of the point process. A modular inference procedure consisting of a combination between Gibbs and Metropolis Hastings steps is put forward. We recover expectation maximization as a special case. Our general approach is illustrated for contagion following geometric Brownian motion and exponential Langevin dynamics.

Our sampling procedure scales linearly with the number of required events and does not require stationarity of the point process. paragraphs: Hawkes processes model events whose occurrence can increase the intensity of subsequent events. This paper extends that idea by allowing the strength of self-excitation itself to evolve according to a stochastic differential equation. The resulting model is designed for situations where events and intensities reinforce one another and contagion strengths are correlated over time.

The authors develop both simulation and fitting procedures for this richer process. They generalize an existing simulation algorithm to handle stochastic excitation levels. Its sampling cost grows linearly with the number of required events, and it does not require the point process to be stationary. Those properties make the simulation procedure relevant to changing event dynamics.

For inference, the paper proposes a modular hybrid Markov chain Monte Carlo method combining Gibbs and Metropolis–Hastings steps. Expectation maximization is recovered as a special case of the approach. Illustrations use contagion governed by geometric Brownian motion and exponential Langevin dynamics. Together, these contributions provide a modeling framework and computational procedures for event sequences with randomly evolving excitation strength.
summary.tldr: The paper extends Hawkes processes with randomly evolving excitation strengths and develops efficient simulation and modular inference procedures.

title: Hawkes Processes with Stochastic Excitations

abstract: This paper reports theoretical and empirical investigations on the use of quasi-Newton methods to minimize the Optimal Bellman Residual (OBR) of zero-sum two-player Markov Games. First, it reveals that state-of-the-art algorithms can be derived by the direct application of Newton’s method to different norms of the OBR. More precisely, when applied to the norm of the OBR, Newton’s method results in the Bellman Residual Minimization Policy Iteration (BRMPI) and, when applied to the norm of the Projected OBR (POBR), it results into the standard Least Squares Policy Iteration (LSPI) algorithm. Consequently, new algorithms are proposed, making use of quasi-Newton methods to minimize the OBR and the POBR so as to take benefit of enhanced empirical performances at low cost. Indeed, using a quasi-Newton method approach introduces slight modifications in term of coding of LSPI and BRMPI but improves significantly both the stability and the performance of those algorithms. These phenomena are illustrated on an experiment conducted on artificially constructed games called Garnets.
originalAbstract: This paper reports theoretical and empirical investigations on the use of quasi-Newton methods to minimize the Optimal Bellman Residual (OBR) of zero-sum two-player Markov Games. First, it reveals that state-of-the-art algorithms can be derived by the direct application of Newton’s method to different norms of the OBR. More precisely, when applied to the norm of the OBR, Newton’s method results in the Bellman Residual Minimization Policy Iteration (BRMPI) and, when applied to the norm of the Projected OBR (POBR), it results into the standard Least Squares Policy Iteration (LSPI) algorithm. Consequently, new algorithms are proposed, making use of quasi-Newton methods to minimize the OBR and the POBR so as to take benefit of enhanced empirical performances at low cost. Indeed, using a quasi-Newton method approach introduces slight modifications in term of coding of LSPI and BRMPI but improves significantly both the stability and the performance of those algorithms. These phenomena are illustrated on an experiment conducted on artificially constructed games called Garnets.

paragraphs: This paper studies optimization methods for zero-sum, two-player Markov games through the Optimal Bellman Residual. That residual provides an objective for assessing agreement with the game’s optimality equations. The authors investigate how Newton and quasi-Newton methods relate to algorithms that improve policies by reducing this residual or a projected version of it.

They show that applying Newton’s method to a norm of the Optimal Bellman Residual produces Bellman Residual Minimization Policy Iteration. Applying it to a norm of the projected residual produces Least Squares Policy Iteration. These relationships provide a common optimization interpretation of the two algorithms and motivate replacing their Newton-based updates with quasi-Newton alternatives.

The proposed algorithms require only modest coding changes to the existing methods. The authors report significant improvements in stability and performance at low cost, illustrated through an experiment on artificially constructed games called Garnets. The contribution combines an explanation of familiar policy-iteration methods with practical modifications whose benefits are demonstrated in that experimental setting.
summary.tldr: A Newton-method interpretation of policy iteration motivates quasi-Newton variants that improve stability and performance in experiments on artificial Markov games.

title: Softened Approximate Policy Iteration for Markov Games

abstract: We consider structure discovery of undirected graphical models from observational data. Inferring likely structures from few examples is a complex task often requiring the formulation of priors and sophisticated inference procedures. Popular methods rely on estimating a penalized maximum likelihood of the precision matrix. However, in these approaches structure recovery is an indirect consequence of the data-fit term, the penalty can be difficult to adapt for domain-specific knowledge, and the inference is computationally demanding. By contrast, it may be easier to generate training samples of data that arise from graphs with the desired structure properties. We propose here to leverage this latter source of information as training data to learn a function, parametrized by a neural network, that maps empirical covariance matrices to estimated graph structures. Learning this function brings two benefits: it implicitly models the desired structure or sparsity properties to form suitable priors, and it can be tailored to the specific problem of edge structure discovery, rather than maximizing data likelihood. Applying this framework, we find our learnable graph-discovery method trained on synthetic data generalizes well: identifying relevant edges in both synthetic and real data, completely unknown at training time. We find that on genetics, brain imaging, and simulation data we obtain performance generally superior to analytical methods.

Common methods estimate a penalized precision matrix, so recovering edges follows indirectly from fitting the data. This paper explores learning edge discovery directly, especially when generating example datasets with desired graph properties may be easier than expressing those properties through penalties.

The authors train a neural network to map empirical covariance matrices to estimated graph structures. Synthetic training examples encode the kinds of structure and sparsity the model should recognize. summary.tldr: A neural network trained on synthetic graphs learns to infer edges from covariance matrices and generalizes well in reported real-data evaluations.

title: Learning to Discover Sparse Graphical Models

abstract: We introduce a notion of algorithmic stability of learning algorithms—that we term hypothesis stability —that captures stability of the hypothesis output by the learning algorithm in the normed space of functions from which hypotheses are selected. The main result of the paper bounds the generalization error of any learning algorithm in terms of its hypothesis stability. The bounds are based on martingale inequalities in the Banach space to which the hypotheses belong. We apply the general bounds to bound the performance of some learning algorithms based on empirical risk minimization and stochastic gradient descent.

The main result of the paper bounds the generalization error of any learning algorithm in terms of its hypothesis stability. The bounds are based on martingale inequalities in the Banach space to which the hypotheses belong. We apply the general bounds to bound the performance of some learning algorithms based on empirical risk minimization and stochastic gradient descent.

paragraphs: A learning algorithm produces a prediction function, and a central theoretical question is how its performance on training data relates to performance beyond that data. This paper approaches that question through hypothesis stability: a measure of stability expressed directly in the normed space containing the functions the algorithm can output.

The main contribution is a general bound connecting generalization error to this form of stability. Measuring stability at the level of the output function makes the function space itself part of the analysis. The proof uses martingale inequalities in a Banach space, providing mathematical tools for controlling fluctuations of quantities that take values in that space.

The authors then apply their general bounds to particular learning algorithms based on empirical risk minimization and stochastic gradient descent. These applications show how the framework can support analysis of familiar learning procedures. The result supplies a way to bound generalization through hypothesis stability; it does not claim that every algorithm automatically has favorable stability.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds generalization error through stability measured directly in the function space of a learning algorithm’s outputs.

title: Algorithmic Stability and Hypothesis Complexity

abstract: We study active object tracking, where a tracker takes as input the visual observation (i.e. frame sequence) and produces the camera control signal (e.g., move forward, turn left, etc). Conventional methods tackle the tracking and the camera control separately, which is challenging to tune jointly. It also incurs many human efforts for labeling and many expensive trial-and-errors in real-world. To address these issues, we propose, in this paper, an end-to-end solution via deep reinforcement learning, where a ConvNet-LSTM function approximator is adopted for the direct frame-to-action prediction. We further propose an environment augmentation technique and a customized reward function, which are crucial for a successful training. The tracker trained in simulators (ViZDoom, Unreal Engine) shows good generalization in the case of unseen object moving path, unseen object appearance, unseen background, and distracting object. It can restore tracking when occasionally losing the target. With the experiments over the VOT dataset, we also find that the tracking ability, obtained solely from simulators, can potentially transfer to real-world scenarios.

paragraphs: Active object tracking requires a system to observe a target and move its camera to keep tracking it. Separately designing the tracking and camera-control components makes joint tuning difficult and can require substantial labeling and real-world trial and error. This paper instead learns a direct mapping from visual observations to camera actions through deep reinforcement learning.

The model combines a convolutional network with an LSTM to predict actions from frame sequences. Training also uses environment augmentation and a customized reward function, both identified as crucial to success. The tracker learns in the ViZDoom and Unreal Engine simulators, placing the acquisition of tracking behavior within controlled simulated environments.

The trained tracker generalizes in the reported tests to unfamiliar target motion, appearances, backgrounds, and distracting objects. It can also regain tracking after occasionally losing its target. Experiments using the VOT dataset suggest that skills learned solely in simulation can potentially transfer to real-world scenarios. That transfer result is presented as evidence of potential, while the simulation tests demonstrate several specific forms of generalization.
summary.tldr: A reinforcement learning tracker maps video directly to camera actions, generalizes across simulated changes, and shows potential for real-world transfer.

title: End-to-end Active Object Tracking via Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We propose a primal-dual based framework for analyzing the global optimality of nonconvex low-rank matrix recovery. Our analysis are based on the restricted strongly convex and smooth conditions, which can be verified for a broad family of loss functions. In addition, our analytic framework can directly handle the widely-used incoherence constraints through the lens of duality. We illustrate the applicability of the proposed framework to matrix completion and one-bit matrix completion, and prove that all these problems have no spurious local minima. Our results not only improve the sample complexity required for characterizing the global optimality of matrix completion, but also resolve an open problem in Ge et al. (2017) regarding one-bit matrix completion. Numerical experiments show that primal-dual based algorithm can successfully recover the global optimum for various low-rank problems.

paragraphs: Recovering a low-rank matrix leads to nonconvex optimization problems, where a central concern is whether local minima can be worse than the global optimum. This paper proposes a framework for examining that question through primal-dual analysis, connecting the original recovery problem with its dual description.

The analysis assumes restricted strong convexity and smoothness, conditions the authors say can be verified for a broad family of loss functions. It also handles incoherence constraints directly through duality. These assumptions and constraints are part of the mathematical setting in which the authors establish their results, rather than a claim about every nonconvex matrix recovery problem.

The framework is applied to matrix completion and one-bit matrix completion, establishing the absence of spurious local minima in the analyzed settings. It improves the sample complexity needed to characterize global optimality for matrix completion and resolves a previously open question for one-bit completion. Numerical experiments further show successful recovery of global optima by a primal-dual algorithm across several low-rank problems.
summary.tldr: A primal-dual framework establishes global optimality properties for low-rank recovery under restricted convexity and smoothness conditions.

title: A Primal-Dual Analysis of Global Optimality in Nonconvex Low-Rank Matrix Recovery

abstract: We study the fair variant of the classic k-median problem introduced by (Chierichetti et al., NeurIPS 2017) in which the points are colored, and the goal is to minimize the same average distance objective as in the standard $k$-median problem while ensuring that all clusters have an “approximately equal” number of points of each color. (Chierichetti et al., NeurIPS 2017) proposed a two-phase algorithm for fair $k$-clustering. In the first step, the pointset is partitioned into subsets called fairlets that satisfy the fairness requirement and approximately preserve the k-median objective. In the second step, fairlets are merged into k clusters by one of the existing k-median algorithms. The running time of this algorithm is dominated by the first step, which takes super-quadratic time. In this paper, we present a practical approximate fairlet decomposition algorithm that runs in nearly linear time.

(Chierichetti et al., NeurIPS 2017) proposed a two-phase algorithm for fair $k$-clustering. In the first step, the pointset is partitioned into subsets called fairlets that satisfy the fairness requirement and approximately preserve the k-median objective. In the second step, fairlets are merged into k clusters by one of the existing k-median algorithms. paragraphs: The paper studies a fairness-constrained version of k-median clustering. Points carry colors representing groups, and every cluster must contain approximately equal numbers of points of each color. The optimization objective remains the usual average distance objective, so the problem combines compact clusters with a specific requirement on group composition.

An existing two-stage approach first divides the data into small subsets called fairlets. These subsets satisfy the fairness requirement while approximately preserving the clustering objective. A standard k-median algorithm then merges the fairlets into the requested number of clusters. The main computational bottleneck is creating the fairlets, which previously required more than quadratic time.

The authors introduce a practical approximate fairlet decomposition algorithm with nearly linear running time. The contribution directly accelerates the costly first stage of this established framework. It makes the decomposition substantially more scalable while retaining an approximation-based approach to fair clustering, with fairness understood through the stated color-balance requirement.
summary.tldr: A nearly linear-time approximate fairlet decomposition accelerates a key bottleneck in color-balanced k-median clustering.

title: Scalable Fair Clustering

abstract: Optimization of machine learning models is commonly performed through stochastic gradient updates on randomly ordered training examples. This practice means that each fraction of an epoch comprises an independent random sample of the training data that may not preserve informative structure present in the full data. We hypothesize that the training can be more effective with self-similar arrangements that potentially allow each epoch to provide benefits of multiple ones. We study this for “matrix factorization” – the common task of learning metric embeddings of entities such as queries, videos, or words from example pairwise associations. We construct arrangements that preserve the weighted Jaccard similarities of rows and columns and experimentally observe training acceleration of 3%-37% on synthetic and recommendation datasets. Principled arrangements of training examples emerge as a novel and potentially powerful enhancement to SGD that merits further exploration.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient training commonly presents examples in random order. Although this spreads examples through an epoch, smaller portions may fail to preserve informative structure found in the full dataset. This paper investigates whether carefully arranging examples can make training more effective by ensuring that partial passes retain useful relationships present in the complete data.

The authors study this idea for matrix factorization, where embeddings of entities such as queries, videos, or words are learned from pairwise associations. They construct self-similar arrangements that preserve weighted Jaccard similarities among rows and columns. Their hypothesis is that such structure can let a single epoch deliver some of the benefits normally associated with multiple passes.

Experiments on synthetic and recommendation datasets show training acceleration ranging from 3% to 37%. The results support example arrangement as a potentially useful addition to stochastic gradient training in the studied setting. They leave the broader proposition appropriately exploratory: the paper demonstrates gains for matrix factorization and presents principled ordering as a direction deserving further investigation.
summary.tldr: Structure-preserving arrangements of training examples accelerate matrix-factorization training by 3%–37% in the reported experiments.

title: Self-similar Epochs: Value in arrangement

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) are a popular class of machine learning models that have been successfully applied to a range of problems. Their major advantage lies in their ability to explicitly incorporate a sparse and discrete dependency structure between data points. Unfortunately, GNNs can only be used when such a graph-structure is available. In practice, however, real-world graphs are often noisy and incomplete or might not be available at all. With this work, we propose to jointly learn the graph structure and the parameters of graph convolutional networks (GCNs) by approximately solving a bilevel program that learns a discrete probability distribution on the edges of the graph. This allows one to apply GCNs not only in scenarios where the given graph is incomplete or corrupted but also in those where a graph is not available. We conduct a series of experiments that analyze the behavior of the proposed method and demonstrate that it outperforms related methods by a significant margin.

We conduct a series of experiments that analyze the behavior of the proposed method and demonstrate that it outperforms related methods by a significant margin.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks use explicit connections between data points to organize learning. That advantage becomes a difficulty when the available graph is noisy, incomplete, or missing. This paper addresses the problem by making the graph itself something to learn alongside the parameters of a graph convolutional network.

The method learns a discrete probability distribution over graph edges. It does this by approximately solving a bilevel optimization problem, coupling the learning of structure with the learning of network parameters. The connections are therefore part of the model's learning process instead of being treated as a fully reliable input supplied beforehand.

This formulation allows graph convolutional networks to be used when an existing graph needs correction and when no graph is available at all. The authors run experiments analyzing the behavior of the method and report that it outperforms related approaches by a significant margin. The contribution is a way to retain the benefits of discrete dependency structure while learning that structure in settings where it cannot simply be assumed.
summary.tldr: Jointly learning edge probabilities and network parameters enables graph convolutional learning with corrupted, incomplete, or absent graphs.

title: Learning Discrete Structures for Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Structured models of decision making often assume an agent is aware of all possible states and actions in advance. This assumption is sometimes untenable. In this paper, we learn Bayesian Decision Networks from both domain exploration and expert assertions in a way which guarantees convergence to optimal behaviour, even when the agent starts unaware of actions or belief variables that are critical to success. Our experiments show that our agent learns optimal behaviour on both small and large decision problems, and that allowing an agent to conserve information upon making new discoveries results in faster convergence.

Our experiments show that our agent learns optimal behaviour on both small and large decision problems, and that allowing an agent to conserve information upon making new discoveries results in faster convergence.

paragraphs: Decision-making models often assume an agent already knows every possible state and action. This paper studies a more open-ended situation: an agent may initially be unaware of actions or belief variables that are essential for success. Learning must therefore expand the agent’s understanding of the decision problem as well as improve its choices.

The proposed method learns Bayesian Decision Networks using both exploration of the domain and assertions supplied by an expert. These two sources let the agent acquire information through experience and guidance. The framework guarantees convergence to optimal behavior even when the initial representation omits critical actions or belief variables.

Experiments show the agent learning optimal behavior on both small and large decision problems. They also examine what happens when new discoveries alter its understanding of the task. Allowing the agent to preserve information it has already acquired produces faster convergence. This finding makes information retention a consequential part of learning under unawareness: expanding a model need not discard all earlier progress.
summary.tldr: An agent learns decision networks through exploration and expert guidance, converging to optimal behavior despite initially unknown actions or variables.

title: Learning Structured Decision Problems with Unawareness

abstract: Variational autoencoders (VAEs) have received considerable attention, since they allow us to learn expressive neural density estimators effectively and efficiently. However, learning and inference in VAEs is still problematic due to the sensitive interplay between the generative model and the inference network. Since these problems become generally more severe in high dimensions, we propose a novel hierarchical mixture model over low-dimensional VAE experts. Our model decomposes the overall learning problem into many smaller problems, which are coordinated by the hierarchical mixture, represented by a sum-product network. In experiments we show that our models outperform classical VAEs on almost all of our experimental benchmarks. Moreover, we show that our model is highly data efficient and degrades very gracefully in extremely low data regimes.ow data regimes.

Our model decomposes the overall learning problem into many smaller problems, which are coordinated by the hierarchical mixture, represented by a sum-product network. paragraphs: Variational autoencoders learn probability models through a generative model and an inference network that must work together. Their interaction can make learning and inference difficult, especially in high dimensions. This paper addresses that difficulty by decomposing the overall modeling problem into smaller, lower-dimensional pieces.

The proposed architecture is a hierarchical mixture of VAE experts. Each expert handles a smaller problem, and a sum-product network represents the hierarchy that coordinates them. This makes decomposition part of the probability model itself: the experts contribute within an organized mixture rather than being treated as unrelated models.

In experiments, the hierarchical models outperform classical VAEs on almost all of the evaluated benchmarks. The authors also report strong data efficiency and a gradual decline in performance when training data becomes extremely scarce. Together, these results support the usefulness of coordinating smaller VAE problems, particularly when high-dimensional learning or limited data makes a single VAE difficult to train effectively. The empirical claim retains exceptions among the tested benchmarks.
summary.tldr: A sum-product hierarchy coordinates low-dimensional VAE experts, improving most tested benchmarks and remaining effective with very little data.

title: Hierarchical Decompositional Mixtures of Variational Autoencoders

abstract: One of the most surprising and exciting discoveries in supervised learning was the benefit of overparameterization (i.e. training a very large model) to improving the optimization landscape of a problem, with minimal effect on statistical performance (i.e. generalization). In contrast, unsupervised settings have been under-explored, despite the fact that it was observed that overparameterization can be helpful as early as Dasgupta & Schulman (2007). We perform an empirical study of different aspects of overparameterization in unsupervised learning of latent variable models via synthetic and semi-synthetic experiments. We discuss benefits to different metrics of success (recovering the parameters of the ground-truth model, held-out log-likelihood), sensitivity to variations of the training algorithm, and behavior as the amount of overparameterization increases. We find that across a variety of models (noisy-OR networks, sparse coding, probabilistic context-free grammars) and training algorithms (variational inference, alternating minimization, expectation-maximization), overparameterization can significantly increase the number of ground truth latent variables recovered.
