paragraphs: Overparameterization means fitting a model with more capacity than a smaller representation would require. Its benefits have received substantial attention in supervised learning, but this paper investigates unsupervised latent variable models. Here, a key question is whether a larger model helps recover the hidden variables responsible for generating the observed data.

The authors conduct synthetic and semi-synthetic experiments across noisy-OR networks, sparse coding, and probabilistic context-free grammars. They examine training through variational inference, alternating minimization, and expectation-maximization. The study considers recovery of the ground-truth model's parameters and held-out log-likelihood, as well as sensitivity to the training algorithm and changes as the degree of overparameterization increases.

The central reported finding is that overparameterization can substantially increase the number of true latent variables recovered across the studied models and training methods. This is an empirical result about recovering hidden structure, rather than a universal guarantee for larger models. The breadth of the experiments makes it relevant beyond one model family and shows why excess capacity deserves attention in unsupervised learning as well as supervised prediction.
summary.tldr: Experiments show that overparameterization can substantially improve recovery of true latent variables across several unsupervised models and training algorithms.

title: Empirical Study of the Benefits of Overparameterization in Learning Latent Variable Models

abstract: Dataset replication is a useful tool for assessing whether improvements in test accuracy on a specific benchmark correspond to improvements in models’ ability to generalize reliably. In this work, we present unintuitive yet significant ways in which standard approaches to dataset replication introduce statistical bias, skewing the resulting observations. We study ImageNet-v2, a replication of the ImageNet dataset on which models exhibit a significant (11-14%) drop in accuracy, even after controlling for selection frequency, a human-in-the-loop measure of data quality. We show that after remeasuring selection frequencies and correcting for statistical bias, only an estimated 3.6% of the original 11.7% accuracy drop remains unaccounted for. We conclude with concrete recommendations for recognizing and avoiding bias in dataset replication. Code for our study is publicly available: https://git.io/data-rep-analysis.

paragraphs: Replicating a benchmark offers a way to check whether rising test accuracy reflects better generalization. That comparison depends on how the replacement dataset is assembled and measured. This paper shows that standard replication procedures can introduce substantial statistical bias, making observed performance differences misleading even when the replication appears to control for data quality.

The study examines ImageNet-v2, where models show an accuracy decline of 11–14% relative to ImageNet. The decline persists after controlling for selection frequency, a quality measure involving human judgments. The authors remeasure those frequencies and correct statistical bias, revisiting how much of the observed gap the replication actually leaves unexplained.

After those adjustments, the authors estimate that 3.6% remains unaccounted for from the original 11.7% accuracy drop they analyze. This substantially changes the interpretation of the raw gap while retaining an estimated unexplained remainder. The paper also gives recommendations for identifying and avoiding replication bias. Its message is that replication can inform generalization assessment, but the statistical behavior of the replication process itself must be examined.
summary.tldr: Remeasuring data-selection frequencies and correcting replication bias substantially reduces the unexplained ImageNet-v2 accuracy gap.

title: Identifying Statistical Bias in Dataset Replication

abstract: Many applications, including natural language processing, sensor networks, collaborative filtering, and federated learning, call for estimating discrete distributions from data collected in batches, some of which may be untrustworthy, erroneous, faulty, or even adversarial. Previous estimators for this setting ran in exponential time, and for some regimes required a suboptimal number of batches. We provide the first polynomial-time estimator that is optimal in the number of batches and achieves essentially the best possible estimation accuracy.
originalAbstract: Many applications, including natural language processing, sensor networks, collaborative filtering, and federated learning, call for estimating discrete distributions from data collected in batches, some of which may be untrustworthy, erroneous, faulty, or even adversarial. Previous estimators for this setting ran in exponential time, and for some regimes required a suboptimal number of batches. We provide the first polynomial-time estimator that is optimal in the number of batches and achieves essentially the best possible estimation accuracy.

paragraphs: Estimating a discrete distribution means learning how probability is spread across distinct possible outcomes. In many applications, observations arrive in batches rather than as one undifferentiated dataset. The paper considers the difficult case where some batches may be unreliable, faulty, or deliberately adversarial, so the estimator must tolerate corrupted groups of observations.

Earlier estimators for this setting required exponential running time. In some regimes, they also needed more batches than were optimal. These are separate obstacles: an estimator can demand too much computation even when enough data are available, or require too much data even if its calculation could otherwise be performed.

The authors provide the first polynomial-time estimator for this setting that is optimal in the number of batches and achieves essentially the best possible estimation accuracy. The result addresses computational cost, batch requirements, and accuracy together. Its relevance extends to the batched-data settings named in the abstract, including sensor networks, collaborative filtering, natural language processing, and federated learning, where unreliable data sources can complicate distribution estimation.
summary.tldr: The paper gives a polynomial-time estimator for corrupted batches that uses an optimal number of batches and achieves essentially optimal accuracy.

title: Optimal Robust Learning of Discrete Distributions from Batches

abstract: We study the properties of a leave-node-out jackknife procedure for network data. Under the sparse graphon model, we prove an Efron-Stein-type inequality, showing that the network jackknife leads to conservative estimates of the variance (in expectation) for any network functional that is invariant to node permutation. For a general class of count functionals, we also establish consistency of the network jackknife. We complement our theoretical analysis with a range of simulated and real-data examples and show that the network jackknife offers competitive performance in cases where other resampling methods are known to be valid. In fact, for several network statistics, we see that the jackknife provides more accurate inferences compared to related methods such as subsampling.

paragraphs: The network jackknife estimates uncertainty by repeatedly leaving a node out of a network and examining how a statistic changes. This paper studies when that procedure has theoretical support. Its analysis uses the sparse graphon model, providing a setting in which to reason about the variability of statistics computed from network data.

The authors prove an Efron-Stein-type inequality for any network functional that is unchanged by relabeling nodes. Under the model, the jackknife variance estimate is conservative in expectation. That means the guarantee concerns its average behavior, rather than promising an overestimate for every individual network. For a general class of count functionals, they additionally establish consistency of the procedure.

Simulated and real-data examples complement the theory. The jackknife performs competitively in settings where other resampling methods are known to be valid, and it yields more accurate inference than related methods such as subsampling for several statistics. The work therefore provides both model-based justification and empirical support for a relatively direct approach to uncertainty estimation on networks.
summary.tldr: Under a sparse graphon model, the network jackknife gives conservative variance estimates in expectation and is consistent for a class of count statistics.

title: On the Theoretical Properties of the Network Jackknife

abstract: We propose a novel Stochastic Frank-Wolfe (a. k. a. conditional gradient) algorithm for constrained smooth finite-sum minimization with a generalized linear prediction/structure. This class of problems includes empirical risk minimization with sparse, low-rank, or other structured constraints. The proposed method is simple to implement, does not require step-size tuning, and has a constant per-iteration cost that is independent of the dataset size. Furthermore, as a byproduct of the method we obtain a stochastic estimator of the Frank-Wolfe gap that can be used as a stopping criterion. Depending on the setting, the proposed method matches or improves on the best computational guarantees for Stochastic Frank-Wolfe algorithms. Benchmarks on several datasets highlight different regimes in which the proposed method exhibits a faster empirical convergence than related methods. Finally, we provide an implementation of all considered methods in an open-source package.

paragraphs: The paper develops a stochastic Frank-Wolfe algorithm for smooth constrained objectives expressed as finite sums, with a generalized linear prediction structure. This setting includes empirical risk minimization with sparse, low-rank, and other structured constraints. The practical goal is to optimize such models efficiently as the number of data points grows.

The proposed method is simple to implement, avoids step-size tuning, and has constant per-iteration cost independent of dataset size. It also produces a stochastic estimate of the Frank-Wolfe gap, which can serve as a stopping criterion. This connects the optimization updates with a way to assess when further computation is no longer needed.

Depending on the setting, the method matches or improves the best computational guarantees for stochastic Frank-Wolfe algorithms. Dataset benchmarks identify regimes where it converges faster empirically than related methods. The authors also release implementations of the compared algorithms in an open-source package, supporting practical comparison of the theoretical and observed advantages across the relevant optimization settings.
summary.tldr: A stochastic Frank-Wolfe method avoids step-size tuning and offers dataset-size-independent iteration cost plus a stochastic stopping criterion.

title: Stochastic Frank-Wolfe for Constrained Finite-Sum Minimization

abstract: Recently, a new recurrent neural network (RNN) named the Legendre Memory Unit (LMU) was proposed and shown to achieve state-of-the-art performance on several benchmark datasets. Here we leverage the linear time-invariant (LTI) memory component of the LMU to construct a simplified variant that can be parallelized during training (and yet executed as an RNN during inference), resulting in up to 200 times faster training. We note that our efficient parallelizing scheme is general and is applicable to any deep network whose recurrent components are linear dynamical systems. We demonstrate the improved accuracy of our new architecture compared to the original LMU and a variety of published LSTM and transformer networks across seven benchmarks. For instance, our LMU sets a new state-of-the-art result on psMNIST, and uses half the parameters while outperforming DistilBERT and LSTM models on IMDB sentiment analysis.

paragraphs: The Legendre Memory Unit is a recurrent neural network with a linear time-invariant memory component. This paper uses that structure to build a simplified variant whose training can be parallelized. The model can still run recurrently during inference, so the computational organization used for training need not be the same as the one used to process inputs afterward.

The authors report training speedups of up to 200 times. They also describe the parallelization scheme as applicable to deep networks whose recurrent components are linear dynamical systems. This identifies the structural condition that makes the scheme useful beyond the particular LMU architecture studied.

Across seven benchmarks, the new architecture improves accuracy relative to the original LMU and a range of published LSTM and transformer networks. It establishes a reported state-of-the-art result on permuted sequential MNIST. On IMDB sentiment analysis, it outperforms the compared DistilBERT and LSTM models while using half the parameters. The findings show that the simplified architecture can combine faster training with strong predictive performance in the evaluated sequence tasks.
summary.tldr: A simplified Legendre Memory Unit enables parallel training with reported speedups up to 200 times while retaining recurrent inference and improving benchmark accuracy.

title: Parallelizing Legendre Memory Unit Training

abstract: We introduce an approach for understanding control policies represented as recurrent neural networks. Recent work has approached this problem by transforming such recurrent policy networks into finite-state machines (FSM) and then analyzing the equivalent minimized FSM. While this led to interesting insights, the minimization process can obscure a deeper understanding of a machine’s operation by merging states that are semantically distinct. To address this issue, we introduce an analysis approach that starts with an unminimized FSM and applies more-interpretable reductions that preserve the key decision points of the policy. We also contribute an attention tool to attain a deeper understanding of the role of observations in the decisions. Our case studies on 7 Atari games and 3 control benchmarks demonstrate that the approach can reveal insights that have not been previously noticed.

paragraphs: Recurrent neural networks can represent control policies whose decisions depend on internal state. One way to understand such policies is to convert them into finite-state machines and examine the resulting transitions. Earlier approaches then minimize the machine, reducing its size by merging states that can be treated as equivalent.

This paper identifies an interpretability cost of that minimization: states with different semantic meanings can be merged, hiding distinctions that help explain how the policy operates. The proposed analysis starts from an unminimized machine and applies reductions chosen to preserve key decision points. The aim is a representation that remains manageable while retaining distinctions useful for understanding behavior.

The authors also introduce an attention tool to examine the role of observations in decisions. Case studies on seven Atari games and three control benchmarks reveal insights that earlier analyses had not noticed. The contribution shows how the choice of simplification procedure affects what an analyst can learn from an extracted policy representation, even when minimizing the machine initially seems like a natural step.
summary.tldr: Interpretability-focused reductions preserve meaningful decision points in finite-state representations of recurrent policies and reveal previously unnoticed behavior.

title: Re-understanding Finite-State Representations of Recurrent Policy Networks

abstract: Smooth dynamics interrupted by discontinuities are known as hybrid systems and arise commonly in nature. Latent ODEs allow for powerful representation of irregularly sampled time series but are not designed to capture trajectories arising from hybrid systems. Here, we propose the Latent Segmented ODE (LatSegODE), which uses Latent ODEs to perform reconstruction and changepoint detection within hybrid trajectories featuring jump discontinuities and switching dynamical modes. Where it is possible to train a Latent ODE on the smooth dynamical flows between discontinuities, we apply the pruned exact linear time (PELT) algorithm to detect changepoints where latent dynamics restart, thereby maximizing the joint probability of a piece-wise continuous latent dynamical representation. We propose usage of the marginal likelihood as a score function for PELT, circumventing the need for model-complexity-based penalization. The LatSegODE outperforms baselines in reconstructive and segmentation tasks including synthetic data sets of sine waves, Lotka Volterra dynamics, and UCI Character Trajectories.

paragraphs: Hybrid trajectories combine smooth evolution with sudden jumps or switches in the governing dynamics. Latent ordinary differential equation models can represent irregularly sampled time series, but are not designed for these interruptions. LatSegODE addresses this by combining smooth latent dynamics with explicit detection of where one segment ends and another begins.

The approach applies when a latent ODE can be trained on the smooth flows between discontinuities. It uses the pruned exact linear time algorithm, PELT, to select changepoints where the latent dynamics restart. The segmentation seeks a high joint probability for the resulting piecewise continuous representation, tying boundary placement to how well the model explains the trajectory.

The authors propose marginal likelihood as PELT’s scoring function, avoiding the need for a model-complexity-based penalty. They report better reconstruction and segmentation than the evaluated baselines on sine-wave data, Lotka–Volterra dynamics, and UCI Character Trajectories. The contribution is a way to preserve smooth modeling within segments while explicitly accommodating discontinuities between them.
summary.tldr: LatSegODE combines latent ODEs with changepoint detection to reconstruct and segment trajectories containing jumps or changing dynamics.

title: Segmenting Hybrid Trajectories using Latent ODEs

abstract: While semi-supervised learning (SSL) has received tremendous attentions in many machine learning tasks due to its successful use of unlabeled data, existing SSL algorithms use either all unlabeled examples or the unlabeled examples with a fixed high-confidence prediction during the training progress. However, it is possible that too many correct/wrong pseudo labeled examples are eliminated/selected. In this work we develop a simple yet powerful framework, whose key idea is to select a subset of training examples from the unlabeled data when performing existing SSL methods so that only the unlabeled examples with pseudo labels related to the labeled data will be used to train models. The selection is performed at each updating iteration by only keeping the examples whose losses are smaller than a given threshold that is dynamically adjusted through the iteration. Our proposed approach, Dash, enjoys its adaptivity in terms of unlabeled data selection and its theoretical guarantee. Specifically, we theoretically establish the convergence rate of Dash from the view of non-convex optimization. Finally, we empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in comparison with state-of-the-art over benchmarks.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning uses unlabeled examples alongside labeled data, often by assigning predictions as temporary labels. The paper identifies a problem with two common selection strategies: using every unlabeled example or accepting only predictions above a fixed confidence threshold. Either strategy can discard useful correct pseudo-labels or include too many incorrect ones.

Dash adds an adaptive selection mechanism to existing semi-supervised methods. At each update, it retains unlabeled examples only when their losses fall below a threshold that changes over training. The intended selection favors pseudo-labels related to the labeled data, making the choice of training examples responsive to the learning process.

The authors establish a convergence rate for Dash through an analysis of nonconvex optimization. They also evaluate it against leading methods on benchmark tasks and report evidence of effectiveness. The contribution links a simple, changing loss cutoff with theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation. Its significance is the ability to adapt which unlabeled examples influence learning as training progresses, rather than committing to one fixed selection rule throughout.
summary.tldr: Dash adaptively selects pseudo-labeled examples using a changing loss threshold, with convergence analysis and supporting benchmark results.

title: Dash: Semi-Supervised Learning with Dynamic Thresholding

abstract: With the fast development of algorithmic governance, fairness has become a compulsory property for machine learning models to suppress unintentional discrimination. In this paper, we focus on the pre-processing aspect for achieving fairness, and propose a data reweighing approach that only adjusts the weight for samples in the training phase. Different from most previous reweighing methods which usually assign a uniform weight for each (sub)group, we granularly model the influence of each training sample with regard to fairness-related quantity and predictive utility, and compute individual weights based on influence under the constraints from both fairness and utility. Experimental results reveal that previous methods achieve fairness at a non-negligible cost of utility, while as a significant advantage, our approach can empirically release the tradeoff and obtain cost-free fairness for equal opportunity. We demonstrate the cost-free fairness through vanilla classifiers and standard training processes, compared to baseline methods on multiple real-world tabular datasets. Code available at https://github.com/brandeis-machine-learning/influence-fairness.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether changing the importance of individual training examples can improve fairness while preserving predictive performance. Its intervention happens during training: examples receive different weights, changing how much they contribute to learning. The approach therefore addresses fairness through the training data rather than requiring a specialized classifier.

The central distinction is the level at which weights are chosen. Previous reweighing methods commonly give the same weight to every example within a group. Here, the authors estimate each example’s influence on both a fairness quantity and predictive utility. They then compute individual weights subject to constraints covering both objectives, allowing examples within the same group to contribute differently.

Experiments with standard classifiers and training procedures on multiple real-world tabular datasets support the approach. For equal opportunity, the authors report fairness improvements without an observed utility cost, whereas the compared methods sacrifice utility. This is an empirical result for the studied fairness objective and settings, showing that the usual tradeoff can sometimes be avoided.
summary.tldr: Weighting individual training examples by their influence improves equal opportunity without an observed predictive utility cost in the reported experiments.

title: Achieving Fairness at No Utility Cost via Data Reweighing with Influence

abstract: NDCG, namely Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain, is a widely used ranking metric in information retrieval and machine learning. However, efficient and provable stochastic methods for maximizing NDCG are still lacking, especially for deep models. In this paper, we propose a principled approach to optimize NDCG and its top-$K$ variant. First, we formulate a novel compositional optimization problem for optimizing the NDCG surrogate, and a novel bilevel compositional optimization problem for optimizing the top-$K$ NDCG surrogate. Then, we develop efficient stochastic algorithms with provable convergence guarantees for the non-convex objectives. Different from existing NDCG optimization methods, the per-iteration complexity of our algorithms scales with the mini-batch size instead of the number of total items. To improve the effectiveness for deep learning, we further propose practical strategies by using initial warm-up and stop gradient operator. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate that our methods outperform prior ranking approaches in terms of NDCG. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time that stochastic algorithms are proposed to optimize NDCG with a provable convergence guarantee. Our proposed methods are implemented in the LibAUC library at https://libauc.org.

paragraphs: NDCG is a widely used measure of ranking quality, but efficiently optimizing it with deep models presents challenges. This paper develops stochastic methods for surrogate objectives corresponding to NDCG and its top-K variant. The aim is to make training scalable while also providing convergence guarantees for the resulting nonconvex optimization problems.

The authors formulate the NDCG surrogate as a compositional optimization problem and the top-K surrogate as a bilevel compositional problem. They then derive algorithms whose per-iteration cost scales with minibatch size rather than the total number of items. That distinction matters for large ranking problems because a training step need not grow with the entire item collection.

For deep learning, the method also includes practical strategies involving an initial warm-up and a stop-gradient operator. Experiments across multiple datasets show better NDCG than prior ranking approaches. The theoretical guarantees concern convergence of the proposed surrogate optimization procedures; the experiments separately demonstrate improvements in the ranking metric itself. Together, these contributions connect a mathematically analyzed objective with a training approach intended for large-scale use.
summary.tldr: The paper develops convergent stochastic algorithms for NDCG surrogates whose iteration costs scale with minibatch size, and reports improved ranking performance.

title: Large-scale Stochastic Optimization of NDCG Surrogates for Deep Learning with Provable Convergence

abstract: Our theoretical understanding of deep learning has not kept pace with its empirical success. While network architecture is known to be critical, we do not yet understand its effect on learned representations and network behavior, or how this architecture should reflect task structure.In this work, we begin to address this gap by introducing the Gated Deep Linear Network framework that schematizes how pathways of information flow impact learning dynamics within an architecture. Crucially, because of the gating, these networks can compute nonlinear functions of their input. We derive an exact reduction and, for certain cases, exact solutions to the dynamics of learning. Our analysis demonstrates that the learning dynamics in structured networks can be conceptualized as a neural race with an implicit bias towards shared representations, which then govern the model’s ability to systematically generalize, multi-task, and transfer. We validate our key insights on naturalistic datasets and with relaxed assumptions. Taken together, our work gives rise to general hypotheses relating neural architecture to learning and provides a mathematical approach towards understanding the design of more complex architectures and the role of modularity and compositionality in solving real-world problems. The code and results are available at https://www.saxelab.org/gated-dln.

paragraphs: Network architecture shapes which representations a model learns, but explaining that influence mathematically is difficult. This paper introduces Gated Deep Linear Networks to study how pathways of information flow affect learning dynamics. Although the framework uses deep linear networks, its gates allow the overall model to compute nonlinear functions of the input.

The authors derive an exact reduction of the learning dynamics and exact solutions in certain cases. Their analysis describes learning as a neural race with an implicit preference for shared representations. Those shared representations then influence systematic generalization, learning multiple tasks, and transfer. The framework thus connects architectural pathways to the representations that emerge during training and to the behaviors those representations support.

The paper validates its main insights on naturalistic datasets and under relaxed assumptions. It also develops general hypotheses about the relationship between architecture and learning, including the roles of modularity and compositionality. The exact mathematical results apply within the analyzed framework and specified cases, while the broader contribution is an approach for reasoning about the design of more complex architectures.
summary.tldr: Gated Deep Linear Networks reveal learning dynamics with a bias toward shared representations that shape generalization, multitasking, and transfer.

title: The Neural Race Reduction: Dynamics of Abstraction in Gated Networks

abstract: Learning the long-range interactions on large-scale mesh-based physical systems with flat Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and stacking Message Passings (MPs) is challenging due to the scaling complexity w.r.t. the number of nodes and over-smoothing. Therefore, there has been growing interest in the community to introduce multi-scale structures to GNNs for physics simulation. However, current state-of-the-art methods are limited by their reliance on the labor-heavy drawing of coarser meshes or building coarser levels based on spatial proximity, which can introduce wrong edges across geometry boundaries. Inspired by the bipartite graph determination, we propose a novel pooling strategy, bi-stride to tackle the aforementioned limitations. Bi-stride pools nodes on every other frontier of the Breadth-First-Search (BFS), without the need for the manual drawing of coarser meshes and, avoid wrong edges introduced by spatial proximity. Additionally, it enables a reduced number of MP times on each level and the non-parametrized pooling and unpooling by interpolations, similar to convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), which significantly reduces computational requirements. Experiments show that the proposed framework, BSMS-GNN , significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency in representative physics-based simulation scenarios.

paragraphs: Physical simulations on meshes often require information to travel between distant parts of a system. A flat graph neural network can accomplish this through repeated message passing, but increasing the number of passes raises computational costs and can oversmooth representations. Multiscale networks offer another route, provided their coarser graphs preserve the geometry appropriately.

This paper introduces bi-stride pooling, which selects nodes from alternating breadth-first-search frontiers. The construction uses graph connectivity instead of requiring manually drawn coarse meshes or relying on spatial proximity. That distinction matters because points that are close in space can lie across a geometry boundary, where proximity-based connections would introduce incorrect edges.

The resulting BSMS-GNN uses fewer message-passing steps at each scale and interpolation-based pooling and unpooling without learned parameters. These choices reduce the computational requirements of multiscale processing. Experiments in representative physical simulation scenarios report substantial improvements in both accuracy and efficiency over existing methods, supporting the usefulness of connectivity-based coarsening for the evaluated mesh systems.
summary.tldr: BSMS-GNN builds mesh hierarchies through graph-based bi-stride pooling, improving accuracy and computational efficiency in the reported physical simulations.

title: Efficient Learning of Mesh-Based Physical Simulation with Bi-Stride Multi-Scale Graph Neural Network

abstract: Noting the importance of factorizing (or disentangling) the latent space, we propose a novel, non-probabilistic disentangling framework for autoencoders, based on the principles of symmetry transformations that are independent of one another. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first deterministic model that is aiming to achieve disentanglement based on autoencoders using only a reconstruction loss without pairs of images or labels, by explicitly introducing inductive biases into a model architecture through Euler encoding. The proposed model is then compared with a number of state-of-the-art models, relevant to disentanglement, including symmetry-based models and generative models. Our evaluation using six different disentanglement metrics, including the unsupervised disentanglement metric we propose here in this paper, shows that the proposed model can offer better disentanglement, especially when variances of the features are different, where other methods may struggle. We believe that this model opens several opportunities for linear disentangled representation learning based on deterministic autoencoders.

paragraphs: Disentangled representations aim to separate underlying factors of variation within a model's latent space. This paper proposes a deterministic autoencoder framework built around symmetry transformations that act independently. The goal is to encourage a structured representation while training the model only to reconstruct its inputs.

The key design choice is to put the relevant inductive biases into the architecture through Euler encoding. The framework does not require image pairs or labels, and its training objective uses only reconstruction loss. This makes the architecture responsible for encouraging factor separation. The authors describe the approach as, to their knowledge, the first deterministic autoencoder model pursuing disentanglement under this combination of conditions.

Evaluation compares the framework with relevant state-of-the-art symmetry-based and generative models using six disentanglement metrics, including a new unsupervised metric. The reported results show that the model can achieve better disentanglement, particularly when features have different variances. That finding suggests architectural structure can help in a setting where other methods may struggle, while the claimed advantage remains an empirical possibility supported by the evaluation.
summary.tldr: A deterministic autoencoder uses architectural symmetry biases to improve disentanglement with reconstruction loss alone, especially for features with unequal variances.

title: Orthogonality-Enforced Latent Space in Autoencoders: An Approach to Learning Disentangled Representations

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) aims to train machine learning models for multiple clients without sharing their own private data. Due to the heterogeneity of clients’ local data distribution, recent studies explore the personalized FL that learns and deploys distinct local models with the help of auxiliary global models. However, the clients can be heterogeneous in terms of not only local data distribution, but also their computation and communication resources. The capacity and efficiency of personalized models are restricted by the lowest-resource clients, leading to sub-optimal performance and limited practicality of personalized FL. To overcome these challenges, we propose a novel approach named pFedGate for efficient personalized FL by adaptively and efficiently learning sparse local models. With a lightweight trainable gating layer, pFedGate enables clients to reach their full potential in model capacity by generating different sparse models accounting for both the heterogeneous data distributions and resource constraints. Meanwhile, the computation and communication efficiency are both improved thanks to the adaptability between the model sparsity and clients’ resources. Further, we theoretically show that the proposed pFedGate has superior complexity with guaranteed convergence and generalization error. Extensive experiments show that pFedGate achieves superior global accuracy, individual accuracy and efficiency simultaneously over state-of-the-art methods. We also demonstrate that pFedGate performs better than competitors in the novel clients participation and partial clients participation scenarios, and can learn meaningful sparse local models adapted to different data distributions.

paragraphs: Personalized federated learning develops distinct models for clients whose private data follow different distributions. This paper emphasizes that clients also differ in computing power and communication resources. When model design is constrained by the least capable participants, other clients may be unable to use their available capacity effectively.

The proposed pFedGate method learns sparse local models through a lightweight trainable gating layer. It generates different sparse models that account for both local data and resource constraints. By adapting sparsity to each client's resources, the method aims to improve computation and communication efficiency while allowing clients to use more suitable model capacities.

Its experiments report simultaneous improvements in global accuracy, individual accuracy, and efficiency over leading alternatives. Additional evaluations cover newly participating clients and partial participation, where pFedGate also performs better than competitors. The learned sparse models adapt meaningfully to different data distributions, supporting personalization along both statistical and resource dimensions.
summary.tldr: pFedGate personalizes sparse federated models to each client's data and resources, improving accuracy and efficiency in the reported experiments.

title: Efficient Personalized Federated Learning via Sparse Model-Adaptation

abstract: Generating unlabeled data has been recently shown to help address the few-shot hypothesis adaptation (FHA) problem, where we aim to train a classifier for the target domain with a few labeled target-domain data and a well-trained source-domain classifier (i.e., a source hypothesis), for the additional information of the highly-compatible unlabeled data. However, the generated data of the existing methods are extremely similar or even the same. The strong dependency among the generated data will lead the learning to fail. In this paper, we propose a diversity-enhancing generative network (DEG-Net) for the FHA problem, which can generate diverse unlabeled data with the help of a kernel independence measure: the Hilbert-Schmidt independence criterion (HSIC). Specifically, DEG-Net will generate data via minimizing the HSIC value (i.e., maximizing the independence) among the semantic features of the generated data. By DEG-Net, the generated unlabeled data are more diverse and more effective for addressing the FHA problem. Experimental results show that the DEG-Net outperforms existing FHA baselines and further verifies that generating diverse data plays an important role in addressing the FHA problem.

paragraphs: Few-shot hypothesis adaptation starts with a well-trained classifier from a source domain and only a small labeled dataset from a target domain. Generated unlabeled examples can provide additional information for adapting the classifier. However, the paper identifies a weakness in existing approaches: generated examples can be extremely similar or even identical, making the extra data strongly dependent.

DEG-Net addresses this problem by explicitly encouraging diversity among generated examples. It uses the Hilbert-Schmidt independence criterion, a kernel-based measure of dependence, on the examples’ semantic features. Minimizing this measure encourages independence in those features. The objective therefore targets diversity in the generated data’s semantic representation, rather than merely increasing the number of available examples.

The authors report that DEG-Net produces more diverse and more useful unlabeled data, and outperforms existing few-shot hypothesis adaptation baselines in their experiments. The findings support the role of generated-data diversity in adaptation: additional examples help when they provide varied information, while repeated or highly dependent examples can undermine learning.
summary.tldr: DEG-Net encourages semantic independence among generated examples to improve classifier adaptation with few labeled target-domain samples.

title: Diversity-enhancing Generative Network for Few-shot Hypothesis Adaptation

abstract: Random masks define surprisingly effective sparse neural network models, as has been shown empirically. The resulting sparse networks can often compete with dense architectures and state-of-the-art lottery ticket pruning algorithms, even though they do not rely on computationally expensive prune-train iterations and can be drawn initially without significant computational overhead. We offer a theoretical explanation of how random masks can approximate arbitrary target networks if they are wider by a logarithmic factor in the inverse sparsity $1 / \log(1/\text{sparsity})$. This overparameterization factor is necessary at least for 3-layer random networks, which elucidates the observed degrading performance of random networks at higher sparsity. At moderate to high sparsity levels, however, our results imply that sparser networks are contained within random source networks so that any dense-to-sparse training scheme can be turned into a computationally more efficient sparse-to-sparse one by constraining the search to a fixed random mask. We demonstrate the feasibility of this approach in experiments for different pruning methods and propose particularly effective choices of initial layer-wise sparsity ratios of the random source network. As a special case, we show theoretically and experimentally that random source networks also contain strong lottery tickets.

paragraphs: Randomly chosen masks can produce sparse neural networks that compete with dense networks and sophisticated pruning methods, despite requiring little initial selection overhead. This paper offers a theoretical explanation: random masked networks can approximate arbitrary target networks when given sufficient additional width, with the required widening tied to sparsity.

The authors establish a logarithmic relationship between the needed overparameterization and inverse sparsity. They also show that this widening requirement is necessary at least for three-layer random networks, helping explain performance degradation at higher sparsity. At moderate to high sparsity levels, their results show that random source networks contain still-sparser networks that can serve as targets for subsequent training and pruning.

This supports replacing a dense-to-sparse procedure with a more computationally efficient sparse-to-sparse procedure constrained by a fixed random mask. Experiments demonstrate feasibility across different pruning methods, and the authors propose effective initial layer-wise sparsity allocations. They also show theoretically and experimentally that random source networks contain strong lottery tickets, further connecting random initialization masks to useful sparse subnetworks.
summary.tldr: Theory and experiments explain when random sparse networks contain useful subnetworks, supporting efficient training that starts sparse.

title: Why Random Pruning Is All We Need to Start Sparse

abstract: We consider solving partial differential equations (PDEs) with Fourier neural operators (FNOs), which operate in the frequency domain. Since the laws of physics do not depend on the coordinate system used to describe them, it is desirable to encode such symmetries in the neural operator architecture for better performance and easier learning. While encoding symmetries in the physical domain using group theory has been studied extensively, how to capture symmetries in the frequency domain is under-explored. In this work, we extend group convolutions to the frequency domain and design Fourier layers that are equivariant to rotations, translations, and reflections by leveraging the equivariance property of the Fourier transform. The resulting $G$-FNO architecture generalizes well across input resolutions and performs well in settings with varying levels of symmetry. Our code is publicly available as part of the AIRS library (https://github.com/divelab/AIRS).

paragraphs: Fourier neural operators work in the frequency domain to help solve partial differential equations. The paper asks how these models can incorporate symmetries associated with changes of coordinates. If an input is rotated, translated, or reflected, an equivariant model transforms its output correspondingly, making those relationships part of its architecture.

The authors extend group convolutions into the frequency domain and use the Fourier transform’s equivariance properties to construct suitable layers. This produces G-FNO, a Fourier neural operator designed to respect rotations, translations, and reflections. The work addresses a gap between well-studied symmetry methods in physical space and less-explored symmetry handling in frequency-based models.

The reported results show that G-FNO generalizes well across input resolutions and performs well in settings with different levels of symmetry. These findings support the usefulness of incorporating symmetry directly into Fourier layers. They also indicate that the architecture can remain effective across the varied symmetry settings evaluated, connecting a mathematical design principle with practical behavior on PDE problems.
summary.tldr: G-FNO builds rotation, translation, and reflection equivariance into Fourier layers and reports good performance across resolutions and varying symmetry levels.

title: Group Equivariant Fourier Neural Operators for Partial Differential Equations

abstract: Finding meaningful representations and distances of hierarchical data is important in many fields. This paper presents a new method for hierarchical data embedding and distance. Our method relies on combining diffusion geometry, a central approach to manifold learning, and hyperbolic geometry. Specifically, using diffusion geometry, we build multi-scale densities on the data, aimed to reveal their hierarchical structure, and then embed them into a product of hyperbolic spaces. We show theoretically that our embedding and distance recover the underlying hierarchical structure. In addition, we demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method and its advantages compared to existing methods on graph embedding benchmarks and hierarchical datasets.

paragraphs: Hierarchical data needs representations and distances that reflect its underlying organization. This paper introduces a method that combines diffusion geometry, an approach used in manifold learning, with hyperbolic geometry. The combination is designed to reveal hierarchical structure and then represent it in a geometric space suited to the method’s distance construction.

The first step builds densities over the data at multiple scales using diffusion geometry. These multiscale descriptions are intended to expose the hierarchy instead of representing the data at only one scale. The method then embeds those descriptions into a product of hyperbolic spaces. Both the embedding and the associated distance are central outputs of the approach.

The authors provide theoretical results showing recovery of the underlying hierarchical structure through their embedding and distance. They also evaluate the method on graph-embedding benchmarks and hierarchical datasets, reporting advantages over existing methods. The contribution links a theoretical account of hierarchy recovery with empirical evidence that the resulting representation and distance are useful.
summary.tldr: The method combines multiscale diffusion densities with hyperbolic embeddings to represent and recover hierarchical structure.

title: Hyperbolic Diffusion Embedding and Distance for Hierarchical Representation Learning

abstract: We introduce MABe22, a large-scale, multi-agent video and trajectory benchmark to assess the quality of learned behavior representations. This dataset is collected from a variety of biology experiments, and includes triplets of interacting mice (4.7 million frames video+pose tracking data, 10 million frames pose only), symbiotic beetle-ant interactions (10 million frames video data), and groups of interacting flies (4.4 million frames of pose tracking data). Accompanying these data, we introduce a panel of real-life downstream analysis tasks to assess the quality of learned representations by evaluating how well they preserve information about the experimental conditions (e.g. strain, time of day, optogenetic stimulation) and animal behavior. We test multiple state-of-the-art self-supervised video and trajectory representation learning methods to demonstrate the use of our benchmark, revealing that methods developed using human action datasets do not fully translate to animal datasets. We hope that our benchmark and dataset encourage a broader exploration of behavior representation learning methods across species and settings.

paragraphs: MABe22 is a benchmark for evaluating what machine-learned representations capture about animal behavior. It brings together video and movement trajectories from biological experiments involving interacting mice, beetles and ants, and groups of flies. These settings broaden evaluation beyond the human-action datasets commonly used to develop behavior-learning methods.

The data include 4.7 million mouse frames with video and pose tracking, another 10 million mouse frames with pose alone, 10 million beetle–ant video frames, and 4.4 million fly pose frames. Accompanying analysis tasks test whether learned representations retain information about behavior and experimental conditions, including strain, time of day, and optogenetic stimulation.

The authors evaluate several leading self-supervised methods for video and trajectory representation learning. Their results show that methods developed around human actions do not transfer fully to animal data. The benchmark therefore supplies both varied recordings and concrete ways to judge their representations, supporting comparisons grounded in the information that biological analyses need to recover.
summary.tldr: MABe22 evaluates learned animal-behavior representations across species and reveals incomplete transfer from methods developed on human actions.

title: MABe22: A Multi-Species Multi-Task Benchmark for Learned Representations of Behavior

abstract: Machine learning-driven human behavior analysis is gaining attention in behavioral/mental healthcare, due to its potential to identify behavioral patterns that cannot be recognized by traditional assessments. Real-life applications, such as digital behavioral biomarker identification, often require the discovery of complex spatiotemporal patterns in multimodal data, which is largely under-explored. To fill this gap, we propose a novel model that integrates uniquely designed Deep Temporal Sets (DTS) with Evidential Reinforced Attentions (ERA). DTS captures complex temporal relationships in the input and generates a set-based representation, while ERA captures the policy network’s uncertainty and conducts evidence-aware exploration to locate attentive regions in behavioral data. Using child-computer interaction data as a testing platform, we demonstrate the effectiveness of DTS-ERA in differentiating children with Autism Spectrum Disorder and typically developing children based on sequential multimodal visual and touch behaviors. Comparisons with baseline methods show that our model achieves superior performance and has the potential to provide objective, quantitative, and precise analysis of complex human behaviors.

paragraphs: Behavioral analysis can require finding patterns spread across time, space, and multiple types of observations. This paper studies that challenge using sequential visual and touch behaviors. Its motivation is that machine learning may identify complex behavioral patterns that traditional assessments do not readily recognize, potentially supporting quantitative behavioral analysis.

The proposed model combines Deep Temporal Sets with Evidential Reinforced Attentions. Deep Temporal Sets captures temporal relationships and converts the input into a set-based representation. The attention component represents uncertainty in its policy network and uses that evidence to guide exploration of relevant regions in the behavioral data. Together, the components address both how behavior unfolds and where the model should focus.

The evaluation uses child-computer interaction data to distinguish children with Autism Spectrum Disorder from typically developing children. The authors report better performance than the comparison methods. These findings support the model’s usefulness for the studied behavioral discrimination task and its potential for objective analysis; the stated contribution is a pattern-discovery approach, rather than an established clinical diagnostic procedure.
summary.tldr: DTS-ERA combines temporal representations and uncertainty-aware attention to identify patterns in multimodal behavioral sequences.

title: Deep Temporal Sets with Evidential Reinforced Attentions for Unique Behavioral Pattern Discovery

abstract: This paper introduces a novel Token-and-Duration Transducer (TDT) architecture for sequence-to-sequence tasks. TDT extends conventional RNN-Transducer architectures by jointly predicting both a token and its duration, i.e. the number of input frames covered by the emitted token. This is achieved by using a joint network with two outputs which are independently normalized to generate distributions over tokens and durations. During inference, TDT models can skip input frames guided by the predicted duration output, which makes them significantly faster than conventional Transducers which process the encoder output frame by frame. TDT models achieve both better accuracy and significantly faster inference than conventional Transducers on different sequence transduction tasks. TDT models for Speech Recognition achieve better accuracy and up to 2.82X faster inference than conventional Transducers. TDT models for Speech Translation achieve an absolute gain of over 1 BLEU on the MUST-C test compared with conventional Transducers, and its inference is 2.27X faster. In Speech Intent Classification and Slot Filling tasks, TDT models improve the intent accuracy by up to over 1% (absolute) over conventional Transducers, while running up to 1.28X faster. Our implementation of the TDT model will be open-sourced with the NeMo (https://github.com/NVIDIA/NeMo) toolkit.

paragraphs: Conventional transducers process encoder outputs frame by frame when converting an input sequence into output tokens. The Token-and-Duration Transducer, or TDT, adds a second prediction: how many input frames an emitted token covers. That duration tells the model how far it can advance through the input during inference.

The architecture extends an RNN-Transducer with a joint network producing separate, independently normalized distributions over tokens and durations. Predicting duration makes frame skipping part of the model’s output mechanism. The stated benefit is faster inference while retaining, and in the reported experiments improving, task accuracy across several sequence-transduction applications.

For speech recognition, the paper reports better accuracy and inference up to 2.82 times faster than conventional transducers. Speech translation improves by more than one absolute BLEU point on MUST-C while running 2.27 times faster. In speech intent classification and slot filling, reported intent-accuracy gains reach over one absolute percentage point, with speedups up to 1.28 times. These task-specific results support learning how far to advance alongside what to emit.
summary.tldr: TDT predicts tokens and their durations together, enabling frame skipping that improves reported inference speed and accuracy.

title: Efficient Sequence Transduction by Jointly Predicting Tokens and Durations

abstract: Model-Based Reinforcement Learning (RL) is widely believed to have the potential to improve sample efficiency by allowing an agent to synthesize large amounts of imagined experience. Experience Replay (ER) can be considered a simple kind of model, which has proved effective at improving the stability and efficiency of deep RL. In principle, a learned parametric model could improve on ER by generalizing from real experience to augment the dataset with additional plausible experience. However, given that learned value functions can also generalize, it is not immediately obvious why model generalization should be better. Here, we provide theoretical and empirical insight into when, and how, we can expect data generated by a learned model to be useful. First, we provide a simple theorem motivating how learning a model as an intermediate step can narrow down the set of possible value functions more than learning a value function directly from data using the Bellman equation. Second, we provide an illustrative example showing empirically how a similar effect occurs in a more concrete setting with neural network function approximation. Finally, we provide extensive experiments showing the benefit of model-based learning for online RL in environments with combinatorial complexity, but factored structure that allows a learned model to generalize. In these experiments, we take care to control for other factors in order to isolate, insofar as possible, the benefit of using experience generated by a learned model relative to ER alone.

paragraphs: A learned environment model can generate imagined experience to supplement an agent’s real observations. Yet value functions also generalize from data, so it is not obvious why learning a separate model should help beyond replaying stored experience. This paper examines when model-based generalization adds useful information.

A theorem motivates how learning a model as an intermediate step can restrict the possible value functions more than directly applying the Bellman equation to observed data. An illustrative neural-network experiment shows a similar effect in a more concrete setting. The proposed benefit therefore concerns the constraints supplied by model learning, not simply the amount of generated experience.

Further online reinforcement-learning experiments study environments with combinatorial complexity and factored structure that a model can generalize over. The authors control other factors as far as possible to isolate benefits over experience replay alone. Their results support model-generated experience in these structured settings, connecting its usefulness to the model’s ability to generalize across the underlying environment.
summary.tldr: Theory and experiments explain how learned environment models can improve reinforcement learning beyond replay through useful structural generalization.

title: The Benefits of Model-Based Generalization in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Identifying layers within text-to-image models which control visual attributes can facilitate efficient model editing through closed-form updates. Recent work, leveraging causal tracing show that early Stable-Diffusion variants confine knowledge primarily to the first layer of the CLIP text-encoder, while it diffuses throughout the UNet. Extending this framework, we observe that for recent models (e.g., SD-XL, DeepFloyd), causal tracing fails in pinpointing localized knowledge, highlighting challenges in model editing. To address this issue, we introduce the concept of mechanistic localization in text-to-image models, where knowledge about various visual attributes (e.g., "style", "objects", "facts") can be mechanistically localized to a small fraction of layers in the UNet, thus facilitating efficient model editing. We localize knowledge using our method LocoGen which measures the direct effect of intermediate layers to output generation by performing interventions in the cross-attention layers of the UNet. We then employ LocoEdit, a fast closed-form editing method across popular open-source text-to-image models (including the latest SD-XL) and explore the possibilities of neuron-level model editing. Using mechanistic localization, our work offers a better view of successes and failures in localization-based text-to-image model editing.

paragraphs: Editing a text-to-image model efficiently requires identifying which internal layers influence the visual attribute to be changed. Earlier causal-tracing work found localized knowledge in early Stable Diffusion variants, but this paper reports that the same approach fails to pinpoint localized knowledge in newer models such as SD-XL and DeepFloyd. This creates a practical obstacle for localization-based editing.

The authors introduce mechanistic localization, focusing on layers’ direct effects on generated outputs. Their method, LocoGen, intervenes in the UNet’s cross-attention layers to identify where attributes such as style, objects, and facts can be controlled. Under this approach, knowledge about these attributes can be localized to a small fraction of UNet layers.

The paper then uses LocoEdit, a fast closed-form editing method, across popular open-source text-to-image models including SD-XL. It also explores editing at the level of individual neurons. The contribution links localization to an actionable editing mechanism and offers an account of why localization-based edits succeed or fail, even when an earlier tracing procedure does not identify a clear location.
summary.tldr: LocoGen identifies layers that directly control visual attributes, enabling fast closed-form edits in text-to-image models including SD-XL.

title: On Mechanistic Knowledge Localization in Text-to-Image Generative Models

abstract: Predictive Coding (PC) is a theoretical framework in cognitive science suggesting that the human brain processes cognition through spatiotemporal prediction of visual world. Existing studies have developed spatiotemporal prediction neural networks based on the PC theroy, emulating its two core mechanisms: Correcting predictions from residuals and Hierarchical learning. However, these models do not show the enhancement of prediction skills on real-world forecasting tasks, and ignore the Precision Weighting mechanism of PC theory. Precision weight posits that the brain allocates more attention to signals with lower Precision, contributing to the the cognitive ability of human brains. This work introduces the Cognitive Diffusion Probabilistic Models (CogDPM) which demonstrates the connection between diffusion probabilistic models and PC theory. CogDPM features a precision estimation method based on the hierarchical sampling capabilities of diffusion models, and allocate the guidance with precision weights estimated by the inherent property of diffusion models. We experimentally show that the precision weights is an estimator of model’s predictability on the rigid body and fluid motion dataset. We also apply CogDPM to real-world prediction tasks using the U.K. precipitation and ERA surface wind datasets. Our results demonstrate that CogDPM outperforms both existing domain-specific operational models and general deep prediction models in providing more proficient forecasting.

Existing studies have developed spatiotemporal prediction neural networks based on the PC theroy, emulating its two core mechanisms: Correcting predictions from residuals and Hierarchical learning. However, these models do not show the enhancement of prediction skills on real-world forecasting tasks, and ignore the Precision Weighting mechanism of PC theory. Precision weight posits that the brain allocates more attention to signals with lower Precision, contributing to the the cognitive ability of human brains. This work introduces the Cognitive Diffusion Probabilistic Models (CogDPM) which demonstrates the connection between diffusion probabilistic models and PC theory. CogDPM features a precision estimation method based on the hierarchical sampling capabilities of diffusion models, and allocate the guidance with precision weights estimated by the inherent property of diffusion models. We experimentally show that the precision weights is an estimator of model’s predictability on the rigid body and fluid motion dataset. We also apply CogDPM to real-world prediction tasks using the U.K. precipitation and ERA surface wind datasets. Our results demonstrate that CogDPM outperforms both existing domain-specific operational models and general deep prediction models in providing more proficient forecasting.

paragraphs: CogDPM connects diffusion models with predictive coding, a cognitive theory of how predictions help organize visual processing over space and time. Earlier prediction networks inspired by this theory used hierarchical learning and corrections based on prediction residuals. According to the paper, they did not demonstrate improved forecasting on real-world tasks and omitted the theory’s precision-weighting mechanism.

The proposed model uses diffusion models’ hierarchical sampling to estimate precision and then uses those estimates to weight guidance. In the account adopted by the paper, lower-precision signals receive greater attention. The method therefore brings an additional predictive-coding mechanism into the forecasting process, rather than relying only on hierarchical prediction and residual correction.

Experiments on rigid-body and fluid-motion data show that the estimated weights reflect the model’s predictability. The authors also evaluate forecasting on U.K. precipitation and ERA surface wind datasets, reporting improvements over both domain-specific operational models and general deep prediction models. These findings support the usefulness of the proposed weighting mechanism in the evaluated forecasting settings.
summary.tldr: CogDPM uses diffusion-derived precision estimates to guide forecasting, with reported gains on motion, precipitation, and surface wind tasks.

title: CogDPM: Diffusion Probabilistic Models via Cognitive Predictive Coding

abstract: Using feature attributions for post-hoc explanations is a common practice to understand and verify the predictions of opaque machine learning models. Despite the numerous techniques available, individual methods often produce inconsistent and unstable results, putting their overall reliability into question. In this work, we aim to systematically improve the quality of feature attributions by combining multiple explanations across distinct methods or their variations. For this purpose, we propose a novel approach to derive optimal convex combinations of feature attributions that yield provable improvements of desired quality criteria such as robustness or faithfulness to the model behavior. Through extensive experiments involving various model architectures and popular feature attribution techniques, we demonstrate that our combination strategy consistently outperforms individual methods and existing baselines.

paragraphs: Feature attributions explain a model's prediction by assigning importance to its input features. Different attribution techniques can disagree, and a single method can produce unstable explanations. This paper asks whether combining several explanations can systematically improve their quality, making the choice of combination a problem to optimize.

The authors derive optimal convex combinations of attributions from different methods or variations of a method. In a convex combination, the weights are nonnegative and sum to one. The optimization targets desired explanation criteria, such as robustness or faithfulness to the model's behavior, and provides provable improvements for those criteria.

Experiments across multiple model architectures and popular attribution techniques show that the combination strategy consistently outperforms the individual methods and existing baselines considered. The contribution is an optimization-based way to aggregate explanations with both theoretical and empirical support. Its guarantees concern the selected quality criteria, so the improvement should be understood in terms of what the combination is designed to measure and preserve.
summary.tldr: Optimizing convex combinations of feature attributions yields provable improvements in selected explanation criteria and strong experimental results.

title: Provably Better Explanations with Optimized Aggregation of Feature Attributions

abstract: Given the black box nature of machine learning models, a plethora of explainability methods have been developed to decipher the factors behind individual decisions. In this paper, we introduce a novel problem of black box (probabilistic) explanation certification. We ask the question: Given a black box model with only query access, an explanation for an example and a quality metric (viz. fidelity, stability), can we find the largest hypercube (i.e., $\ell_{\infty}$ ball) centered at the example such that when the explanation is applied to all examples within the hypercube, (with high probability) a quality criterion is met (viz. fidelity greater than some value)? Being able to efficiently find such a trust region has multiple benefits: i) insight into model behavior in a region, with a guarantee; ii) ascertained stability of the explanation; iii) explanation reuse, which can save time, energy and money by not having to find explanations for every example; and iv) a possible meta-metric to compare explanation methods. Our contributions include formalizing this problem, proposing solutions, providing theoretical guarantees for these solutions that are computable, and experimentally showing their efficacy on synthetic and real data.

paragraphs: An explanation of one model decision may also be useful for nearby inputs, but its reliability across that neighborhood needs assessment. This paper formalizes probabilistic explanation certification for a black-box model accessible only through queries. The inputs are an example, its explanation, and a chosen quality measure such as fidelity or stability.

The problem is to find the largest centered hypercube within which the explanation meets a specified quality criterion with high probability. This region is called a trust region. Framing the task this way turns a single-example explanation into a regional statement, while making the probabilistic nature of the assurance explicit.

The authors propose solutions with computable theoretical guarantees and demonstrate their effectiveness on synthetic and real data. Such regions can support explanation reuse, provide insight into regional model behavior, and establish explanation stability. They may also serve as a measure for comparing explanation methods. The contribution is thus both a certification problem and methods for giving explanations a defined, probabilistically supported scope.
summary.tldr: The paper develops query-based methods to probabilistically certify regions where an existing model explanation satisfies a chosen quality criterion.

title: Trust Regions for Explanations via Black-Box Probabilistic Certification

abstract: Instruction-guided speech editing aims to follow the user’s natural language instruction to manipulate the semantic and acoustic attributes of a speech. In this work, we construct triplet paired data (instruction, input speech, output speech) to alleviate data scarcity and train a multi-task large language model named InstructSpeech. To mitigate the challenges of accurately executing user’s instructions, we 1) introduce the learned task embeddings with a fine-tuned Flan-T5-XL to guide the generation process towards the correct generative task; 2) include an extensive and diverse set of speech editing and processing tasks to enhance model capabilities; 3) investigate chain-of-thought reasoning for free-form semantic content editing; and 4) propose a hierarchical adapter that effectively updates a small portion of parameters for generalization to new tasks. To assess instruction speech editing in greater depth, we introduce a benchmark evaluation with contrastive instruction-speech pre-training (CISP) to test the speech quality and instruction-speech alignment faithfulness. Experimental results demonstrate that InstructSpeech achieves state-of-the-art results in eleven tasks, for the first time unlocking the ability to edit speech’s acoustic and semantic attributes following a user’s instruction. Audio samples are available at https://InstructSpeech.github.io

paragraphs: InstructSpeech aims to edit both what speech says and how it sounds by following natural-language instructions. To address scarce training data, the researchers construct examples pairing an instruction with input and output speech. These triplets train a multitask language model to connect a requested change with the corresponding audio transformation.

The system combines learned task embeddings with a fine-tuned Flan-T5-XL model to guide generation toward the appropriate task. Training covers diverse speech editing and processing tasks, and the authors investigate chain-of-thought reasoning for free-form changes to semantic content. A hierarchical adapter supports generalization to new tasks by updating only a small portion of the model’s parameters.

The paper also introduces an evaluation benchmark using contrastive instruction-speech pretraining to assess speech quality and how faithfully the output follows the instruction. Experiments report state-of-the-art results on eleven tasks. The contribution brings instruction interpretation, acoustic editing, and content editing into one framework, with evaluation explicitly considering whether the resulting speech matches the user’s requested transformation.
summary.tldr: InstructSpeech learns to modify speech content and acoustic attributes from natural-language instructions, reporting state-of-the-art results on eleven tasks.

title: InstructSpeech: Following Speech Editing Instructions via Large Language Models

abstract: The growing significance of RNA engineering in diverse biological applications has spurred interest in developing AI methods for structure-based RNA design. While diffusion models have excelled in protein design, adapting them for RNA presents new challenges due to RNA’s conformational flexibility and the computational cost of fine-tuning large structure prediction models. To this end, we propose RNAFlow, a flow matching model for protein-conditioned RNA sequence-structure design. Its denoising network integrates an RNA inverse folding model and a pre-trained RosettaFold2NA network for generation of RNA sequences and structures. The integration of inverse folding in the structure denoising process allows us to simplify training by fixing the structure prediction network. We further enhance the inverse folding model by conditioning it on inferred conformational ensembles to model dynamic RNA conformations. Evaluation on protein-conditioned RNA structure and sequence generation tasks demonstrates RNAFlow’s advantage over existing RNA design methods.

paragraphs: Designing RNA requires accounting for both its sequence and its flexible three-dimensional conformations. RNAFlow addresses protein-conditioned RNA sequence and structure generation using flow matching. The paper highlights two challenges behind this design: RNA can adopt varied conformations, and fine-tuning a large structure-prediction network can be computationally costly.

RNAFlow's denoising network combines an RNA inverse-folding model with a pretrained RosettaFold2NA network. Inverse folding contributes sequence generation within the structure-denoising process. This integration allows the structure-prediction network to remain fixed during training, simplifying the learning problem while retaining that network as part of sequence-and-structure generation.

To better represent RNA's dynamic conformations, the authors further condition the inverse-folding model on inferred conformational ensembles. This supplies information about multiple conformations within the design process. Evaluations on protein-conditioned RNA sequence and structure generation show advantages over existing RNA design methods. The contribution brings flexible-structure modeling and a fixed pretrained predictor together in a joint design framework, addressing both conformational variability and the stated training-cost challenge.
summary.tldr: RNAFlow combines inverse folding, flow matching, and a fixed structure predictor to generate protein-conditioned RNA sequences and structures.

title: RNAFlow: RNA Structure & Sequence Design via Inverse Folding-Based Flow Matching

abstract: Retrieval pipelines are an integral component of many machine learning systems. However, they perform poorly in domains where documents are long (e.g., 10K tokens or more) and where identifying the relevant document requires synthesizing information across the entire text. Developing long-context retrieval encoders suitable for these domains raises three challenges: (1) how to evaluate long-context retrieval performance, (2) how to pretrain a base language model to represent both short contexts (corresponding to queries) and long contexts (corresponding to documents), and (3) how to finetune this model for retrieval under the batch size limitations imposed by GPU memory constraints. To address these challenges, we first introduce LoCoV1, a 12 task benchmark constructed to measure long-context retrieval where chunking is not possible or not effective. We next present the M2-BERT retrieval encoder, an 80M parameter state-space encoder model built from the Monarch Mixer architecture, capable of scaling to documents up to 32K tokens long. We describe a pretraining data mixture which allows this encoder to process both short and long context sequences, and a finetuning approach that adapts this base model to retrieval with only single-sample batches. Finally, we validate the M2-BERT retrieval encoder on LoCoV1, finding that it outperforms competitive Transformer-based models by at least 22.2 points, despite containing 90× fewer parameters.
