paragraphs: Finding a relevant document becomes difficult when the document is long and relevance depends on information spread across its text. Dividing it into smaller pieces may fail to preserve what makes it relevant. This paper addresses the linked problems of evaluating such retrieval, representing short queries alongside long documents, and training within GPU memory limits.

The authors introduce LoCoV1, a benchmark with 12 tasks where splitting documents into chunks is impossible or ineffective. They also build M2-BERT, an 80-million-parameter retrieval encoder based on the Monarch Mixer architecture. This state-space model handles documents of up to 32,000 tokens. A pretraining mixture supports both short and long sequences, while the retrieval fine-tuning method works with batches containing just one sample.

On LoCoV1, the encoder exceeds the competitive Transformer-based models by at least 22.2 points while using 90 times fewer parameters. The result ties the benchmark and training design together: the paper demonstrates strong retrieval performance specifically where understanding a long document as a whole matters.
summary.tldr: LoCoV1 evaluates retrieval across long documents, and M2-BERT delivers strong results with a compact encoder and single-sample training batches.

title: Benchmarking and Building Long-Context Retrieval Models with LoCo and M2-BERT

abstract: Latent generative models (e.g., Stable Diffusion) have become more and more popular, but concerns have arisen regarding potential misuse related to images generated by these models. It is, therefore, necessary to analyze the origin of images by inferring if a particular image was generated by a specific latent generative model. Most existing methods (e.g., image watermark and model fingerprinting) require extra steps during training or generation. These requirements restrict their usage on the generated images without such extra operations, and the extra required operations might compromise the quality of the generated images. In this work, we ask whether it is possible to effectively and efficiently trace the images generated by a specific latent generative model without the aforementioned requirements. To study this problem, we design a latent inversion based method called LatentTracer to trace the generated images of the inspected model by checking if the examined images can be well-reconstructed with an inverted latent input. We leverage gradient based latent inversion and identify a encoder-based initialization critical to the success of our approach. Our experiments on the state-of-the-art latent generative models, such as Stable Diffusion, show that our method can distinguish the images generated by the inspected model and other images with a high accuracy and efficiency. Our findings suggest the intriguing possibility that today’s latent generative generated images are naturally watermarked by the decoder used in the source models. Code: https://github.com/ZhentingWang/LatentTracer.

paragraphs: LatentTracer asks whether an image can be attributed to a particular latent generative model without adding a watermark or modifying training or generation. This addresses a constraint of tracing methods that require extra operations before an image is examined. The goal is model-specific attribution: distinguishing images from the inspected model from other images.

The method searches for a latent input that allows the inspected model to reconstruct the image well. It uses gradient-based latent inversion, with an encoder supplying the starting point. The authors identify this encoder-based initialization as critical to the approach's success, connecting effective attribution to how the reconstruction search begins.

Experiments with latent generative models, including Stable Diffusion, show high attribution accuracy and efficiency. The findings suggest that the decoder may leave a naturally occurring signature in generated images, even without an artificial watermark. The paper presents this as an intriguing possibility supported by the results, rather than a universal guarantee that every generated image can be traced.
summary.tldr: LatentTracer uses encoder-initialized latent inversion to attribute images to a specific generator without adding artificial watermarks.

title: How to Trace Latent Generative Model Generated Images without Artificial Watermark?

abstract: This paper rethinks Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM), which is originally formulated as a zero-sum game where the weights of a network and a bounded perturbation try to minimize/maximize, respectively, the same differentiable loss. To fundamentally improve this design, we argue that SAM should instead be reformulated using the 0-1 loss. As a continuous relaxation, we follow the simple conventional approach where the minimizing (maximizing) player uses an upper bound (lower bound) surrogate to the 0-1 loss. This leads to a novel formulation of SAM as a bilevel optimization problem, dubbed as BiSAM. BiSAM with newly designed lower-bound surrogate loss indeed constructs stronger perturbation. Through numerical evidence, we show that BiSAM consistently results in improved performance when compared to the original SAM and variants, while enjoying similar computational complexity. Our code is available at https://github.com/LIONS-EPFL/BiSAM.

paragraphs: Sharpness-Aware Minimization trains a network against bounded changes to its weights. In its original formulation, one player adjusts the network to reduce a differentiable loss while another chooses a perturbation to increase that same loss. This paper argues that improving the method requires reconsidering what the two players optimize.

The authors start from the zero-one loss, which records whether a prediction is correct, and use different continuous approximations for the two roles. The minimizing player uses an upper bound on this loss, while the maximizing player uses a lower bound. This produces BiSAM, a bilevel formulation in which the two optimization problems are linked rather than sharing an identical objective.

With a newly designed lower-bound surrogate, BiSAM constructs stronger perturbations. The reported numerical evidence shows consistent performance improvements over original SAM and its variants while retaining similar computational complexity. The findings suggest that changing the relationship between the training and perturbation objectives can improve SAM without requiring a more computationally expensive approach in the stated complexity comparison.
summary.tldr: BiSAM gives the training and perturbation players different surrogate objectives, producing stronger perturbations and improved empirical performance at similar computational complexity.

title: Improving SAM Requires Rethinking its Optimization Formulation

abstract: When reading a story, humans can quickly understand new fictional characters with a few observations, mainly by drawing analogies to fictional and real people they already know. This reflects the few-shot and meta-learning essence of humans’ inference of characters’ mental states, i.e., theory-of-mind (ToM), which is largely ignored in existing research. We fill this gap with a novel NLP dataset in a realistic narrative understanding scenario, ToM-in-AMC. Our dataset consists of $\sim$1,000 parsed movie scripts, each corresponding to a few-shot character understanding task that requires models to mimic humans’ ability of fast digesting characters with a few starting scenes in a new movie. We further propose a novel ToM prompting approach designed to explicitly assess the influence of multiple ToM dimensions. It surpasses existing baseline models, underscoring the significance of modeling multiple ToM dimensions for our task. Our extensive human study verifies that humans are capable of solving our problem by inferring characters’ mental states based on their previously seen movies. In comparison, all the AI systems lag $>20%$ behind humans, highlighting a notable limitation in existing approaches’ ToM capabilities. Code and data are available at https://github.com/ShunchiZhang/ToM-in-AMC

paragraphs: People can often understand a new fictional character after seeing only a few scenes, drawing on experience with other people and stories. This paper turns that ability into a language-understanding evaluation. Its focus is theory of mind: inferring characters’ mental states from limited observations and transferring relevant understanding from previously encountered narratives.

The authors introduce ToM-in-AMC, a dataset containing approximately 1,000 parsed movie scripts. Each script supplies a task requiring rapid character understanding from a movie’s opening scenes. They also develop a prompting method that explicitly considers multiple dimensions of theory of mind, allowing the evaluation to examine the contribution of those dimensions.

The prompting approach outperforms the compared baseline models. A human study finds that participants can solve the task by using mental-state inferences informed by movies they have previously seen. All evaluated AI systems trail humans by more than 20%. Together, these results identify a substantial gap on this particular form of character understanding while showing benefits from modeling several theory-of-mind dimensions.
summary.tldr: ToM-in-AMC tests rapid character understanding from movie scripts and reveals a substantial gap between evaluated AI systems and humans.

title: Few-Shot Character Understanding in Movies as an Assessment to Meta-Learning of Theory-of-Mind

abstract: The best arm identification problem requires identifying the best alternative (i.e., arm) in active experimentation using the smallest number of experiments (i.e., arm pulls), which is crucial for cost-efficient and timely decision-making processes. In the fixed confidence setting, an algorithm must stop data-dependently and return the estimated best arm with a correctness guarantee. Since this stopping time is random, we desire its distribution to have light tails. Unfortunately, many existing studies focus on high probability or in expectation bounds on the stopping time, which allow heavy tails and, for high probability bounds, even not stopping at all. We first prove that this never-stopping event can indeed happen for some popular algorithms. Motivated by this, we propose algorithms that provably enjoy an exponential-tailed stopping time, which improves upon the polynomial tail bound reported by Kalyanakrishnan et al. (2012). The first algorithm is based on a fixed budget algorithm called Sequential Halving along with a doubling trick. The second algorithm is a meta algorithm that takes in any fixed confidence algorithm with a high probability stopping guarantee and turns it into one that enjoys an exponential-tailed stopping time. Our results imply that there is much more to be desired for contemporary fixed confidence algorithms.

paragraphs: Best-arm identification asks which alternative is best while spending as few experiments as possible. In the fixed-confidence setting, an algorithm decides when to stop based on the data and must meet a correctness guarantee. Its stopping time is therefore random, making unusually long runs an important part of its behavior.

The paper shows that common stopping-time guarantees can leave this behavior insufficiently controlled. Expectation bounds can allow heavy tails, while high-probability bounds can even permit a nonzero chance of never stopping. The authors prove that this never-stopping event can occur for some popular algorithms and develop alternatives with exponentially decaying stopping-time tails.

One construction combines Sequential Halving with a doubling strategy. A second is a general transformation that accepts a fixed-confidence algorithm with a high-probability stopping guarantee and produces one with an exponential tail. These results strengthen control over rare, prolonged runs, showing why average or high-probability experiment counts alone do not fully capture the timeliness of active experimentation.
summary.tldr: The paper constructs best-arm identification algorithms with exponentially decaying stopping-time tails, addressing rare prolonged or never-ending runs.

title: Fixing the Loose Brake: Exponential-Tailed Stopping Time in Best Arm Identification

abstract: Machine learning has increasingly been employed to solve NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems, resulting in the emergence of neural solvers that demonstrate remarkable performance, even with minimal domain-specific knowledge. To date, the community has created numerous open-source neural solvers with distinct motivations and inductive biases. While considerable efforts are devoted to designing powerful single solvers, our findings reveal that existing solvers typically demonstrate complementary performance across different problem instances. This suggests that significant improvements could be achieved through effective coordination of neural solvers at the instance level. In this work, we propose the first general framework to coordinate the neural solvers, which involves feature extraction, selection model, and selection strategy, aiming to allocate each instance to the most suitable solvers. To instantiate, we collect several typical neural solvers with state-of-the-art performance as alternatives, and explore various methods for each component of the framework. We evaluated our framework on two typical problems, Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) and Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP). Experimental results show that our framework can effectively distribute instances and the resulting composite solver can achieve significantly better performance (e.g., reduce the optimality gap by 0.88% on TSPLIB and 0.71% on CVRPLIB) than the best individual neural solver with little extra time cost.

To instantiate, we collect several typical neural solvers with state-of-the-art performance as alternatives, and explore various methods for each component of the framework. Experimental results show that our framework can effectively distribute instances and the resulting composite solver can achieve significantly better performance (e.g., reduce the optimality gap by 0.88% on TSPLIB and 0.71% on CVRPLIB) than the best individual neural solver with little extra time cost.

paragraphs: Neural solvers for combinatorial optimization have different strengths, so the best solver overall may not be the best choice for every problem instance. This paper finds complementary performance among existing solvers and develops a framework for coordinating them. Its goal is to route each instance to the solver or solvers most suited to it.

The framework has three components: extracting instance features, building a selection model, and choosing a selection strategy. The authors assemble several strong existing neural solvers as alternatives and investigate different implementations of these components. This makes instance-level selection the central mechanism for improving the combined system.

Experiments cover the Traveling Salesman Problem and Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem. The composite solver outperforms the best individual neural solver with little additional time cost, with reported optimality-gap reductions of 0.88% on TSPLIB and 0.71% on CVRPLIB. These results show that complementary solver behavior can translate into practical gains when a selection mechanism assigns work effectively, making coordination a productive direction alongside improvements to individual solvers.
summary.tldr: Instance-level selection combines complementary neural solvers into a stronger optimization system with little additional runtime in the reported evaluations.

title: Neural Solver Selection for Combinatorial Optimization

abstract: Test-time training (TTT) methods explicitly update the weights of a model to adapt to the specific test instance, and they have found success in a variety of settings, including most recently language modeling and reasoning. To demystify this success, we investigate a gradient-based TTT algorithm for in-context learning, where we train a transformer model on the in-context demonstrations provided in the test prompt. Specifically, we provide a comprehensive theoretical characterization of linear transformers when the update rule is a single gradient step. Our theory (i) delineates the role of alignment between pretraining distribution and target task, (ii) demystifies how TTT can alleviate distribution shift, and (iii) quantifies the sample complexity of TTT including how it can significantly reduce the eventual sample size required for in-context learning. As our empirical contribution, we study the benefits of TTT for TabPFN, a tabular foundation model. In line with our theory, we demonstrate that TTT significantly reduces the required sample size for tabular classification (3 to 5 times fewer) unlocking substantial inference efficiency with a negligible training cost.

paragraphs: Test-time training adapts a model's weights using information available for the current test instance. This paper studies that idea for in-context learning, where a prompt contains demonstrations of the target task. The proposed setup trains the transformer on those demonstrations, making them a source of explicit adaptation.

The theoretical analysis focuses on linear transformers updated with a single gradient step. It characterizes how alignment between pretraining and the target task affects adaptation, explains how test-time training can alleviate distribution shift, and quantifies sample complexity. Within this setting, the analysis shows how adaptation can substantially reduce the number of examples eventually needed for in-context learning.

The empirical study applies test-time training to TabPFN, a foundation model for tabular data. The authors report that tabular classification requires three to five times fewer samples, with substantial inference-efficiency gains and negligible training cost. These findings align with the theory's account of sample savings, while the formal characterization itself remains specific to the analyzed linear-transformer update.
summary.tldr: Theory explains sample savings from test-time adaptation, and TabPFN experiments report three to five times fewer required classification samples.

title: Test-Time Training Provably Improves Transformers as In-context Learners

abstract: We introduce Adjoint Sampling, a highly scalable and efficient algorithm for learning diffusion processes that sample from unnormalized densities, or energy functions. It is the first on-policy approach that allows significantly more gradient updates than the number of energy evaluations and model samples, allowing us to scale to much larger problem settings than previously explored by similar methods. Our framework is theoretically grounded in stochastic optimal control and shares the same theoretical guarantees as Adjoint Matching, being able to train without the need for corrective measures that push samples towards the target distribution. We show how to incorporate key symmetries, as well as periodic boundary conditions, for modeling molecules in both cartesian and torsional coordinates. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through extensive experiments on classical energy functions, and further scale up to neural network-based energy models where we perform amortized conformer generation across many molecular systems. To encourage further research in developing highly scalable sampling methods, we plan to open source these challenging benchmarks, where successful methods can directly impact progress in computational chemistry. Code & and benchmarks provided at https://github.com/facebookresearch/adjoint_sampling.

paragraphs: Adjoint Sampling learns diffusion processes for drawing samples from an energy function or an unnormalized probability density. Its central computational contribution is to permit many more gradient updates than energy evaluations and model samples. This matters because learning progress can continue without requiring an equally large increase in those sampling and evaluation operations.

The method is an on-policy approach grounded in stochastic optimal control. It inherits the theoretical guarantees of Adjoint Matching and can train without additional corrective procedures that move samples toward the desired distribution. The framework also incorporates symmetries and periodic boundaries, supporting molecular descriptions based on either Cartesian positions or torsional coordinates.

The experiments cover classical energy functions and larger energy models represented by neural networks. For the latter, the authors demonstrate amortized conformer generation across multiple molecular systems: a learned sampling approach supports generating molecular configurations across many systems. Together, these results support the method’s stated scalability and its relevance to computational chemistry.
summary.tldr: Adjoint Sampling scales diffusion-based energy sampling by enabling many training updates per energy evaluation or model sample.

title: Adjoint Sampling: Highly Scalable Diffusion Samplers via Adjoint Matching

abstract: Protein dynamics play a crucial role in protein biological functions and properties, and their traditional study typically relies on time-consuming molecular dynamics (MD) simulations conducted in silico. Recent advances in generative modeling, particularly denoising diffusion models, have enabled efficient accurate protein structure prediction and conformation sampling by learning distributions over crystallographic structures. However, effectively integrating physical supervision into these data-driven approaches remains challenging, as standard energy-based objectives often lead to intractable optimization. In this paper, we introduce Energy-based Alignment (EBA), a method that aligns generative models with feedback from physical models, efficiently calibrating them to appropriately balance conformational states based on their energy differences. Experimental results on the MD ensemble benchmark demonstrate that EBA achieves state-of-the-art performance in generating high-quality protein ensembles. By improving the physical plausibility of generated structures, our approach enhances model predictions and holds promise for applications in structural biology and drug discovery.

paragraphs: Protein function depends on motion and on the different conformations a protein can occupy. Studying these dynamics traditionally involves costly molecular dynamics simulations. Generative models offer a faster route to sampling structures, but learning from crystallographic structures leaves a challenge: incorporating physical feedback into the distribution of structures they generate.

The paper introduces Energy-based Alignment, or EBA, to address this challenge. It calibrates generative models using feedback from physical models, adjusting the balance among conformational states according to their energy differences. The target therefore includes how frequently different states appear in an ensemble, beyond whether individual structures look plausible. This addresses a setting where standard energy-based training objectives often make optimization intractable.

On the molecular dynamics ensemble benchmark, EBA achieves the reported state of the art for generating high-quality protein ensembles. The results support using physical feedback to improve the plausibility of generated structures and model predictions. The authors also identify structural biology and drug discovery as promising applications, presenting these as potential uses of the improved ensembles.
summary.tldr: EBA uses physical energy feedback to calibrate protein conformation generators and improve the quality of their generated ensembles.

title: Aligning Protein Conformation Ensemble Generation with Physical Feedback

abstract: We propose Noise Conditional Variational Score Distillation (NCVSD), a novel method for distilling pretrained diffusion models into generative denoisers. We achieve this by revealing that the unconditional score function implicitly characterizes the score function of denoising posterior distributions. By integrating this insight into the Variational Score Distillation (VSD) framework, we enable scalable learning of generative denoisers capable of approximating samples from the denoising posterior distribution across a wide range of noise levels. The proposed generative denoisers exhibit desirable properties that allow fast generation while preserve the benefit of iterative refinement: (1) fast one-step generation through sampling from pure Gaussian noise at high noise levels; (2) improved sample quality by scaling the test-time compute with multi-step sampling; and (3) zero-shot probabilistic inference for flexible and controllable sampling. We evaluate NCVSD through extensive experiments, including class-conditional image generation and inverse problem solving. By scaling the test-time compute, our method outperforms teacher diffusion models and is on par with consistency models of larger sizes. Additionally, with significantly fewer NFEs than diffusion-based methods, we achieve record-breaking LPIPS on inverse problems.

paragraphs: Noise Conditional Variational Score Distillation, or NCVSD, transfers knowledge from pretrained diffusion models into generative denoisers. These denoisers approximate samples from a denoising posterior across many noise levels. The method builds on the finding that an unconditional score function implicitly characterizes the scores of those posterior distributions.

The authors incorporate that relationship into Variational Score Distillation. At high noise levels, the learned denoiser supports one-step generation starting from Gaussian noise. It also permits multiple sampling steps to improve quality when more inference computation is available. A further property is zero-shot probabilistic inference, supporting flexible and controllable sampling.

Experiments examine class-conditional image generation and inverse problems. With increased test-time computation, NCVSD outperforms its teacher diffusion models and matches larger consistency models. For inverse problems, the authors report record-breaking LPIPS results with substantially fewer function evaluations than diffusion-based methods. These findings support a distillation approach that offers fast generation while retaining the ability to refine samples through additional computation.
summary.tldr: NCVSD distills diffusion models into denoisers supporting one-step generation, iterative improvement, and zero-shot probabilistic inference.

title: Noise Conditional Variational Score Distillation

abstract: In this work, we study the online convex optimization problem with curved losses and delayed feedback. When losses are strongly convex, existing approaches obtain regret bounds of order $d_{\max} \ln T$, where $d_{\max}$ is the maximum delay and $T$ is the time horizon. However, in many cases, this guarantee can be much worse than $\sqrt{d_{\mathrm{tot}}}$ as obtained by a delayed version of online gradient descent, where $d_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the total delay. We bridge this gap by proposing a variant of follow-the-regularized-leader that obtains regret of order $\min\{\sigma_{\max}\ln T, \sqrt{d_{\mathrm{tot}}}\}$, where $\sigma_{\max}$ is the maximum number of missing observations. We then consider exp-concave losses and extend the Online Newton Step algorithm to handle delays with an adaptive learning rate tuning, achieving regret $\min\{d_{\max} n\ln T, \sqrt{d_{\mathrm{tot}}}\}$ where $n$ is the dimension. To our knowledge, this is the first algorithm to achieve such a regret bound for exp-concave losses. We further consider the problem of unconstrained online linear regression and achieve a similar guarantee by designing a variant of the Vovk-Azoury-Warmuth forecaster with a clipping trick. Finally, we implement our algorithms and conduct experiments under various types of delay and losses, showing an improved performance over existing methods.

paragraphs: Online optimization makes successive decisions before all feedback from earlier decisions has arrived. Curvature in the loss functions can improve learning guarantees, but existing guarantees for strongly convex losses depend on the longest delay. The paper observes that this dependence can produce a worse bound than one based on the square root of total delay.

For strongly convex losses, the authors modify follow-the-regularized-leader to obtain a regret bound taking the smaller of two quantities: maximum outstanding observations times log T, and the square root of total delay. Here T is the time horizon. This allows the guarantee to reflect both the backlog of missing feedback and accumulated delay.

For exp-concave losses, an adaptive delayed Online Newton Step method similarly combines a curvature-sensitive bound with the square-root total-delay bound; its first term includes dimension and maximum delay. The authors also obtain a related guarantee for unconstrained online linear regression using a modified forecaster with clipping. Experiments across different losses and delay patterns report improved performance, supporting the practical relevance of adapting to more than the single longest delay.
summary.tldr: New online optimization algorithms combine curvature-sensitive guarantees with total-delay bounds to handle delayed feedback more effectively.

title: Exploiting Curvature in Online Convex Optimization with Delayed Feedback

abstract: Continual learning is crucial for applying machine learning in challenging, dynamic, and often resource-constrained environments. However, catastrophic forgetting — overwriting previously learned knowledge when new information is acquired — remains a major challenge. In this work, we examine the intermediate representations in neural network layers during continual learning and find that such representations are less prone to forgetting, highlighting their potential to accelerate computation. Motivated by these findings, we propose to use auxiliary classifiers (ACs) to enhance performance and demonstrate that integrating ACs into various continual learning methods consistently improves accuracy across diverse evaluation settings, yielding an average 10% relative gain. We also leverage the ACs to reduce the average cost of the inference by 10-60% without compromising accuracy, enabling the model to return the predictions before computing all the layers. Our approach provides a scalable and efficient solution for continual learning.

paragraphs: Continual learning trains models as new information arrives, creating the risk that learning something new will overwrite earlier knowledge. This paper examines how that forgetting appears across a neural network's layers. The authors find that intermediate representations are less prone to forgetting, suggesting that useful retained knowledge is available before the final layer.

They attach auxiliary classifiers to make predictions from these intermediate representations. Integrating these classifiers into several continual-learning methods consistently improves accuracy across the evaluated settings, with an average relative gain of 10%. The approach therefore makes intermediate representations directly useful for prediction within existing continual-learning systems.

The same classifiers also allow predictions to exit the network before every layer has been computed. In the reported evaluations, this reduces average inference cost by 10–60% without sacrificing accuracy. The findings link knowledge retention and computational efficiency: representations that better preserve earlier learning can also support earlier decisions. This makes auxiliary classifiers relevant to continual learning in dynamic environments where inference resources are constrained.
summary.tldr: Auxiliary classifiers exploit intermediate representations to improve continual-learning accuracy and reduce inference cost through early exits.

title: Improving Continual Learning Performance and Efficiency with Auxiliary Classifiers

abstract: The locate-then-edit paradigm has shown significant promise for knowledge editing (KE) in Large Language Models (LLMs). While previous methods perform well on single-hop fact recall tasks, they consistently struggle with multi-hop factual recall tasks involving newly edited knowledge. In this paper, leveraging tools in mechanistic interpretability, we first identify that in multi-hop tasks, LLMs tend to retrieve knowledge with implicit subject information from deeper MLP layers, unlike single-hop tasks, which rely on shallow layers. This distinction explains the poor performance of current methods in multi-hop queries, as they primarily focus on editing shallow layers with single-hop edit prompts, leaving deeper layers unchanged. To address this, we propose IFMET, a novel locate-then-edit KE approach designed to edit both shallow and deep MLP layers. Beyond single-hop editing prompts, IFMET further incorporates multi-hop editing prompts to locate and modify knowledge across different stages of reasoning. Experimental results demonstrate that IFMET significantly improves performance on multi-hop factual recall tasks, overcoming the limitations of previous locate-then-edit methods.

paragraphs: Knowledge editing aims to change facts stored in a language model. Existing locate-then-edit methods can succeed when a question directly asks for the edited fact, yet struggle when answering requires several linked factual steps. This paper investigates why a successful direct edit may fail to carry through a longer chain of recall.

Using mechanistic interpretability tools, the authors find that multi-hop tasks tend to retrieve knowledge involving implicit subjects from deeper MLP layers. Single-hop recall instead relies on shallower layers. Earlier methods largely target those shallow layers using single-hop prompts, leaving deeper retrieval pathways unchanged. This gives a concrete explanation for the mismatch between direct recall and multi-hop performance.

IFMET responds by locating and editing knowledge in both shallow and deep MLP layers. It uses multi-hop editing prompts alongside single-hop prompts to reach different stages of reasoning. Experiments show significant improvements on multi-hop factual recall. The contribution is therefore both diagnostic and procedural: it identifies a depth-related retrieval difference and uses that finding to broaden where edits are applied.
summary.tldr: IFMET edits shallow and deep model layers using single-hop and multi-hop prompts to improve recall that depends on newly edited facts.

title: Locate-then-edit for Multi-hop Factual Recall under Knowledge Editing

abstract: Autoregressive models have emerged as a powerful generative paradigm for visual generation. The current de-facto standard of next token prediction commonly operates over a single-scale sequence of dense image tokens, and is incapable of utilizing global context especially for early tokens prediction. In this paper, we introduce a new autoregressive design to model a hierarchy from a few low-resolution image tokens to the typical dense image tokens, and delve into a thorough hierarchical dependency across multi-scale image tokens. Technically, we present a Hierarchical Masked Autoregressive models (Hi-MAR) that pivot on low-resolution image tokens to trigger hierarchical autoregressive modeling in a multi-phase manner. Hi-MAR learns to predict a few image tokens in low resolution, functioning as intermediary pivots to reflect global structure, in the first phase. Such pivots act as the additional guidance to strengthen the next autoregressive modeling phase by shaping global structural awareness of typical dense image tokens. A new Diffusion Transformer head is further devised to amplify the global context among all tokens for mask token prediction. Extensive evaluations on both class-conditional and text-to-image generation tasks demonstrate that Hi-MAR outperforms typical AR baselines, while requiring fewer computational costs.

paragraphs: Autoregressive image models commonly predict a dense sequence of image tokens at a single scale. Early predictions have limited access to global context, even though they help determine the image's overall structure. Hi-MAR addresses this issue by organizing generation into a hierarchy that begins with a small number of low-resolution tokens.

In the first phase, the model predicts these coarse tokens as intermediary pivots that represent global structure. Later autoregressive phases use the pivots as additional guidance when modeling dense image tokens. This gives detailed predictions an explicit source of structural context. A new Diffusion Transformer head further strengthens global information exchange among tokens for masked-token prediction.

The authors evaluate Hi-MAR on both class-conditional generation and text-to-image generation. It outperforms the typical autoregressive baselines considered while requiring less computation. The results support a generation strategy in which a compact global representation guides subsequent detail, connecting improvements in image modeling with a more computationally efficient hierarchy.
summary.tldr: Hi-MAR generates low-resolution token pivots to guide detailed image generation, outperforming typical autoregressive baselines with less computation.

title: Hierarchical Masked Autoregressive Models with Low-Resolution Token Pivots

abstract: Pre-Layer Normalization (Pre-LN) is the de facto choice for large language models (LLMs) and is crucial for stable pretraining and effective transfer learning. However, Pre-LN incurs repeated statistical-computation overhead and remains vulnerable to the curse of depth, where hidden-state magnitudes and variances grow as the number of layers increases, destabilizing training. Efficiency-oriented normalization-free methods such as Dynamic Tanh (DyT) improve throughput but remain fragile at depth. To jointly address stability and efficiency, we propose Bounded Hyperbolic Tanh (BHyT), a drop-in replacement for Pre-LN. BHyT combines a tanh nonlinearity with explicit, data-driven input bounding to keep activations within a non-saturating range. It prevents depth-wise growth in activation magnitude and variance and provides a theoretical stability guarantee. For efficiency, BHyT computes exact statistics once per block and replaces a second normalization with a lightweight variance approximation. Empirically, BHyT demonstrates improved stability and efficiency during pretraining, achieving an average of 1.6% faster training and an average of 1.77% higher token generation throughput compared to RMSNorm, while maintaining strong pretraining-only and post-SFT performance across language understanding and reasoning benchmarks[Code is available at: https://github.com/MLAI-Yonsei/BHyT].

paragraphs: Deep language models need mechanisms that keep internal activations stable as information passes through many layers. Pre-layer normalization helps, but repeatedly computing statistics adds overhead, and activation magnitudes and variances can still grow with depth. The paper also identifies fragility at depth in efficiency-focused normalization-free methods such as Dynamic Tanh.

summary.tldr: BHyT combines bounded tanh activations with cheaper normalization statistics to improve depth stability and modestly increase training and generation speed.

title: Bounded Hyperbolic Tangent: A Stable and Efficient Alternative to Pre-Layer Normalization in Large Language Models

abstract: Recent work on Neural Network-based methods for nonlinear control use Lyapunov Functions to obtain controllers with guarantees of stability. However, Lyapunov-based methods are fundamentally limited: they cannot be used for smooth blending with formal Region of Attraction (RoA) expansion guarantees, and also fail to certify stability when unstable equilibria or saddle points are present. Density functions provide an alternate stability certificate, and address these limitations by certifying almost everywhere stability, and enable smooth blending of controllers. Learning valid density certificates is challenging due to integrability constraints, and the effect of density-based blending controllers on RoAs is not well understood. In this work, we provide the first guarantee that controllers blended with density functions yield RoAs containing the union of the RoAs achieved by the constituent controllers. Then, we propose a novel exponential characterization of density functions that provably satisfies the integrability condition, and introduce Neural Control Density Functions (NCDFs), that leverage this new parameterization. We also extend NCDFs for synthesizing safe-stable controllers by combining NCDFs with control barrier functions (NCDF-CBFs). Our experiments show that blended controllers obtain superior RoAs to state-of-the-art methods like Neural Lyapunov Control and Sum-of-Squares based techniques.

It uses density functions as stability certificates, addressing limitations of Lyapunov-based methods for smooth blending and systems containing unstable equilibria or saddle points.

The central theoretical result guarantees that controllers blended using density functions have a region of attraction containing the union of the constituent controllers’ regions. The certificates establish almost-everywhere stability, allowing exceptional states rather than requiring convergence from every state. To make these certificates easier to learn, the authors introduce an exponential parameterization that provably satisfies the required integrability condition.

The resulting Neural Control Density Functions are also combined with control barrier functions to synthesize controllers addressing safety and stability together. Experiments report larger regions of attraction than Neural Lyapunov Control and Sum-of-Squares methods. The work therefore links a guarantee about combining controllers with a learnable certificate and an extension for safety.
summary.tldr: Neural density certificates enable smooth controller blending with guarantees that the combined region of attraction contains those of its constituent controllers.

title: Blending Neural Control Density Functions for Stabilization and Safety

abstract: Pretrained Transformers can perform in-context learning (ICL) from a few demonstrations, but this ability can fail sharply when the test distribution differs from pretraining—a common deployment setting. We study attention temperature as a simple inference-time control for improving ICL robustness under such shifts. In a high-dimensional linear-regression framework, we analyze a Transformer with "approximate softmax" attention, which preserves softmax’s normalization and temperature-dependent selectivity while remaining tractable. We derive a closed-form expression for the ICL generalization error under distribution shift, and show that it is minimized by an explicit optimal attention temperature. This characterization yields interpretable guidance by linking the best temperature to moments of the pre-softmax attention scores, and predicts when temperature adjustment can recover near Bayes-optimal performance. We validate the theory with extensive simulations, and further demonstrate gains for pretrained LLMs on question-answering benchmarks under distribution shift induced by noisy in-context demonstrations. Overall, attention temperature emerges as a principled, lightweight knob for improving the robustness of ICL in pretrained Transformers.

title: Optimal Attention Temperature Improves the Robustness of In-Context Learning under Distribution Shift in High Dimensions

abstract: Current evaluation for Large Language Model (LLM) code agents predominantly focus on generating functional code in single-turn scenarios, which fails to evaluate the agent’s capability for continuous code optimization and multi-turn iterative development. To bridge this gap, we introduce CATArena, a framework designed to evaluate the evolutionary capabilities of code agents via iterative tournaments. Agents engage in multi-turn tournaments and continuously refine their code through self-reflection and peer-learning based on comprehensive execution feedback. For evaluation, we propose a dual-metric system to decouple static generation proficiency from evolutionary potential. Extensive experiments reveal that an agent’s evolutionary potential is not strictly correlated with its initial proficiency. Our analysis further reveals that current agents struggle to concurrently leverage both peer-learning and self-reflection for effective performance gains. Furthermore, the results validate CATArena’s high extensibility and resistance to variance tasks, establishing it as a continuous and reliable standard for assessing the evolutionary capability of LLM code agents.

paragraphs: A coding agent can produce a strong first solution yet struggle to improve it after testing. CATArena evaluates this distinction through repeated tournaments, extending assessment beyond whether an agent generates functional code in a single attempt. Its central question is how effectively an agent develops its code over multiple rounds.

During tournaments, agents receive execution feedback and refine their programs using both reflection on their own work and learning from peers. A dual-metric evaluation separates initial code-generation proficiency from the ability to improve. This makes development over time a distinct object of measurement, rather than allowing the quality of the first submission to stand in for iterative capability.

The experiments find that initial proficiency does not strictly track improvement potential. They also show that current agents have difficulty benefiting from peer-learning and self-reflection simultaneously. The authors report evidence of extensibility and robustness across task variation. Together, these findings support evaluating code agents through their response to feedback as well as through their initial output.
summary.tldr: CATArena uses iterative coding tournaments to distinguish agents’ initial coding ability from their capacity to improve through feedback.

title: CATArena: Evaluating Evolutionary Capabilities of Code Agents via Iterative Tournaments

abstract: Deepfake audio detectors often fail to generalize to unseen attacks, in part due to spectral bias: neural networks prioritize low-frequency structure while under-exploiting subtle high-frequency (HF) artifacts left by generative models. We introduce SONAR (Spectral-cONtrastive Audio Residuals), a frequency-guided framework that explicitly enforces representation-level consistency between semantic content and HF residuals. Unlike prior frequency-aware or dual-stream detectors that treat HF cues as auxiliary features, SONAR encourages structured interaction between content and noise representations in latent space. The model employs a dual-path architecture in which an XLSR encoder captures low-frequency content, while a parallel branch with learnable, value-constrained 1D SRM (Spatial Rich Model) high-pass filters distills HF residuals. The two representations are fused via frequency cross-attention and trained with a Jensen–Shannon alignment loss that promotes LF–HF consistency for genuine audio and amplifies inconsistency for deepfakes. Evaluated on ASVspoof 2021 and in-the-wild benchmarks, SONAR achieves state-of-the-art performance in a single run setting and converges faster than strong baselines. By mitigating the effects of spectral bias through frequency-guided alignment, SONAR provides a fully data-driven and architecture-agnostic approach to generalizable audio deepfake detection.

The significance is that high-frequency information is integrated through a structured learning objective rather than merely added as another feature stream. The results support frequency-guided alignment as a data-driven approach to improving generalization, with the reported evidence grounded in those benchmark evaluations.
summary.tldr: SONAR improves audio deepfake detection by learning how speech content and high-frequency residuals agree in genuine recordings and diverge in fakes.

title: SONAR: Spectral-Contrastive Audio Residuals for Generalizable Deepfake Detection

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are vulnerable to malicious inputs, posing serious risks in high-stakes applications. Although existing detection-based defenses achieve strong empirical performance, they generally lack explicit control over the false acceptance rate (FAR), a critical safety requirement in sensitive deployment scenarios. This challenge is further complicated by two practical constraints: the lack of malicious calibration samples and the streaming nature of real-world inputs. To address these challenges, we propose OSCS, a novel framework for online FAR control without requiring malicious calibration data. OSCS leverages detection scores produced by existing defenses and employs recursive density estimation to estimate benign probability from the test stream. Based on these estimates, OSCS performs real-time accept/reject decisions while provably satisfying a user-specified FAR target. Theoretically, we show that OSCS controls the FAR up to a vanishing excess term under mild assumptions. Extensive experiments on backdoor and jailbreak attack tasks further demonstrate the effectiveness of OSCS, showing that it consistently achieves robust FAR control across diverse attack settings while outperforming existing baselines.

paragraphs: OSCS addresses a gap between detecting malicious language-model inputs and explicitly controlling how often such inputs are accepted. A defense can perform well empirically without providing control at a user-chosen false acceptance rate. The paper focuses on the practical setting where inputs arrive as a stream and malicious calibration examples are unavailable.

The framework builds on detection scores from existing defenses. It uses recursive density estimation on the test stream to estimate benign probabilities, then makes accept-or-reject decisions in real time. This adds an online selection mechanism to existing detection signals, connecting the decision process to a specified false acceptance target.

Under mild assumptions, the theory bounds the false acceptance rate by the target plus an excess term that vanishes. The qualification matters: the guarantee is expressed through that bound rather than exact finite-stream equality to the target. Experiments involving backdoor and jailbreak attacks show robust false acceptance control across diverse settings and stronger performance than the evaluated baselines.
summary.tldr: OSCS uses streaming detection scores to control false acceptance up to a vanishing excess term under mild assumptions, without malicious calibration data.

title: OSCS: Online Selection with Provable FAR Control for LLM Safety

abstract: Recent work has shown that the computations of Transformers can be simulated in the RASP family of programming languages. These findings have enabled improved understanding of the expressive capacity and generalization abilities of Transformers. In particular, Transformers have been suggested to length-generalize exactly on problems that have simple RASP programs. However, it remains open whether trained models actually implement simple interpretable programs. In this paper, we present a general method to extract such programs from trained Transformers. The idea is to faithfully re-parameterize a Transformer as a RASP program and then apply causal interventions to discover a small sufficient sub-program. In experiments on small Transformers trained on algorithmic and formal language tasks, we show that our method often recovers simple and interpretable RASP programs from length-generalizing transformers. Our results provide the most direct evidence so far that Transformers internally implement simple RASP programs.

paragraphs: A Transformer can solve a task without making its internal algorithm easy to inspect. Prior work connects Transformer computation to the RASP family of programming languages and suggests a relationship between simple RASP programs and generalization to longer inputs. That connection leaves a separate question: whether trained models actually implement such interpretable programs.

The paper proposes extracting programs directly from trained Transformers. It first faithfully re-parameterizes a model as a RASP program. It then uses causal interventions to identify a smaller sub-program sufficient for the computation being studied. This process moves from a complete computational description toward a compact explanation supported by interventions.

Experiments use small Transformers trained on algorithmic and formal language tasks. For models that generalize to longer inputs, the method often recovers simple, interpretable RASP programs. The finding supports the idea that these models can internally implement compact algorithms. Its force comes from recovering sufficient programs from trained computations, while the reported success remains frequent rather than universal and is demonstrated in the small-model settings studied.
summary.tldr: The paper extracts compact RASP programs from trained Transformers, often revealing interpretable algorithms in small models that generalize to longer inputs.

title: Discovering Interpretable Algorithms by Decompiling Transformers to RASP

abstract: Retrieval quality is the primary bottleneck for accuracy and robustness in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Current evaluation relies on heuristically constructed query sets, which introduce a hidden intrinsic bias. We formalize retrieval evaluation as a statistical estimation problem, showing that metric reliability is fundamentally limited by the evaluation-set construction. We further introduce semantic stratification, which grounds evaluation in corpus structure by organizing documents into an interpretable global space of entity-based clusters and systematically generating queries for missing strata. This yields (1) formal semantic coverage guarantees across retrieval regimes and (2) interpretable visibility into retrieval failure modes. Experiments across multiple benchmarks and retrieval methods validate our framework. The results expose systematic coverage gaps, identify structural signals that explain variance in retrieval performance, and show that stratified evaluation yields more stable and transparent assessments while supporting more trustworthy decision-making than aggregate metrics.

paragraphs: A retrieval system's evaluation depends on which questions it is asked. If a query collection misses substantial parts of the underlying document corpus, its aggregate scores can give an incomplete picture of performance. This paper formalizes retrieval evaluation as statistical estimation and shows that evaluation-set construction fundamentally limits the reliability of reported metrics.

The proposed semantic stratification method starts from the structure of the corpus. It organizes documents into an interpretable global space of entity-based clusters, then systematically generates queries for strata that lack coverage. This connects the test questions to identifiable parts of the document collection and provides formal semantic coverage guarantees across retrieval regimes.

Experiments across multiple benchmarks and retrieval methods reveal systematic coverage gaps and structural signals that explain variation in performance. Stratified evaluation produces more stable assessments while making retrieval failures easier to interpret. The contribution is an evaluation framework: it helps users understand which parts of a corpus are represented in testing and where a retriever struggles.
summary.tldr: Semantic stratification builds retrieval evaluations around corpus coverage, producing more stable scores and clearer explanations of retrieval failures.

title: Coverage, Not Averages: Semantic Stratification for Trustworthy Retrieval Evaluation

abstract: Neural Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) excel at reconstructing watertight manifolds but fail on thin structures and open boundaries due to strict inside—outside constraints. Conversely, Unsigned Distance Fields (UDFs) accommodate general geometries but suffer from gradient singularities at the zero-level set, hindering optimization and extraction. We introduce Metric—Phase Fields (MPFs), a decoupled implicit representation that separates metric proximity from topological phase. Given an unoriented point cloud, MPFs learn (i) an unsigned metric field $r$ and (ii) a smooth phase field $\theta$, for which we derive a bounded phase indicator $P=\tanh(\beta\theta)$ that provides soft inside—outside cues where they are meaningful. We couple the two fields via a gated-metric formulation with a residual phase injection to obtain a signed implicit function with stable near-surface gradients. The phase coefficient $\beta$ is learnable, allowing MPFs to adaptively control the sharpness of the phase transition and the degree of saturation of the soft sign indicator. Experiments on both synthetic and scanned thin-shell and thin-plate shapes demonstrate that MPFs preserve thin and layered structures more faithfully than recent SDF-based methods, while also enabling more robust training and more reliable surface extraction than UDF-based approaches. Check out MPFs-GitHub for source code and test models.

Signed distance functions impose an inside-outside distinction that causes problems for thin structures and open boundaries. Unsigned distance fields handle broader geometries, but their gradients become singular at the surface, complicating both training and surface extraction.

Metric–Phase Fields separate two roles normally coupled in a signed representation. An unsigned metric field learns proximity to the surface, while a smooth phase field supplies soft inside-outside information where that distinction is meaningful. It also trains more robustly and extracts surfaces more reliably than unsigned-distance approaches. The results support treating distance and phase as separate but coordinated quantities.
summary.tldr: Metric–Phase Fields separate surface distance from soft inside-outside information to improve thin-structure reconstruction and stabilize training and surface extraction.

title: Metric—Phase Fields: Decoupling Distance and Sign for Thin-Structure Reconstruction from Unoriented Point Clouds

abstract: Protein automodeling from cryo-EM density maps faces unique challenges in enforcing physicochemical validity and managing conformational heterogeneity. Current solvers are often limited to static predictions or require computationally intensive heuristic searches. We present CryoACE, an end-to-end framework that reconstructs precise atomic graphs for both homogeneous and heterogeneous structures. Our method features two key innovations: an atom-centric reconstruction paradigm, where density features are sampled directly at atomic coordinates and iteratively recycled to refine structures—replacing expensive voxel convolutions for efficient multimodal fusion—and a training-free guidance mechanism that leverages predicted local resolution priors to resolve dynamic ambiguity. Validated on a newly constructed high-quality dataset, CryoACE significantly outperforms existing baselines on static benchmarks and, for the first time, unveils atomic-level dynamic conformations on complex real-world datasets like EMPIAR-10345 without relying on pre-built static structures. We release our code, model weights, and dataset to facilitate future research.

paragraphs: Building protein structures from cryo-electron microscopy density maps requires recovering atomic arrangements that make physical and chemical sense. The problem becomes harder when the observed protein occupies multiple conformations. CryoACE addresses both homogeneous and heterogeneous structures through an end-to-end system that reconstructs atomic graphs.

Its reconstruction process samples density features directly at atomic coordinates and repeatedly recycles those features to refine the structure. This atom-centered approach replaces expensive voxel convolutions and supports efficient fusion of multiple information sources. A separate training-free guidance mechanism uses predicted local resolution information to help resolve ambiguity associated with structural dynamics.

The authors validate CryoACE on a newly constructed, high-quality dataset and report significant gains over existing methods on static benchmarks. They also report recovering atomic-level dynamic conformations in complex real datasets, including EMPIAR-10345, without pre-built static structures. The findings connect accurate static reconstruction with the harder task of representing conformational variation, rather than restricting automated model building to a single fixed protein arrangement.
summary.tldr: CryoACE reconstructs atomic protein structures and dynamic conformations by refining density features directly at atomic coordinates.

title: CryoACE: An Atom-centric Framework for Accurate and Automated Model Building in Cryo-EM

abstract: The diversity of post-training data is critical for effective downstream performance in large language models (LLMs). Many existing approaches to constructing post-training data quantify diversity using text-based metrics that capture linguistic variation, but such metrics provide only weak signals for the task-relevant features that determine downstream performance. In this work, we introduce Feature Activation Coverage (FAC) which measures data diversity in an interpretable feature space. Building upon this metric, we further propose a diversity-driven data synthesis framework, named FAC Synthesis, that first uses a sparse autoencoder to identify missing features from a seed dataset, and then generates synthetic samples that explicitly reflect these features. Experiments show that our approach consistently improves both data diversity and downstream performance on various tasks, including instruction following, toxicity detection, reward modeling, and behavior steering. Interestingly, we identify a shared, interpretable feature space across model families (i.e., LLaMA, Mistral, and Qwen), enabling cross-model knowledge transfer. Our work provides a solid and practical methodology for exploring data-centric optimization of LLMs.

paragraphs: Diverse post-training data can improve a language model’s downstream performance, but linguistic variety is only a weak indicator of task-relevant variety. Two collections may differ substantially in wording without covering the features that matter to the model. This paper measures diversity in an interpretable feature space through Feature Activation Coverage, or FAC.

FAC Synthesis turns that measure into a data-generation procedure. It uses a sparse autoencoder to identify features missing from an initial dataset, then generates samples that explicitly express those features. The objective is to fill representational gaps in the seed data. This connects the choice of new examples to the model’s feature coverage rather than relying solely on surface differences between texts.

Experiments report consistent improvements in both diversity and downstream performance across instruction following, toxicity detection, reward modeling, and behavior steering. The researchers also identify a shared interpretable feature space across LLaMA, Mistral, and Qwen, enabling cross-model knowledge transfer. These findings support feature coverage as a practical guide for targeted synthetic-data construction.
summary.tldr: FAC Synthesis generates examples that fill missing interpretable features, improving data diversity and downstream language-model performance.

title: Less is Enough: Synthesizing Diverse Data in LLM Feature Space with Sparse Autoencoders

abstract: LLM parameter editing methods commonly rely on computing an ideal target hidden-state at a target layer (referred as anchor point) and distributing the target vector to multiple preceding layers (commonly known as backward spreading) for cooperative editing. Although widely used for a long time, its underlying basis have not been systematically investigated. In this paper, we first conduct a systematic study of its foundations, which helps clarify its capability boundaries, practical considerations, and potential failure modes. Then, we propose a simple and elegant alternative that replaces backward spreading with forward-propagation. Instead of optimizing the target at the last editing layer, we optimize the anchor point at the first editing layer, and then propagate it forward to obtain accurate and mutually compatible target hidden-states for all subsequent editing layers. This approach achieves the same computational complexity as existing methods while producing more accurate layer-wise targets. Our method is simple, without interfering with either the computation of the initial target hidden state or any other components of the subsequent editing pipeline, and thus constituting a benefit for a wide range of LLM parameter editing methods.

paragraphs: Language-model parameter editing often starts by computing a desired internal hidden state at an anchor layer. To coordinate edits across several layers, existing methods commonly distribute that target backward to preceding layers. This paper systematically investigates the basis of that practice, examining its capability boundaries, practical considerations, and potential failure modes.

The proposed alternative changes where the anchor is placed and how other targets are obtained. It optimizes the target at the first editing layer, then propagates that state forward through the model. Subsequent editing layers receive targets derived from this forward computation, producing layer-specific hidden states that are mutually compatible with the propagated anchor.

The paper reports more accurate targets with the same computational complexity as existing approaches. The change leaves the initial hidden-state target computation and the other components of the editing pipeline intact, making it applicable to a wide range of parameter-editing methods. Its contribution is specifically a revised construction of coordinated layer targets, grounded in the model's forward propagation rather than a backward distribution of a later-layer target.
summary.tldr: Forward replay constructs more accurate, compatible editing targets by optimizing an early-layer anchor and propagating it through subsequent layers.

title: From Backward Spreading to Forward Replay: Revisiting Target Construction in LLM Parameter Editing

abstract: Sparse Matrix-Vector Multiplication (SpMV) is a fundamental operation in the inference of sparse Large Language Models (LLMs). Because existing SpMV methods perform poorly under the low, unstructured sparsity ($30-90%$) commonly observed in pruned LLMs, unstructured pruning provides only limited memory reduction and speedup. We propose **MACKO-SpMV**, a GPU-optimized format and kernel co-designed to reduce storage overhead while remaining compatible with the GPU’s execution model. This enables efficient SpMV for unstructured sparsity without specialized hardware units or precomputation. We identify memory bandwidth as the primary limiting factor of SpMV and analyze the storage overhead of MACKO. At $50%$ sparsity, MACKO is the first approach to achieve $1.5\times$ memory reduction and $1.2-1.5\times$ speedup over the dense baseline as well as substantial improvements over other SpMV methods: cuSPARSE ($2.8-13.0\times$), Sputnik ($1.9-2.6\times$), and DASP ($2.2-2.5\times$). An LLM pruned with Wanda to sparsity $50%$ requires $1.5\times$ less memory and achieves $1.5\times$ faster inference at fp16 precision. As a result, **unstructured pruning at $50%$ sparsity becomes practical** for real-world LLM workloads and **bridges the efficiency gap with structured 2:4 sparsity**.
originalAbstract: Sparse Matrix-Vector Multiplication (SpMV) is a fundamental operation in the inference of sparse Large Language Models (LLMs). We propose **MACKO-SpMV**, a GPU-optimized format and kernel co-designed to reduce storage overhead while remaining compatible with the GPU’s execution model. This enables efficient SpMV for unstructured sparsity without specialized hardware units or precomputation. We identify memory bandwidth as the primary limiting factor of SpMV and analyze the storage overhead of MACKO. At $50%$ sparsity, MACKO is the first approach to achieve $1.5\times$ memory reduction and $1.2-1.5\times$ speedup over the dense baseline as well as substantial improvements over other SpMV methods: cuSPARSE ($2.8-13.0\times$), Sputnik ($1.9-2.6\times$), and DASP ($2.2-2.5\times$). As a result, **unstructured pruning at $50%$ sparsity becomes practical** for real-world LLM workloads and **bridges the efficiency gap with structured 2:4 sparsity**.

paragraphs: Removing model weights does not automatically deliver proportional memory savings or faster inference. For the unstructured sparsity found in pruned language models, existing sparse matrix-vector multiplication methods can incur substantial overhead. MACKO addresses this by designing a sparse storage format and GPU computation kernel together, with memory bandwidth identified as the main bottleneck.

The format reduces storage overhead while fitting the GPU’s execution model. It supports unstructured sparsity without specialized hardware units or precomputation. This matters because the positions of surviving weights need not follow a prescribed pattern, yet the implementation still has to store and process them efficiently enough to outperform a dense representation.

At 50% sparsity, the paper reports a 1.5-fold memory reduction and a 1.2–1.5-fold speedup over the dense baseline, alongside improvements over other sparse methods. A language model pruned with Wanda achieves 1.5-fold lower memory requirements and 1.5-fold faster fp16 inference. These results support the practical value of unstructured pruning at that sparsity and narrow its efficiency gap with structured 2:4 sparsity.
summary.tldr: MACKO co-designs sparse storage and GPU execution to make 50% unstructured pruning yield practical memory and inference gains.

title: MACKO: Sparse matrix-vector multiplication for low sparsity

abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) or verifiable rewards (RLVR), the standard paradigm for aligning LLMs or building recent SOTA reasoning models, is highly sensitive to noise from inconsistent or erroneous rewards. Yet, the interaction between such noise and widely used group-based policy optimization methods remains underexplored. We introduce a noise-robust Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and Done Right GRPO (Dr.GRPO) framework that explicitly models reward corruption as Bernoulli noise. Our method applies noise correction after estimating reward flip probabilities to debias the learning signal, yielding unbiased gradient estimates. Theoretical analysis shows that group-based methods inherently mitigate individual-level noise, and our correction strategy amplifies this robustness. Empirically, we observe consistent improvements across math and code tasks when applying our noise correction to standard reward model usage, with particular gains of up to 6.7 percentage points in accuracy on math tasks and 1.5 on code tasks under realistic reward model conditions. This work bridges label-noise correction from supervised learning with modern RLHF, offering both theoretical insights and a practical algorithm for noisy real-world deployment.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning for language models depends on rewards that may be inconsistent or wrong. Such errors can distort the training signal, including when optimization compares groups of generated responses. This paper studies how reward noise interacts with GRPO and Dr.GRPO and develops corrections for both methods.

The framework explicitly models reward corruption as Bernoulli noise, meaning that reward errors are represented through probabilistic flips. It estimates flip probabilities and then corrects the learning signal to remove bias. Within this framework, the authors derive unbiased gradient estimates. Their theory also shows that group-based optimization already mitigates noise affecting individual examples, and that the proposed correction strengthens this robustness.

Experiments applying the correction with reward models show consistent improvements across mathematics and coding tasks. Reported gains reach 6.7 percentage points in math accuracy and 1.5 points in code accuracy under realistic reward-model conditions. The work connects techniques for correcting noisy labels in supervised learning to policy optimization, offering both an account of existing group-level robustness and a method for improving it.
summary.tldr: Correcting estimated reward-flip noise gives GRPO and Dr.GRPO unbiased gradients within the proposed framework and improves tested math and code accuracy.

title: Noise-corrected GRPO: From Noisy Rewards to Unbiased Gradients

abstract: Pre-trained diffusion models have emerged as powerful generative priors for both unconditional and conditional sample generation, yet their outputs often deviate from the characteristics of user-specific target data. Such mismatches are especially problematic in domain adaptation tasks, where only a few reference examples are available and retraining the diffusion model is infeasible. Existing inference-time guidance methods can adjust sampling trajectories, but they typically optimize surrogate objectives such as classifier likelihoods rather than directly aligning with the target distribution. We propose MMD Guidance, a training-free mechanism that augments the reverse diffusion process with gradients of the Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) between generated samples and a reference dataset. MMD provides reliable distributional estimates from limited data, exhibits low variance in practice, and is efficiently differentiable, which makes it particularly well-suited for the guidance task. Our framework naturally extends to prompt-aware adaptation in conditional generation models via product kernels. Also, it can be applied with computational efficiency in latent diffusion models (LDMs), since guidance is applied in the latent space of the LDM. Experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks demonstrate that MMD Guidance can achieve distributional alignment while preserving sample fidelity. The project code is available at https://github.com/matinamehdizadeh/MMD-Guidance.

paragraphs: A pretrained diffusion model may generate convincing samples whose characteristics still differ from a user's reference data. Adapting the model is especially challenging when only a few examples are available and retraining is infeasible. MMD Guidance addresses this setting by changing the sampling process using a direct measure of distributional mismatch.

The method adds gradients of Maximum Mean Discrepancy between generated samples and a reference dataset to reverse diffusion. This steers generation toward the reference distribution. The authors motivate MMD through its estimation behavior with limited data, low observed variance, and efficient differentiability. These properties make it suitable for repeatedly guiding samples during generation.

The framework extends to prompt-aware conditional generation through product kernels and can operate efficiently inside the latent space of latent diffusion models. Experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks show that it can improve distributional alignment while preserving sample fidelity. The stated result is that adaptation can happen at inference time, with the reference dataset influencing generation without requiring additional model training.
summary.tldr: MMD Guidance adapts diffusion sampling toward a reference distribution without retraining, with experiments showing alignment gains while preserving sample fidelity.

title: MMD Guidance: Training-Free Distribution Adaptation for Diffusion Models via Maximum Mean Discrepancy Guidance

abstract: We study the corruption-robustness of in-context reinforcement learning (ICRL), focusing on the Decision-Pretrained Transformer (DPT, Lee et al., 2023). To address the challenge of reward poisoning attacks targeting the DPT, we propose a novel adversarial training framework, called Adversarially Trained DPT (AT-DPT). Our method simultaneously trains a population of attackers to minimize the true reward of the DPT by poisoning environment rewards, and a DPT model to infer optimal actions from the poisoned data. We evaluate the effectiveness of our approach against standard bandit algorithms, including robust baselines designed to handle reward contamination. Our results show that AT-DPT significantly outperforms them in bandit settings under a learned attacker, and generalizes to more complex environments such as adaptive attackers and MDPs. It shows promise in ICRL as a meta-RL approach to learning effective corruption-robust algorithms.
