paragraphs: In-context reinforcement learning uses contextual experience to guide action selection. This paper examines what happens when an attacker corrupts the rewards in that experience, focusing on the Decision-Pretrained Transformer. Such poisoning can make the feedback used for decision-making disagree with the true reward the agent should maximize.

The proposed Adversarially Trained DPT trains the decision model alongside a population of attackers. The attackers learn to alter environment rewards in ways that reduce the model's true reward, while the model learns to infer optimal actions from the corrupted data. Training therefore makes reward corruption an active part of the learning problem.

In bandit experiments under a learned attacker, the resulting model significantly outperforms standard algorithms, including robust baselines designed for contaminated rewards. The authors also report generalization to adaptive attackers and more complex Markov decision processes. These findings suggest that adversarial training can help in-context reinforcement learning acquire effective corruption-resistant decision strategies, with the evidence extending beyond the initial bandit setting to the additional environments tested.
summary.tldr: Training a decision transformer against learned reward-poisoning attackers improves its reported robustness in bandits and more complex environments.

title: Robust In-Context Reinforcement Learning Under Reward Poisoning Attacks

abstract: Diffusion policies offer a powerful and expressive parameterization for continuous control. Yet, their integration with reinforcement learning remains conceptually and algorithmically challenging. In this work, we address this gap by introducing a noisy-space action-value (Q-)function that assigns values to diffusion latents through the distribution of executed actions induced by the denoising process. We show that this construction admits a precise semantic interpretation and derive a noisy-space policy gradient (NSPG) that optimizes noisy latents using only clean action space value estimates. Building on this result, we formulate a KL-regularized policy improvement over noisy latents and show that the resulting objective admits a diffusion-compatible regression form, avoiding backpropagation through the denoising process. Empirical results on state-based D4RL benchmarks and vision-based OGBench tasks demonstrate that the proposed noisy-space objective provides a principled and effective basis for training diffusion policies in offline reinforcement learning. Project webpage: https://mahmoud-selim.github.io/NSPG/

paragraphs: Diffusion policies represent continuous-control actions through a denoising process, but connecting that process to reinforcement-learning objectives is challenging. This paper introduces a value function for the noisy latent variables used by the policy. Their value is defined through the distribution of executed actions that denoising those variables ultimately produces.

That construction gives noisy-space values a precise interpretation in terms of actual actions. The authors derive a noisy-space policy gradient that improves noisy latents using value estimates from the clean action space alone. They then formulate policy improvement with a KL regularizer and show that its objective can be expressed as regression compatible with diffusion training.

The regression formulation avoids backpropagating through the denoising process, directly addressing a complication of optimizing diffusion policies. Experiments on state-based D4RL benchmarks and vision-based OGBench tasks support the effectiveness of the resulting objective in offline reinforcement learning. The central contribution is a principled connection between latent-space optimization and action-space value, together with a practical training form that uses that connection.
summary.tldr: A noisy-space policy gradient trains diffusion policies from clean action values without backpropagating through denoising.

title: Noisy-Space Policy Gradient for Diffusion Policies in Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Deploying GRPO on Flow Matching models has proven effective for text-to-image generation. However, existing paradigms typically propagate an outcome-based reward to all preceding denoising steps without distinguishing the local effect of each step. Moreover, current group-wise ranking mainly compares trajectories at matched timesteps and ignores within-trajectory dependencies, where certain early denoising actions can affect later states via delayed, implicit interactions. We propose TurningPoint-GRPO (TP-GRPO), a GRPO framework that alleviates step-wise reward sparsity and explicitly models long-term effects within the denoising trajectory. TP-GRPO makes two key innovations: (i) it replaces outcome-based rewards with step-level incremental rewards, providing a dense, step-aware learning signal that better isolates each denoising action’s “pure" effect, and (ii) it identifies turning points—steps that flip the local reward trend and make subsequent reward evolution consistent with the overall trajectory trend—and assigns these actions an aggregated long-term reward to capture their delayed impact. Turning points are detected solely via sign changes in incremental rewards, making TP-GRPO efficient and hyperparameter-free. Extensive experiments also demonstrate that TP-GRPO exploits reward signals more effectively and consistently improves generation.

paragraphs: Training a flow-based image generator with a reward on its final image leaves an attribution problem: individual denoising decisions receive feedback that does not distinguish their contributions. Comparing different generation trajectories at matching timesteps also overlooks how an early decision can influence later states. This paper introduces TurningPoint-GRPO to account for both immediate and delayed effects.

The method first replaces final-outcome rewards with incremental rewards at individual steps. These provide denser feedback intended to better isolate each action’s local contribution. It then identifies turning points, where the local reward trend reverses and subsequent changes align with the trajectory’s overall trend. Those actions receive an aggregated reward representing their longer-term impact, supplementing the immediate feedback.

Turning-point detection relies only on sign changes in incremental rewards, avoiding extra hyperparameters for that detection mechanism. The reported experiments show more effective use of reward signals and consistent improvements in generation. The contribution is a more structured assignment of credit across the sampling process, including decisions whose benefits appear later.
summary.tldr: TurningPoint-GRPO improves flow-based image generation by assigning rewards to immediate denoising effects and selected steps with delayed influence.

title: Alleviating Sparse Rewards by Modeling Step-Wise and Long-Term Sampling Effects in Flow-Based GRPO

abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) achieve high accuracy on time series classification (TSC) but remain opaque, hindering deployment in sensitive domains. Existing post-hoc TSC explanation methods rely on a single attribution perspective and incur high per-instance computational cost, limiting real-time use. We propose XMA, a framework that unifies multiple post-hoc explainers at the instance level and amortizes the cost of explanation into a learned inference pass. Instance-level Multi-Expert Knowledge Distillation (IMEKD) selects, per instance, the attribution map with the highest combined faithfulness and robustness score from a pool of XAI experts. Objective-Regularized Amortized Optimization Explanation (ORAOE) trains an explainer DNN to reproduce this instance-best supervision while directly optimizing differentiable faithfulness and robustness objectives, letting the student refine beyond any individual teacher. Faithfulness-Preserving Segmentation (FPS) converts point-wise maps into contiguous segments without changing their faithfulness score. Across four synthetic datasets, MIT-ECG with cardiologist-verified ground truth, and 11 multivariate UEA benchmarks on three DNN architectures, XMA attains the best AUPRC on all synthetic and MIT-ECG benchmarks among compared methods, and the highest faithfulness on 7 of 11 and robustness on 8 of 11 UEA datasets, while amortizing explanation into a lightweight learned explainer rather than relying on per-instance optimization.

paragraphs: Explaining a time-series classifier can require expensive optimization for every input, and individual explanation methods offer only one attribution perspective. XMA combines several explainers and shifts much of that work into training a separate neural explainer. Once learned, the explainer produces an attribution map through an inference pass.

The student learns from this instance-specific choice while also directly optimizing differentiable versions of those objectives, allowing refinement beyond an individual teacher. On eleven multivariate UEA datasets, it leads in faithfulness on seven and robustness on eight. These results support learning from complementary explainers while preserving a lightweight inference path, with the strongest explanation method allowed to vary by input.
summary.tldr: XMA learns a fast time-series explainer from instance-specific expert choices and directly optimizes explanation faithfulness and robustness.

title: Unified Time Series Explanations via Amortized Optimization and Instance-level Multi-Expert Knowledge Distillation

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) require substantial compute, and thus energy, at inference time. While quantizing weights and activations is effective at improving efficiency, naive quantization of LLMs can significantly degrade performance due to large magnitude outliers. This paper describes FPTQuant, which introduces three novel, lightweight, and expressive function-preserving transforms (FPTs) to facilitate quantization of transformers: (1) a mergeable pre-RoPE transform for queries and keys, (2) a mergeable transform for values, (3) a cheap, dynamic scaling transform. By leveraging the equivariances and independencies inherent to canonical transformer operation, we designed these FPTs to maintain the model’s function while shaping the intermediate activation distributions to be more quantization friendly. FPTQuant requires no custom kernels and adds virtually no overhead during inference. The FPTs are trained both locally to reduce outliers, and end-to-end such that the outputs of the quantized and full-precision models match. FPTQuant enables static INT4 quantization with minimal overhead and shows SOTA speed-up of up to 3.9x over FP. Empirically, FPTQuant has an excellent accuracy-speed trade-off—it is performing on par or exceeding most prior work and only shows slightly lower accuracy compared to a method that is up to 29% slower.

paragraphs: Quantizing a language model reduces numerical precision to improve inference efficiency, but unusually large values can cause substantial accuracy loss. FPTQuant addresses this by reshaping intermediate activations before quantization. Its transforms preserve the underlying model function while making the numerical distributions easier to represent at low precision.

The method introduces three transforms: one for queries and keys before rotary positional encoding, one for values, and a dynamic scaling operation. The first two can be merged into the model, while the third is inexpensive. Their design uses symmetries and independencies in standard transformer operations. Training both suppresses outliers locally and encourages the quantized model’s outputs to match full-precision outputs end to end.

FPTQuant enables static four-bit integer quantization without custom kernels and with virtually no inference overhead. The authors report speedups of up to 3.9 times over full precision. Accuracy matches or exceeds most compared prior methods; the method with slightly better accuracy can be up to 29% slower. These results position FPTQuant as an effective accuracy–speed compromise in the reported evaluations.
summary.tldr: FPTQuant reshapes transformer activations with function-preserving transforms, enabling efficient four-bit quantization and reported speedups of up to 3.9 times over full precision.

title: FPTQuant: Function-Preserving Transforms for LLM Quantization

abstract: While diffusion language models (DLMs) have achieved competitive performance in text generation, improving their reasoning ability with reinforcement learning remains an active research area. Here, we introduce d2, a reasoning framework tailored for masked DLMs. Central to our framework is a new policy gradient algorithm that relies on accurate estimates of the sampling trajectory likelihoods. Because computing these likelihoods naively is computationally expensive for masked DLMs, we develop a family of estimators tailored to distinct model classes. For DLMs that support a sampling algorithm called any-order decoding, we propose d2-AnyOrder, which achieves exact trajectory likelihood with a single model pass. Through an empirical study of widely used DLMs, we show that any-order decoding is not universally supported in practice. For standard masked diffusion models, we propose d2-StepMerge, which approximates the trajectory likelihood, trading off compute for approximation accuracy in an analytically tractable manner. Empirically, d2 significantly outperforms widely-used RL baselines when applied to popular DLMs, and sets a new state-of-the-art performance for DLMs on logical reasoning tasks (Countdown and Sudoku) and math reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K and MATH500). We provide the code along with a blog post on the project page: https://guanghanwang.com/d2

paragraphs: The d2 framework improves reasoning in masked diffusion language models through reinforcement learning. Its central challenge is estimating the likelihood of the sampling trajectory that produced an answer. The proposed policy gradient algorithm depends on accurate trajectory estimates, but computing them directly can be expensive for this class of language model.

The authors develop different estimators for different model capabilities. For models that support any-order decoding, d2-AnyOrder computes an exact trajectory likelihood in a single model pass. Their empirical investigation finds that widely used diffusion language models do not universally support this decoding method. For standard masked diffusion models, d2-StepMerge instead provides an approximation with an analytically tractable trade-off between computational expense and estimation accuracy.

In the reported experiments, d2 substantially outperforms widely used reinforcement learning baselines on popular diffusion language models. It also achieves new state-of-the-art results for diffusion language models on Countdown, Sudoku, GSM8K, and MATH500. The contribution links stronger reasoning to practical likelihood estimation while explicitly accounting for differences in which decoding procedures models support.
summary.tldr: d2 improves diffusion-model reasoning with reinforcement learning estimators that compute exact or approximate sampling-trajectory likelihoods according to model capabilities.

title: d2: Improving Reasoning in Diffusion Language Models via Trajectory Likelihood Estimation

abstract: Vision-Text Compression (VTC) offers a scalable path for long-context multimodal modeling by rendering textual data into dense visual tokens. While recent Vision-Language Models (VLMs) demonstrate high decoding fidelity (OCR) on such inputs, they exhibit a severe reasoning gap: models that reason robustly on native text often fail on visually compressed equivalents, particularly in long-range retrieval and multi-step deduction. We identify a phenomenon of post-training transfer failure, where standard supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning on visual prompts yield marginal gains compared to their textual counterparts. To address this, we propose CoRe (Coordinated Reasoning), a training framework that enforces lockstep consistency between the reasoning processes of textual and visual modalities. By treating the text-conditioned policy as a dynamic anchor, CoRe aligns the visual-conditioned policy via step-wise distribution matching, seamlessly integrating into both SFT and RL pipelines. Extensive evaluations across mathematical reasoning, long-context memory, and tabular retrieval benchmarks show that CoRe significantly outperforms standard visual post-training, recovering up to 70% of the performance gap relative to the textual upper bound and effectively activating latent reasoning capabilities in the compressed visual modality.

paragraphs: Vision-text compression represents textual material visually, allowing dense visual tokens to carry long contexts. The paper identifies a gap between reading this material and reasoning with it: models can decode the words accurately yet struggle with retrieval across long inputs or deductions requiring several steps. Strong reasoning on ordinary text therefore does not automatically transfer to its visually compressed equivalent.

The authors find that standard supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning on visual prompts make only limited progress relative to training on text. Their proposed CoRe framework coordinates the two forms of reasoning. It uses the text-conditioned policy as an evolving reference and matches the visual-conditioned policy’s output distributions at successive reasoning steps. This coordination fits into both supervised and reinforcement-learning pipelines.

Across mathematical reasoning, long-context memory, and table retrieval, CoRe substantially improves on standard visual post-training. It recovers up to 70% of the performance gap against the textual upper bound. That result indicates that explicitly coordinating reasoning across modalities can help models use capabilities that ordinary visual post-training struggles to activate.
summary.tldr: CoRe aligns visual reasoning with text-based reasoning during training, recovering up to 70% of the gap caused by visual text compression.

title: Awakening Visual Reasoning: Mitigating Post-Training Failure in Vision-Text Compression

abstract: Analog in-memory computing (AIMC) performs computation directly within resistive crossbar arrays, offering an energy-efficient platform to scale large vision and language models. However, non-ideal analog device properties make the training on AIMC devices challenging. In particular, its update asymmetry can induce a systematic drift of weight updates towards a device-specific symmetric point (SP), which typically does not align with the optimum of the training objective. To mitigate this bias, most existing works assume the SP is known and pre-calibrate it to zero before training by setting the reference point as the SP. Nevertheless, calibrating AIMC devices requires costly pulse updates, and residual calibration error can directly degrade training performance. In this work, we present the first theoretical characterization of the pulse complexity of SP calibration and the resulting estimation error. We further propose a dynamic SP estimation method that tracks the SP during model training, and establishes its convergence guarantees. In addition, we develop an enhanced variant based on chopping and filtering techniques from digital signal processing. Numerical experiments demonstrate both the efficiency and effectiveness of the proposed method.

title: Dynamic Symmetric Point Tracking: Tackling Non-ideal Reference in Analog In-memory Training

abstract: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) empowers Large Language Models (LLMs) with exceptional performance on specialized tasks, but it yields dense, high-dimensional delta parameters that pose severe storage and distribution challenges. Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)-based compression offers a compact representation for such delta parameters, but existing methods adopt heuristic quantization without clarifying underlying mechanisms, leading to poor generalizability. In this work, we propose PrinMix, a rigorous SVD-based framework that models quantization as an optimization problem, grounding the design in mathematical mechanisms. We first theoretically derive quantization error and identify a key singular-value-dominated scaling mechanism, which mathematically proves the necessity of mix-precision quantization. We then model the quantization scheme as a 0/1 Integer Linear Programming (ILP) problem, which yields optimal bit-budget-constrained solutions without empirical assumptions. Furthermore, PrinMix integrates a Reconstruction Target Correction (RTC) method to compensate for errors from the $\mathbf{V}$-then-$\mathbf{U}$ sequential quantization process. Extensive experiments confirm PrinMix performs well: for 7B LLMs, PrinMix outperforms SOTA Delta-CoMe on challenging benchmarks by 22.3% on AIME2024 and 6.1% on GQA.

title: Principled SVD-based Delta Compression via Quantization Error Minimization

abstract: While Visual Multi-Agent Systems (VMAS) promise to enhance comprehensive abilities through inter-agent collaboration, empirical evidence reveals a counter-intuitive "scaling wall": increasing agent turns often degrades performance while exponentially inflating token costs. We attribute this failure to the information bottleneck inherent in text-centric communication, where converting perceptual and thinking trajectories into discrete natural language inevitably induces semantic loss. To this end, we propose L$^{2}$-VMAS, a novel model-agnostic framework that enables inter-agent collaboration with dual latent memories. Based on such a design, we decouple the perception and thinking while dynamically synthesizing dual latent memories. Additionally, we introduce an entropy-driven proactive triggering that replaces passive information transmission with efficient, on-demand memory access. Extensive experiments among backbones, sizes, and multi-agent structures demonstrate that our method effectively breaks the "scaling wall" with superb scalability, improving average accuracy by 2.7-5.4% while reducing total token usage by 21.3-44.8%. The codes will be publicly released.

paragraphs: Adding more rounds of collaboration to a visual multi-agent system does not necessarily improve its answers. The paper reports an empirical pattern in which performance can decline while token costs rise exponentially. The framework dynamically synthesizes these memories, giving agents a different means of sharing information. It also uses an entropy-driven trigger for proactive memory access, so information is accessed on demand rather than transmitted passively throughout the interaction.

The reported results show average accuracy improvements of 2.7%–5.4% alongside reductions in total token usage of 21.3%–44.8%. summary.tldr: L²-VMAS separates perceptual and reasoning memories to improve visual multi-agent collaboration while reducing token use.

title: Dual Latent Memory for Visual Multi-agent System

abstract: Long-context large language model (LLM) inference has become the norm for today’s AI applications. However, it is severely bottlenecked by the increasing memory demands of its KV cache. Previous works have shown that self-speculative decoding with sparse attention, where tokens are drafted using a subset of the KV cache and verified in parallel against the full KV cache, speeds up inference in a lossless manner. However, they rely on a standalone KV selection algorithm to select the KV entries used for drafting and overlook the fact that the criticality of each KV entry is inherently computed during verification. In this paper, we propose Vegas, a self-speculative decoding method with verification-guided sparse attention. Vegas identifies critical KV cache entries as a byproduct of verification and computes attention only over these entries when drafting subsequent tokens. This not only improves the draft token acceptance rate but also incurs low KV selection overhead, thereby improving decoding throughput. Vegas achieves a 1.25$\times$–2.81$\times$ speedup in decoding throughput over default vLLM and a 1.15$\times$–1.29$\times$ speedup over state-of-the-art sparse attention-based self-speculative decoding methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/platformxlab/vegas.

paragraphs: Long-context language-model inference is constrained by the memory demands of the key-value cache. Sparse self-speculative decoding speeds generation by drafting tokens using only part of that cache, then verifying them in parallel against the full cache. Verification preserves the lossless behavior of this approach, but selecting a useful cache subset introduces its own overhead.

Vegas reuses information already computed during verification to identify important cache entries. Subsequent drafting attends only to those entries. This connects the verification and drafting stages more closely: the full-cache check also supplies guidance for the next sparse draft, reducing the need for a separate cache-selection procedure.

The method improves draft-token acceptance while keeping selection overhead low. Reported decoding-throughput gains range from 1.25 to 2.81 times over default vLLM and from 1.15 to 1.29 times over leading sparse self-speculative methods. The findings show that verification can serve two purposes at once, checking candidate tokens and informing a more efficient next round of drafting.
summary.tldr: Vegas reuses verification attention to choose cache entries for speculative drafting, improving token acceptance and decoding throughput.

title: Vegas: Self-Speculative Decoding with Verification-Guided Sparse Attention

abstract: Improving LLM performance on downstream tasks sometimes requires leveraging auxiliary datasets during post-training. In practice, however, developers face constraints on compute, labeling, and licensing costs that preclude using all available data, necessitating principled dataset-level selection. These constraints are increasingly shaped by dataset marketplaces, where data acquisition is governed by budgets and negotiation. We study dataset valuation as a subset selection problem during LLM post-training. Our goal is to identify and weight auxiliary datasets so as to maximize target task performance given constrained budgets. We first show that commonly used gradient alignment scores provide a reasonable yet incomplete valuation signal, as they ignore redundancy among datasets. To address this, we propose a scalable convex dataset-level valuation method based on kernel mean matching (KMM) in gradient space, which jointly accounts for alignment with the target task and redundancy across auxiliary datasets. Through extensive experiments across diverse post-training settings and tasks, we show that our approach consistently outperforms existing valuation baselines, achieving stronger performance with low computational overhead. Our results position dataset valuation as a practical decision tool for post-training data selection in market-constrained large language model settings.

paragraphs: Choosing auxiliary datasets for language-model post-training involves more than finding potentially useful data. Compute, labeling, and licensing budgets can prevent developers from using everything available. This paper treats dataset valuation as a selection and weighting problem: decide which collections to use so that a target task benefits within those constraints.

A common valuation signal measures whether a dataset's training gradients align with the target task. The authors show that this signal is useful but incomplete because it overlooks redundancy. Several datasets can each appear relevant while providing overlapping information. Their method uses kernel mean matching in gradient space to consider target alignment and overlap jointly through a scalable convex formulation.

This changes the decision from evaluating datasets only in isolation to assessing how they fit together as a collection. Across diverse post-training tasks and settings, the method consistently outperforms the tested valuation baselines with low computational overhead. The findings support dataset valuation as a practical tool for allocating limited data budgets, including settings where acquisition costs and marketplace negotiations shape the available choices.
summary.tldr: A convex valuation method selects post-training datasets by jointly accounting for target-task relevance and redundancy.

title: Convex Dataset Valuation for Post-Training

abstract: Existing offline feed-forward methods for joint scene understanding and reconstruction on long image streams often perform global computation over an ever-growing set of past observations, causing runtime and GPU memory to increase rapidly with sequence length. We propose Streaming Semantic Gaussian Splatting (S2GS), a strictly causal and incremental framework that builds a 3D Gaussian semantic field from image streams without accessing future frames or reprocessing historical observations. S2GS continuously updates scene geometry, appearance, and instance-level semantics through a geometry–semantic decoupled dual-backbone design. The geometry branch performs causal modeling for incremental Gaussian updates, while the semantic branch leverages a 2D foundation vision model and a query-driven decoder to predict masks and identity embeddings. Query-level contrastive alignment and lightweight online association with an instance memory further stabilize temporal identities. Experiments show that S2GS matches or outperforms strong offline baselines, while substantially improving long-horizon scalability: it processes over 1,000 frames with much slower runtime and GPU memory growth, whereas offline global-processing baselines typically run out of memory at around 80 frames under the same setting. Project Page: https://stdcoutzrh.github.io/projects/s2gs/.

paragraphs: Reconstructing and understanding a scene from a long image stream can become expensive when every update revisits an expanding history. S2GS builds a semantic 3D Gaussian field incrementally. It is strictly causal: it uses no future frames and does not reprocess historical observations.

The framework separates geometry and semantics into two branches. The geometry branch updates the Gaussian representation causally. The semantic branch combines a 2D foundation vision model with a query-driven decoder that predicts object masks and identity embeddings. Query-level contrastive alignment and lightweight association with an instance memory help maintain consistent object identities over time. These components let the scene representation update geometry, appearance, and individual-object information together.

Experiments show performance matching or exceeding strong offline baselines while runtime and GPU memory grow much more slowly. S2GS processes over 1,000 frames; under the same setting, offline methods using global processing typically run out of memory around 80 frames. The result demonstrates the practical scaling benefit of incremental processing in the tested setting.
summary.tldr: S2GS incrementally reconstructs and labels 3D scenes from image streams, maintaining object identities while substantially improving long-sequence scalability.

title: S2GS: Streaming Semantic Gaussian Splatting for Online Scene Understanding and Reconstruction

abstract: Planning-driven model-based (modelic) reinforcement learning has achieved impressive success in continuous control tasks but predominantly relies on zero-order optimizers like Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI). While robust for global exploration, MPPI updates actions solely through sampling and neglects the smooth return gradients inherent in structured dynamics that guide fine-grained search. To complement MPPI’s robustness with gradient-guided precision, we first propose Langevin Rollout Optimization (LaRO), which leverages return gradients to refine actions via Langevin dynamics, achieving reliable local convergence without sacrificing multimodal exploration. This is supported by a score-augmented world model that jointly learns dynamics and a score function within a unified latent space, facilitating efficient and accurate gradient estimation for real-time planning. Second, we combine MPPI and LaRO through a simple yet effective choice mechanism, termed Maximum Look-Ahead Planning (MLAP). Finally, we instantiate MLAP within the latest BOOM algorithm, replacing its MPPI-only planner and yielding BOOM-L. Empirical results on the DeepMind Control Suite and Humanoid Bench demonstrate that BOOM-L consistently outperforms strong baselines in both sample efficiency and final performance.

MPPI supports broad exploration, but its updates do not use the smooth return gradients available in structured dynamics. This paper introduces Langevin Rollout Optimization to add gradient-guided refinement to action planning.

title: Langevin Rollout Optimization for Modelic Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Modern large-scale LLM pretraining benefits from utilizing Pipeline Parallelism; however, synchronous implementations leave GPUs idle during pipeline bubbles, wasting computational resources. Asynchronous Pipeline Parallelism eliminates these bubbles, maximizing throughput at the cost of gradient staleness. Among asynchronous schedules, PipeDream-2BW is particularly appealing: unlike the original PipeDream schedule, it ensures a constant one-step gradient delay regardless of pipeline depth. However, its adoption remains limited due to the common belief that optimizing under staleness is fundamentally unstable. In this work, we challenge this assumption, demonstrating that degradation under one-step delay depends strongly on optimizer choice rather than being an intrinsic limitation. We provide the first comprehensive empirical analysis showing that while AdamW, the predominant optimizer at the time when PipeDream-2BW was introduced, indeed suffers from severe degradation, recent methods like Muon exhibit strong robustness under a one-step delay. We introduce an optimizer-agnostic Error Feedback-inspired correction to further mitigate delay effects. We provide supporting theoretical analysis demonstrating convergence for Muon with and without this correction. Extensive evaluation on models up to 10B parameters confirms that our strategies bridge the performance gap with synchronous training, highlighting the practical potential of asynchronous pipeline parallelism at scale.

paragraphs: Pipeline parallel training divides a language model across devices, but synchronized schedules can leave GPUs idle. Asynchronous execution removes these pipeline bubbles at the cost of using delayed gradients. The paper studies PipeDream-2BW, whose gradient delay remains one step regardless of pipeline depth, and asks whether that delay necessarily causes unstable optimization.

The empirical analysis finds that the consequences depend strongly on the optimizer. AdamW suffers severe degradation in the studied setting, whereas Muon is substantially more robust to a one-step delay. The authors also introduce an optimizer-agnostic correction inspired by error feedback to further reduce delay effects. Supporting theory establishes convergence for Muon with and without the correction.

Evaluations on models with up to 10 billion parameters show that the proposed strategies bridge the performance gap with synchronous training. The result challenges treating gradient staleness alone as a sufficient reason to avoid asynchronous pipelines. In the investigated one-step-delay setting, optimizer choice and correction mechanisms make a material difference to training quality.
summary.tldr: Muon and an error-feedback-inspired correction mitigate one-step gradient delay, bridging the reported training-quality gap between asynchronous and synchronous pipelines.

abstract: We introduce a framework, which we call Divide-by-2 (DB2), for extending support vector machines (SVM) to multi-class problems. DB2 offers an alternative to the standard one-against-one and one-against-rest algorithms. For an $N$ class problem, DB2 produces an $N-1$ node binary decision tree where nodes represent decision boundaries formed by $N-1$ SVM binary classifiers. This tree structure allows us to present a generalization and a time complexity analysis of DB2. Our analysis and related experiments show that, DB2 is faster than one-against-one and one-against-rest algorithms in terms of testing time, significantly faster than one-against-rest in terms of training time, and that the cross-validation accuracy of DB2 is comparable to these two methods.

paragraphs: Divide-by-2, or DB2, organizes support vector machines into a hierarchy for problems with more than two classes. The paper presents it as an alternative to the familiar one-against-one and one-against-rest approaches. Its central choice is to arrange binary classification decisions in a tree, giving the overall multiclass classifier an explicit decision structure.

For a problem with N classes, DB2 constructs a binary decision tree with N−1 classifier nodes. Each node contains a decision boundary learned by a binary SVM. This organization provides the basis for analyzing both generalization and computational complexity, connecting the arrangement of classifiers to the cost of learning and making predictions.

The analysis and experiments report faster testing than both comparison methods and significantly faster training than one-against-rest. Cross-validation accuracy is reported as comparable to both. The stated benefit is therefore a computational improvement while retaining similar measured predictive accuracy; the abstract does not claim a corresponding training-speed advantage over one-against-one.
summary.tldr: DB2 arranges binary SVMs in a decision tree, improving reported prediction speed while maintaining comparable cross-validation accuracy.

title: A hierarchical method for multi-class support vector machines

abstract: The problem of inferring haplotypes from genotypes of single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) is essential for the understanding of genetic variation within and among populations, with important applications tothe genetic analysis of disease propensities and other complex traits. Theproblem can be formulated as a mixture model, where the mixture componentscorrespond to the pool of haplotypes in the population. The size of this poolis unknown; indeed, knowing the size of the pool would correspond to knowingsomething significant about the genome and its history. Thus methods for fitting the genotype mixture must crucially address the problem of estimating a mixture with an unknown number of mixture components. In this paper we present a Bayesian approach to this problem based on a nonparametric prior known as the Dirichlet process. The model also incorporates a likelihood that captures statistical errors in the haplotype/genotype relationship. We apply our approach to the analysis of both simulated andreal genotype data, and compare to extant methods.

paragraphs: The paper addresses inferring haplotypes from SNP genotype data, a problem important for understanding genetic variation and studying complex traits. It represents the population's haplotype pool through a mixture model, with components corresponding to haplotypes. A central difficulty is that the number of components is unknown and is itself biologically informative.

The authors use a Bayesian approach based on a Dirichlet process prior to address that uncertainty. This makes the unknown size of the haplotype pool part of the inference problem rather than a quantity assumed known in advance. The model also includes a likelihood that accounts for statistical errors in the relationship between haplotypes and observed genotypes.

Together, these choices address uncertainty about both the composition of the population and the observations used to reconstruct it. The approach is applied to simulated and real genotype data and compared with existing methods. The stated contribution is this Bayesian formulation and its evaluation; the abstract does not report a particular superiority result from those comparisons.
summary.tldr: A Dirichlet process mixture models an unknown haplotype pool while accounting for statistical errors in genotype relationships.

title: Bayesian haplo-type inference via the dirichlet process

abstract: We introduce a family of kernels on discrete data structures within the general class of decomposition kernels. A weighted decomposition kernel (WDK) is computed by dividing objects into substructures indexed by a selector. Two substructures are then matched if their selectors satisfy an equality predicate, while the importance of the match is determined by a probability kernel on local distributions fitted on the substructures. Under reasonable assumptions, a WDK can be computed efficiently and can avoid combinatorial explosion of the feature space. We report experimental evidence that the proposed kernel is highly competitive with respect to more complex state-of-the-art methods on a set of problems in bioinformatics.
originalAbstract: We introduce a family of kernels on discrete data structures within the general class of decomposition kernels. A weighted decomposition kernel (WDK) is computed by dividing objects into substructures indexed by a selector. Two substructures are then matched if their selectors satisfy an equality predicate, while the importance of the match is determined by a probability kernel on local distributions fitted on the substructures. Under reasonable assumptions, a WDK can be computed efficiently and can avoid combinatorial explosion of the feature space. We report experimental evidence that the proposed kernel is highly competitive with respect to more complex state-of-the-art methods on a set of problems in bioinformatics.

paragraphs: This paper introduces weighted decomposition kernels for comparing discrete structured objects. The basic approach divides each object into substructures and builds a similarity measure from matches between those parts. Each substructure has a selector that determines whether it can be matched with a substructure from another object.

A match occurs when the selectors satisfy an equality condition. The importance of that match is then determined by a probability kernel applied to local distributions fitted to the substructures. The method therefore separates eligibility for matching from the weight assigned to the match, combining structural decomposition with information from local probability distributions.

Under reasonable assumptions, the authors show that these kernels can be computed efficiently and can avoid a combinatorial explosion in the feature space. Experiments on a set of bioinformatics problems find the proposed kernel highly competitive with more complex contemporary methods. The contribution is a family of structured-data similarities that combines selective matching and probability-based weighting, with conditional computational advantages and empirical evidence of competitive performance.
summary.tldr: Weighted decomposition kernels compare selected substructures using local probability distributions and show competitive results on bioinformatics problems.

title: Weighted decomposition kernels
Online multiclass learning by interclass hypothesis sharing

abstract: Residual gradient (RG) was proposed as an alternative to TD(0) for policy evaluation when function approximation is used, but there exists little formal analysis comparing them except in very limited cases. This paper employs techniques from online learning of linear functions and provides a worst-case analysis to compare these two types of algorithms when linear function approximation is used. No statistical assumptions are made on the sequence of observations. In particular, our results suggest that RG may result in smaller temporal differences, while TD(0) is more likely to yield smaller prediction errors. These phenomena can be observed even in two simple Markov chain examples.

No statistical assumptions are made on the sequence of observations. paragraphs: The paper compares two approaches to policy evaluation with linear function approximation: TD(0) and residual gradient. Residual gradient had been proposed as an alternative, but formal comparisons were largely confined to limited cases. The authors develop a worst-case analysis to clarify how the two approaches can differ when estimating a policy's value.

Their analysis uses techniques from online learning of linear functions and makes no statistical assumptions about the observation sequence. This is a significant feature of the comparison: the reasoning does not depend on observations following a particular statistical pattern. It also distinguishes temporal differences from prediction errors, keeping two measures of an algorithm's behavior separate.

The results suggest that residual gradient may produce smaller temporal differences, while TD(0) is more likely to produce smaller prediction errors. These are qualified conclusions, not a claim that one method always wins. Two simple Markov chain examples exhibit the same phenomena, illustrating why success at reducing temporal differences need not imply the strongest predictive performance.
summary.tldr: A worst-case analysis suggests residual gradient may reduce temporal differences more, while TD(0) is more likely to reduce prediction errors.

title: A worst-case comparison between temporal difference and residual gradient with linear function approximation

abstract: We address the problem of computing the optimal Q-function in Markov decision problems with infinite state-space. We analyze the convergence properties of several variations of Q-learning when combined with function approximation, extending the analysis of TD-learning in (Tsitsilis and Van Roy, 1996) to stochastic control settings. We identify conditions under which such approximate methods converge with probability 1. We conclude with a brief discussion on the general applicability of our results and compare them with several related works.
originalAbstract: We address the problem of computing the optimal Q-function in Markov decision problems with infinite state-space. We analyze the convergence properties of several variations of Q-learning when combined with function approximation, extending the analysis of TD-learning in (Tsitsilis and Van Roy, 1996) to stochastic control settings. We identify conditions under which such approximate methods converge with probability 1. We conclude with a brief discussion on the general applicability of our results and compare them with several related works.

paragraphs: The paper studies computing the optimal Q-function in Markov decision problems with infinitely many states. Its focus is on Q-learning combined with function approximation, where the learned function provides a representation of action values across that state space. The central question is whether the resulting learning procedures converge.

The authors analyze several variations of approximate Q-learning. Their work extends an earlier analysis of temporal-difference learning to stochastic control settings, bringing the convergence question into a setting concerned with choosing actions. Studying multiple variations allows the paper to address a family of approximate learning procedures rather than a single isolated update rule.

The main result identifies conditions under which these methods converge with probability one. The conditions are essential to the claim: the paper does not assert convergence for every combination of Q-learning and function approximation. It also discusses the applicability of its results and their relationship to related work. The contribution is a conditional theoretical foundation for convergence in an infinite-state control setting.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies conditions ensuring probability-one convergence for several Q-learning methods with function approximation in infinite-state problems.

title: An analysis of reinforcement learning with function approximation

abstract: We introduce into the classical Perceptron algorithm with margin a mechanism of unlearning which in the course of the regular update allows for a reduction of possible contributions from �very well classified� patterns to the weight vector. The resulting incremental classification algorithm, called Margin Perceptron with Unlearning (MPU), provably converges in a finite number of updates to any desirable chosen before running approximation of either the maximal margin or the optimal 1-norm soft margin solution. Moreover, an experimental comparative evaluation involving representative linear Support Vector Machines reveals that the MPU algorithm is very competitive.
originalAbstract: We introduce into the classical Perceptron algorithm with margin a mechanism of unlearning which in the course of the regular update allows for a reduction of possible contributions from �very well classified� patterns to the weight vector. The resulting incremental classification algorithm, called Margin Perceptron with Unlearning (MPU), provably converges in a finite number of updates to any desirable chosen before running approximation of either the maximal margin or the optimal 1-norm soft margin solution. Moreover, an experimental comparative evaluation involving representative linear Support Vector Machines reveals that the MPU algorithm is very competitive.

paragraphs: The Margin Perceptron with Unlearning modifies the classical margin-based Perceptron by allowing some previous contributions to its weight vector to shrink. During an ordinary update, the method can reduce contributions associated with examples that are already very well classified. Here, unlearning describes this adjustment within training.

The resulting method remains an incremental classification algorithm. The authors prove that it reaches a chosen approximation of either the maximum-margin solution or the optimal 1-norm soft-margin solution after finitely many updates. The desired approximation is selected before running the algorithm, making the target accuracy part of the procedure’s setup.

This result connects a relatively direct update mechanism with optimization targets associated with margin-based classification. The paper also compares the method experimentally with representative linear support vector machines and reports that it is highly competitive. The theoretical result establishes finite convergence to the specified approximation, while the experiments address practical comparative performance. Together, they support unlearning as a useful modification to the margin Perceptron.
summary.tldr: The Margin Perceptron with Unlearning reduces contributions from well-classified examples and provably reaches a preselected approximation to margin-optimal solutions in finitely many updates.

title: The Margin Perceptron with Unlearning

abstract: The principle of maximum entropy provides a powerful framework for statistical models of joint, conditional, and marginal distributions. However, there are many important distributions with elements of interaction and feedback where its applicability has not been established. This work presents the principle of maximum causal entropy--an approach based on causally conditioned probabilities that can appropriately model the availability and influence of sequentially revealed side information. Using this principle, we derive models for sequential data with revealed information, interaction, and feedback, and demonstrate their applicability for statistically framing inverse optimal control and decision prediction tasks.
originalAbstract: The principle of maximum entropy provides a powerful framework for statistical models of joint, conditional, and marginal distributions. However, there are many important distributions with elements of interaction and feedback where its applicability has not been established. This work presents the principle of maximum causal entropy--an approach based on causally conditioned probabilities that can appropriately model the availability and influence of sequentially revealed side information. Using this principle, we derive models for sequential data with revealed information, interaction, and feedback, and demonstrate their applicability for statistically framing inverse optimal control and decision prediction tasks.

paragraphs: Maximum entropy provides a framework for constructing statistical models, but applying it to interactions requires accounting for when information becomes available. In a sequential setting, information may be revealed gradually and influence later decisions. Feedback adds another connection between what happens now and what can be observed or chosen afterward.

The paper introduces maximum causal entropy to represent these information relationships. Its foundation is causally conditioned probabilities, which account for the availability and influence of sequentially revealed side information. The key modeling concern is therefore the timing of information: a description of sequential behavior must reflect what was available at the relevant point in the interaction.

Using this principle, the authors derive models for sequential data involving revealed information, interaction, and feedback. They demonstrate its applicability to statistical formulations of inverse optimal control and decision prediction. The contribution supplies a framework for these tasks that explicitly incorporates information flow, extending the reach of entropy-based modeling to the interactive settings considered.
summary.tldr: Maximum causal entropy extends entropy-based modeling to sequential interactions by accounting for when information becomes available.

title: Modeling Interaction via the Principle of Maximum Causal Entropy

abstract: The majority of value function approximation based reinforcement learning algorithms available today, focus on approximating the state (V) or state-action (Q) value function and efficient action selection comes as an afterthought. On the other hand, real-world problems tend to have large action spaces, where evaluating every possible action becomes impractical. This mismatch presents a major obstacle in successfully applying reinforcement learning to real-world problems. In this paper we present a unified view of V and Q functions and arrive at a new space-efficient representation, where action selection can be done exponentially faster, without the use of a model. We then describe how to calculate this new value function efficiently via approximate linear programming and provide experimental results that demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
originalAbstract: The majority of value function approximation based reinforcement learning algorithms available today, focus on approximating the state (V) or state-action (Q) value function and efficient action selection comes as an afterthought. On the other hand, real-world problems tend to have large action spaces, where evaluating every possible action becomes impractical. This mismatch presents a major obstacle in successfully applying reinforcement learning to real-world problems. In this paper we present a unified view of V and Q functions and arrive at a new space-efficient representation, where action selection can be done exponentially faster, without the use of a model. We then describe how to calculate this new value function efficiently via approximate linear programming and provide experimental results that demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

paragraphs: Value-based reinforcement learning must both estimate how promising situations or actions are and select an action to take. With large action sets, evaluating every candidate can become impractical. This paper argues that efficient action selection needs to shape the value representation itself, rather than being considered only after that representation is chosen.

The authors develop a unified view of state-value and state-action-value functions, leading to a new space-efficient representation. In this representation, action selection can be exponentially faster without using a model. The contribution therefore addresses the cost of making a decision as well as the space required to represent the values supporting it.

The paper also describes how to compute the new value function efficiently using approximate linear programming. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach. The stated speed advantage concerns action selection, linking the representation directly to the large-action-set problem; the additional computation method provides a way to learn the quantities needed to use that representation.
summary.tldr: A unified value-function representation supports space-efficient storage and exponentially faster action selection without a model.

title: Generalized Value Functions for Large Action Sets
